events.title: Chancellor rejects calls to raise Capital Gains Tax in Budget
events.summary: Chancellor John Healey says he wants to avoid an investor exodus from the UK Published 20 October 2026, 02:31 BST Chancellor John Healey has dismissed calls from some Labour MPs to increase Capital Gains Tax (CGT). Cabinet ministers Wes Streeting and Louise Haigh both previously voiced support for raising CGT before Andy Burnham became prime minister in July. Ahead of next week's Budget, as first reported by the Times , external , Healey is minded not to increase CGT - which is imposed on the profit people make when they sell an asset that has increased in value, such as shares in a company or properties which are not primary residences. The move followed warnings that it could end up costing the government money if wealthy people leave the country or defer selling off assets. If you pay income tax at the basic rate then CGT is charged at 18%. For higher and additional rate income tax payers, the CGT rate is 24%. Last year, HMRC estimated that lifting the higher rate of CGT by 10% would reduce the Treasury's receipts by £3.6bn in 2028-9. The chancellor gave an indication of his approach last month in a speech when he spoke about the importance of businesses and self-employed people making profits. "I want to see this country as a country of wealth creation. I want our government decisions and policies to raise the levels of confidence, and investment, and profit in British business," Healey said. Burnham has faced warnings against lifting CGT. His former adviser and Goldman Sachs Chief Economist Lord Jim O'Neill suggested it would send "the wrong message to business". But influential Labour figures had pushed for equalising CGT and income tax, with the former generally attracting a lower tax rate. Louise Haigh, a key ally of the prime minister, had suggested capital gains should go up to be closer to income tax, before she became Burnham's first secretary of state. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting called for a "wealth tax that works" in May, shortly after resigning as a minister in former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer's government. He had argued that equalising CGT with income tax would address an unfair system that was "penalising work". Healey had already ruled out levelling the two tax rates, according to the Financial Times , external . Asked about the government's plans for CGT on BBC Breakfast, Communities Secretary Angela Rayner would not speculate on the Budget. Pressed over whether rejecting calls to increase the tax was a win for the rich, she said the government had already taken steps to give people "breathing space" and help with the cost of living. It comes after senior banking executives told the BBC they expect Healey to raise taxes on the sector. UK banks have been reporting bumper profits, leading to calls from unions for higher taxes. Healey is due to set out his tax and spending plans at his first Budget on 28 October, against the backdrop of the US-Iran war which has led to rising prices. The chancellor is under pressure to find measures to ease the cost of living and fund an increase for defence at his spending review next year. The chancellor's options for raising money are limited as Labour's 2024 manifesto pledged not to increase income tax, National Insurance and VAT, the three big revenue raisers. The government is also restricted in how much it can borrow due to its self-imposed rules on debt. In a pre-Budget speech on Tuesday, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch is expected to urge the government to cut spending and reduce its borrowing. She will tell the prime minister and the chancellor to "live within our means" and signpost her party's plan to save £70bn in cuts, including to welfare and overseas development aid. The Liberal Democrats have said the government could raise £14bn partly by introducing a windfall tax on the profits of banks. The party's deputy leader Daisy Cooper said the money could go towards cutting fuel duty, rail and bus fares and VAT for hospitality businesses. events.title: A modest increase in bank taxes is not the end of the world for lenders | Nils Pratley
events.summary: A modest increase in bank taxes is not the end of the world for lenders As long as Healey doesn’t go overboard, a small turn on surcharge dial will not seriously undermine flow of capital E veryone is familiar with the banks’ plea: raising taxes on them amounts to taxing the nation’s growth. If you increase how much banks pay, goes the argument, less interest will be paid on deposits and loans will cost slightly more, meaning we’ll all be worse off eventually. In terms of economic theory, it’s coherent, it should be said: in an ideal world, a chancellor would strive to lower costs of capital at every opportunity. In the real world, however, John Healey faces multiple competing demands, even from within a business lobby that extends well beyond the banks. As this newspaper revealed last week , the chancellor is likely to increase bank taxes in his budget next week. In the current climate of trying to “stay the course” on the fiscal rules by finding some money from somewhere, tapping the banks is a reasonable policy. Or, at least, better than most alternatives. First, today’s conditions for banks are plainly gentle: defaults are historically low and interest rates are high. Banks’ returns on tangible equity – a better guide to how they are doing than pure profitability – are heading towards 20%. Most non-financial firms would love such a number. Provided Healey doesn’t go overboard, the flow of capital is not going to be seriously undermined when the starting point for banks’ returns is so good. Second, all the indications suggest Healey will indeed opt only for tweaks. If the mechanism is the surcharge that banks pay on top of corporation tax at 25%, then an increase to 8%, from 3%, would amount to £2bn-ish extra from across the sector. He may not even go that far. Analysts at UBS calculate that a doubling of the surcharge to 6% would reduce UK banks’ profits only by about 2% on average, with a roughly 3%-4% impact for the domestic-focused banks, meaning NatWest and Lloyds. That cannot be called a violent change in the operating climate, or a devastating blow for the shareholders or the equity-incentivised executives. Dividends or share buybacks may be trimmed a bit, but the share prices for both banks are up by a fifth in the past year. Third, we’ll have to wait to see whether any move by Healey is part of a wider financial services package that could include bank-pleasing elements. There’s always scope for another hack at the thicket of regulations, for instance. Or help on capital buffers. And, if Healey is really as pro-growth as he claims, he’d consider this column’s perennial pre-budget suggestion to scrap or cut stamp duty on shares – a move that would seriously improve UK companies’ cost of capital (see Tax Policy Associates’ paper ) and do wonders for banks’ wealth-management divisions. The point is that a small turn on the surcharge dial is better than other ways of extracting the odd billion or two for the banks. A windfall tax would be too arbitrary. Changing the way banks’ deposits are remunerated at the Bank of England would look like interference in the central bank’s independence. The surcharge is a well-understood mechanism. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning None of which, one suspects, will stop the howls of complaints from banks, or halt the grumbles about the loss of competitiveness versus other financial centres. But an extra £2bn, or less, from the financial services sector simply doesn’t sound like a gamechanger if Healey acts as expected. Even JP Morgan’s Jamie Dimon, who likes to play politics at budget-time with his proposed new London headquarters , might reflect that some other European capitals – Paris, say – don’t look like a bed of roses.

events.summary: Analysts say idle factories in Europe could be prime targets as Chinese carmakers look to localise production They plan to either splash out billions of yuan to set up their own factories or tap international marques’ idle plants to build their vehicles, looking to sustain a sales boom in one of the world’s major automotive markets. “Global growth shifts from exporting vehicles to Europe to producing them locally, from price-led market share gains to margin-led positioning, and from a single export channel to a multimarket footprint,” Morgan Stanley analysts said in a research note issued last week after Beijing and Brussels agreed on an import quota for Chinese-made hybrid vehicles. “Such a development would favour Chinese EV leaders with the scale, balance sheets and European manufacturing plans already in motion to pivot quickly.”

events.title: Landholders and politicians push for tougher laws on renewable energy developments
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Landholders push for more regulations amid renewables rollout Glenn Franz and his parents own a property next to Wambo Wind Farm. ( ABC Southern Qld: Brandon Long ) About 12 community action groups have come together to discuss the challenges landholders face amid growth in the renewable energy sector. The group is calling for a minimum 3-kilometre setback from residences and up-front decommissioning bonds. Regional Voices Queensland will continue advocating for better protections for those impacted by renewable energy projects. A coalition of rural community groups is demanding tougher laws governing renewable energy developments, including mandatory turbine setbacks, stricter decommissioning rules and stronger protections for neighbouring landholders. Regional Voices Queensland (RVQ), a loose alliance of about 12 community action groups representing communities affected by renewable energy projects across the state, brought landholders, farming industry representatives and politicians together for its first major meeting today at the Franz family farm beside the Wambo Wind Farm at Diamondy, 280 kilometres north-west of Brisbane. The meeting, co-organised by Member for Maranoa David Littleproud, focused on reforms to planning laws, with more than 70 participants travelling from communities including the Southern Downs and other parts of regional Queensland. Regional Voices Queensland members are demanding tougher laws governing renewable energy developments. ( ABC Southern Qld: Brandon Long ) RVQ chair and Property Rights Australia board member, Jim Willmott, described the alliance as a "supergroup" formed after community organisations dealing with individual projects identified common concerns. Queensland's wind farm code has not allowed developers to comply simply by meeting a specified separation distance since 2024. Projects must meet all of the code's performance outcomes, including noise criteria at neighbouring dwellings. David Littleproud says affected landholders wanted clarity around the issue. ( ABC Southern Qld: Brandon Long ) Mr Littleproud said affected landholders were seeking practical safeguards rather than opposing renewable energy outright. "They're not asking for anything irrational," he said. "They're actually being quite considered and it's coming from a lived experience." Farm co-owner Glenn Franz, who does not host the turbines, said the experience of living beside the wind farm had highlighted gaps in existing protections, particularly around visual amenity and the financial risks associated with dismantling turbines at the end of their operational lives. "We've got 13 wind turbines surrounding us within a 3km zone," Mr Franz said. "There's got to be safeguards for the future. "It'd be nice to have the security up front, not as a pay-as-you-go-down-the-track sort of scheme." Karl Stefanovic interviewed landholders at the meeting. ( ABC Southern Qld: Brandon Long ) The Wambo Wind Farm, a joint venture between state-owned Stanwell and energy infrastructure group Cubico, received planning approval in 2020. Mr Franz said while the project was well advanced, other communities were at the start of the process and could learn from the Diamondy community's experience. Anna Lethbridge and Brendan Taylor from AgForce attended the meeting. ( ABC Southern Qld: Brandon Long ) AgForce policy adviser Anna Lethbridge said safeguards needed to extend beyond project hosts to neighbouring producers, including protections against contamination and impacts on agricultural accreditation. "From an AgForce perspective, we're not opposed to renewables," Ms Lethbridge said. Queensland regulates wind farm developments through its planning and environmental assessment framework, including State Code 23 and applicable approval conditions. Since 2025, new wind farm applications must undergo impact assessment and provide financial security for decommissioning. However, RVQ is concerned the wording is vague and could still leave landholders or taxpayers liable. Developers must now also negotiate a community benefit agreement with the relevant council before lodging an application.

events.title: Burnham vows end to 'rip-off parking charges' under new rules
events.summary: Drivers will be given the right to challenge "rip-off" private parking charges and more grace when using private providers under new rules set out by Andy Burnham. The prime minister announced the changes after drivers repeatedly raised concerns penalties issued by private providers were too harsh and left motorists unfairly punished. In one case, a woman was taken to court in a £1,906 claim after taking longer than five minutes to pay at a car park in Derby . The charge was eventually dropped . Private car parks already have an industry code of practice, but the RAC motoring group said the government's changes would protect drivers from the "poor practices of some private parking companies". Burnham said: "Being a few minutes late back to your car or typing one digit of your number plate wrong shouldn't end with a hefty fine landing on your doormat. "These charges leave people feeling ripped off and out of pocket, so I'm putting a stop to them." A guaranteed five-minute period to decide whether to park A 10-minute window to leave without facing a penalty Cancellation of charges for issues drivers can't control, like vehicle breakdowns in car parks Cancellation of charges for honest mistakes such as stopping to check directions, as well as for medical emergencies or broken ticket machines Maximum charges of £20 on appeal for slip-ups like forgetting a parking permit, entering the wrong vehicle registration, or forgetting to confirm the registration in the machine when parking A freeze on the maximum parking charge at £100, which is the same limit as the current private parking Code of Practice Operators who do not comply risk losing access to DVLA data, making it far more difficult to pursue the car's owner even if they do issue a charge. 'I got fined £11k over a five-minute parking rule' Published 1 August 2024 Firm told to pay £10,240 in five-minute parking row Published 5 April 2025 Private car parks are different to council-owned car parks and streets. RAC analysis of government data showed a record 17 million private parking tickets were issued in 2025-26, a 17% increase from a year earlier. With each charge worth up to £100, the data, analysed by the Press Association and the RAC Foundation, suggests drivers could collectively face private parking charges worth more than £4.6m each day. The yellow and black envelope of a Penalty Charge Notice, or PCN, is a dreaded sight for motorists returning to their car. The AA said some drivers pay up even if they have done nothing wrong, just to avoid the hassle. It said people felt they would not get a fair hearing if they appealed against their fines, with many saying they feared legal action. The government's Private Parking Code of Practice has been seven years in the making. In 2019, an act of Parliament was passed to create a code but the code was withdrawn in 2022, due to "resistance from the private parking industry", according to the RAC. The current industry Code of Practice, created by the British Parking Association and the International Parking Community, was introduced in 2024 and updated last year after a review . Angela Rayner, communities and housing secretary, told BBC Breakfast that parking "shouldn't be a way of making money, quite frankly". Asked if the changes were an admission that motorists have been "ripped off" by parking companies for years, she said: "We're calling time on it. They have regulated themselves and they have their appeals process but we're giving it more meat now." Asked why the government has not called for lower price caps on fines, Rayner said: "We've frozen them now and what we're saying is that there is a proportionate response to when people don't follow the rules when they are parking." Derek Millard-Smith from the British Parking Association told BBC Breakfast the group welcomed the changes as it would "increase trust". When asked about calls to drop the cost of fines, he said that "deterrents work". "We know dog fouling, rail fare dodging, littering - all those levels are around £100 or more because that is a level that is deemed sufficient to change behaviours. "What we are trying to do is educate people so they don't do what we don't want them to do." The new code will apply in England, Scotland and Wales after motorists said they wanted independent oversight of the private parking industry. Both the AA and the RAC said the new code was a good first step but did not go far enough. "There is still a huge amount of work to do, such as tackling the scourge of debt recovery fees," said Jack Cousens, head of roads policy at the AA. "Ultimately, we need to stop charges being issued in the first place, especially where the driver has done nothing wrong." The RAC's head of policy, Simon Williams, also called for the banning of debt recovery fees and said the current industry-run appeals bodies should be replaced by a single independent one.

events.title: Job vacancies fall as small firms cut back on recruitment
events.summary: Published 20 October 2026, 07:19 BST Job vacancies in the UK have seen their largest fall since the start of the year as smaller businesses cut back on recruitment, official figures indicate. Vacancies fell by 21,000 in the three months to September to 691,000, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS), which said small firms were citing labour costs as a key factor in scaling back hiring. Energy costs have risen since the Iran war began, and companies have also said that increases in National Insurance and the minimum wage have made it more expensive to employ staff. The ONS figures also showed the unemployment rate fell to 4.7% in the three months to August, the lowest for more than a year. The figures are the last official snapshot of the jobs market before Chancellor John Healey presents his first Budget next week. ONS deputy director of labour market statistics, David Freeman, said the labour market remained "broadly flat", with the latest data showing the employment rate edging up and "a small drop in unemployment". "The number of workers on payroll remains slightly down over the same period, though data for the most recent month suggests that might be starting to level off," he said. "The number of vacancies has seen its largest fall since the start of the year, concentrated mainly within smaller businesses, which cite increased labour costs as a key factor." The number of job vacancies fell to its lowest level in more than five years, the figures indicated, with the largest decrease in construction jobs. Average earnings excluding bonuses rose 3.7% in the three months to August. Taking inflation into account, wages grew 0.8% in real terms. Pat McFadden, the Secretary of State for Work and Pensions, said the figures "show the resilience of our labour market" with the UK's employment rate "now the third highest in the G7, despite a backdrop of global uncertainty". However, he said that "too many young people still find themselves locked out of employment". The government is working with industry "to bring young people back into the labour market and prevent them from drifting into the welfare system", he added. The latest ONS figures showed the unemployment rate for those aged 16 to 24 was 15.6% in the June to August quarter. While that was down from 16.4% in the March to May period, it was still higher than the rate of 14.6% seen in the June-to-August period last year. Separate ONS figures have indicated that nearly one million young people in the UK are not in education, employment or training - or "Neet" On Monday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham warned the UK faces an "economic catastrophe and moral failure" due to high levels of youth unemployment. Ashley Webb, senior UK economist for Capital Economics, said the fall in the unemployment rate was "unexpected", and that it suggests the labour market "continues to recover". But "with businesses' energy costs likely to fall only slowly, we still think hiring will stay subdued," he said. Louise Murphy, senior economist at the Resolution Foundation, said the labour market "has performed poorly in recent years as the number of jobs has fallen and pay growth weakened". But she added that the UK's "recent bout of economic resilience may finally be creating some green shoots", pointing to "rising employment levels and private sector wage growth stabilising". The quality of ONS statistics has been criticised in recent years, with a review last year finding "deep seated" issues with the body . The Labour Force Survey, which it uses to report payroll and employment figures, has suffered from low response rates. In an update on Tuesday, the ONS said that response levels had improved, but that "some volatility" remained in the statistics. Have you been affected by the issues raised in this story? events.title: U.S. Treasury yields move lower as investors await housing, employment data
events.summary: U.S. Treasury yields inched lower on Tuesday as investors awaited further economic data and continued to weigh the inflationary backdrop ahead of the Federal Reserve's interest rate decision next week. The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield was down 2 basis points to 5.114%, while the 30-year Treasury bond also fell 2 basis points to 5.45%. Meanwhile, the 2-year Treasury note yield was broadly flat at 4.757%. One basis point is equal to 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions. Investors will parse housing starts and monthly pending home sales data for September, due later on Tuesday morning, and weekly ADP employment change figures. Weekly initial jobless claims will be released on Thursday, and the S&P Global Composite PMI Flash will be out on Friday. Investors are anticipating the Fed's next interest rate decision, due next week. The latest figures for the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, the personal consumption expenditures index, will also be released. Traders are now pricing in an 82% chance of the Fed holding interest rates steady, according to the CME FedWatch Tool .

events.title: Oil wavers near five-month high as Iran threats vie with flows
events.summary: Hostilities have recently flared up in the Strait of Hormuz. Brent oil stayed near a five-month high at just below US$110 a barrel as traders weighed Iran’s threats in the Strait of Hormuz against strong crude flows from the Persian Gulf. Iran said it had “no choice” but to assert control over Hormuz, while US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said Gulf flows had recovered to about 80% of prewar levels. Geopolitical risks keep prices high as attacks on tankers continue; Brent has risen about 80% in 2026, and Iraq’s exports have topped 3.4 million barrels a day in October. Brent oil fluctuated near a five-month high as traders weighed the risk of further Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz against robust crude flows from the Persian Gulf. The global benchmark was just below US$110 a barrel, near the highest since May, while the most-active West Texas Intermediate contract was close to US$99. Iran has “no choice” but to assert control over Hormuz to safeguard the country’s security, First Vice-President Mohammad Reza Aref said on Oct 19 , according to a report from state-run news agency IRNA. Despite a recent flare-up in hostilities around the waterway , crude exports from the Gulf have continued at an accelerated pace. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright told Fox News that flows had recovered to about 80% of their prewar level, although refined-product shipments remained constrained. Brent has surged about 80% in 2026 as widening conflicts in the Middle East and between Russia and Ukraine disrupt energy supplies. Refined products have rallied even harder, with European diesel futures surging. Renewed attacks on tankers and energy infrastructure are keeping geopolitical risk elevated even as Persian Gulf crude flows recover. “The risks to oil prices clearly lie to the upside,” said Hamad Hussain, a commodities economist at Capital Economics. The escalation in attacks on ships raises the possibility of a “renewed fall in oil supply and a continued rise in prices”, he added. Iran’s Aref said the Islamic Republic could ensure safe passage through Hormuz for friendly nations, but warned that the “the US is now the cause of the current situation and must pay the price”. He made the comments during a meeting in Tajikistan with Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin. Iraq is among Persian Gulf producers that have ramped up crude flows, with the country’s oil minister saying exports have exceeded 3.4 million barrels a day so far in October . Shipments are now close to prewar levels after the OPEC member offered deep discounts to regional benchmarks. Meanwhile, the Trump administration is authorising the sale of sanctioned oil tankers so they can legitimately ship crude, according to Wright. The move is aimed at expanding capacity as the US-Iran war strains supply and drives up freight costs. He estimated there are about 1,600 vessels in the global “dark fleet”. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Pound jumps after surprise fall in UK unemployment rate, but vacancies dry up amid ‘jobs drought’ – business live
events.summary: Introduction: UK unemployment rate falls in pre-budget boost Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets and the world economy. The UK unemployment rate has fallen, in a pre-budget boost to chancellor John Healey, but the number of vacancies available for workers continues to shrink. The latest data on the UK labour market, just released, shows that the UK unemployment rate fell to 4.7% in June to August, down from 4.9% a month ago. That’s better than expected – City economists had forecast a rise to 5%. In its final snapshot of Britain’s jobs market ahead of the budget in two week’s time, the Office for National Statistics reports that employment rose, by 102,000 jobs, to 34.577m in the last quarter. The number of people unemployed fell by 47,000 in the quarter to 1.712m, and there was a small (16,000) drop in the number of people ‘economically inactive’, to 9.091m. But worryingly, the number of vacancies has seen its largest fall since the start of the year, falling by 21,000 in the last quarter. That pulled the number of vacancies down to 691,000 in July to September, down from over 1.2m in early 2022. This is the first time the total has been below 700,000 since February to April 2021. This is mainly from smaller firms, who continue to suggest that they may not be recruiting because of increased labour costs. That’s a reference to the higher employer National Insurance Contributions (NICs) brought in by Healey’s predecessor, Rachel Reeves, and the rise in the minimum wage, which have made it costlier to hire staff. 10am BST: ZEW index of eurozone economic sentiment 10am BST: Eurozone construction output for August 2.30pm BST: BIST Committee questions Secretary of State Jonathan Reynolds 43m ago McFadden: UK's employment rate now the third highest in the G7 55m ago Pound jumps after UK jobs report 1h ago UK suffering 'jobs drought' as vacancies drop 2h ago Public sector pay outpaces private sector, but.... 2h ago Real wage growth remains weak 2h ago A mixed picture on wage growth 2h ago Construction led fall in vacancies 2h ago Introduction: UK unemployment rate falls in pre-budget boost The FTSE 100 share index has dropped by 45 points, or 0.42%, to 10,719 points, adding to yesterday’s losses. That has helped to pull the pan-European Stoxx 600 index down by 0.4%. France’s CAC index has lost 0.3% while Germany’s DAX is down 0.7%. Investors remain concerned that the protests that rocked France last weekend will hamper efforts to cut spending. France appears to be heading for a fiscal crisis which could lead to contagion and potentially a recession in the euro-zone. However, several factors mean the contagion risks to other countries’ bond markets and economies are lower than they were during the sovereign debt crisis of the early 2010s. McFadden: UK's employment rate now the third highest in the G7 Secretary of State for Work and Pensions Pat McFadden says: “Today’s figures show the resilience of our labour market with unemployment falling and the UK’s employment rate now the third highest in the G7, despite a backdrop of global uncertainty. “But too many young people still find themselves locked out of employment. That’s why are working with industry, to bring young people back into the labour market and prevent them from drifting into the welfare system. “The hospitality and retail sectors have committed to 200,000 jobs for young people not in education, work or training through this partnership, to give them the opportunities they need to get started and build a successful career.” The pound has rallied after Britain’s unemployment rate fell unexpectedly this morning to 4.7%. Sterling has gained half a cent against the US dollar to $1.3352, as the City welcomes the news that employment rose in the last quarter. The pound is also up 0.2% against the euro to €1.1888, close to the 17-month high touched yesterday. Traders may be concluding that a stronger-than-expected jobs market will give the Bank of England confidence to raise interest rates to fight inflation. Chris Beauchamp , chief market analyst at IG says sterling is “rampant” after the UK employment data. “This data has caught the market on the hop, with traders scrambling to respond and boost exposure to the pound. Good news has been a touch more prevalent for the UK of late, which is just the kind of framing the government needs heading into the budget, though signs of more resilience in the labour market do of course mean the BoE has more room to respond to higher inflation.” The money markets indicate there’s a 95.5% chance that the Bank raises interest raatest at its next meeting in November, to 4%. Three further rate rises are expected in 2027. events.title: Alberta voters reject a move toward independence in referendum backing Canadian unity
events.summary: Voters in Canada’s oil-rich province of Alberta have rejected a proposal to begin a process toward independence EDMONTON, Alberta -- Voters in Canada’s oil-rich Alberta province overwhelmingly backed remaining in Canada, with early referendum results Tuesday delivering a boost to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s push for national unity amid U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war and annexation threats . With more than 1 million votes counted, 77% supported remaining in Canada , while 23% backed beginning a process toward separation, according to unofficial results from Elections Alberta. The referendum wasn't a direct vote on independence. Approval would have set Alberta on a path toward a future vote on separation from Canada . “Albertans made a clear choice,” Carney said. “They chose unity, to build together, and to take care of each other. Above all, Albertans chose Canada.” Carney said that the result would allow Canadians to move forward together and accelerate efforts to diversify trade, develop major infrastructure projects and make Canada a global energy powerhouse , with Alberta at its center. Alberta's separatists, however, saw a silver lining. “We don’t have the final results. I think the numbers are going to fluctuate, but it is fair to say that at least a quarter of Albertans feel that Alberta needs to be treated better,” said Keith Wilson, a leader of the separatist movement. Alberta Premier Danielle Smith welcomed the early results, saying they showed widespread support for remaining in Canada. “Albertans have voted for a stronger Alberta in a united Canada,” Smith posted on social media. Smith, who called the referendum amid pressure from separatists within her governing United Conservative Party, or UCP, despite opposing independence, said that she would address the province Tuesday evening about the results and Alberta’s future. “We are a solid country that’s united from coast to coast to coast,” Thomas Lukaszuk, a former Alberta deputy premier who led the Forever Canadian campaign against separation, told supporters. Results were delayed after late openings forced more than 100 polling stations to extend voting hours Monday. Alberta, home to the world’s fourth-largest proven oil reserves , is cowboy country and a conservative stronghold whose political culture has long had more in common with the American West than much of Canada. Resentment toward Canada's federal government in Ottawa runs deep, but hasn't traditionally translated into widespread support for independence. Despite the proposal’s apparent failure, separatist leaders have said they turned a fringe cause into a movement that won't disappear. Carney earlier urged Albertans to deliver a decisive vote for unity. “Vote like Canada’s future depends on it, because it does,” he told a rally on Friday in Edmonton, where he grew up. 2 dead, 11 injured after Kansas mother drives onto soccer field during game: Police Iran updates: Trump admin prepares options, including 'mother of all bombs' Bend, Oregon, shooting: Suspect ID'd, had attended elementary school, police say Separatist parties traditionally attracted only 1% or 2% of the vote, former Premier Jason Kenney said. Anger over COVID-19 restrictions helped mobilize activists who later embraced the separatist movement, he said. Trump’s trade war and threats to make Canada the 51st U.S. state have helped Carney rally support in Alberta, where Liberal prime ministers have historically been unpopular. Separatist advocate Jeff Rath said that he would be thrilled if 30% of Albertans voted to begin the separation process. He wants Smith ousted as UCP leader and said that the party could splinter, potentially creating a new pro-independence party. Dustin Degenhardt, a Wainwright voter, said that Albertans have long been mistreated by Canada's federal government. “Alberta has essentially been treated as, you know, a colony,” he said after voting Monday. “They want to take and take and take from us, and not return anything.” Taylor MacIsaac, another Wainwright voter, backed separation. “I think it’ll be good for Alberta to separate personally, as a very conservative individual that grew up in rural Alberta,” she said. Dave Malka, 59, of Edmonton, criticized spending money on a “referendum on a referendum” rather than healthcare. With Trump threatening Canada, Malka said, “It seems to be happening at the absolute worst time when we should be united; instead we’re fighting among ourselves.” Jake Graham, 35, of Calgary, attended a Carney rally wearing maple leaf pants and a Canada hockey jacket. He hopes that the vote ends the debate. “I hope this squashes this for a long time to come and that it’s clear and decisive, that these grumblings disappear for a while and we can be a united Canada,” he said. events.title: Zuckerberg spent years building on Apple’s terms. His $100 billion-plus AI bet is about owning everything
events.summary: Mark Zuckerberg says he knew he was taking an enormous risk when he greenlit Meta’s AI buildout—a commitment he pegged at as much as $200 billion—before there was any proof it would work. “We’re going to write this check for, like, I don’t know, like $100 billion, $200 billion,” Zuckerberg said on a recent episode of Cheeky Pint , the podcast hosted by Stripe cofounder John Collison. “I’m like, ‘Alex, are you sure this is going to work?’” Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer, appeared alongside Zuckerberg and said decisions of that size get made “long before there’s proof points around whether or not even the thing is working.” He added: “It’s like the opposite of Lean Startup.” The episode was released Oct. 12, the same day Meta launched Muse Wonder , the first frontier-class model from the superintelligence lab Wang leads . Meta has guided for as much as $145 billion in capital expenditures this year , much of it on AI infrastructure. Much of that money is going toward what Zuckerberg describes as a “full-stack” operation. “Meta is a full-stack tech company,” he said. “We build our own data centers, we build our own chips, we build our own low-level infrastructure.” Lessons from the smartphone wars Zuckerberg’s push to own the full stack may stem from his nearly two-decade rivalry with Apple and Google, which control the world’s dominant smartphone platforms. Facebook’s iPhone app launched in July 2008, followed by an Android app in September 2009 . Its mobile years that followed were marked by friction with the platform owners, some of it self-inflicted. Zuckerberg repeatedly sought workarounds to the limits those platforms imposed. In 2013, Facebook pushed updates to its Android app outside the Google Play store, prompting Google to ban the practice . In 2019, Apple shut down a Facebook “Research” app that paid users, including teens, up to $20 a month for sweeping access to their phone data. The biggest blow came in 2021, when Apple began letting iPhone users block apps from tracking them —a change Meta later said would cost it about $10 billion in 2022 alone. Zuckerberg has said that experience shapes his approach to AI. “One of my formative experiences has been building our services constrained by what Apple will let us build on their platforms,” he wrote in a 2024 post on Meta’s website . Speaking with Collison, Zuckerberg said owning the stack is “less about wanting to own a platform for its own sake. It’s about being able to build the best things.” The cost of going it alone Unlike Amazon , Microsoft , and Google, Meta doesn’t run a cloud business that rents its data centers to outside customers, so it shoulders those costs itself. Zuckerberg said a one-gigawatt AI data center costs $50 billion to $60 billion to build and roughly $15 billion a year to operate. Meta’s Hyperion campus in Louisiana is designed to scale to five gigawatts. That could change. In July, Bloomberg reported that Meta is building a cloud business to sell AI computing power and is also weighing selling raw computing capacity. Weeks later, Zuckerberg confirmed the cloud plans on Meta’s earnings call. On Cheeky Pint , he framed all that compute as a hedge. “…If like the cost is whatever, $15 billion a gigawatt, we could get like a lot more for that,” Zuckerberg said. “So I think that you, in order for it not to work out, it’s not just that we have to fail, AI overall has to fail.” The bet on agentic commerce Meta’s full-stack ambitions don’t stop at data centers. Zuckerberg and Wang want Muse Wonder and the more powerful Muse Wonder Full to drive Muse, Meta’s personal AI agent , which can act on people’s behalf. “The best personal agent should feel like a team of experts in your corner,” Wang said. “Your legal team, and your finance team, and your medical team.” Wang said he uses Muse to “source increasingly obscure teas from increasingly obscure vendors of tea.” Zuckerberg said he set up an Instacart account specifically for Muse, which orders ingredients for weekend baking projects with his 3-year-old daughter. He went from using Instacart maybe twice a year to “once or twice a week.” That vision of full-fledged agentic commerce could, paradoxically, disrupt Meta’s main profit engine. Advertising made up about 98% of Meta’s revenue last quarter, and eMarketer projects the company’s worldwide ad revenue will reach $243.46 billion this year, surpassing Google’s for the first time . Meta’s future business model But if AI agents compare prices, check delivery dates, read reviews, and ultimately make purchase decisions, who are the ads for? Collison raised a version of that question on the podcast, suggesting that a business that “only succeeds by overcharging consumers” would rationally want to keep agents out. Zuckerberg countered that few businesses have tried to block agents and that those that do are likely to lose out. “We have way more businesses that are calling us asking to integrate deeply,” he said. He argued agents could grow commerce overall: “Is the total addressable market for all of commerce just increasing dramatically?” Zuckerberg also sketched how Meta could make money beyond ads. “Subscriptions is going to be a big one,” he said. Muse is free to use, with paid plans at $20 and $100 a month for heavier users. On commerce, he floated taking “a small cut of what you are saving or making for people.” And on Meta’s July earnings call , he pitched business agents as working “just like the ad system”: “We will get paid when we deliver results for those businesses.” What Zuckerberg hasn’t addressed directly, on the podcast or the earnings call, is whether agents will eat into the ad impressions that generate nearly all of Meta’s revenue today. For now, Wall Street isn’t pressing the point. Bank of America analyst Justin Post wrote last week that Meta is “ back on offense with AI ,” naming rising AI spending—not agents—as the top risk. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Cumulative impacts of data centre gas plants overlooked, court hears
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Data centre developer takes Southern Highlands power plant fight to court Gundungurra man Dane Shanahan voiced his opposition to the project during the open-air Land and Environment Court hearing. ( ABC Illawarra: Penny Burfitt ) Nakar Property is appealing in the Land and Environment Court after its application to build a 16-megawatt gas-fired power plant in the Southern Highlands was refused. Community members urged the court to consider all three of the power plants proposed for the site. Lawyers for the applicant and the council will present evidence in coming days. A court has heard the "cumulative impacts" of a series of gas plants proposed to run data centres in the Southern Highlands are being ignored as a result of fragmented planning decisions. Seven community members gave evidence at the site of the development in Moss Vale on Tuesday morning, kicking off a three-day hearing in the Land and Environment Court. The court is considering developer Nakar Property's appeal of a refusal by Wingecarribee Shire Council for one of its projects on the site. The application was for a 16-megawatt gas-fired power plant and battery storage system to power data centres. Separately, the developer has secured approval for another gas-fired plant on the site, a 14MW facility, and is seeking state government approval for a third, 673MW plant. More than 100 community members gathered on the site ahead of the Land and Environment Court hearing. ( ABC Illawarra: Penny Burfitt ) A crowd of more than 100 community members, Land and Environment Court Commissioner Nicola Targett, and representatives for the council and the applicant gathered in an open field in Moss Vale for the first day of the hearing. The first community member to address the court was Dane Shanahan, who introduced himself by his Gundungurra name, Mullyang. The emerging knowledge-holder for the region's traditional landowners told the court his name meant "eagle" and, as he outlined his community's concerns about the project, two wedge-tailed eagles appeared in the sky above the open-air court. After the proceedings, Mr Shanahan described the appearance of the birds as an "ancestral presence". He was one of several speakers to urge the commissioner to consider the application for the 16MW facility in the broader context of the development. "Each piece is being presented as small — each piece is being assessed on its own and no-one is looking at the whole," Mr Shanahan told the court. The court is only assessing the appeal lodged by Nakar Property for the 16MW facility and battery, but Gabby Kent, who lives 1 kilometre from the proposed site, agreed with Mr Shanahan's argument. "The planning processes may be separate, but the cumulative impacts to my family … and my community are not," she said. Will McCarthy says the project needs to be looked at as a whole. ( ABC Illawarra: Penny Burfitt ) Will McCarthy, whose home overlooks the development, echoed those sentiments. "At some point the planning system needs to stand back at look at the development as a whole," he told the commissioner. The court heard the applicant had submitted an amended plan for the development to speakers and parties ahead of the hearing. That submission included changes such as painting exhaust stacks green to address visual amenity, and adding some onsite solar power generation. Mr Shanahan told the court no Gundungurra people had been consulted as part of the development application's Aboriginal Heritage Assessment, despite the cultural significance of a waterway that would be cut off by the project. "It is as significant to the Gundungurra as Genesis is to Christians," he said. "The applicant has proposed to reshape an ancestral waterway without asking the people [whether] it will scar." The power plant and battery would provide power to data centres on Cloud Carrier's Moss Vale site. ( Supplied: Cloud Carrier ) Jacqueline Duc raised concerns about the health impacts of pollutants, telling the court carcinogens from gas power-plants had been linked to lung and childhood cancers. She also raised concerns about the project being located within the Sydney water catchment, saying its tributaries eventually flowed into Warragamba Dam, which supplied 80 per cent of the city's drinking water. The applicant's lawyer, James Smith, did not question any of the community speakers. The court will hear from the applicant's attorney and the council's representative, Michael Staunton, in coming days.

events.title: What’s making Europe so angry? The frustration behind the protests
events.summary: Violent protests have erupted in several European countries over dissatisfaction with living costs. Demonstrations in France saw protesters set city halls ablaze and attack police officers. "The European economy is not growing as much as the U.S.," a Portuguese minister told CNBC. Anger over the cost of living and pressure on public services has brought hundreds of thousands of protesters onto streets across several European countries, with grievances ranging from expensive housing to poor conditions in schools and universities. France saw the largest demonstrations at the weekend, with more than 500,000 people marching. Most protested peacefully, but some looted and vandalized shops, set fire to city halls and attacked police officers. Separate protests also took place in Italy, Spain, Portugal and Albania on Saturday and Sunday. Their immediate triggers differed, although high fuel and energy costs formed part of the backdrop in several countries. The wars in Iran and Ukraine have pushed diesel prices sharply higher across the continent. There's no one "single trigger" for the riots, Capital Economics' Chief Europe Economist Andrew Kenningham told CNBC. The increase in energy costs may be playing a role, but the increase is smaller than in 2022, at the onset of the Russia-Ukraine war, when there were no comparable violent protests, he added. Nevertheless, the demonstrations pose a shared challenge for governments: how to improve living conditions and maintain public services while supporting households and keeping strained public finances in check. The demonstrations in France began last month when high school students criticized poor schooling conditions, including shoddy facilities and teacher shortages. They have since evolved into broader protests over living standards and declining public services. In Spain, housing protests began in September after an 87-year-old woman, Maricarmen Abascal, was evicted following a 230% rent increase by an investment fund. She died a fortnight later. Thousands of protesters also took to the streets in Portugal on Saturday to demonstrate against soaring housing costs and the cost of living. "People obviously are protesting on the cost of living with diesel and fuel prices, but mainly on housing costs, which have been increasing substantially all over Europe, but also particularly in Portugal," Miranda Sarmento, Portugal's minister of state and finance, said Monday. In Albania, protesters were angry about poor university conditions and high tuition fees, and called for the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama. Some threw Molotov cocktails and other objects at the police and set fire to cars and litter bins. In Italy, a march in central Milan on Saturday over living costs also ended violently, with rioters attacking the police with stones and paving blocks and setting fire to barricades. "The underlying problem is that politicians are not able to offer hope of a better life for many Europeans because the economy is growing only slowly and governments have built up huge debts, leaving them little scope to support higher public spending or to cut taxes," Capital Economics' Kenningham said. The escalation of violence in France in particular is due to a "conjugation of different elements," said Douglas Yates, a professor at the American Graduate School in Paris. "This was a storm that turned into a hurricane," Yates told CNBC's Steve Sedgwick. "There was this inflation, which has brought out the cost-of-living protesters who would have been disgruntled at any rate." Yates said another factor is France's 2027 presidential election, as opposition parties seek to capitalize on growing public discontent with President Emmanuel Macron . Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has proposed a 2027 budget aimed at narrowing France's deficit , projected at 5.4% of gross domestic product this year. Measures include freezing the civil service pay index and tightening reimbursement for sick leave. "Finally there's the students, the poor students who started this by making reasonable demands for having their dilapidated infrastructure repaired and perhaps getting some air conditioners installed in the classrooms, and so these three forces have come together and created an out-of-control hurricane," Yates added. The economic backdrop has also deteriorated. In the second quarter of 2026, France's unemployment rate rose to 8.3%, representing 2.7 million people, according to Insee, the national statistics bureau . The unemployment rate among 15- to 24-year-olds climbed to 21.6%. Consumer prices rose 3.1% in September from a year earlier, up from 2.4% in August, according to final Insee data. Energy prices jumped 21.3%. Meanwhile, purchasing power per consumption unit is projected to fall 0.7% in 2026, according to Insee figures, cited by Le Monde .

events.title: Gulf states to boost diesel shipments to struggling France
events.summary: The UAE, Saudi Arabia and Bahrain are to sell France the equivalent of 10 per cent of its diesel consumption in the coming weeks, Elysee sources have said. The aim is to bring energy prices down in Europe, which have fuelled protests and public anger in France. “The greater the quantity, the lower the price. It’s quite simple,” an adviser to French President Emmanuel Macron said. A large part of the deal was obtained by Mr Macron during a tour of the Gulf that started on Monday with visits to Kuwait and the UAE. He is also set travel to Bahrain and Qatar. France previously obtained guarantees from Saudi Arabia to sell 95,000 tonnes of diesel in October and November, bringing the total to 190,000 tonnes over two months. In addition, the UAE and Bahrain are in the coming weeks expected to separately sell 100,000 tonnes of diesel to France for an unknown duration. “These are political commitments obtained from countries in the region because they know us and they know we are reliable – because we have been there during every critical moment, notably by deploying air defence capabilities,” the adviser said. Sales are to go through French energy company TotalEnergies, whose chief executive, Patrick Pouyanne, has accompanied Mr Macron on his Gulf tour. UAE and France sign AI and tech deals The UAE and France have signed deals in energy, artificial intelligence and advanced technology as the countries strengthen investment and economic ties. The preliminary agreements were signed in the presence of Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, and Mr Macron in the UAE capital. Three agreements focused on AI and advanced technology were signed with French start-up AMI Labs to strengthen research and technological co-operation and explore new applications across several fields, Abu Dhabi Media office reported. The deals cover Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence, Abu Dhabi’s G42 and computing company Analog. MBZUAE is to focus on strengthening co-operation with AMI Labs in AI research and development, while G42 aims to establish a framework for strategic co-operation in cloud computing infrastructure and AI models. Analog’s deal with AMI Labs is related to exploring opportunities to integrate AI models into robotics and physical AI applications and opening new avenues for developing intelligent systems and expanding their use in industrial and technology sectors. The UAE and France will also boost co-operation in the energy sector, with Adnoc Gas and Schneider Electric signing an initial pact to assess advanced technology and opportunities for operational improvements to help enhance efficiency and improve the performance of energy systems. Adnoc Refining and Technip Energies also signed two contracts relating to a refining capacity enhancement project and a sustainable aviation fuel project. “These agreements demonstrate both countries’ commitment to broadening economic and investment co-operation, strengthening integration between their industrial, technological and research capabilities, and opening new avenues for public-private partnerships to support the development of innovative and sustainable solutions in shared priority sectors,” Abu Dhabi Media office said.

Hello, this is Hui Jie writing to you from Singapore. Welcome to another edition of CNBC's Daily Open. The tech trade staged a comeback as investors pile into the sector in the U.S., but the same sentiment did not cross the Pacific. However, public listings are very much on the table in Asia, with firms jostling for a piece of India's Jio IPO and venture capitalist Jenny Lee saying that startups in the region were 'speeding' toward IPOs. After a week defined by investors trimming exposure to the tech sector, some have cautiously begun to buy back in. The Nasdaq Composite advanced more than 1% on Monday stateside, with tech leading the charge. Chip heavyweight Nvidia added 1.4%, and Tesla jumped 3.8%. Alphabet shares advanced about 1%. However, the same sentiment did not seem to carry over to Asia on Tuesday, with the tech-heavy Kospi in South Korea leading losses in the region and down over 4%. Japanese tech stocks were also mostly lower, with the Nikkei 225 down 1.6%. In Europe, however, Nvidia is increasing its investments in the continent's artificial intelligence sector, unveiling plans to back four German startups as the country pushes to strengthen its position in industrial AI. The investments are part of the U.S. chipmaker's nearly $10 billion commitment to invest in companies, universities and research institutions across Europe, as announced at the Invest in Germany Summit in Berlin on Monday. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who described the technology as a major opportunity for the country's economy, told small and medium enterprises to "please open your doors for AI to make use of your data." "This is a real secret and a real advantage for Germany to make use of all the data which is already available in our companies," Merz said. IPO fever is slowly getting some attention in Asia, where newly formed companies are reaching the initial public offering stage far sooner than they used to, according to venture capitalist Jenny Lee. In the West, companies like to stay private a little longer, but Asian firms are leaning toward a more accelerated timeline, according to Lee, senior managing partner at Granite Asia. "On average the holding period before a company goes public is eight to 10 years," Lee said in an interview. "But currently, the later stage companies we are seeing are actually preparing for IPOs when they are four to five years old." events.title: Oil majors face spending test from Iran war windfall cash
events.summary: The severe disruption of the Strait of Hormuz has pushed energy prices to multi-year highs. Oil majors are set for a big third-quarter profit jump after the US-Israeli war on Iran lifted energy prices and refining margins. Investors want to see whether Shell, BP, TotalEnergies, Chevron and Exxon keep spending discipline or start a costly spending spree. BP is using cash to cut debt, while Shell and TotalEnergies may raise buybacks; BP plans a strategy update on 15 December. LONDON – Oil majors are set to post a big jump in third-quarter profit as the US-Israeli war on Iran has boosted refining and trading results, while investors will monitor how wisely they use their cash piles and whether they resist a spending spree. The severe disruption of the Strait of Hormuz since US-Israeli airstrikes began the war in February has pushed energy prices to multi-year highs, allowing trading desks to profit from the volatility. In a sector notorious in the past for boom and bust, the majors have all promised this time to refrain from losing control of costs in what is one of the highest-earning years for global oil producers in recent memory. Shell, BP and TotalEnergies all expect refining margins to increase three- to fourfold in the third quarter from a year ago, with Shell guiding for a record high of US$42 a barrel. TotalEnergies expects cash flow from its refining and chemicals business to double to around US$4 billion (S$5.11 billion) from the previous quarter. Exxon signalled that higher refining margins in the quarter could boost downstream profit by US$4.5 billion versus the previous quarter. Are majors adapting their spending plans? As oil majors report third-quarter results at the end of October, investors are asking whether they will stick to their existing spending plans in times of exceptional earnings, wrote RBC Capital Markets analyst Biraj Borkhataria in a research note. So far, Chevron and Exxon have used the money to pay down debt. Investors in Chevron will monitor investment in Venezuela and its progress towards extending its contract to operate the TCO joint venture in Kazakhstan, which is developing the country’s largest oilfield, analysts said. HSBC expects Shell to announce a US$3.5 billion buyback for the fourth quarter, after it reduced the pace of its buyback programme to a quarterly US$3 billion earlier in 2026. After the oil major’s trading update last week, investment bank TPH called BP its favourite name among European majors. It said BP’s underlying profit could exceed US$7 billion, versus US$5.7 billion in the second quarter, boosted by refining and gas marketing and trading. That cash is going towards repairing BP’s balance sheet. Citi data shows BP’s net debt to operating cash flow falling from 1.7 times at the end of 2025, the highest of the five biggest majors, to an expected 0.8 times by the third quarter. BP is likely to discuss its future capital allocation during its third-quarter earnings announcement, HSBC said, as BP hits a target to reduce its net debt about a year early, also helped by pausing its buyback programme in 2026. BP has flagged a strategy update on Dec 15. “We believe the priority will remain firmly on deleveraging, with stable capex and no buyback resumption before 2028,” said HSBC’s Kim Fustier and Sadnan Ali in a note. Shell and Total are due to report on Oct 29 while BP, Chevron and Exxon are due on Oct 30. REUTERS

events.title: Larry Page could dodge nearly $15 billion in taxes after leaving California and spending $173 million on a Miami compound
events.summary: In just a couple of weeks, Californians will vote on ballot measure Prop 40 —a highly debated measure that would require a one-time 5% tax on the state’s billionaires who lived there as of Jan. 1, 2026.  While some billionaires like Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang are “ perfectly fine ” with the measure, others left the state ahead of the cutoff. One was Larry Page, the 53-year-old Google cofounder who had ties to California for decades and began severing them after the wealth tax proposal . He’s currently worth $292 billion , so he would have owed nearly $15 billion had he stayed. In late December, Koop, Page’s family office, was converted out of California and incorporated in Delaware, Fortune ’s Sasha Rogelberg previously reported. Other organizations linked to Page, including Flu Lab LLC, One Aero, and Oceankind, were also incorporated in Delaware that month, after previously being in California, Rogelberg’s analysis of state filings found. Meanwhile, he spent big on homes on the other side of the country. Page bought two Miami estates for a combined $173.4 million, The Wall Street Journal reported early this year, citing people familiar with the matter. One was a $101.5 million , 11,855-square-foot property in the Coconut Grove neighborhood, according to the WSJ. Redfin reported this was the most expensive U.S. home sale of December and the fourth most expensive sale of 2025. Page also purchased a nearby property for $71.9 million, Miami-Dade property records show .  Page isn’t the only tech billionaire to trade the West Coast for Miami as states move to tax the rich. Amazon founder Jeff Bezos left Seattle for Miami in late 2023, later selling his Hunts Point mansion for a record $63 million . He now lives in a $237 million Miami compound with his wife, Lauren Sánchez Bezos. Washington has since passed a 9.9% tax on household income above $1 million. Voters there decide Nov. 3 whether to repeal it. Former Starbucks CEO Howard Schultz followed a similar path. He announced his move from Seattle to Miami in March, around the time Washington lawmakers were advancing the millionaires tax. He reportedly paid $44 million for a Miami penthouse. To be sure, Bezos said he moved to be closer to his parents, and Schultz wrote the couple was “enjoying the sunshine of South Florida and its allure to our kids on the East Coast.” Google cofounder Sergey Brin, who moved to the Nevada side of Lake Tahoe and also bought a Miami home , and venture capitalist Peter Thiel also left California for Miami ahead of the Prop 40 cutoff. Florida has no income, capital gains, or wealth tax. While a one-time levy may prompt the move, the lack of income taxes also appeals to the ultrawealthy: It’s “a huge boon for us,” Miami developer Robert Rivani , who moved from Los Angeles, told Fortune . Some brokers say the ultrawealthy are leaving California reluctantly. “They want to stay in the state of California, because they love where they’re at, and they never thought of moving,” Compass agent Michael Martirena told Fortune ’s Marco Quiroz-Gutierrez . “But they work very hard for their money, and they said they like their pocketbook much more.” Still, the departures have already cut into what Prop 40 could raise. Page, Brin, Thiel, and former Uber CEO Travis Kalanick alone would have owed about $29 billion, according to a recent Fortune estimate. That’s more than a fourth of the measure’s projected $100 billion . Opponents have spent more than $187 million fighting the measure , compared with about $32 million from supporters. Two billionaire-backed countermeasures, Props 41 and 42, would nullify Prop 40 if either draws more votes. Even if it passes, the Jan. 1 residency date is likely to be challenged in court, according to the California Budget & Policy Center . California weighs factors like time spent in the state and business ties when deciding who counts as a resident. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts WA woman stranded in Bali hospital after horror fall while on holiday Estelle Ravenscroft is being treated at a hospital in Bali after having a fall. ( Supplied: Marilyn Jones ) A 79-year-old woman is in a Bali hospital in a serious condition after breaking multiple bones when she fell at a restaurant. Estelle Ravenscroft's family are fundraising to bring her home because she is not covered by insurance. The Insurance Council of Australia is urging travellers to persist in efforts to obtain insurance before heading overseas. A West Australian grandmother is facing a potential bill of $100,000 to return home to Australia after falling down stairs at a Bali restaurant. Estelle Ravenscroft, 79, and her husband Keith remain in Bali, where Ms Ravenscroft is in the intensive care unit at a local hospital. Ms Ravenscroft broke both her legs in the fall. The harrowing ordeal has been exacerbated by mounting medical expenses as Ms Ravenscroft is not covered by insurance. Mr Ravenscroft said it was difficult to obtain travel insurance, because of their age. Indonesia is not among the 11 countries with which Australia has a reciprocal arrangement for publicly-funded emergency care. Ms Ravenscroft's family said the 79-year-old had gone for lunch at a restaurant and fallen down the stairs, which had no rails. Speaking this morning, Mr Ravenscroft said his wife had pulled through after a nine-hour operation at a local hospital. "She's sitting up now, but there are some difficulties breathing, and issues with transfusions, but she's pulled through the operation OK, which is really fantastic." Estelle Ravenscroft broke multiple bones when she fell at a restaurant. ( Supplied: Leonie Walsh ) The couple's family has appealed to the community for help with expenses through an online fundraising website. Mr Ravenscroft said travel insurance was increasingly difficult to obtain as people aged. "When you get a certain age, you'll find having the insurances that you think you can have, are not available," he said. "I'd prefer not to go into that, because I'm here at the moment to make sure that my wife is OK. I want to get her home. The family wants to get her home." Ms Ravenscroft's sister Marilyn Jones said the family was grateful for the support offered by the WA community. Estelle Ravenscroft was on holiday with her husband in Bali when she fell at a restaurant. ( Supplied: Marilyn Jones ) "The amount daily is climbing," she said. Ms Jones said she was aware of commentary around the couple's lack of adequate travel insurance. "It's pulled us down terribly," she said. "There are some not very nice people out there, but there are also some wonderful people out there. National Seniors Australia chief executive Chris Grice urged older Australians to investigate all options for travel insurance before travelling overseas. ''So I just feel so badly for someone who is caught in a foreign land, who perhaps can't get home because of the costs involved." He said he was aware of seniors who struggled to get travel insurance as they aged, but urged people to persist. "It depends on age and existing conditions," he said. "It doesn't mean they can't get cover. It all depends on how they are being treated." He said people needed to try and speak directly to an insurer, rather than apply online, if they had concerns. An Insurance Council of Australia spokesperson said its thoughts were with the Ravenscrofts and acknowledged the strain many households were under. "While cost of living is putting pressure on household budgets, a single overseas medical emergency, evacuation, or trip cancellation can cost far more than the premium of even a comprehensive policy," she said.

events.title: An Ohio court’s ruling against $776 million in vouchers reignites the fight over who should pay for private school
events.summary: Ohio gives parents taxpayer-funded vouchers to send their children to private schools. But those schools still get to cherry-pick which children they accept. That contradiction sits at the center of an Ohio appeals court ruling that declared the state’s EdChoice voucher program unconstitutional on Oct. 15. The Tenth District Court of Appeals upheld a June 2025 lower-court decision, finding that the program uses public money to secure “a separate system of non-public schools” at the expense of public education. For families using the vouchers, nothing changes immediately. The ruling is on hold pending an appeal, and Ohio Attorney General Andy Wilson said the program would continue uninterrupted as the state asks the Ohio Supreme Court to review the case. How EdChoice went from a rescue program to universal vouchers Created in 2005 and launched the following year, EdChoice was originally designed to help children assigned to chronically underperforming public schools attend private schools using state-funded tuition assistance. In 2013, lawmakers created EdChoice Expansion , initially allowing kindergarten students whose family income was at or below 200% of the federal poverty guidelines to qualify, regardless of how their local public schools performed. Eligibility was then extended one grade at a time. Then, in 2023, Republican lawmakers removed the income limit altogether, making EdChoice Expansion available to families regardless of income. Families earning up to 450% of the federal poverty guidelines—about $135,000 for a family of four at the time—could receive full scholarships, while those earning more qualified for smaller awards. The legal fight began in January 2022, when six public school districts, four students and the Ohio Coalition for Equity and Adequacy of School Funding sued the state, arguing that EdChoice violated Ohio’s constitutional requirement to maintain a “thorough and efficient system of common schools.” In June 2025, a Franklin County judge declared EdChoice unconstitutional. The state appealed and lost again this month. Why the court says public schools pay the price So what exactly went wrong with a program originally designed to help children escape struggling public schools? For one, the appeals court found that private schools receiving vouchers retain discretion to decide which students to accept. The judges cited admission policies that allowed private schools to reject students with behavioral problems, disabilities or poor academic performance. Public schools, meanwhile, must continue educating eligible children in their districts, regardless of how expensive their needs may be. That creates a financial problem. When students leave public schools, districts can lose the state funding tied to those students. But their buildings still need maintenance, school buses still need to run, and teachers still need to be paid. (Some Ohio districts have even cut high school bus service while still busing students to private and charter schools to avoid state penalties.) The students can leave. The bills don’t necessarily leave with them. And if private schools enroll children who cost less to educate, public schools may be left with a greater share of students who need more expensive support. The court also found that families in many rural counties have substantially fewer opportunities to use EdChoice vouchers. Of the 154 private schools where at least three-quarters of students use vouchers, 44% are in just three counties: Cuyahoga, Franklin and Hamilton, home to Cleveland, Columbus and Cincinnati. Ohio spent about $776 million on its two EdChoice programs in fiscal 2025—$492.7 million on EdChoice Expansion scholarships and $283.1 million on traditional EdChoice scholarships—covering more than 140,000 students. Meanwhile, the appeals court found that public schools were not receiving all the money the state’s own funding plan called for. According to the appeals court ruling , Ohio public schools received about $7.1 billion in state funding in fiscal 2024, roughly $700 million less than the $7.8 billion they would have received under the state’s fully funded school-funding formula. That same year, Ohio spent $677.6 million on EdChoice vouchers. The judges found that EdChoice and public school funding drew from the same line item in the state budget. Aaron Rausch, chief of budget and school funding at the Ohio Department of Education and Workforce, testified that if the voucher money were no longer going to private schools, the state could direct it back to public schools. In other words, Ohio was spending hundreds of millions of dollars on private-school tuition while falling short of fully funding its public-school formula. The state had planned to phase in its school-funding formula over several years, so the $700 million gap can’t simply be blamed on EdChoice. But the court concluded that the phase-in had “by all meaningful measures, been abandoned,” and that voucher spending was competing with money that could otherwise support public schools. The court also cited a sworn statement detailing the financial problems facing one of the districts that sued. Marnisha Brown, superintendent of the Richmond Heights Local School District outside Cleveland, said the district couldn’t afford to repair a broken elementary-school boiler and heating pumps, pay competitive teacher salaries or offer programs including band, art, music, drama and foreign languages. The district also couldn’t win voter approval for a school levy. Those problems don’t prove that EdChoice alone caused its financial difficulties, but they illustrate the strain facing public schools. Most new voucher users weren’t leaving public schools And there’s another twist. You might think a program originally designed to help children escape struggling public schools would mostly benefit students leaving those schools. But among first-time recipients of its expanded version, that wasn’t the case. Of roughly 25,700 students who received an EdChoice Expansion scholarship for the first time in fiscal 2025, only about 6,100, or 24%, had attended public schools the year before, according to Ohio’s Legislative Service Commission. The other three-quarters weren’t coming from an Ohio public school. Ohio isn’t just helping children leave struggling public schools. It’s also paying private-school tuition for students who weren’t attending public schools to begin with. What critics and supporters are saying Democratic state Sen. Willis E.
