events.title: Strangers are paying up to $150 for empty seats at weddings all because one couple ran out of date-night ideas—20,000 people have signed up
events.summary: Jeff and Karina Besen have a standing date night every week. After 19 years of marriage, they ran out of things to do. “One day, Jeff literally looked at me and said, ‘Hey, wouldn’t it be fun if we could get dressed up and go to a wedding?’” Karina told Fortune . Her first answer was you can’t just do that: They didn’t know anyone getting married, they themselves got married and had kids relatively young, and they certainly weren’t going to crash a wedding—just yet. So the two started chatting and wondered if there was a resource where they could get connected to couples having a wedding in their area who needed a seat-filler of sorts. Jeff looked into it and found nothing like it existed. So, the San Diego couple built it. Not a Wedding Crasher , which launched in mid-March, lets couples share unused wedding seats with verified guests, who pay a fee set by the couple to attend the ceremony and reception. And it’s solving a pretty common problem: Jeff said an estimated 10% to 20% of invited guests RSVP no or drop out, and many venues require couples to pay for a minimum headcount whether they fill it or not. “You may have to pay for 100 seats, and you can only get 75 people,” he said. And those empty chairs are costly: The Knot’s 2026 Real Weddings Study found the average cost per wedding guest is $292, and the average guest count is 117. Their website allows to-be newlyweds to list what Jeff called “unused capacity” and get them filled. Listings on the site have ranged from one open seat to 60. How it works Couples sign up as hosts and list how many seats they have open and what they want to charge. Jeff said couples have set prices from $25 to $150 a seat, with an average of about $50. Current listings include a $25 seat outside Nashville and 19 open seats at $70 each at a Las Vegas wedding next month. The Besens review every listing and contact the couple before it goes live, to weed out fake accounts. Guests sign up for free; build a profile with a photo, a short bio and links to their social media; and verify their identity by scanning a government ID and their face through Stripe. They then request a seat with a short note to the couple, who approve or decline from a dashboard. Only after approval does the guest learn the venue name and address. The company takes a 20% platform fee on each seat’s price, plus what Jeff called a “relatively nominal” service fee charged to guests on each transaction. The platform has processed “tens of thousands of dollars” in gross seat payments, Jeff said, of which it keeps 20%. “This is also a largely software business, so we do have pretty high margins,” he said. He added the couple is looking at other ways to expand revenue. From a dozen seats to 20,000 sign-ups Growth has come almost entirely from social media. The Besens make short videos about each new listing and push them to the cities where the weddings are. The site’s first wedding came in May in Los Angeles, and the Besens went themselves. “We are based in San Diego, so fortunately that was relatively close,” Jeff said. “As any good business owner, you should be eating your own dog food, if you will. So we had to go and try it out.” The couple had never crashed a wedding before building the site. “We are fairly private people, and this has totally flipped us upside down,” Jeff said. Karina added they’ve had to learn to put themselves out more publicly, since they now make videos for every new listing. In May, they had sold about a dozen seats and had 300 guests on the platform, but five months later, Jeff said the site has placed close to 1,000 guests who have attended about 60 weddings, and has nearly 20,000 people signed up across the country. Guests have flown across the country to attend, alone, in pairs, and in groups. Some who met as fellow crashers now book weddings together. Gifts aren’t required, though some guests bring them anyway. Couples have their own reasons to sign up beyond filling paid-for seats. Jeff described a recent Atlanta wedding where the couple’s guest list skewed toward older relatives and they wanted people who would get on the dance floor. Many hosts ask for the same thing just to get the party started. “You’re choosing your guests,” Jeff said. A wedding season they missed Before launch, the couple spent months testing the idea on strangers, including comedians outside comedy clubs and vendors at a wedding expo. “Some people said it’s crazy, but most people said it’s a really good idea,” Jeff said. The idea also has a personal side. Karina was 21 and Jeff was 23 when they married, and they had kids by the time she was 23. “You know how some people get to go to weddings every weekend for a year? We didn’t really get to do that,” she said. “We had too much responsibility at home.” Their own wedding ran into the same venue minimums their site now works around. Their preferred venue required at least 100 guests on a Saturday. With only 50 or 60 people, they married on a Sunday instead. Karina said she didn’t expect the personal connections. One guest wrote in her profile that she had always wanted to be an adult flower girl. And it came true, thanks to the site. “That bride that she applied to the wedding actually asked her to be her adult flower girl in the wedding,” Karina said. events.title: Blackwall quadruples valuation to $2.2B as websites wrangle an increasingly crowded internet
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Estonia-based Blackwall , which builds web traffic security tools for hosting providers, said on Tuesday that it has raised $100 million at a $2.2 billion valuation. It builds products that helps websites grapple with the skyrocketing volume of bot traffic, especially AI agents. The Series C was led by AVP, with participation from existing investors Dawn Capital, MMC Ventures and Tera Ventures. Blackwall’s executive chairman, Roi Carthy, told TechCrunch this funding round increased the company’s valuation by 4 times since its previous fundraise in 2025 . Over the past few years, web infrastructure companies like Cloudflare, Akamai, Imperva and Blackwall have found themselves in an increasingly valuable but difficult space: They’re on the frontlines, dealing with DDoS attacks, indiscriminate scraping, botnet farms, malicious requests, and these days, even swarms of AI agents going rogue . But it’s also a chance to make a killing by helping hosting providers and websites deal with all the potentially unwanted traffic. Blackwall, however, isn’t interested in competing with the bigwigs in its space. Instead of selling its platform directly to websites, the company uses a “channel” approach, working with web hosting, managed service and cloud providers to understand their needs, and then handing over a bundle of tools which they can customize. Those providers can then offer Blackwall’s security tools to their own clients under their own branding and retain control of that relationship. There’s money in it for both sides. Co-founder and CEO Nikita Rozenberg told TechCrunch that hosting companies can mix and match security components to build their own solution according to what they want to provide to their end customers, set the prices, and share a cut of the revenue with Blackwall. The company initially gives its customers a free tier showing the traffic and threats hitting their network, but charges for any protection or tools to address the threats. In addition to providing services like threat intelligence, certificate management, DDoS protection and traffic routing, Blackwall examines its customers’ web traffic to differentiate actual visitors and legit AI agents from malicious bots, intruders, and disruptive traffic. Rozenberg said the company uses techniques like digital fingerprinting to identify the software sending a request — for example, Microsoft Office or Codex — to filter out bots. In addition, the company uses its own AI models at customers’ endpoints to analyze the intent and behavior of the requests coming in to differentiate agents sent by a person for a real request versus a malicious bot. In the coming years, Rozenberg sees a big opportunity emerging as AI agents begin interacting and transacting with websites on behalf of their users. This should eventually require systems to manage which agents get access, and on what terms, and how they are authorized to make payments. Blackwall isn’t alone in eyeing that opportunity. Cloudflare’s AI Crawl Control lets website owners allow or block individual AI crawlers, and there’s also an option to charge them for access. But Rozenberg argues that Blackwall’s advantage lies in letting hosting providers offer such traffic management services themselves instead of handing the customer relationship to another security provider. Blackwall plans to use the funding to expand its operations across North America, Europe, Asia-Pacific and the Middle East, and develop more security tooling for hosting, cloud and managed service providers. events.title: The CO2-absorbing building made of old sinks, windscreens and toilets: Ghent’s £17m design museum is a green marvel
events.summary: Inspired by a gothic cathedral partly built using human bones, this gleaming monument to recycling boasts 62,000 bricks derived from construction waste – each made by the public during a two-day brick-making festival M useums often try to reflect the world around them, but rarely are they made so literally of their surroundings as the new design museum in Ghent . Rising above the Belgian city’s medieval tiled rooftops like an angular white watchtower, the new building has vacuumed up the city’s condemned concrete frames, windows, car windscreens, sinks and old toilets, and transformed them, phoenix-like, into a gleaming monument to recycling. “There’s nothing new about reuse,” says Andy Groarke, co-founder of Carmody Groarke , the London-based architects who designed the €20m (£17m) project with local firms Atama and Re-st . “We’ve just forgotten how to do it.” He says the team drew inspiration from Ghent’s 16th-century gothic cathedral, Saint Bavo’s, which was partly built using the white limestone blocks of the 10th-century romanesque basilica that had stood on the same site (recent renovations also ghoulishly uncovered walls made of human bones , femurs and tibias apparently having particularly useful structural properties, with crushed skulls for infill). The new design museum doesn’t quite go that far in its nose-to-tail approach, but almost. The toilet cubicles are a smorgasbord of “biomaterials”, each featuring different tiles made of seaweed, flax, wood terrazzo and volcanic ash (you can scan a QR code for more info while you’re sitting on the loo). Some walls are plastered with local clay, while a chunky column in the entrance hall revels in its earthy layers of rubble dug straight from the building site. But the real innovation is the brick , which was specially developed, tested and certified for the project (funded by a grant from Circular Flanders and Sogent, the city’s development agency). Each brick is made of 63% construction waste, sourced from within 8km of the museum, pulverised and compressed with hydrated lime, saving two-thirds of the embodied carbon of a regular fired clay brick. And the lime will continue to absorb CO2 from the atmosphere as it cures over the coming months and years. “We’re not claiming this is a panacea, or a solution to the climate crisis,” says architect Sian Ricketts, Carmody Groarke’s sustainability lead. “But it is a sort of 82,000-brick proof of concept that you can do something different, with the right collaborators and the right clients.” Developed by East Sussex firm Local Works Studio and Brussels group BC Materials , the bricks were made in a former railway depot nearby, with the public invited to mix the ingredients and press their own blocks during a two-day festival of brickmaking. For €10, you can take one home from the museum shop. Public participation extended to defining the very essence of the museum, too. In keeping with Belgium’s democratic traditions, a “citizens’ panel” of 40 randomly selected Ghent residents was established to inform what the museum should be. Their 100+ recommendations ranged from incorporating unticketed areas, to being able to see work-in-progress, and having plenty of seating, as well as ensuring that the “chic” building didn’t put people off. The result is as locally sourced and collaboratively created as big civic buildings come. “This expansion and renovation are not about creating more museum,” says the outgoing director, Katrien Laporte, “but about creating more than a museum: a community sense-making museum with real social relevance.” The extension fills a leftover plot on the museum’s site, uniting the galleries that were previously spread between an 18th-century rococo mansion, called the Hotel de Coninck, and a troublesome 1990s addition – designed with a moving glass floor that rarely moved, now thankfully banished. The new building stands with the presence of a grand Ghent house, rising in five large storeys, and turning as it climbs to face the city centre, with big picture windows looking out in different directions on each floor. “We wanted it to feel domestic, industrial and civic at once,” says Groarke. It certainly has a bold presence. Not everyone has welcomed its industrial bulk. Concerns have been raised about how the boxy white mass lumbers into view from the city’s quaint historical centre, and there is something slightly clumsy about the form on the skyline, topped with multiple roofs angled in different directions. Silicone joints between stretches of brick don’t help either, reading as unsightly seams from a distance. The museum defended the height as providing never-before-seen views of the city, and it’s true: when you’re on the top floor – a freely accessible public loft – or the roof terrace below, the panoramic vistas of Ghent’s castle and church spires are a treat. Skyline concerns also fade away as you approach the museum at street level.

events.title: Don’t vilify data centers for the wrong reasons — just demand better ones
events.summary: Almost nobody wakes up thinking about a data center. But by the time you’ve checked the weather, paid a bill and answered a few emails, you’ve probably used several. Your bank runs on them, your hospital, your streaming account, every AI tool you’ve tried, and increasingly, more of the public services you rely on. You just never see them. That’s becoming a problem for my industry. In August, supervisors in Pinal County, Arizona, voted down a large data center campus after so many residents turned up to object that the county opened five overflow rooms across three buildings. Some said they hadn’t even heard about the project until several meetings in. Developers have lost similar votes this year in Florida, Virginia and North Carolina. I work on the power systems inside these buildings, in Britain and increasingly in the US. A lot of the backlash is aimed at the wrong target. Some of it is our own fault, and we should own that. Start with water, because that’s what most people worry about. Agriculture accounts for around 72% of the world’s freshwater withdrawals, according to the UN Food and Agriculture Organization. Data centers barely show up in that picture. That’s no comfort if you live next to a new campus in a dry county, and I get that. Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimates US data centers used about 17 billion gallons of water for cooling in 2023, and that could double or even quadruple by 2028. The water used to generate their electricity is roughly 12 times that again, and companies rarely report it. In Britain the picture looks very different. Research for England’s water market operator puts data centers at about 0.2% of non-household water use, a figure the government quoted in Parliament last month. A cooler climate helps, and so do cooling systems that barely use water for most of the year. So national figures don’t tell you much either way. What matters is the specific site, where it is, and how it’s cooled. Why the anger, then? Part of it is simple. The benefits of cloud services and AI are spread across millions of people. The costs, real or imagined, land on one town. Residents see the construction trucks, the new power lines and the backup generators. They don’t see the hospital or the bank that relies on what’s inside. These are also big, windowless, heavily secured buildings. When people can’t easily find out how much water and power a site will use, or who actually benefits, politicians fill the gap with rhetoric. And a data center is an easy stand-in for bigger fears about AI, climate change, jobs and big tech. A planning meeting turns into a vote on the future. I don’t blame people for that. Using AI or watching Netflix doesn’t mean you give up the right to ask how it’s made. So, here’s what I think my industry needs to do. Publish the numbers. Water and energy use, how they’re measured, and how they’ll change as a site grows. That should include the water behind the electricity, not just what goes through the cooling system. Build for the place. A cooling design that works in a cool, wet climate can be the wrong choice in the desert. Water, grid capacity and what the community actually wants should decide where and how we build. Take power seriously. In my experience it’s often a harder problem than water. A large campus can draw as much electricity as a small city. When the grid connection isn’t ready, the fallback is usually on-site gas or diesel generators, and “temporary” tends to last a lot longer than anyone said. Communities are right to ask for a proper connection plan and firm limits on how long those generators run. Treat residents as partners. Tell them early and give them a real say. If we promise jobs, tax revenue or better infrastructure, put numbers on it, not just headlines. The good news is the technology is moving the right way. Newer sites increasingly use air cooling or sealed liquid loops that keep reusing the same water instead of evaporating it. That isn’t universal yet, which is why planning standards matter. Efficiency is also just good business. Power and water drive our costs, our resilience and our ability to grow, so we have every reason to use less of both. But we should prove it with measured results, not targets and press releases. The quickest way to win back trust is site-by-site public reporting, so communities can check what was promised against what was delivered: water, energy, cooling method, backup generation. That lets planners do their jobs properly. They can steer projects away from water-stressed areas, test whether grid plans are realistic, and hear local concerns while designs can still change, instead of telling the community after everything’s been decided. Judge data centers on how well they’re designed, powered, sited and run. Scrutiny on those terms is fair, and we should welcome it. Blanket opposition isn’t. It ignores the services everyone depends on and the improvements that are already here. events.title: Nike’s turnaround is stalling, and its Converse brand is a big reason why
events.summary: Converse makes up just 2.5% of Nike’s sales. Last quarter, it accounted for 20% of the company’s sales decline. Two years into Elliott Hill’s tenure as Nike’s CEO, the 118-year-old maker of the Chuck Taylor is a big drag on a comeback that isn’t coming together, with Converse sales down 28% in the most recent quarter and analysts openly wondering whether Nike will keep it in its portfolio. Converse’s Chuck Taylor high-tops have gone in and out of style over the decades, but the shoe’s vulcanized rubber sole and heavy, stiff profile are out of step with trends right now, and the brand is enduring an unusually long, deep cold streak. Too dependent on one style Nike bought Converse for $305 million in 2003, seeing enormous potential to rehabilitate an iconic brand. Converse had dominated athletic footwear for decades, but by the 1990s, it was reeling, and it ultimately filed for bankruptcy protection in 2001.  Converse started out as a rubber shoe manufacturer in 1908 and early on made items like winterized rubber-soled footwear and galoshes. Then in 1916, it made its first ever basketball shoes, introducing the Converse All-Star the following year. The model became the first real hit in the emerging athletic shoe industry. Converse’s growing popularity accelerated in 1932 when it unveiled a pair redesigned by Chuck Taylor, a semi-pro player and sneaker salesman who worked for the company. The shoes would ultimately bear his name as well as the “All-Star” ankle patch. Generations have worn the style since, from Kurt Cobain to Charli XCX. But now Converse is in its worst slump since the 1990s. Converse hit its peak in 2023, with sales reaching an all-time high of $2.43 billion. But they had more than halved to $1.17 billion last fiscal year. If its current rate of decline continues for the rest of the fiscal year, sales will fall below $1 billion for the first time since 2010.   Analysts blame the falloff on Converse’s inability to innovate and its overreliance on the Chuck Taylor model.  “They’re far too dependent on one item and when that one item cools off, like it is now, there’s no place to hide,” says Matt Powell, a footwear industry veteran now serving as a senior advisor to BCE Consulting. “It’s a fashion business and nothing lasts forever.” Converse is run separately from Nike with its own CEO who reports to Hill. It has a few other shoe models, such as the Jack Purcell, named for a 20th-century Canadian badminton star, that is having some success, but Chuck Taylors account for the lion’s share of the business. (Vans, owned by VF Corp, has had a similarly hard time in recent years for the same reason: over-reliance on skater shoes in its distinctive checkered patterns.) Frank O’Brien—The Boston Globe/Getty Images Rivals are winning over the same shoppers Converse sits in a tricky spot in the shoe market between casual footwear, fashion sneakers, and lifestyle shoes. Over the past few years, that space has become much more crowded, with brands from On Running to APL to Deckers Brands’ HOKA to New Balance managing to meet consumers’ changing tastes. Powell says Adidas , which has found enormous success tweaking its classic models, can serve as a model for Converse. The German athletic brand has kept its classic Samba shoe hyper relevant by introducing new variations, such as its recent slip-on version. Still, Converse’s sales hemorrhage raises fair questions about whether this is more than a cyclical decline. “We’ve never seen a 44% decline in demand for a brand,” BNP Paribas Equity Research senior analyst Laurent Vasilescu wrote, citing Converse’s sales deterioration in the fiscal quarter that ended in November 2025. The analyst said he wouldn’t be surprised if Nike ultimately decided to sell off Converse. Last month, Nike CEO Hill said he was focusing on getting Converse “back to financial health.” A Nike spokesperson said, “Converse remains an important part of the portfolio” and declined to provide specific details on how Hill planned to revive the brand, adding that the company would provide an update at Nike’s investor day next month. Nike’s last remaining acquisition In recent years, Nike has sold off most of the brands it acquired: Cole Haan, Umbro, Starter, Bauer, and Hurley, leaving just Converse. Vasilescu says Converse could meet the same fate, given its recent performance and the parent company’s need to focus on fixing other ailing parts of its business, like sales in China and its Jordan brand.  Powell sees a lot of life left in Converse—as part of Nike or otherwise—especially if it launches versions that are less heavy, less stiff, and more breathable.  “If and when this shoe hits again, it’s going to be ridiculously successful,” he says. events.title: Morocco’s not-so-new government faces new challenges
events.summary: The new cabinet has doubled down on continuity at a time of regional turmoil and domestic anxiety. On October 16, King Mohammed VI of Morocco appointed a new government headed by Prime Minister Fatima Zohra Al Mansouri. This is the first time in Moroccan history that a woman is leading the government – a precedent that was covered widely in international media. In the Moroccan context, however, what is important is that Al Mansouri hails from the Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM), which won the most seats in parliamentary elections in September. The party was founded by Ali Himma, a close associate and adviser to the king. PAM, which has formed a coalition with three other parties, dominates the new government. This signals continuity rather than potential for change. When thinking about what trajectory the new government is likely to take, it is important to consider PAM’s evolution. The party was established in 2008 with the aim of countering the rise of political Islam in Morocco and in particular, the Justice and Development Party (PJD). The Arab Spring, which saw mass protests across the country, brought changes to the Moroccan political scene, allowing more space for political forces like the PJD and, to an extent, curbing the influence of the establishment, known as the Makhzen. In 2011, Himma distanced himself from PAM and became an adviser to the king. Yet, the party continued to be perceived by other political groups as tied to the Makhzen. For years, PAM carried the stigma of its origins, but it persisted in trying to gain acceptance. In the 2016 elections, it challenged the PJD and secured the second-biggest number of votes, thus establishing itself as a legitimate political force. Yet this was still not enough to enable it to lead the government. The party subsequently reinvented itself by rejuvenating its ranks and gaining experience in public affairs through its participation in the 2021 government as a coalition partner. In the latest elections, PAM finally won. This election victory, however, needs to be put into perspective: 62 percent of eligible voters stayed away from the polls. On election day, the authorities had to call on people to go out and vote. Apart from the low turnout, there were suspicions of irregularities, but because in some cases the official election records were not released, observers and political parties were unable to obtain tangible evidence. There was also the familiar phenomenon of influential figures being brought into political parties at the last minute to boost electoral prospects. For example, just two months before the election, Faouzi Laaqjea, president of the Royal Moroccan Football Federation, whose popularity stems from the achievements of Moroccan football, officially joined PAM. To secure a majority in parliament, the party has had to form a coalition with forces which had previously questioned its legitimacy. While PAM has gained legitimacy through this alliance, the other parties and their leaders may now lose credibility. The newly formed government has retained more than half the members of its predecessor, not to mention the so-called sovereign ministries, which fall directly within the king’s reserved powers. Some Moroccans are already asking what was the point of holding elections if the same people are brought back to govern. The new government has an ambitious programme to respond to growing domestic pressure as the cost-of-living crisis deepens. At the first Council of Ministers meeting chaired by the king on October 17 , a 2027 Finance Bill was put forward that featured greater emphasis on addressing social issues, citizens’ purchasing power and youth inclusion. However, this agenda is facing an unfavourable international economic and financial environment, marked by rising energy prices and increasing costs of inputs for some of Morocco’s leading sectors, including phosphate production. The state-owned OCP Group, which is in charge of phosphate extraction and the industrial processing of phosphate derivatives and is one of Morocco’s principal sources of wealth, is now experiencing difficult times. There are also concerns about the potential effects of El Nino, which could bring more dry weather and threaten food security in a country that just endured seven consecutive years of drought. Tourism, another major source of revenue, could also suffer from the global slowdown in travel, rising transport costs and the uncertainties arising from tensions in the Gulf and Europe. The circumstances are therefore far from favourable for the new government, and public opinion appears broadly sceptical. Last but not least, this government will face an experienced and outspoken opposition, represented by both the Islamist PJD and the radical left. Even the ministers holding the so-called sovereign portfolios face serious challenges. The foreign minister must contend with public opposition to the normalisation of relations with Israel.

events.title: Alberta voters reject separation from Canada, early results show
events.summary: With more than one million votes counted, about 76 percent supported remaining in Canada. Alberta residents have voted to remain ⁠part of Canada in the province’s first-ever referendum on separation, in a much-needed win for Prime Minister Mark Carney as he ‌attempts to unify the country amid an ongoing trade war with the United States. With more than one million votes counted, about 77 percent supported remaining in Canada, compared with 23 percent who backed beginning a process that could lead to separation, early results showed on Tuesday. list 1 of 3 Could Alberta trigger Canada’s Brexit moment? list 2 of 3 Carney says he and Trump have agreed to ‘intensify’ trade negotiations list 3 of 3 Canada’s Carney secures deal for pipeline to expand oil exports beyond US The vote was not a direct referendum on independence but would have set oil-rich Alberta on a path towards a future vote on separation from Canada. Carney welcomed the result and said Albertans had made a “clear choice” in favour of unity. “They chose unity, to build together, and to take care of each other,” he said in a statement on X. Jeffrey Rath, a top leader of the secessionist Alberta Prosperity Project, told reporters his push for an independent Alberta will “absolutely” continue, despite the result from Monday’s vote. “We’ve learned a lot of lessons from this fight,” he said. Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, a conservative, said she voted against independence but called the referendum to settle an issue that has divided the province. She has said a win for the federalists would close the secession question. Alberta has the world’s fourth-largest proven oil reserves, and much of the secessionist momentum has been driven by anger over oil industry management. Smith has blamed Carney’s predecessor Justin Trudeau for igniting the secessionist fire, accusing him of trying to crush oil production to advance his pro-climate agenda. Alberta’s independence push has also drawn sustained interest from the allies of US President Donald Trump, including Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who called Alberta Washington’s “natural partner”. Elon Musk, the world’s richest person and eminent Trump supporter, also posted on X that Alberta “should separate”. Carney, who grew up in Alberta, has worked to improve relations between the province and Ottawa since taking office last year. He has partnered with Smith on advancing a new pipeline to export more Alberta bitumen overseas, a project considered a nonstarter during Trudeau’s tenure.

events.title: Hiring in the UAE rebounds in third quarter despite uncertainty fuelled by Middle East conflict
events.summary: Hiring in the UAE rebounded in the third quarter of the year to 4 per cent, the highest across the Gulf , as business demand recovers, a report has found. After hiring in the country dropped by 4 per cent in the second quarter, demand recovered from the mid-year slowdown and by September new export business was growing at its fastest pace in almost two years, Cooper Fitch said its third quarter employment index. Companies remain cautious about the year ahead, the report added. Across the Gulf, hiring returned to growth in the third quarter, rising 2 per cent following a 3 per cent decline in the previous quarter. In Saudi Arabia, recruitment rose 1.5 per cent, while Oman recorded 0.5 per cent growth. Hiring, however, fell by 1 per cent in Qatar , 2 per cent in Kuwait and 2 per cent in Bahrain. The Iran war, which began on February 28, has had a significant impact on regional economies, with the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz affecting oil-exporting countries. The International Monetary Fund, in a report this month, projected the UAE 's economy to contract by 3.9 per cent this year before rebounding at a 7.7 per cent growth rate in 2027, as long as shipping routes normalise and the strait reopens. The fund also expects Saudi Arabia 's economy to contract 3.3 per cent this year, while Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar are forecast to see double-digit contractions of 11.3 per cent, 16.7 per cent and 15.6 per cent, respectively, in 2026. Oman is the only Gulf member to see positive economic growth in 2026 at 4.1 per cent. However, all the six states are anticipated to post growth in 2027, the IMF said. The contraction in Gulf hiring "lasted a single quarter and the market is now back within the modest growth range seen through 2025", Cooper Fitch said. "Growth extended across a wider range of functions than in the previous quarter, with paused mandates resuming in sectors such as energy." Sectors hiring Hiring in energy recorded the sharpest increase at 7 per cent across the Gulf in the July-September period. Mandates stalled during the regional tensions returned steadily as conditions eased, the report said. "Clients resumed searches where they left off. In the UAE, growth came from across the energy market, including nuclear and renewables," it added. The delivery of Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030 pipeline also supported the sector's growth. "Project directors, commissioning specialists and contracts leaders remained difficult to secure. Candidates with scarce technical skills continued to receive multiple offers, keeping the market firmly in their favour," the report added. Hiring in finance grew 5 per cent, strategy rose 6 per cent – its first increase of 2026, while real estate and software employment was up 4 per cent. Recruitment in sales and marketing rose 3 per cent in the third quarter, "reflecting cautious confidence rather than a broad hiring rebound", while human resources grew 2 per cent, the report said. However, hiring in banking declined 4 per cent, while investment management fell by 5 per cent "after a strong run of hiring earlier in the year, driven by regional platform expansion and fund activity". While hiring picked up in the third quarter, it remained selective, Cooper Fitch said. "Clients focused on advancing active searches and securing specialist capability rather than broad expansion, and several markets and parts of financial services saw lower activity," it said. Looking ahead to the fourth quarter, it remains to be seen whether the improvement can be sustained. "Business demand has provided a firmer base, but costs remain elevated and visibility on trade and shipping is still limited," the report said. "Competition for scarce specialist talent has also intensified, adding pressure on employers seeking to secure critical capability."

events.title: U.S. bans DeepSeek from government agency systems amid AI rift with China
events.summary: The Trump administration has banned DeepSeek-related technology from federal civilian agency IT systems, including third-party products and services built using its AI models. The DHS order, issued in July and made public Monday, also bars federal civilian agencies from procuring DeepSeek products and services. The DHS cited concerns over potential transfers of sensitive U.S. government data to China and security vulnerabilities in DeepSeek's models. The Trump administration banned Chinese AI startup DeepSeek from civilian U.S. government agencies, citing security concerns. The Department of Homeland Security on Monday made public the order requiring federal civilian agencies to remove DeepSeek-related technology from their IT systems and barring them from procuring DeepSeek products and services. The ban applies to federal civilian agency IT systems, including third-party products and services developed using the company's technology. The move comes amid intensifying geopolitical tensions between Washington and Beijing, with artificial intelligence emerging as a key battleground in the two countries' race for technological dominance. The order, originally issued on July 24, applies to federal civilian agencies, including the Treasury, State and Justice departments, but it excludes the Department of Defense. Since DeepSeek burst onto the scene at the start of 2025, several U.S. government agencies have imposed various restrictions. Congress restricted the use of DeepSeek in intelligence community systems in December 2025. Earlier that year in March, U.S. Commerce Department bureaus told staff DeepSeek was banned on government devices, Reuters reported at the time. The Defense Information Systems Agency moved to block access to DeepSeek models in January 2025, according to reports from Bloomberg. DeepSeek's AI models "present multiple threat vectors," the latest DHS order states, citing concerns over potential access to sensitive data by Chinese authorities and potential cybersecurity vulnerabilities. The agency also warned that using DeepSeek's AI models could result in sensitive U.S. government data being transferred to China, potentially providing intelligence on American citizens and government programs. The models may also contain malware or other security vulnerabilities, the agency said, citing open-source research that identified multiple critical vulnerabilities in DeepSeek's iOS app. Executive agencies can request exceptions to the order, including delays in compliance, by submitting a written justification to the DHS within 60 days of the order's issuance. DeepSeek and China's Embassy in the U.K. did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.

events.title: Apple breaks its silence on the privacy crackdown that’s roiled the online ad industry
events.summary: John Ternus' Apple is waging war on advertising identifiers. Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images Apple roiled the ad industry with an unexpected new crackdown on web trackers. The tech giant has now issued a rationale for why it's stamping out "identity resolution." The ad industry has concerns Apple's latest privacy move may hamper targeting and measurement. Apple's latest privacy crackdown left the online ad industry scrambling for answers. Now, the tech giant has finally offered some. Late on Monday, Apple published a blog post laying out its rationale for new restrictions that block technology used to identify and track consumers across websites. The changes are implemented through WebKit, the browser engine that powers Safari and other browsers on iPhones and iPads. Apple said the change was designed to target " identity resolution ," a method adtech companies use to connect separate data points about users — such as email addresses, phone numbers, IP addresses, browsing history, or information about the device they're using — to identify and track them across devices. The method grew in popularity as many web browsers, including Apple's Safari, began phasing out third-party tracking cookies , the small files dropped on a user's device that were traditionally used for web tracking. The ad industry deploys tracking to precisely target specific audiences and measure whether their campaigns are working. In its blog post , Apple said that while users might readily offer their email address to log in to a website or sign up for a newsletter, most wouldn't expect it to also be shared with other companies for invisible tracking purposes. "It's not enough to block cross-site cookies to prevent cross-site tracking today because the tracking industry has not stopped trying to track users on the web," Apple said. "They have ushered into what they call the post cookie era and in our latest releases we have put strong protection in place." The blog post explains that Apple is implementing "domain-level" blocking, a broad intervention designed to ensure that identity providers can't circumvent the restriction by changing how they send data. Apple took the adtech industry by surprise earlier this month when it came to light that it had begun blocking the domains operated by several companies that offer alternative identifiers, without warning. The blocked domains included those operated by The Trade Desk , LiveRamp, ID5, Permutive, and Audigent. The initial rollout also blocked The Trade Desk's ability to serve ads at all on Apple-operated browsers. Apple rolled out a fix a few days later that restored The Trade Desk's ad-serving domain from being blocked alongside its advertising identifier, Unified ID 2.0. The ad industry braces for fallout The ad industry is now bracing for impact as more users begin updating their devices to iOS 27. Ad pros previously told CMO Insider that the change will make it harder for advertisers to identify and reach people across the open web. Industry insiders said that by effectively shrinking the pool of users they can target, advertisers are expecting less reach, higher prices to reach the audiences they can still identify, and more difficulty in controlling how often people see an ad and measuring whether their campaigns worked. Identity resolution has become widespread across the open web. An academic paper published in September that analyzed 600,000 websites over 41 months found that 83.76% of those sites were using alternative identifiers by May 2025. If advertising becomes less effective on the open web, marketers could funnel more of their budgets into so-called "walled garden" platforms like Meta and Google, which aren't as heavily reliant on alternative identifiers because they have reams of their own logged-in user data. Apple, too, has a growing advertising business within its App Store and apps, including News and Maps. Apple isn't backing down There are still unanswered questions about Apple's exact definition of an identity resolution provider, and the company has already demonstrated it can add domains to its block list without warning. There's also an indication Apple is only getting started. First reported by AdExchanger, Apple has also created a broader block list that can dynamically block potentially hundreds of adtech, martech, and data companies. Affected companies may not realize they've been added to the list until they begin experiencing disruptions. In Monday's blog post, Apple linked to its long-standing tracking-prevention policy , which acknowledges that its blocking rules may have unintended impacts. Those include disrupting the funding of websites that use targeted or personalized advertising, advertising measurement, and fraud prevention. The policy states that while Apple will try to limit unintended impact, "when faced with a tradeoff, we will typically prioritize user benefits over preserving current website practices." Ever since Apple launched its Intelligent Tracking Prevention feature in 2017, the tech giant has been locked in a cat-and-mouse game with the adtech industry, which has persistently developed workarounds to its privacy updates. Adtech companies have argued that these techniques were necessary to help publishers effectively monetize their websites with ads while still maintaining user privacy. Apple, which has long held that "privacy is a fundamental human right ," makes it clear in its policy that it won't allow workarounds to proceed on its watch. "We treat circumvention of shipping anti-tracking measures with the same seriousness as exploitation of security vulnerabilities," the Apple policy states. "If a party attempts to circumvent our tracking prevention methods, we may add additional restrictions without prior notice." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.summary: Trump, Netanyahu and the Iran question How Iran war fallout may shape US elections Trump calls for Zelenskyy to be replaced as negotiator, while Ukraine’s president says arms shipments delayed. United States President Donald Trump says someone other than Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy should negotiate on Kyiv’s behalf in talks to end Russia’s war. “Zelenskyy is a man that should have had settled this war a long time ago. If he would’ve listened to me, he would have made a much better deal a long time ago,” Trump told reporters outside the White House on Monday. “Maybe it’s time for Zelenskyy to get somebody else to negotiate.” list 1 of 3 Russia’s war on Ukraine ‘must be brought to an end’, Zelenskyy says list 2 of 3 Rubio says there was no US pause in intelligence sharing with Ukraine list 3 of 3 Children among six killed in Russian drone strike on Ukraine park The US president has been verbally swiping at his Ukrainian counterpart for several days as a rift between the leaders deepens. On Sunday, Trump claimed on Truth Social that Zelenskyy does not want to end the war. Earlier this month, he called for him to be replaced as president , and labelled him a “warmonger” over Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil refineries . Trump has also defended sanctions waivers for Russia, saying in the same Truth Social post that he wants to keep Moscow at the negotiating table. Zelenskyy said the decision “will hurt Ukraine” and strengthen Russian President Vladimir Putin’s war effort. Trump also announced plans on October 9 for Russia to supply more than 300,000 metric tonnes of diesel to US and global markets to tackle fuel prices that have soared since the US and Israel launched a war on Iran in late February. The decision has angered not only Kyiv, but also European partners and US officials, who say it rewards Moscow while it continues its four-and-a-half-year war on Ukraine. Zelenskyy told US senators at a meeting on Monday that decisions taken by the Trump administration “are hard to explain between friends”. He said arms shipments had been delayed and intelligence sharing restricted. “We also know that … the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles that our partners have already paid for through the PURL (Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List) programme,” he said. To his knowledge, he added, one missile package was waiting for the signature of US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. He also said several European countries were ready to transfer Patriot interceptor missiles from their own stockpiles but were awaiting US approval. In remarks posted in a video on Telegram, Zelenskyy said that on three occasions in the past week, Ukraine had not received the advance warning of Russian attacks generally provided by its partners. Last week, Zelenskyy suggested a disruption of Starlink services in Ukraine was “deliberate”. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio rejected the claim. The sparring comes as Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff is ⁠set to travel to Norway this week for the next round of negotiations on ending the war in Ukraine, the Reuters news agency reported, citing three people familiar with the matter. Two of the sources said they expected Zelenskyy to attend the meetings. The Oslo discussions are expected to include Zelenskyy, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, representatives of the E4 – made up of the United Kingdom, France, Germany, and Poland – the European Union, and NATO.

events.title: Palestine weekly: Israeli settlers attack journalist and diplomats
events.summary: Shackled, bleeding, raped: Abuse in Israeli prisons Does Trump have real leverage over Netanyahu? Settler olive harvest attacks top 2025 total, journalist and diplomats attacked as Israel halts Gaza commercial imports. With more than a month left of the olive harvest season to go, United Nations deputy spokesperson Farhan Haq said on Friday that the UN’s Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) had recorded more than 200 Israeli attacks on Palestinian farmers since September 1, eclipsing the 185 that OCHA documented across the entire 2025 harvest season. The attacks have already killed one Palestinian, injured more than 120 and damaged more than 2,500 trees. The Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission recorded 34 Israeli attacks on Friday that injured at least 19 people , with another 40 on Saturday. list 1 of 3 Benny Gantz drops out of Israel’s election race list 2 of 3 How HSBC’s Sharia fund invested millions in Israeli war-linked firms list 3 of 3 The night watch: Palestinians protecting their homes from settler pogroms Israeli settlers are carrying out such widescale attacks and thefts with backing from some religious figures. On Friday, Rabbi Dov Lior, spiritual guide of National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power party, ruled that settlers may take olives from Palestinian orchards, proclaiming “Jews are permitted to harvest olives even in areas far from Jewish settlements in order to publicly demonstrate our ownership of the land and thereby fulfill the commandment of conquering the land”. “An olive tree today is more significant in the campaign for Judea and Samaria [the occupied West Bank] than an M16 rifle,” said one post in a settler chat group this week. “Settlers are stealing the Palestinian olive crop on a vast scale, never seen before in my 22-year history of working on this issue,” said Sarit Michaeli, formerly the international advocacy director of the Israeli human rights group B’Tselem. Under this ideological push, dozens of attacks on olive harvesters have been reported each day. On October 16, in Abu Falah, northeast of Ramallah, about 80 masked settlers armed with clubs charged at Palestinians picking olives . During the attack, Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine, 63, fell and was beaten for more than 10 minutes by settlers, videos and her own account attest. She suffered broken ribs and needed hand surgery, while her camera, phone and passport were stolen. Israeli activist Jonathan Pollak reported that soldiers later shot a village council member, Abdel Jaber Obeid, in the thigh. Then, on Saturday, masked settlers with clubs attacked a delegation visiting Taybeh, east of Ramallah, that included Belgium’s consul general, French and Polish diplomats, and church representatives. A window of a Belgian consulate vehicle was smashed. French mayor Bernard Baudoux, 78, was kicked and beaten during the attack. In response to these incidents, United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington was “very disturbed”, while US Ambassador Mike Huckabee called Levine’s attack “a despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards”. France demanded arrests and the European Union said it expected “full accountability”. In response, Israel’s military called the Taybeh attack “severe”, and leader of the Yashar party, Gadi Eisenkot, described settler violence as “Jewish terror under the auspices of the government of Israel”, according to The Times of Israel. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office, however, offered a conditional condemnation of Levine’s attack, saying questions remained about “who initiated the violence”. After the attack in Taybeh, his office equivocated on the matter, too, remarking that “the more serious the accusation, the stronger the evidence required”. On Monday, police and the domestic intelligence agency Shin Bet launched “Operation Olive Leaf”, arresting 10 Israelis in raids near Ofra and Shiloh in connection to these attacks on foreign journalists and diplomats. However, no other arrests or investigations have been announced for the dozens of other settler attacks against Palestinians reported this weekend alone. Beyond the headline incidents, masked settlers – often alongside soldiers – targeted farmers, flocks, homes and land. Settlers beat two women in Beit Lid on Tuesday and injured an American citizen, Haytham Tayseer, in Burqa on Thursday, leaving him with deep head wounds. Six people, including four women and a child, were injured in Ma’in, in Masafer Yatta, on Saturday, the Red Crescent said. Settlers burned four vehicles in Turmus Aya, including a civil defence vehicle, and set fire to a mosque in Mikhmas , the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported. Settlers stabbed to death about 20 sheep in Kafr Malek, Mayor Najeh Rustum told Al Jazeera. Bulldozers uprooted hundreds of olive trees in Kafr Malek, and settlers cut down 120 olive trees in Kisan, near Bethlehem, Wafa reported.

events.summary: FIFA punishes Egypt’s head coach, forward and team manager for their comments after their World Cup loss to Argentina. Egypt’s head coach Hossam Hassan and forward Mostafa Zico have paid the price for criticising the referee after their World Cup knockout loss to Argentina, with FIFA suspending the duo for three and five matches, respectively. FIFA’s Disciplinary Committee handed down the sanctions, the Egyptian Football Association (EFA) said in a statement on Monday. list 1 of 4 Decision on Senegal’s AFCON final appeal to be made by end of November list 2 of 4 Ronaldo banned for 30 days, fined $285 over spat with coach Jesus list 3 of 4 Mohamed Salah sets Turkish Super Lig record for Trabzonspor list 4 of 4 Spain punished by FIFA for Islamophobic chants during Egypt friendly Hossam’s twin brother, Ibrahim, who is the national team’s manager, was also given a three-match suspension. The EFA said it had submitted a request to the committee, seeking “the detailed reasons and justifications for the decisions”. The national football body is planning to appeal after assessing the legal aspects of the punishment. The suspensions could rule Hossam and Ibrahim Hassan out of Egypt’s upcoming matches against Malawi in the next rounds of Africa Cup of Nations qualifying in November, as well as the first match of the March international window. Zico will be unavailable until June. Egypt were knocked out in the round of 16 by Argentina, who came from 2-0 down to win the tense encounter in Atlanta, United States, on July 6. The Pharaohs were left furious after a number of controversial calls went against them, including a disallowed goal early in the second half, and a member of their coaching staff was red-carded in the aftermath of the winning goal. Hassan claimed his side was “cheated” out of a place in the quarterfinals after Argentina’s stunning late comeback. “I do not want to put it nicely and talk about hard luck. We have been cheated unfairly today; we have suffered injustice,” Hassan said in an explosive post-match news conference. Egypt had a Zico goal ruled out when they were leading 1-0 as the video assistant referee (VAR) intervened to spot a foul on Lisandro Martinez much earlier in the move. Zico then put Egypt on the brink of a place in the last eight for the first time by doubling their lead. However, the defending champions hit back as Cristian Romero reduced the arrears before Lionel Messi, who had a first-half penalty saved, smashed in the equaliser with his eighth goal of the tournament. The controversy did not end there, though, as in the build-up to Argentina’s winner scored by Enzo Fernandez, Egypt believe they should have instead been awarded a penalty for a pull by Alexis Mac Allister on Hamdy Fathy. “We haven’t seen respect or fair play. There has not been respect or fair play,” Hassan said. “A penalty was ruled out; it was not even checked by VAR. A second goal was remarkably disallowed. There has not even been a VAR check when we have all seen the image of the [shirt] being pulled back.” Zico had a goal ruled out for a foul in the build-up, before Egypt’s players appealed for a penalty near the end when the score was 2-2. However, FIFA refereeing chief Pierluigi Collina defended the officiating in the match, saying such allegations could provoke threats against referees and their families.

events.title: Southeast Asia’s haze crisis will persist until polluters pay
events.summary: Cheap land clearing imposes enormous costs across borders. ASEAN must change the economic incentives that keep the fires burning. Senior international affairs analyst at the Indonesia Strategic and Economics Action Institution. Across Southeast Asia, the haze has returned with a familiar cruelty. Malaysia has closed schools as air quality deteriorated, Singapore has experienced dangerous levels of air pollution, and even parts of the Philippines have been affected, underscoring how far the smoke has travelled. In Indonesia, meanwhile, forest and peatland fires, a major source of the region’s haze, have threatened communities and livelihoods, particularly in parts of Kalimantan. What begins as land burning in one country can become a public health emergency across an entire region. The immediate response is predictable: extinguish fires, distribute masks and seek regional cooperation. All are necessary, but none explains why the emergency keeps returning. Malaysian children missing school, Singaporean residents breathing polluted air, Filipino communities exposed to drifting smoke and Indonesian families living near burning land all bear different costs from the same regional failure. Dry weather and El Nino can intensify fires, but many are deliberately started to clear land for agriculture. The deeper question is why practices that create enormous public losses can remain attractive to those who benefit from them. When the gains from cheap land preparation are concentrated while the costs of smoke are dispersed across communities and national borders, the market signal is distorted and political responsibility becomes easier to evade. The haze is therefore not merely an environmental emergency or a test of diplomatic goodwill. It disrupts ordinary life, strains public services and exposes how easily environmental costs can be shifted away from those who create them. It is a failure of economic accountability. Unless Southeast Asia changes who pays for the damage, how land-clearing decisions are monitored and what consequences follow proven violations, each dry season will bring another round of emergency measures followed by familiar arguments over blame. The economics of cheap land clearing Fire can be an inexpensive way to clear vegetation, especially where land governance is weak, alternative methods are costly and enforcement is uncertain. The private calculation is straightforward: spend less on land preparation and capture the returns. The fires cause respiratory illness, lost working days, school closures and transport disruption, while also damaging ecosystems and releasing greenhouse gases. Those costs are rarely borne in full by those responsible for the burning. The World Bank’s assessment of Indonesia’s 2015 fire crisis estimated losses of at least $16.1bn, equivalent to 1.9 percent of that year’s gross domestic product (GDP). Government figures put the area burned between June and October at 2.6 million hectares. The bank linked the fires to cheap land preparation, drought and weak enforcement. Its estimate covered agriculture, trade, tourism, transport, healthcare and emergency response, but excluded some long-term health damage and lost ecosystem services. That figure is not a price tag for the 2026 fires. It shows the scale of losses a recurrent crisis can impose. More recent estimates put the area burned in Indonesia this year at between 637,000 and 900,000 hectares, while Ministry of Health data recorded 283,270 cases of respiratory illness linked to the fires in seven provinces as of October 13. In West Kalimantan province, fires have also threatened communities and livelihoods, underscoring that Indonesians living beside the flames bear costs long before smoke reaches neighbouring countries. This is the central economic distortion: the cost of burning is not fully reflected in the decision to burn. When benefits accrue privately, but health costs, lost income and ecological damage are borne by society, fire can remain economically attractive even when its total cost is enormous. Small farmers need affordable, practical alternatives to burning; companies must face credible liability when evidence links them to fires; and peatlands need sustained restoration and water management, not emergency attention only when smoke becomes politically embarrassing. Smoke travels across borders, but responsibility and enforcement remain largely national. Tracing pollution to a particular fire, identifying those responsible and proving cross-border harm can be difficult. A satellite hotspot is a warning signal, but not by itself proof of who started a fire or whether a company is liable. The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) is not without rules. Its Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution was signed in 2002 and entered into force in 2003; Indonesia ratified it in 2014. The region also has a Haze-Free Roadmap and a strategy for sustainable peatland management for 2023-30.

events.title: ‘No real sense of appeal’: Vinted sellers complain of unfair account ‘bans’
events.summary: Some users claim online marketplace’s automated systems stack odds against them when sales go wrong A fter Catherine Warrilow sold a Zara necklace for £6 on Vinted, she packed it up and posted it off, just as she had done with many things before. Only this time the buyer claimed the parcel arrived empty. Warrilow, 47, from Oxford, provided Vinted with photos and videos of the package, including date-stamped Ring doorbell footage of her leaving the house to post it. But she says the resale platform refunded the buyer and left her out of pocket. “I challenged Vinted on what evidence they had and asked them to supply it, but they simply said ‘based on our evidence’ and ‘our evidence suggests’ and could not explain what that was,” she says. “The photos from the buyer showed that all of the parcel tape I’d used had been removed.” Vinted has become a giant of the secondhand economy. In 2025, users traded €10.8bn (£9.1bn) worth of goods through the platform – a 47% increase on the previous year. It generated €1.1bn in revenue and made a €62m profit. It now operates across 26 markets and has expanded beyond clothes into books, toys, sports goods and collectibles, as well as building its own shipping and payments businesses. It is a success story, but some sellers feel that the odds are stacked against them. Warrilow had used the app for five years, usually selling items her children had outgrown or things she had “fallen out of love with”. After having problems as a buyer, too, she had had enough. In both cases, “small amounts” of money were lost, Warrilow says. “But the principle of the lack of support led me to start a survey.” She did this on the website she set up called Sad Vinted Faces . Within two days, hundreds of people had responded. Since then, she says, more than 6,400 cases have been collected. One of the users who claimed, via Warrilow’s website, that she had had a bad experience, was Maggie, who did not want to give her last name. She says she sold a pair of Birkenstock Boston clogs for £72. When the buyer disputed their authenticity, she provided photographs of the shoes, and a bank statement showing she had bought them from Office. But Vinted decided the shoes were counterfeit, she says. The buyer was refunded and kept them, and Maggie permanently lost her account. “What upset me the most was not just the financial loss, but the feeling that my evidence was never properly considered,” Maggie says. “I had no meaningful opportunity to explain my case, or have it reviewed by a real person.” The consumer expert Martyn James says he has been “flooded” with messages from people who say they were accused of selling counterfeit goods and then had their Vinted accounts, and their money, frozen. “This problem has been bubbling away for a while,” he says. Part of the issue, he says, appears to be the use of automated systems in dealing with disputes. “AI is all well and good as a first line of investigation,” he says. “It is fine to use it to speed things up. But a service cannot exist without the service part, and that has to involve a human being.” He adds: “There seems to be no real sense of appeal. The company is acting as judge and jury, but there is money at play and it is not as straightforward as that.” According to Vinted, all appeals are handled by human reviewers, including Warrilow’s cases. Victoria Chamberlain-Ralphs has built a business selling clothes for clients who do not have time to do it themselves on Vinted. She says her problems started when she was made to convert her account to a “Pro” one, which took her offline for six weeks. “They said that our wardrobe was too big: we have 700 clients, which was, at that time, 18,000 items. They said that they had no capacity to get us back on. “We were emailing constantly, and they said they ‘would get around to it’.” She adds: “I told them I have staff to pay. I have clients asking why their items are not online, and I have a building to pay for.” In three years, Chamberlain-Ralphs says she has had her account shut down about 12 times. “I got banned last Thursday,” she says. “It was a permanent ban due to ‘fraudulent activity’.” She says Vinted gave her no explanation. She had 42 outstanding orders, all of which were cancelled when her account was banned. Five hours later, she says, it was reinstated. “They said it was ‘a false alarm’,” she says. “But that has cost me.” She says her account was also banned in November 2025 after she was accused of selling a fake item of clothing. “I rang one of my clients and got a receipt from Amazon for the trousers I was selling, and proved it was not fake – but they did not remove the ban.” According to Vinted, accounts will be suspended if Pro members repeatedly breach its “catalogue rules,” which prohibit counterfeit and dangerous items, or commercial activity that is not centred on secondhand goods.

events.title: Googlebook review: Google’s new laptops are woefully underbaked
events.summary: Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more . Great hardware let down by software flaws on these pricey machines that combine ChromeOS with Android G oogle’s attempt to create a new type of laptop to compete with Windows and macOS machines is finally here, combining the best of ChromeOS and Android into the new Googlebook. With advanced links to Android phones and the best of Google built in, can these Googlebooks really compete with a MacBook Air or Surface Laptop? I took two for a spin to find out. For years, Chromebooks have been the boss of budget laptops, but Googlebooks take a different, far more premium approach. Made by a range of traditional PC makers, including Acer, Asus, Dell, HP and Lenovo, they start at £999 (€1,099/ $899 / A$2,299 ) – a far cry from the £160 Chromebooks. While Google does not make these machines directly, it has set strict hardware quality standards that the laptops must reach. That includes backlit keyboards, haptic trackpads, fingerprint readers, crisp touchscreens, decent speakers and modern fast chips with at least 16GB of RAM. It is a list of specs you should expect with a premium Windows PC, but those start at a much higher price, primarily thanks to RAMageddon . As such, the Acer Googlebook 14 and the Asus Googlebook 14 I’ve been testing have excellent hardware with satisfying keyboards, great trackpads and quality screens. The Acer is a convertible that allows the screen to fold over the back of the device turning into a tablet of sorts. It is 1.14kg and 13.9mm thick, with a glossy 14in 3K OLED screen and a smooth aluminium-magnesium body, costing £999.99 . The Asus is a traditional laptop with a matt 14in 3K OLED screen and a magnesium-alloy body that weighs just 0.99kg and is 11mm thick, costing £1,199.99 . Top quality hardware aside, anyone familiar with a Chromebook would be forgiven for thinking it was ChromeOS running on these machines. It has the familiar taskbar at the bottom, Chrome-based web apps and access to Android apps. But the software is essentially Android underneath, which means getting it up and running is just like setting up an Android phone: scan the QR code with your phone, enter a passcode and transfer your apps and accounts. It is all done and dusted in about four minutes, which is faster than setting up a modern Windows 11 machine even if you know all the shortcuts. Access to the full gamut of Android apps is the Googlebook’s biggest strength and its greatest weakness. Practically any app you have on your phone can be installed and run on the laptop. But almost all those phone apps are just that, mobile versions, with most not even aware that they are not installed on a phone. Those that have at least some tailoring to the laptop form come in a few different types, categorised by Google broadly under “compatible with desktop”, which means they should support mouse and keyboard controls; “optimised for desktop”, which means they should scale properly to the laptop’s display; and “made for desktop”, which are a handful of Android apps redesigned with the laptop in mind. Only the last category really seems to make any difference to the quality of the app, and even then most of them are still not of the same calibre as their equivalents found on Windows or macOS. Even Google’s apps are a mixed bag. Google Calendar can only show one account at any one time, so you can’t see your personal, work and shared calendars on one screen like you can on Android. Google Docs starts as its own app, but when you actually open a document it just becomes another Chrome window hidden behind the Chrome logo on the task bar, not the Docs logo. The Files app shows your Google Drive files, but you can’t pin locations to the side bar to quickly access your commonly used folders, making it a time-consuming dig through endless folders to find things each time. Even the Chrome browser is not quite up to par with its Windows or macOS counterpart, lacking features such as split-screen tabs, the auto-hiding vertical tab bar or the ability to have multiple profiles, such as a personal and work account. Google has an app-gap problem and one that will only be solved if developers are convinced Googlebook OS is going to take off and be worth spending time and money making better apps for. Bring your Android phone into your Googlebook The other big selling point is deep integration with your Android phone. Google calls this “better together”, which is a collection of features that mirror capabilities of iPhones with Macs or Microsoft’s Link to Windows. Some of the features are like magic. You can search the files on your phone straight from the Files app on the laptop without plugging it in, see your notifications from your phone, continue tasks on your laptop from your phone and even use apps cast from your phone. As useful as these features sound, many are not up to scratch.

events.title: Hollywood AI-listers: is the technology ready to rival flesh-and-blood film stars?
events.summary: Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more . As a freaky Val Kilmer doppelganger stars in a new western and faux starlet Tilly Norwood is set for her feature debut, experts are split on whether mainstream adoption is a long way down the line – or just around the corner ‘D on’t fear the dead – and don’t fear me.” An exact facsimile of a young Val Kilmer , not quite dead and not quite alive, utters that baiting line in the trailer for the new western As Deep as the Grave. Director Coerte Voorhees knows exactly what he is doing – this is an AI-created version of the late actor, approved by his family but bringing with it a heap of controversy about whether such technology could make flesh-and-blood thespians redundant. Not just yet, judging by the extended glimpse of the film released earlier this year : it looks like a thirtysomething Kilmer, if a robot version had been sent back to the 1920s American wilderness by Skynet and, as well as being strangely rigid, had forgotten to download his voice, let alone his signature air of spacey shrewdness. Kilmer’s estate signed off on it, citing his enthusiasm for new technology that expands storytelling, but surely he would have been dismayed by this freaky doppelganger. Many reacted with revulsion to last year’s unveiling of AI “starlet” Tilly Norwood . After her appearance in an introductory “comedy” sketch, Emily Blunt described her as “really, really scary” – underscoring the depth of feeling around the idea of synthetic performers supplanting real ones. What you might call the Norwood injunction – the feeling of a tech-driven agenda imposing something no one asked for – deepened with the announcement the AI-lister will be soon appear in feature-length film Misaligned . Tim Webber, the chief creative officer at British VFX powerhouse Framestore, is sceptical about whether fully AI-generated actors can ever capture the complexity of our inner lives. “AI models are trained on the surface of things – the pixels of internet images, if they’re image models. To get to the level where it’s a human performance, where there’s genuine emotion involved, is a long way further down,” he says. So AI acting, scraping the external texture of past performances, would seem to be the inverse of something like method acting – whose acolytes excavate their internal psyche and emotions in the interests of authenticity. But AI acting is undeniably becoming more realistic. Higgsfield AI – one of many companies currently pushing the possibilities of AI video – recently claimed to have “eliminated” the uncanny valley: that nagging phoneysimilitude effect that has plagued even sophisticated recent CGI reincarnations, such as the de-aged Indiana Jones in The Dial of Destiny . Having released two full-length, entirely AI-generated features this year, Higgsfield’s content lead Adil Alimzhanov is bullish. This new frontier of completely AI-generated films is liberating for artists, he says, and shortcuts laborious Hollywood production structures. The two online-only releases – Hell Grind , a 95-minute action fantasy, and The Cully Hill Boys, a 115-minute Guy Ritchie-esque caper comedy – completed the equivalent of shooting and post-production in a fortnight and a month respectively (not counting time spent on the scripts). Despite actors’ qualms, the future can’t be resisted, says Alimzhanov, 23, who used his own face for Hell Grind’s protagonist. “We can’t fight new tools simply because they transform industries. If you draw a parallel with when cars first came out, if we’d fought that, everybody would still be riding horses today.” Hell Grind and The Cully Hill Boys are essentially extended ads for Higgsfield’s suite of AI content-creation tools. But they show swift progression on the AI acting front. In Hell Grind, released in May, the skate-rat characters only seem to be able to crank out a single emotion per 15-second shot (the limit of the Chinese video-AI model used, Seedance 2.0). The Cully Hill Boys, which came out three months later, is far more engaging, with enough convincing repartee and comic timing to qualify it as quite funny. Its lead trio of grime rappers on the lam are AI-generated likenesses of real-life streetball player Matt Kiatipis, MMA fighter Israel Adesanya and livestreamer N3on – testament to the gen Z, AI-native short-form creators Higgsfield aims to attract. Though there is something quaint about the idea of an “actor” in the age of AI. If bespoke characters can be generated for every film, why have an intermediary play a “role”? Written by a human being, Tim Planagan, The Cully Hill Boys was assembled in 30-second chunks, made possible by this summer’s release of Seedance 2.5. But prompting your way towards something dramatically convincing is labour-intensive.
