events.title: Who exactly will be affected by the UK review of benefits for young people?
events.summary: Around one in eight 16- to 24-year-olds are ‘Neet’ – and Alan Milburn is hinting that the overhaul of their support may be controversial With nearly 1 million young people not in education, employment or training (a cohort known as “Neets”), the government and its advisers have signalled that welfare benefits may be cut to fund more job support for them. What may change and who will be affected? Why are politicians talking about Neets? Ministers are expected to make a major policy announcement in November on plans to tackle what has been called a “generational challenge” and a “moral crisis” – the persistent number of young people in the UK who are out of work, not in college or training, or economically inactive . The head of the government-commissioned review of young people and work , Alan Milburn, has been vigorously preparing the ground in media interviews for what he has hinted will be a major – and potentially controversial – overhaul of employment and benefits support for young people. An estimated 960,000 16- to 24-year-olds are currently classified as Neet according to official estimates – around one in eight young people – with this number forecast to rise to 1.25m by the early 2030s. Although the concept of Neets has been around for more than three decades, Milburn has warned the current cohort are different: not simply jobless but estranged from the world of work. Some 45% of 24-year-old Neets have never had a job. He says urgent action is needed to prevent this group becoming a “lost generation”. It is partly the labour market: fewer entry-level roles and apprenticeships for young people, a decline in “Saturday jobs” that leave them less prepared for work, and in many areas, few decent job opportunities of any kind. It is also about the failure of state institutions – schools, the NHS, the welfare system – to prepare them for work. And, says Milburn, it is crucially about the increasing number of young people with “work-limiting health conditions” who he says have become economically marginalised because of their anxiety, depression or neurodevelopmental conditions such as autism. Milburn says that while the welfare system is not the cause of the Neet crisis, it exacerbates it by failing to provide enough meaningful advice and support to young people, especially those with health conditions. Plenty want to work, but job centre interactions with young people are often limited and “administrative” – paying their cash benefits – rather than providing a springboard for them to participate in work or training. The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) does have two major employment schemes, the Youth Guarantee and Pathways to Work, with budgets of around £6bn over three years, but Milburn is sceptical about their ability to reach Neets. Why does the government say it needs to cut benefits for young people? In theory, ministers could invest in new and improved employment support schemes aimed at Neets without cutting benefits. But they insist benefit savings are needed to fund their vision. They say disability benefit spending on 16- to 24-year-olds – currently £800m a year on universal credit health and £3.2bn on personal independence payment (Pip) – is spiralling out of control. In addition, Milburn is adamant that the design of disability benefits can “trap” young people with incomes of £2,000 a month, while incentivising them not to look for work. For every £1 the DWP spends on employment support for young people, £25 is spent on benefits, says Milburn – a ratio he says must be rebalanced. What benefits will be cut or reformed, how – and who will it affect? Ministers and Milburn alike are tight-lipped about any changes, but they are likely to focus on universal credit health and Pip, and the mood music is they will be radical . There is speculation either or both could be cut entirely or dramatically restricted. Some on the right have called for benefits to be removed for young people with so-called “mild” mental health or autism conditions, though because most young Pip claimants have multiple conditions this is unlikely to save significant amounts. A parallel review of Pip by welfare minister Stephen Timms has ruled out means-testing of Pip. Milburn said young people with complex and enduring disabilities will be exempt from any benefit cuts . What are the risks of cutting disability benefits for young people? Campaigners say better job support is essential – but cutting benefits for a cohort already on low incomes will simply drive up poverty and hardship , making it harder for them to get a job. They argue that in many areas there simply aren’t the jobs or opportunities, however comprehensive the job support. Around a third of the 1 million Neets are not claiming benefits, so in theory any changes won’t affect them. The political risk for ministers is that changes spark a repeat of last year’s backbench rebellion on disability benefit cuts, which forced a humiliating government U-turn.

events.title: Copper is outshining gold this year. Investors say the rally can survive an AI correction
events.summary: Copper has rallied nearly 16% this year, with strong demand driven by artificial intelligence, power grids and defense spending. Ivanhoe Electric CEO Taylor Melvin says relatively “inelastic” demand from technology and defense could help copper withstand an AI-driven tech pullback. U.S. tariff uncertainty, low Chinese inventories and tight supply are reinforcing investors’ bullish outlook for copper. Copper is becoming increasingly strategic to governments and industries as artificial intelligence, power-grid investment and defense spending increase demand for the industrial metal, investors say. The metal — a key component in electronics, construction and transportation, and often seen as a barometer of economic activity — has outperformed gold this year, as the need to secure reliable supplies has intensified. Copper has rallied 15.8% year-to-date, and is up more than 30% over the past 12 months. By comparison, gold futures have slipped 4.11% year-to-date, and are down 4.52% over the past 12 months. Spot gold is 4.89% lower over the past 12 months, and 4% down year-to-date. Speaking to CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe," Ivanhoe Electric CEO Taylor Melvin said countries, regions and industries are increasingly focused on securing access to metals for national security, economic growth and technology infrastructure. Melvin said that shift has helped support copper prices. "It's certainly a good time to be in copper mining globally, and specifically in the United States," said Melvin, whose Arizona-based mining and exploration company focuses on copper, gold, silver, nickel and cobalt. "We're really in a world right now where the metals that we used to refer to, and still do, as critical metals are really becoming strategic metals, in every sense of the word," said Melvin, who spoke as LME Week, the annual gathering of the global metals industry, began in London on Monday. That shift comes as investors question the sustainability of AI spending and the hyperscaler build-out, which has led to a recent wobble in tech stocks. But Melvin said he expects copper to withstand the recent volatility. "It's a new pocket of demand, and it really is almost an inelastic demand for copper," he said of the tech sector's need for the metal. "It's hard to think that one of these large-scale technology companies is going to make an investment decision on a hyperscale data center based on the cost of copper." He added: "That same inelasticity applies to another demand pocket that's emerging, which is national security, national defense budgets. So when you look at copper demand, the impact of technology, artificial intelligence infrastructure, I think we can all agree that that market is growing. "There certainly has been a bit of a retrench, a retreat, in those [tech] valuations. But two things can be true at the same time — you can have a capital market move in sentiment on equity values… but it can also be true that those industries are growing, and they're going to be a source of incremental demand for our metal." The rally has also been supported by uncertainty over whether the U.S. will impose a tariff on refined copper. In 2025, the Commerce Department recommended a 15% tariff beginning Jan. 1, 2027, but no final decision on the proposed levy has been publicly announced. "Because of the potential for US tariffs, a large share of the world's copper is now stored in the U.S., and it isn't clear those stocks will be available to the rest of the market," said Iain Pyle, senior investment director at Aberdeen Investments and co-manager of the abrdn Future Minerals Fund. "At the same time, Chinese inventories look exceptionally low and premiums there are rising." In an Oct. 15 note, Pyle called copper the "clearest example" of a market where supply cannot keep up with demand. "Higher incentives will be needed in the form of sustained higher copper prices. "There is still some risk of a pullback around tariff announcements, but we see the underlying fundamentals as clearly bullish, and the potential for a spike in prices has increased."

events.title: Inquiry urges halt to plan to burn Sydney's waste in regional towns
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Energy-from-waste inquiry recommends moratorium on proposed incinerators Topic: Recycling and Waste Management There has been strong opposition in Parkes to a proposed energy-from-waste facility. ( ABC News: Joanna Woodburn ) A NSW parliamentary inquiry into waste-to-energy facilities has handed down 22 recommendations. The committee advised that two incinerator proposals in Parkes and Goulburn should be halted pending an independent review. The NSW government has until early 2027 to respond to the recommendations. A New South Wales parliamentary inquiry into energy-from-waste facilities has recommended that the state government reject plans to burn Sydney's waste in regional communities. The select committee on proposed energy-from-waste technology made 22 recommendations after holding seven hearings across 2025 and 2026. The committee recommended that development applications to build incinerators in Tarago near Goulburn and Parkes be knocked back. The chair of the committee, Nationals MLC Nichole Overall, today told NSW parliament it was clear the technology was not appropriate to be built in the communities. "Given the absence of numerous critical elements, significantly the lack of social licence and community acceptance including from local councils and Aboriginal land councils," Ms Overall said. Nichole Overall chaired the select committee's inquiry into energy-from-waste facilities. ( ABC News: Lisa Glenday ) Environment Protection Authority regulations limit the construction of energy-from-waste facilities to four locations in NSW: Tomago, West Lithgow, Parkes, and the southern Goulburn-Mulwaree precinct. "The government, proponents and advocates state that these facilities are safe wherever they are located," Ms Overall said. Existing landfill capacity in Greater Sydney is expected to be reached by 2030, with advocates for incinerators highlighting the technology as a potential solution. The scoping report for the proposed $1 billion Parkes Energy Recovery facility in the New South Wales central west was published by the NSW Planning Department on Tuesday. A sign shows opposition to the proposed Parkes waste-to-energy facility. ( Supplied: Parkes Clean Future Alliance ) If approved, the site would have capacity to process 732,000 tonnes of waste per annum by thermally treating household and industrial rubbish. Almost all of the waste processed would be transferred by rail from Sydney to the site, before being converted into up to 80 megawatts of base load power daily. If approved, the Parkes Energy Recovery facility would have capacity to process 730,000 tonnes of waste per year. ( Supplied: Parkes Energy Recovery ) Ms Overall said the committee heard from residents in opposition to the development throughout the hearings. "Waste is best managed as close to its source as possible," she said. "Transporting hundreds of thousands of tonnes of metropolitan waste to regional facilities, hundreds of kilometres away adds to cost, emissions and impacts." Parkes resident Erik Lensson welcomed the committee's recommendation for the state government to reject the incinerator proposal. "It is entirely unsuitable," he said. Ed Nicholas says the project is safe and, if approved, will deliver benefits to the region. ( ABC News: Laurence Curson ) In a statement, Parkes Energy Recovery director Ed Nicholas said while the technology is new to Australia, it has been embraced in developing countries around the world. "It's a pity that the inquiry wasn't able to visit an operating facility as part of their investigation," Mr Nicholas said. "Had they done so, they would have seen for themselves how best-practice facilities, such as the one we are proposing for Parkes, work in both rural and urban areas to strict environmental standards. "We are committed to listening to feedback … and demonstrating the real benefits this project can bring at every stage." Veolia is proposing to build the Woodlawn Advanced Energy Recovery Centre near Tarago. ( Supplied: Veolia ) Veolia is proposing to process 380,000 tonnes of non-recyclable waste from Sydney each year at the company's existing Woodlawn site near Tarago. If approved, it would generate enough electricity for up to 40,000 homes. The proposal is before the NSW Planning Department and is awaiting a response to submissions from Veolia. Veolia have been contacted for comment. The committee received more than 1,400 submissions, the majority in opposition to the technology's development.

events.title: Bono says U2 has got no problem with charging wealthy fans more to see the band live
events.summary: Bono says U2 has long tried to keep its best concert seats within reach for fans. VALERY HACHE/AFP via Getty Images Bono says U2 has little say over what fans pay to see the band live. Still, the band has long tried to make prime seats more accessible. The band also has no issue with wealthier fans paying a premium, Bono says. For decades, U2 has sold out some of the world's biggest venues. Bono says the band has one longstanding way of making those shows more accessible. On The New York Times' "The Interview" podcast, Bono said U2 has "very little" say over ticket prices for its live shows. Still, he said, the band has long worked to make some front-row seats less expensive. "What we do in our band is we take the best seats in the house — we've done this all our life — and make sure that they're often the most affordable," Bono said. That doesn't mean U2 objects to charging some fans a premium. "We also have no problem separating rich people from their money," Bono said. "You know, as we say, rich people have feelings, too. If they want to pay very high prices, we've no problem." Bono said the aim is for fans to feel good about what they are paying for. He said U2 shows have "a level of depth" where people who don't normally agree politically can "feel safe." "If they're in America, we want people to feel really good about the choice to pay a ticket — and probably pay too much for it — to see us," Bono said. U2 performed 40 nights at the Sphere in Las Vegas from September 2023 through March 2024. The official announcement said tickets for the residency started at $140, and that the venue's larger capacity would allow "60% of tickets to be priced under $300," alongside a "limited number of premium-priced tickets" at each show. High ticket prices have become a defining feature of the modern concert experience. The average ticket price for the top 100 tours rose from $96.17 in 2019 to $132.62 in 2025, per data from Pollstar , a music industry trade publication. Dynamic pricing , which allows prices to rise with demand, has helped drive costs higher. On the secondary market , tickets can also be relisted at far higher prices than their original face value. There are also longstanding concerns about consolidation in the ticketing industry. In April, a federal jury found Live Nation liable for antitrust violations , determining that its market monopoly led Ticketmaster to overcharge customers by $1.72 per ticket from May 2020 to 2024. Sports fans are facing the same sticker shock. A Business Insider analysis of past ticket data found that a Category 1 ticket to this year's World Cup final cost $10,990 in April's open sale. At the previous seven World Cups, the equivalent ticket cost between $988 and $1,783 in today's dollars. Read the original article on Business Insider

( ABC News ) Whyalla's six football clubs are facing an uncertain future in the wake of job losses at the steelworks. Members from the clubs say it is unlikely the Upper Spencer Gulf city will have enough players and volunteers to keep all six clubs, with future mergers possible. More certainty is expected for the town after a decision on a buyer is made. Football in Whyalla is facing an uncertain future as the region grapples with the flow-on effects of mass redundancies at the steelworks, with local clubs concerned a drop in player numbers could lead to their demise. Last month, the state government revealed that the steelworks' blast furnace, which had been shut down for months, would not be restarted and, as a result, the plant's direct workforce to be reduced from 1,700 to 1,200 people . A further 300 contractors were also expected to be impacted, and it is unknown how many workers will chase employment opportunities elsewhere and consequently leave the Upper Spencer Gulf city. Last week, more than 250 workers who accepted redundancies finished up at the steelworks . Roopena Football Club is one of the six which make up the Whyalla Football League, and president Robert Brereton said each club was bracing for player shortages. "I think every club in Whyalla at the moment probably doesn't fully understand what season 2027 is going to look like for them," he said. The blast furnace at the Whyalla steelworks has been shut down, resulting in job losses. ( ABC News: Brant Cumming ) He said it was not just players clubs could lose, but volunteers. "Every one of those teams has a level of volunteer support and we've noticed over the journey that it's difficult to find the volunteers needed to keep all the sports on the park." The steel city's population peaked in the mid-1970s, when about 33,000 people were living in the region, but the latest figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics show it had fallen to about 21,400 in 2021. Greg Flanegan from the North Whyalla Football Club said it was likely the number of clubs in the league needed to reduce. "With the expansion of Whyalla getting so strong we went to six clubs, and Port Augusta and Pirie just stayed the same. I don't know that we'll ever get back to that." Greg Flanegan says Whyalla may need to drop down to four clubs. ( ABC News ) President of the Central Whyalla Football Club, Richard Wallace, said he felt "a little bit nervous" about the future of the league. "In the current form — six teams, and we're one team that's been struggling a little bit, if you lose too many people it's pretty hard to keep your club going so it doesn't look good but we're going to hang in there. Whyalla hangs in," he said. He said amalgamation was not on the table for his club "at the moment", but the concept was "not completely a bad thing", noting clubs like Woodville-West Torrens and the Brisbane Lions had won premierships in the years following mergers. "I'm hopeful for the future of footy, and Whyalla. I've got to be," he said. Richard Wallace says the next couple of years will be tough for Whyalla and its football clubs. ( ABC News ) Mr Brereton said the South Australian National Football League had "basically given clubs two options" if considering mergers. "One is one club consumes the other completely, or both clubs fold and form a new club. And the appetite for either of those two options is not high," he said. "All clubs have struggled a bit with that understanding that potentially in a merger one club disappears and 100 years of history goes with it, or they both lose their 100 years of history and a new club forms and they continue on like that.

events.title: Former Google chief Eric Schmidt’s 1% Anthropic stake set to pay huge windfall
events.summary: Eric Schmidt invested tens of millions of dollars in Anthropic’s Series A fundraising round. Eric Schmidt owns about 1% of Anthropic from an early Series A bet, which could add billions to his wealth if the AI firm goes public at a huge valuation. Anthropic is preparing an IPO, with marketing due around 9 November and a debut expected by end-2026. Investors see a possible US$1.8 trillion to US$2 trillion value. Big backers include Alphabet, Amazon, Nvidia and Microsoft. The company’s latest US$65 billion funding round pushed its value above OpenAI for the first time. WASHINGTON – Former Google chief executive officer Eric Schmidt owns around 1% of Anthropic thanks to his early investment in the start-up, according to sources familiar with the matter, setting him up for one of the largest individual windfalls from the company’s imminent public market debut . Schmidt invested tens of millions of dollars in Anthropic’s Series A fundraising round, according to the sources, who asked not to be identified because they were not authorised to discuss private matters. It is unclear if he has sold any part of his stake since the initial investment. Schmidt and Anthropic declined to comment. Anthropic’s highly anticipated initial public offering (IPO) is set to generate massive windfalls for its employees and investors. The start-up’s seven co-founders are already worth US$8 billion (S$10.2 billion) each based on its last funding round, fortunes that propelled them onto the Bloomberg Billionaires Index of the world’s 500 richest people. When Schmidt, 71, made his first bet on Anthropic in 2021, it was valued at US$461 million, according to data company Pitchbook. Investors indicated earlier in October that a fair valuation for the company is in the US$1.8 trillion to US$2 trillion ballpark; the high end of that range would value Anthropic at more than 4,300 times its Series A funding round. At that value, the Anthropic stake would boost Schmidt’s net worth by about one-third to nearly US$80 billion, according to Bloomberg’s wealth index. Even using Anthropic’s most recent valuation of US$965 billion, Schmidt adds nearly US$10 billion to his existing fortune of US$57.5 billion. Schmidt has become a prolific technology investor over the past decade and a half, across several investment platforms including TomorrowVentures, Innovation Endeavors and his Hillspire family office, which Pitchbook associates with hundreds of different venture capital bets. His early portfolio focused on consumer internet, software and financial technology, but more recently artificial intelligence has been a major focus, with investments in Mistral AI, Reflection AI and World Labs, as well as Anthropic. If Anthropic’s public stock debuts at a US$2 trillion value, his bet on the company would beat Innovation Endeavors’ own early bet on Uber Technologies in 2011. By the time that company went public in 2019, its value had increased about 1,400-fold to US$82 billion. Anthropic is set to begin formally marketing its IPO as soon as the week of Nov 9, putting it in line to begin trading before the US Thanksgiving holiday, sources familiar with the matter said earlier in October. It is expected to make its debut no later than the end of 2026. The start-up’s major backers include Alphabet, Amazon.com, Nvidia and Microsoft, which have all poured billions into the Claude chatbot maker. Venture firms Altimeter Capital, Dragoneer, Greenoaks and Sequoia Capital also each put more than US$2 billion into the company when they led a US$65 billion funding round in May that tipped Anthropic’s valuation higher than its rival OpenAI for the first time. The company – whose other backers include Menlo Ventures and Spark Capital – expects to match or beat the size of SpaceX’s record-setting US$1.77 trillion June IPO, sources familiar have said. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Software upgrades eat nearly a third of companies’ IT budgets, survey finds
events.summary: Vendor-driven upgrades can add costs and operational risks for IT companies in the AI race. A survey by Origina found large US and British firms spend 28% of software budgets on vendor-driven upgrades, migrations and licence changes they did not choose. The study said 95% paid for upgrades they expected to worsen results, while 80% feared leaving a major vendor would disrupt business. Companies also lost time and money: 84% of senior engineers worked on forced changes, and the latest change cost US$12.87 million a year on average. Large US and British companies spend 28% of their software budgets on average to pay for vendor-driven upgrades, migration and licensing changes they would not have actively chosen, adding avoidable costs and operational risks in the race to adopt AI solutions, a survey by software maintenance provider Origina showed on Oct 20 . These hard-to-avoid recurring costs and operational disruption were described as a “software tax” in the study that surveyed more than 2,000 companies. “When the alternative to an unwanted upgrade is losing support on systems the business runs on, saying yes is often a rational response,” Origina CEO Tomas O’Leary said. The report showed 95% of respondents said they had paid for a vendor-driven upgrade they expected to worsen outcomes, while 80% said leaving a major software vendor would significantly disrupt their business. Another 84% said senior engineering staff “always” or “often” devoted time to vendor-driven software changes rather than innovation or business-focused development. Some 91% said they had retired fully functional hardware in the past three years to comply with vendors’ support deadlines, sacrificing 1.65 years of remaining useful life on average O’Leary said the issue was largely universal and also applied to other regions, with older companies with more entrenched technology stacks facing the biggest challenges. According to the report, the most recent vendor-driven software change resulted in an average annual cost of US$12.87 million (S$16 million) for the surveyed organisations. REUTERS

events.title: Hegseth makes unannounced trip and other Mideast news
events.summary: U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is in the Middle East U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is in the Middle East. Meanwhile, Israeli police have arrested 10 suspects in a wave of settler violence that targeted a U.S. journalist and European diplomats in the occupied West Bank, and Iran-backed Houthi rebels announced attacks in Yemen and across Saudi Arabia. Here's the latest news from the Middle East on Monday. Read our full coverage here . U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has made an unannounced trip to the Middle East. Hegseth announced on social media late Monday U.S. time that he was in the Middle East visiting troops that were on an unspecified, “historic mission.” However, the post also came several hours after Axios reported that Hegseth was in Israel visiting Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. When asked about the visit and the reports, the Pentagon declined to comment. Saudi Arabia has executed a Bangladeshi man and woman after they were convicted of committing “indecent acts” in a mosque in the Muslim holy city of Mecca. Bangladesh said that it wasn't informed before the sentences were carried out and has sought information from Saudi Arabia. The Saudi Interior Ministry said the Bangladeshis were executed because of “the gravity and seriousness of their actions in violating the sanctity of both time and place.” It did not elaborate. Police said 10 suspects were arrested on Monday following violent attacks by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank that prompted heavy criticism of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government. Israeli police didn't identify who attacked the people who had come to support Palestinians during their annual olive harvest. Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine was beaten Friday by a crowd of young male settlers while documenting the scene, leaving her with several broken ribs and vertebrae. Masked settlers also attacked a group of European diplomats on Saturday. Palestinians have been subject to surging attacks, rarely leading to arrests or punishment, rights groups say. Netanyahu’s main rival in the Oct. 27 elections, Gadi Eisenkot, said “a handful of criminals is burning up the last shreds of legitimacy left to the state of Israel.” A money shortage has forced the World Food Program to deny food and cash assistance to 500,000 people in Gaza and 200,000 people in the West Bank, according to its acting director Carl Skau, who urged international donors to provide $450 million to fund hot meals and food parcels for the next six months. Skau said Monday in a video briefing that “life in Gaza remains absolutely brutal” and incredibly dangerous, with U.N. teams recording about 50 attacks per day in the past week, while in the West Bank, he saw burned olive fields, camps and villages. There have been more settler attacks over these first two weeks of the olive harvest than during all of last year, he said. Israel's military said Monday that it would resume coordinating the entry of commercial trucks into Gaza, but warned that future reports of merchants paying taxes to Hamas would lead to their licenses being revoked. The suspension since Wednesday cut off the flow of needed food and goods. COGAT, the Israeli military body that oversees humanitarian affairs in Gaza, cited disagreements between Hamas and the merchants over taxes, and claimed to be communicating a decision made by the merchants. Truckers in Gaza said Israel was using the disagreement as a pretext to fight Hamas’ taxation efforts. They said officials in Gaza called the money a “donation” to pay civil servants rather than a tax. COGAT said Monday that Hamas had withdrawn its demands. 2 dead, 11 injured after Kansas mother drives onto soccer field during game: Police Airman killed rappelling from Alamodome's ceiling in Salute to Armed Forces ceremony Bend, Oregon, shooting: Suspect ID'd, had attended elementary school, police say Iran-backed Houthi rebels killed at least 53 soldiers in ballistic missile strikes on a Yemeni military camp on Monday, making it one of the deadliest attacks on the Saudi-backed government’s forces since rebels shattered a 2022 ceasefire in Yemen’s civil war . The strikes on the al-Alam military camp also wounded 200 recruits, the Shabwa provincial government said. The Houthi rebels also claimed Monday to have carried out six military operations targeting oil infrastructure, airports and military sites across Saudi Arabia. Saudi authorities say recent Houthi missile and drone attacks have killed 19 people and injured more than 350 others. The Saudi Civil Defense issued more danger alerts across parts of the kingdom Monday. Three separate Israeli strikes hit Gaza City, killing at least two people, according to Shifa Hospital, and two 17-year-olds were killed in another strike on Khan Younis in southern Gaza, according to Nasser Hospital. The Israeli military said it struck Hamas militants in each of the attacks on Gaza City. It did not comment on the other attack.

events.title: The world’s finance chiefs see new risks — and less China angst
events.summary: Attendees debated whether global trade imbalances, the AI boom or a debt buildup in advanced economies poses the biggest risk for financial stability. Russian officials' in-person appearance drew rebukes from European leaders and a walkout by nearly half of IMFC delegates. Talk of China subsided in Bangkok as stabilizing ties with Washington led investors to treat it as "any other risk rather than something unique and special," IIF's Tim Adams said. The world's finance chiefs spent last week in Bangkok debating the biggest risk facing the global economy — with debt, artificial intelligence and trade imbalances topping the list. Meanwhile, China, long a main risk factor in these discussions, was no longer at the top of the worry list. The Bangkok meetings were the first in Asia since 2018, when the gathering was held in Bali, Indonesia . Thailand last hosted in 1991, six years before the unpegging of the baht from the U.S. dollar set off the Asian financial crisis. Fast-forward to 2026, and anything from global imbalances to the AI boom or a massive debt buildup in the "Global North" could trigger the next financial crisis, said Kevin Gallagher, director of Boston University's Global Development Policy Center, who spoke with reporters in Beijing after attending the IMF and World Bank meetings. The IMF was upbeat on economies positioned to benefit from the global AI supply chain, such as South Korea, Japan and China, and downbeat on those that aren't, warning that the AI build-out is widening gaps between economies. AI-related borrowing is also pushing up debt levels and competing with governments for capital, which lifts borrowing costs further. The IMF warned that should AI technology fail to deliver the promised productivity gains, it could trigger severe global economic consequences. Gallagher said he's watching whether the IMF, the Federal Reserve and People's Bank of China can coordinate, or end up going in different directions and "make things worse." The U.S. Treasury is at odds with the Fund over its own debt. IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said strong growth alone won't put the U.S. on a sustainable path , with federal debt above $40 trillion. David Zervos, a counselor to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, dismissed the warning. "It's good to remember how messy their forecasts have been in the past," he said. "So take it all with a grain of salt." There were also few signs of coordination. Chinese and U.S. finance officials were seated at a distance at Thursday's G20 finance ministers' and central bank governors' meeting in Bangkok, according to a layout seen by CNBC. Chinese central bank Governor Pan Gongsheng told the International Monetary and Financial Committee Saturday that China supports stronger Fund monitoring of spillovers from "major advanced economies' fiscal risks." He said countries should address their own fiscal deficits, while those running surpluses should boost consumption and investment. 2. Ukraine re-emerges as central flashpoint Russia and Ukraine returned as a central focus of the week's meetings as tensions flared. Russian officials were also back in the room at a G20 finance chiefs' meeting on the margins of the IMF gathering last Thursday. Finance Minister Anton Siluanov attended in person for the second time this year , after an August G20 session in Asheville, North Carolina, drew harsh criticism from European leaders that forced him out of participating in a group photo. German finance minister Lars Klingbeil reiterated his discontent over the Russian delegation's presence, saying in a statement to CNBC that "pretending that Russia's returning as a normal member of the G20 and sitting at the table again — that won't happen with me, and it won't happen with the other Europeans either." Nearly half of IMFC delegates walked out of the room when Siluanov was addressing the group in Russian on Saturday. Ukraine's central bank chief, Andriy Pyshnyi, told Reuters that he was surprised by the large number of finance officials who expressed solidarity with Ukraine, calling it a "deep and emotional moment." After a three-hour meeting Thursday evening, the Group of Seven announced 260 million euros ($300 million) in funding for Ukraine to repair infrastructure at the Chornobyl nuclear power plant, and expect to bring that to 500 million euros — which would pay for the whole project — at a donor conference in Paris next month. The IMF has warned that rising public debt is squeezing governments' room to spend on priorities such as defense. China featured prominently during the IMF meeting in 2018 as the U.S.-China trade war was just kicking off. But this year, panels and interviews had little to say about the country. Tim Adams, president and CEO of the Washington, D.C.-based Institute of International Finance, said China has rarely come up in his conversations during recent visits to Singapore and Bangkok.

events.title: Israel’s elections 2026 explained in maps and charts
events.summary: Shackled, bleeding, raped: Abuse in Israeli prisons Does Trump have real leverage over Netanyahu? Israelis vote on October 27 in the sixth election since 2019. Here’s how the system works and who gets left out. Israelis go to the polls on October 27 to elect the 26th Knesset, in the first general vote since the genocide against Palestinians in Gaza and the wars on Lebanon and Iran. Benjamin Netanyahu, the longest-serving prime minister in Israel’s history, with 19 years in office, is seeking another term while standing trial on corruption charges. His Likud party and the far-right coalition it leads are locked in a close race with a Jewish-led opposition bloc, with neither side appearing on track to win an outright majority in the 120-seat Knesset, Israel’s parliament. About 7.3 million people aged 18 and above are eligible to vote, according to Israel’s Central Elections Committee. Most polling stations open from 7am to 10pm, and anyone still queuing when they close is entitled to vote. Election day is a national holiday. Any party clearing an electoral threshold of 3.25 percent enters parliament, which sits for a four-year term. There are no term limits for a prime minister. Israelis vote for a party, not a candidate. A majority requires 61 of the 120 seats and no party has ever won that outright. Finishing first does not guarantee power. Parties then have 28 days, with a possible extension of up to 14 days, to assemble a coalition reaching 61. If nobody manages it, the country votes again. Seats are shared out in proportion to each party’s share of the national vote, so a party winning 30 percent of votes takes roughly 30 percent of seats. The votes for parties failing to secure 3.25 percent are discarded, which explains why small parties routinely merge before every election. About 7.3 million Israeli citizens are eligible to vote in this election, but they are not the only adults living under the government they choose. Roughly three million adult Palestinians in Gaza, the occupied West Bank and occupied East Jerusalem have no vote in the government that controls their borders, movement and legal status. Jewish Israelis and Palestinian citizens of Israel, who number about 1.2 million, can vote. So can adult settlers among the more than 750,000 Israelis living in the occupied West Bank and occupied East Jerusalem, who help elect the parliament that legislates over the land they live on. Most Palestinians in occupied East Jerusalem hold Israeli residency, not citizenship. They can vote for Jerusalem’s city council but not for the Knesset. The result is a sharp anomaly in the occupied West Bank, where a settler votes and a Palestinian family living nearby, under the same military authority, does not. Most Israeli citizens living abroad also cannot vote, because Israel has no general absentee ballot and requires voters to be physically in the country on election day. Diplomats and state emissaries are the exception, casting their ballots at Israeli missions on October 20. Israelis are dealing with a series of domestic and international issues this election cycle, including: October 7 security failures – Three years on, the government is yet to form a state commission of inquiry into the events of October 7, 2023, when a Hamas-headed attack led to the killing of some 1,200 people, with about 250 taken captive. Israel launched the genocidal war against Palestinians in the wake of the attack, killing at least 74,000 people and leaving most of the besieged territory in ruins. Ultra-Orthodox draft exemptions – Supporters of the exemptions say they protect full-time Torah study, but critics argue they place an unfair military burden on everyone else. Judicial reform – Netanyahu’s push to curb the Supreme Court’s powers, which sparked mass protests before the war on Gaza, remains a deep fault line. Critics see it as a threat to democracy, while supporters argue that the court has overstepped its authority. War and security – The public wants stability but remains wary of concessions in Gaza, the occupied West Bank and Lebanon. Netanyahu promised “total victory”, but Hamas and Hezbollah remain operational. Cost of living – High prices and modest wages are being further squeezed by soaring defence spending. Since 2023, Israel’s defence budget has doubled, increasing pressure on public finances. Netanyahu’s coalition held 60 of the Knesset’s 120 seats when parliament dissolved in July. It comprised Likud with 32 seats, Shas with 11, Religious Zionism with seven, Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Otzma Yehudit with six, and New Hope with four. Shas left the government in July 2025 but remained in the coalition and New Hope will merge into Likud for this election. The opposition held 59 seats: Yesh Atid with 24, Blue and White with eight, United Torah Judaism with seven, Yisrael Beiteinu with six, Hadash-Taal and Raam with five each and Labor with four. Noam’s single seat was unaffiliated.

events.title: Food aid charity under pressure from fuel costs
events.summary: FareShare South West has its distribution hub in Plymouth Soaring fuel prices are putting extra pressure on efforts to get food to thousands of people in need across Devon and Cornwall, the South West's largest food redistribution charity has warned. FareShare South West said demand for food support had risen by 45% since the Covid-19 pandemic, while the cost of collecting and delivering surplus food had increased sharply. The charity, which redistributes surplus food to about 70 organisations across the region, said it was facing the challenge of meeting growing demand while absorbing higher operating costs. Bosses added they were also concerned about the impact on volunteers and staff, many of whom were paying more to travel to their shifts. FareShare South West is an independent charity that obtains surplus food from food producers, farmers, supermarkets and other businesses before it goes to waste. It relies on a mix of government, corporate and independent funding. Recent increases in wholesale oil prices have contributed to higher fuel costs, making travelling and transporting goods more expensive for charities, businesses and households. Ryan Jackson said costs had "increased significantly" It operates from a distribution hub in Plymouth, where about 80 volunteers and four paid staff help sort, organise and load tonnes of surplus food each week. Much of the food, including fresh fruit, vegetables and dairy products, is distributed to charities and community groups. Hub manager Ryan Jackson said: "With petrol rising by 31% and diesel by 41% in the last six months, our costs have increased significantly and those are costs the charity has had to absorb. "At the same time, the number of charities requesting support from FareShare South West has grown across the region." Jamie Henshaw said there "may come a point" when some volunteer cannot afford to come and help The charity said the rising cost of fuel could also affect the people it relied on to keep the service running. Volunteer Jamie Henshaw said: "Everybody's feeling the pinch, but we love what we do. "Volunteers aren't paid, so this comes out of their own pockets. They're giving their time and goodwill. "There may come a point when some simply can't afford to come to work." A crate of apples is ready to be delivered from FareShare's Distribution hub Jackson said prolonged high fuel prices could create further challenges for the charity. "If fuel prices stay high for a long period, it could affect our ability to recruit and retain volunteers," he said. Despite the additional costs, FareShare South West said it remained committed to meeting growing demand. The charity said it planned to move to a larger hub in Plymouth later this year and create more food collection points across the region. events.title: Ukraine identified a slew of foreign parts in Russia's anti-jamming tech. Over 75% are American.
events.summary: The Geran-2 regularly uses the Kometa system to navigate Ukraine's skies and suppress electronic warfare. Sergei Grits/AP Photo A new Ukrainian list of foreign parts in Russia's anti-jamming antenna is filled with US electronics. GUR published a catalog of US digital processors, chips, and other components found in the Kometa. These arrays are used to help Shaheds and Iskander-M missiles navigate and suppress jamming. Over two dozen US processors, chips, and other components have been found in Russia's anti-jamming antenna systems, according to Ukraine's military intelligence. The Ukrainian agency, GUR, published a list of foreign parts on Monday that it said were discovered in 16-element Kometa modules, one of Russia's more advanced systems that help drones and ballistic missiles suppress electronic warfare and navigate the skies. US-headquartered firms produced 28 out of 37 foreign components — or just over three-quarters — listed on Monday, per GUR. Ten American brands and their components were identified in the catalog, posted on GUR's War and Sanctions page. These include digital processors from Intel subsidiary Altera, radio-frequency and precision components from Analog Devices, a memory chip from Micron, and supporting electronics from Texas Instruments. Another three components are built by Chinese companies, while the other six come from Japanese, Taiwanese, and Swiss manufacturers, GUR also indicated. In a statement to Business Insider, a Texas Instruments spokesperson said the company "strongly opposes the use of our chips in Russian military equipment." "Any shipments of TI chips into Russia are illicit and unauthorized. We devote significant time and resources to developing, implementing, and refining policies and procedures to combat illicit diversion and keep chips out of the hands of bad actors," they added. Intel, Analog Devices, and Micron did not immediately respond to requests for comment sent outside regular business hours by Business Insider. The new list from GUR, which regularly publishes information on foreign parts in Russian equipment , comes as the electronic warfare race grows more vital to Ukraine's air defense. Kyiv's forces try to stop Russian drone and missile attacks with a mix of jamming tools and interceptors, but the latter are facing difficulty as Moscow has begun mass-launching faster, jet-powered drones — the slowest of which can fly at about 185 mph. Kometa antenna panels are among the most common anti-jamming tools on Russian long-range weapons, such as Shahed drones, Iskander-M ballistic missiles, and glide bombs. Each antenna receives satellite signals and helps to counter jamming or spoofing. The 16-element Kometa, which essentially has an array of 16 antennas, is one of Russia's newer versions of the system in mass production. Two years ago, Moscow was regularly using eight-element Kometas on its Shaheds instead. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: How is the US economy really doing under President Trump?
events.summary: President Donald Trump has been boasting about the performance of the US economy ahead of the midterm congressional elections, claiming he has boosted incomes, reduced inflation and created jobs. Trump has repeatedly said: "We have the hottest country anywhere in the world." While the overall US economy is faring better than many expected after Trump launched his sweeping "Liberation Day" tariffs in 2025, there's evidence those import taxes and the impact of the US-Israel war with Iran have pushed up inflation, with the harmful effects felt by most American households. The US economy is also being helped by an AI investment boom, and could falter if that spending were to dry up. So how does all this feel for the average American? BBC Verify has looked at whether the evidence supports the president's claims. The overall US economy is growing at a respectable clip by the country's recent historic standards. The latest data shows US GDP , external - which is how economists measure the size of the US economy - currently expanding at an annualised rate of 2.2%. And it has increased by around 3.2% overall since the end of 2024, just before Trump took office for his second term. That is more growth than any other member of the G7 group of leading economies over that period. The US growth rate has been faster than was forecast by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) , external in the immediate wake of Trump's announcement of a swathe of new tariffs on goods coming into the US on 2 April 2025. It downgraded its forecasts at the time, citing the negative impact of Trump's import duties on investment and consumer spending. Though it is important to note that Trump eased the tariffs considerably in the months that followed, reducing the impact that had initially been expected on the economy. The US economy has also been heavily supported in recent years by American technology companies making massive investments in AI, including by constructing data centres around the country. Spending on building data centres , external (excluding the IT hardware to go in them) by US businesses in August 2026 was $5bn, almost double the monthly rate when Trump returned to office. Many American voters wanted to punish Joe Biden in the 2024 presidential election, holding him responsible for the pain caused by a significant spike in prices in the wake of the pandemic. The current rate of US inflation , external is 3.7%. That's still well down on the recent peak rate of 9% under Biden in 2022, but higher than the 3% rate that Donald Trump inherited in January 2025. Economists estimate , external US inflation would have been lower without the new tariffs imposed by Trump since he returned to office. While the impact of the Iran war on global energy prices, with the significant disruption to oil and fuel supplies from the Middle East, has also helped push up US domestic inflation. The price of a gallon of diesel in the US , external - a fuel used not only by drivers but also widely in agriculture and industry - hit a record high of $6.52 in September. The price of some grocery staples , external like beef and coffee have risen since Trump returned to office, though the price of eggs has fallen. And some US retailers have warned , external that rising energy prices caused by the Iran war will make producing food more expensive and raise prices at the till. 3. Household income growth held back Average US household incomes are still rising under Trump. The median income - after adjusting for inflation - rose 2.6% in 2025 to $87,460, the highest on record , external . However, the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy (ITEP) think tank has estimated the combined effects of the following , external on US households: - The expiry of extra government subsidies that had made health insurance cheaper for millions of Americans - Higher-than-expected price rises during Trump's second term, including those linked to tariffs and the Iran war ITEP's conclusion is that the middle fifth of households are, on average, around $1,700 worse off in 2026 than they would have been, while the poorest fifth are around $750 worse off. The richest 1%, by contrast, are estimated to be an average of $12,560 better off than they woud have been, primarily because of Trump's tax cuts. ITEP's estimates about the impact of tariffs on American households of different income levels are broadly similar to those of the Tax Foundation think tank , external . Trump predicted his tariffs would result in America being "flooded with jobs" , external as manufacturing firms set up new factories on US soil to avoid their products being taxed at the border. Since he returned to the White House, an average of 34,000 jobs have been added to the economy each month. ​​But that is significantly down on the 122,000 jobs added each month in the final year of Biden's presidency , external .

events.title: Don’t be fooled. The AI that was supposed to save us time is doing just the opposite | Gaby Hinsliff
events.summary: Don’t be fooled. The AI that was supposed to save us time is doing just the opposite The government says it can transform the state with AI, but it is no match for the resulting stream of machine-generated slop. And we all pay the cost A nother morning, another avalanche of emails. Even after a guilty cull, my inbox is sitting at well over 7,000, but lately I’ve started subscribing to the Quentin Crisp theory of housework: why bother, when after four years or so you stop noticing the accumulating dust? Empty inboxes just fill up again anyway. In theory, email was supposed to save hours of meetings, phone calls and standing over photocopiers. Instead, we just spend hours deleting stuff people wouldn’t have bothered telling us if it had meant picking up the phone, but which they can now spam to their entire database at the click of a button. The glorious ease and convenience of being able to reach the world in seconds came, we now know, with the inconvenience of them being able to reach you right back. And therein lies the challenge to the government’s hopes of AI helping to transform the machinery of the state on the cheap, saving not only time but billions of pounds in public money. It’s early days, but AI seems not so much to be streamlining public service delivery as gumming it up – partly because, as was once the case with email, the public is using it right back at them. In a Substack post last week, the former civil servant Sam Freedman noted that governments around the world seem to be experiencing unusual surges in complaints, requests and responses to regulatory and official bodies since the adoption of ChatGPT. It’s the same story in the courts , with employment tribunal cases in England, Scotland and Wales reportedly rising by 39% in a year thanks in part to claimants using AI to draft claims, while magistrates and judges face a wave of people who can’t afford lawyers using ChatGPT to build cases that often don’t make sense. And all of this needs patient disentangling by a human, on the grounds that just because a defendant is citing precedents that don’t exist, it doesn’t mean there isn’t a genuine grievance buried in there somewhere. Whitehall special advisers complain of departments drowning in AI-generated freedom of information requests, an abuse of a system originally intended to empower individuals. MPs’ offices are similarly swamped by AI-generated letters, all of which need to be read by humans for fear of missing something important from a constituent. How long before public consultations on changing the law become so spammed by slop that they are in essence useless as a measure of what the country actually thinks? There’s a fine line between the noble aim of making it easier for individuals to interact with an otherwise remote state, and making it so easy that the result is an uncontrollable firehose of meaningless machine-generated guff. The obvious answer to this kind of AI flooding is getting AI tools to detect or sift it, but that doesn’t always work when dealing with potentially vulnerable human beings. Constituents who use AI to express themselves in more fancy-sounding language when writing to their MP, for example, still have the right to expect a personal response from a human being. Employers who thought they were being smart by getting AI to sift job applications, meanwhile, are reaping what they sowed, as resentful applicants automate their end of things too and spray-gun applications across the board, rather than concentrating on the jobs they really want. Now neither side can separate the wheat from an avalanche of chaff. The risk of paralysis is likely only to increase if the public starts adopting agentic AI in the kind of numbers big tech fondly imagines. Early adopters might well find agents save them time and hassle. But shortcuts stop being shortcuts once everyone else is using them too, and risk turning into bottlenecks instead. Think of cars, which have vastly shortened journey times compared with travelling by horseback, except in cities at rush hour when too many other people are also trying to shorten theirs. By 2018, central London daytime traffic was moving on average at just over 7mph – about the same speed as a trotting pony. Historically, humans have always learned to develop ways around problems of our own making. We have spam filters for email, congestion charges to keep cars out of cities, and in the long term we could well figure out what kind of frictions we need to put back in the system to make it possible to live with the impact of AI. Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more But for now a useful rule of thumb, if improbable claims start to be made for savings due to AI, will be that more isn’t always better; faster and easier isn’t always more convenient; and time saved in one section of public services has a horrible habit of popping up in another one. Let the Whac-A-Mole begin.

events.title: New Bradford railway station will ‘transform travel across the north’
events.summary: Transport hub will offer through trains between Leeds and Manchester with ‘turn-up-and-go’ service A new railway station will be built in Bradford to “transform how people travel across the north”, the government has announced. The station will be at the heart of the Northern Powerhouse Rail (NPR) scheme , built on the current Bradford Interchange site but allowing through trains between Leeds and Manchester. With the promise of more frequent and faster services, it is expected to support new homes and jobs for the West Yorkshire city, located alongside its Southern Gateway regeneration project and connecting to the proposed tram to Leeds . Approval of the station, which is expected to be built by the mid-2030s, has been regarded by northern leaders as a critical sign of political commitment to improving rail links across the north, after long delays in delivering pledged upgrades. The Department for Transport said that NPR would allow a “turn-up-and-go railway” for passengers from Bradford, with sufficiently frequent trains running across the north for people not to need to check timetables. The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander , said: “Today marks an important milestone for Bradford with a brand-new station that will transform how people travel across the north.” The new station, along with the proposed West Yorkshire mass transit network – better known as the Leeds tram – will bring more than £1bn in economic benefits, according to Bradford council. The mayor of West Yorkshire , Tracy Brabin, said: “Bradford has so much untapped potential, and faster, more frequent trains to Leeds and Manchester, and the transformation of the city centre will help to finally unleash it.” Henri Murison, the chief executive of the Northern Powerhouse Partnership, said the decision to build a new station at Bradford Interchange represented “a long-term commitment to the city and the wider north”. He added: “Confidence is already building here, and this will help build it further.” NPR was first promised by the Conservatives in 2014 but no firm funded plans emerged for the proposed railway linking cities from Liverpool to Hull. The government under Keir Starmer announced in January that NPR would be delivered in three stages, with a funding cap of £45bn, which could be topped up by local contributions. The scheme will start by improving connections on existing lines around Yorkshire. It also includes plans for a new line between Liverpool and Manchester. As mayor of Greater Manchester at the time, Andy Burnham had championed a new underground station for Manchester Piccadilly as part of the project, which the Treasury did not approve. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning The rail industry is also anticipating more work on improving Manchester-Birmingham links to replace the scrapped HS2 northern leg, another transport issue long pushed by Burnham . Northern transport links could be improved further after the mayor of South Yorkshire and other leaders announced plans to bring Doncaster Sheffield airport into public ownership. The combined authority and Doncaster city council are set to buy the airport from Peel Land, hoping to restart freight next year and passenger flights by spring 2028. The airport’s owners shut down operations in November 2022 , regarding it as commercially unviable. However, South Yorkshire’s mayor, Oliver Coppard, said that, subject to formal approval, a deal was now going through that “puts the future of DSA back in our hands and finally gives one of the biggest and best growth opportunities in South Yorkshire the platform for long-term success that it needs and deserves”. He said the government’s devolution agenda had allowed them to now act to resume flights to the city, adding: “When the airport closed, almost everything was against us; the owners did not want to sell, we had no legal powers to intervene or stop the airport from closing, and no backing from the government at the time. Today, the sky’s the limit.”

events.title: Spain-Based Startups Advance Regional Innovation With Barcelona Supercomputing Center
events.summary: The Barcelona Supercomputing Center (BSC) ’s AI Factory Accelerator Programme, now in full operation following a pilot initiative, gives startups access to sovereign compute, technical support and training to support innovation across industries. Many of these companies are also members of the NVIDIA Inception program for cutting-edge startups — and as of today, access to some of the BSC AI Factory services are available through the NVIDIA Inception portal . NVIDIA Inception complements the BSC AI Factory Accelerator Programme by providing members with training through NVIDIA Deep Learning Institute open courses, business mentoring, venture capital connections and other resources. An upcoming extension of MareNostrum 5 — BSC’s public infrastructure serving scientific and technological innovation, powered by NVIDIA accelerated computing — will deliver supercomputing access through the BSC AI Factory and other AI Factories across Europe. BSC AI Factory is among Europe’s first AI factories and the first in Spain, and has delivered more than 800 services to private and public-sector clients since its April 2025 launch. Three Inception members were recently named the BSC AI Factory Accelerator Programme’s AI Champions at the pilot initiative’s demo day: Qatium ’s water-network platform — already used by more than 250 utilities in 16 countries — is now in early production with its Neural Water Intelligence technology, powered by proprietary AI models trained on MareNostrum 5. Built on NVIDIA accelerated computing, the NVIDIA cuGraph library, the NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo framework and NVIDIA Nemotron open models, the technology helps water utilities make better operational decisions every day. OneCareAI , a research spin-off from BSC, used NVIDIA NIM microservices to develop technology designed to identify signs of hidden atrial fibrillation — an irregular heart rhythm — in seemingly normal ECGs, helping clinicians identify patients who may be at risk of stroke before one occurs. Avatia built a voice-first, multi-agent system that provides pharmaceutical companies with agentic coworkers that support sales representatives and give doctors transparent, curated information about medicines, ultimately helping the right treatment reach the right patient sooner. The system taps into NVIDIA NIM microservices, the NVIDIA Nemotron 3 open model family and the open source NVIDIA NeMo Curator library. Other BSC AI Factory startups — Agrikola AI , Elna Health , Lokutor , Montevive AI , Oppy , Pack2Earth and Up2Smart — span precision agriculture, medical imaging and knowledge access, speech services, enterprise security, sales intelligence and sustainable packaging. The cohort reflects the breadth of what advanced intelligence can now unlock: preventing strokes, detecting breast cancer subtypes before biopsy, putting medical knowledge at doctors’ fingertips faster, replacing petroleum-based plastic with biobased compostable materials, protecting crops with robots instead of chemicals and more. events.title: Japan’s 20-year bond auction sees strongest demand on record
events.summary: Japan’s super-long yields have recently approached multi-decade highs, as a global bond selloff driven by escalating tensions in the Middle East and higher oil prices added to inflation and fiscal concerns. Japan’s 20-year bond auction drew record demand, with a bid-to-cover ratio of 5.84. Higher yields and easing fiscal worries brought back domestic buyers. The auction helped push the 20-year yield down by as much as 6 basis points to 3.710%. BNP Paribas said the result showed stronger demand from life insurers and other investors. Markets still worry about Japan’s finances and future bond supply under Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi. Traders now await the Bank of Japan meeting next week for rate clues. TOKYO – Japan’s 20-year government bond auction on Oct 20 saw the strongest demand on record, as elevated yields attracted renewed buying from domestic investors. The bid-to-cover ratio was 5.84, compared with 4.01 at the previous sale, and a 12-month average of 3.73. In another sign of robust investor interest, the tail, or gap between average and lowest-accepted prices, was 0.07, compared with 0.15 in September . The yield for the tenor fell as much as 6 basis points to 3.710% after the results. Ryutaro Kimura, senior bond strategist at BNP Paribas Asset Management, said the “positive outcome” was “a reflection of recovering demand from domestic investors, driven by high interest-rate levels and easing fiscal concerns”. Life insurers have strengthened their net buying of super-long bonds again since June, underscoring the recovery in demand, he said. Earlier in October , the 20-year JGB yield climbed to levels last seen in the mid-1990s, while the 30-year yield hit a record high. The rise in yields reflects persistent concerns over Japan’s fiscal outlook , as investors are focused on how Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi will fund her planned sales-tax cut on food and soft drinks without further straining the nation’s finances. Takaichi has sought to ease market concerns, saying her administration aims to build a strong economy and achieve fiscal sustainability, while pledging to appropriately manage JGB issuance in next fiscal year’s budget. Against that backdrop, investors have been watching to see if elevated yields will draw demand from domestic institutional buyers. Fukoku Mutual Life Insurance, the first life insurer to outline its plans for the fiscal second half, said it sees scope to move a bit more from foreign bonds into yen bonds as yields have risen more than expected. Mark Cranfield, Bloomberg’s markets live strategist, said: “That’s stunning demand for a 20-year JGB auction; indeed, it is the best on record for the duration and sets up a faster pace of yield curve flattening. “It is exceedingly rare to see any JGB auction with a bid-to-cover above 5.0, and it’s even more remarkable in 20-year, which has seen a decidedly mixed record over the past two years.” He added: “There is a very large unknown component in the buying, which suggests that foreigners have stepped up to participate. Showing confidence that the BOJ will deliver on a steady path of interest rate hikes.” A major test for Japanese bonds will come at the Bank of Japan’s policy meeting next week. While markets widely expect the central bank to keep rates unchanged, with overnight index swaps pricing in about a 6.2% chance of a hike, traders will look to Governor Kazuo Ueda’s post-decision press conference for signals on the pace and scope for further tightening. events.title: Cisco's president said he used personal AI agents to screen $9,000 worth of his yearly subscriptions
events.summary: Cisco's president and product chief, Jeetu Patel, shared how he's used personal AI agents. Bloomberg/Getty Images Cisco's president, Jeetu Patel, said he uses four or five of the most popular personal AI agents. One of them, which costs him $20 a month, recently saved him more than $1,000 in subscription bills. But he said it's important not to give personal AI agents access to work tools or resources. If getting mysterious and surprising subscription bills are the bane of your existence, Cisco's president and product chief, Jeetu Patel , is in the same boat. Patel told Business Insider that said he's been using four to five different personal AI agents , like Meta's Muse, Instinct, and OpenAI's Dots, for things like consolidating news, summarizing earnings calls, and even booking his daughter's concert tickets. But recently, he was impressed by how one agent could slash his subscription bills. He said that the first time he gave a personal AI agent access to his email, the agent told him, "Hey, you've got $9,000 worth of subscriptions that you subscribe to per year. Are you sure you want all of these? It seems like a lot of subscriptions." He told the agent to make him a table of all his subscriptions, how much he spends on each, and how long he's had each. After the agent presented him with the table, he picked out two subscriptions that he didn't need and made the agent cancel them, which it did without difficulty, and sent him cancellation emails. "I'm like, OK, that was kind of creepy how easy it was to do that," Patel said. "And then it saved me 1,000, 1,200 bucks a year just over there. So basically, for the most part, I paid for that agent, at a $20-a-month plan, several times over." The agent also managed to cancel part of his Dropbox subscription — an $11.95 plan he had accidentally subscribed to, even though he had already purchased a 2-terabyte plan. Patel is a big fan of AI agents, both at work and outside it. He said he rarely starts any task now without asking an AI agent to do a "recon job" and give him research and context. But the important thing to remember, he said, was not to give personal AI agents, which are not vetted by employers, access to work tools and resources. He hasn't linked his email or calendar to his personal agents, instead using his internal work agent for those tasks. "These are common-sense things that I think most companies implement, which is, 'Don't give your crown jewels of your source code repository to Muse; it might not be a good idea,'" Patel said. Rogue or not, AI agents have been causing a buzz Personal AI agents have been all the rage in recent months, serving as personal assistants and handling mundane, repetitive tasks like paying bills and buying groceries for their users. While they've been touted as productivity boosters, there have been several instances of users reporting that the agents have performed actions outside their permissions, such as posting bank balances to company Slack channels or misinterpreting instructions, such as ordering 20 pounds of chicken for a dinner for two. Obedient or not, personal AI agents have been causing a buzz, especially for investors. Ross Mayfield, an investment strategist at Baird, told Business Insider's William Edwards ahead of Meta's earnings that Muse is the first big app of the AI era and that it assuages some investors' fears about Big Tech's ballooning AI spending. And Instinct, founded by a 23-year-old , raised $1 billion in its Series C, bringing its valuation to $10 billion. But these new products are coming in a year when there have been several instances of AI agents going rogue and performing unauthorized actions, such as breaking out of sandboxes during security tests and exploiting software vulnerabilities in external companies' websites. This has led companies such as  Bank of America  to invest resources and hire additional personnel to address issues with their legacy software and prevent such hacks. Former and current staffers at frontier AI labs like Anthropic and OpenAI have publicly raised concerns that AI development is progressing too rapidly, without adequate checks and balances. September was characterized by an air of doom and gloom over an "AI apocalypse," in which AI researchers estimated that the technology would kill all of humanity in the next decade.
