events.title: I sold my apartment, cashed out my pension, and took on debt to build a semiconductor startup. I'd do it again.
events.summary: Hans Hasselby-Andersen spent nearly a year raising his first funding after leaving Texas Instruments during the financial crisis. Hans Hasselby-Andersen/Lotus Microsystems Hans Hasselby-Andersen quit Texas Instruments during the 2008 financial crisis with four young kids at home. He sold his apartment, cashed out his pension, and took on debt to build a semiconductor startup. Nine years later, his company, Merus Audio, was acquired by Infineon. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Hans Hasselby-Andersen, 56, CEO of Danish semiconductor startup Lotus Microsystems and cofounder of Merus Audio, which was acquired by Infineon in 2018. The following has been edited for length and clarity. When I quit my job at Texas Instruments in September 2008 to start a semiconductor company, I had four children between the ages of 5 and 14. It was almost the height of the financial crisis. You had Lehman Brothers going down in flames in the US, and the whole credit market was just freezing up. So to jump out at that point and go into fundraising was a big, big step. My manager was looking at me like I was crazy, basically. Thinking back, probably I should have waited a year or so and just cooled off a little bit. But the thing is, once you have an idea and you're really motivated, you can't really wait. You have to go do something about it. I'm an electrical engineer by training. Earlier in my career, I joined a small startup that was acquired by Texas Instruments about five or six months after I arrived. The whole concept of a company being acquired, an exit and all that, was all new to me. It planted a seed in my head that, if the circumstances were right, this was also a path I could take, and not just build my career in a large company. I stayed at Texas Instruments and worked in the audio semiconductor business. I was picking up things from my interactions in the market where I thought there was actually a need for a much more energy-efficient way to drive speakers in products like portable speakers and soundbars. I saw a market need, but I didn't have the technical solution, so my first task was to go out and find a cofounder who could come up with a technical solution for that market. I think that's actually quite unusual for tech startups. Normally, somebody comes up with some technology, and then they go out and try to see where it can be applied. This was the opposite approach. Four kids, one big decision Just before I resigned, I called my bank and asked if I could get a basic bank overdraft facility just to give me some extra headroom to live on. Honestly, I think if I had waited two weeks, I wouldn't have gotten it. It was just when the financial crisis started to really kick in, and I seriously doubt I would've gotten that line of credit. Getting the first funding took the better part of a year. I probably spoke to between 50 and 100 different investors. It's really a dating game. You try to look appealing and interesting from a company point of view, but you mostly get rejections because the investor doesn't invest in your domain, you're too early, you're too late, or you don't fit their profile. I paid out of my own pocket to travel to Japan, South Korea, and Singapore to meet potential customers. I wanted to pressure-test my idea, understand what they were struggling with, what their requirements were, and help mature my business case. Eventually, I raised the equivalent of about $150,000 to $200,000. It was a very small amount, and we spent it in about six months. The minute we got the funding, we knew we had to continue fundraising immediately. My wife, who was a school teacher at the time, has been very, very supportive. She never told me, "This is a stupid idea, go back and find a job." With four kids, you can't just make that decision on your own. When we finally got the company off the ground, my wife and I made some adjustments to minimize the risk for my family. We sold our apartment while we could still make a little money from it and rented instead, so we wouldn't risk having to sell at a loss if the company failed. We also sold our car and leased one instead. I slaughtered my pension and took out the money. I thought, "I need it now. I'm not about to be retired anyway." Throughout the life of a startup company, you're more or less in fundraising mode all the time. You always have to keep your eye on how long you have cash and where you're going to get your next funding. The worst thing that can happen is that you run out of cash. If there's one recommendation I would give first-time founders, it's to prepare for things to take longer than they expect because they always do. If you think you can do something in two years or three years, multiply that by two, at least. If you plan financially for your cash to fund your plan as you lay it out, then you're going to be in a difficult situation because you're going to run out of cash before you've achieved the milestones you set out to achieve. Engineers have to sell, too Starting a company around 40 made me a different kind of founder. There were definitely things I had learned that I wouldn't have been without. I had learned how to communicate with customers, how to find out what the market needed, and how to explain what I was doing and why it was a good idea. Many engineers are obviously good at what they do technically, but they can have a big challenge explaining that to others. When you're standing in front of investors, you have three minutes to explain what you're doing. You have to train to do that elevator pitch. Nine years later, the company I cofounded, Merus Audio, was acquired by Infineon. I stayed on to help with the integration, but I was really not looking to go back into the corporate world. I had already had that experience and I had really come to like the startup life. Today, I'm CEO and an investor at Lotus Microsystems, another semiconductor startup. I'm not a founder this time, but I feel ownership. I feel invested in the company. Would I take that same risk again today as I did with Merus? I think the answer is yes. If you have that mentality of wanting to try something on your own, to build something, that is a major driver inside you. It gives you an enormous amount of energy and motivation. When you do that, you can actually achieve a lot. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: 'Cannot play hide and seek': Minister's warning over haze sends Singapore agricultural stocks lower
events.summary: Minister K Shanmugam said the Singapore Exchange had asked seven firms about their operations and possible links to the haze. Some fire or smoke source points appear associated with First Resources, Bumitama Agri and unlisted First Borneo Plantations. "We will use every legal and regulatory lever at our disposal to exert pressure where it matters," he said. "Companies cannot play hide and seek" with different corporate structures, hoping that will help them, Shanmugam said, revealing that seven companies had been questioned by the Singapore Exchange. Bumitama Agri fell as much as 6.5%, while First Resources dropped to a low of 4.83%. Golden Agri Resources and Wilmar International slipped almost 2%. Shanmugam, who is also home affairs minister for the city-state, said that some of the fires or smoke source points seem to be associated with First Resources, Bumitama Agri, as well as non-listed First Borneo Plantations. "Take, for example, First Resources. It issued a detailed statement on its zero burning policy and firefighting efforts ... but statements, no matter how well drafted, are not good enough. Show us the evidence." The other companies named by the minister were Golden Agri-Resources, Wilmar International, Kencana Agri, Indofood Agri and TSH Resources. The haze has affected businesses and daily life in Singapore and Malaysia in the past few weeks, with the air quality in Singapore hitting levels not seen since 2015. Schools in the state of Johor Bahru in Malaysia have also closed due to the air quality reaching unhealthy levels. "They should not underestimate the Singapore government's determination to act," Shanmugam said, adding, "we will use every legal and regulatory lever at our disposal to exert pressure where it matters, including on their bottom lines, including on their access to financing, and including on their standing with investors." He also revealed that Singapore could even amend laws or introduce new laws "on an urgent basis" to ensure cooperation, if needed. Companies potentially linked to the haze would also be examined if they still meet the standards for government grants or incentives. When asked if Singapore's actions will affect bilateral relations between the city-state and Jakarta, Shanmugam dismissed the concern, saying, "Our people are suffering. What do these experts think we are supposed to do? Shiver in our shoes before we take any action to protect our own people? That's not the Singapore approach." He was responding to a question about an article published by local media outlet CNA , which cited legal experts saying that actions taken by Singapore against haze-causing firms in Indonesia may carry diplomatic implications. "If we think like that, there will be no Singapore, and we do not think there should be any bilateral issues. The Indonesian public is suffering as well, and it is in Indonesia's interests as much as ours to deal with the companies that are causing these problems." He said that Singapore's actions against companies are aligned with the broad policies of Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto. "In fact, we hope to get full cooperation from Indonesia in going after the companies," Shanmugam added

events.title: Arada enters Saudi Arabia with $3.8bn Riyadh project
events.summary: UAE developer Arada is launching a Dh14 billion ($3.8 billion) residential project in Riyadh and plans to build 100,000 homes in Saudi Arabia over the next three to five years as it expands in the kingdom, its chief executive has said. The company will also launch projects in Jeddah and Makkah as the Saudi market opens for foreign investment. “We have a good pipeline coming, and we will probably announce another project by the end of the year,” Ahmed Alkhoshaibi said. “As a group we plan to have 200,000 homes in the next three to five years, with half of that coming in Saudi Arabia.” Arada is jointly owned by Saudi businessman Prince Khaled bin Alwaleed’s KBW Investments and Sharjah-based Basma Group. Following the Saudi announcement, Arada’s pipeline is valued at Dh185 billion across the UAE, Saudi Arabia, the UK, Australia and Syria, comprising more than 70,000 homes. It has completed 17,000 homes so far. Saudi Arabia, the Arab world’s largest economy, has overhauled its property sector, allowing foreigners to buy in designated zones in Riyadh and Jeddah, while introducing “special requirements” for home ownership in Makkah and Madinah from January. It also introduced land tax rules last year to help free up undeveloped land and spur building activity. Riyadh debut Arada’s debut project will be built in the Al Rimal district in Riyadh's north-eastern growth corridor on a plot covering 2.5 million square metres. Apart from 3,500 villas and town houses, it will also have a school, retail outlets and a community centre, as well as sporting facilities and green areas. The project is inspired by Arada's Masaar, a Dh8 billion woodland community development in Sharjah. Units will be sold for between 1,000 and 1,400 Saudi riyals ($267 and $373) per square foot, with construction starting in mid-2027 and completing in five years time, Mr Alkhoshaibi said. Arada KSA, set up in partnership with Saudi property investor Xtopia, will spearhead its expansion in the kingdom, with Mohammed AlDhabaan, chairman of Xtopia as the new chairman of Arada KSA. Arada KSA has access to a significant 10 million square metre land bank across Saudi Arabia with a collective value of Dh49 billion, spanning key strategic locations including Riyadh, Jeddah and Makkah, it said in a separate announcement. Meeting domestic demand Demand for housing in Saudi Arabia is strong as the government pushes to increase home ownership among Saudis. Demand from expatriates following the opening of the sector to foreign buyers is also supporting the market, he said. “The real demand is by the Saudis who need a home, and this is driven further by the government, [which is] pushing for higher home ownership for the Saudis.” “The government's initiative, which we're trying to support, is that they want to provide 300,000 homes delivered in the next three years.” Saudi Arabia has set a target of raising home ownership rates among locals to 70 per cent by 2030 under the Sakani programme – a joint initiative between the Ministry of Housing and the Real Estate Development Fund. By the end of last year, Saudi citizens owning homes exceeded 66 per cent, with one million beneficiaries of government housing support programmes, the Saudi Press Agency reported in January, citing Minister of Municipalities and Housing Majed Al Hogail. Saudi Arabia’s property market was mixed in the second quarter, with nationwide residential transaction values contracting by 26.9 per cent year-on-year to 37.67 billion riyals and the total deal count falling 14.2 per cent, according to the latest CBRE report. The National Residential Price Index, however, grew 2.6 per cent on an annual basis, supported by a 1.1 per cent rise in apartment prices during the quarter. The Al Rimal project will be funded through a Capital Market Authority-regulated investment structure managed by Al Rajhi Capital, an asset-management firm in the kingdom. “We have partnered with Al Rajhi, who will provide the fund management and will also provide the funding. So there is obviously certain equity we put in, but [the] majority is through the fund and the bank,” Mr Alkhoshaibi said. The company is also entering Syria with plans to build a $7 billion “UAE-style” mixed-use real estate project in Damascus in phases over 10 years. The company's property sales are ranging between Dh400 million and Dh700 million a month despite uncertainty over the Iran war, he added. “The external factors will have an impact, but it will be mitigated or reduced by delivering a great product in a great location at a reasonable price, and that's what we've been doing.”

events.title: US Supreme Court to hear case on race in school admissions
events.summary: A group of parents claims local admission policy boosts Black and Latino students while constraining Asian applicants. The United States Supreme Court has agreed to hear a case about the role of race in admissions to selective Maryland middle schools after a group of parents claimed policies discriminated against Asian students in favour of Black and Latino students. The Supreme Court agreed on Monday to hear the parents’ plea on four academically rigorous “magnet” schools in Montgomery County, a suburb on the outskirts of Washington, DC, in the neighbouring state of Maryland. list 1 of 3 US Supreme Court hears challenge to air force UXO detonations in Guam list 2 of 3 US Supreme Court agrees to hear watchdog case on Elon Musk’s DOGE records list 3 of 3 Trump administration sues California over noncitizens on voter rolls The high court said it would weigh whether the parent group has enough evidence of discrimination for the case to move forward. Lower courts previously dismissed the case because Asian-American students were not underrepresented at the specialised-curriculum schools compared with the pool of students that applied. If the Supreme Court rules for the parent group, the Association for Education Fairness, it could revive the lawsuit. The court is expected to hear arguments in the coming months and rule by June. The Montgomery County school district’s selection process was introduced in the 2021-2022 school year during the COVID-19 pandemic. It screens all students for academic potential, and then implements a lottery to randomly assign students from that pool to receive enriched instruction at either a magnet school or a local school. The suit alleged that the screening process makes it harder for Asian-American students, who the challengers said are clustered in “high-performing, low-poverty elementary schools”, to enter the lottery pool. Part of the process ranks a student’s performance by comparing the student’s test scores against those of other students whose family incomes are at a similar level. “Under the applicant pool benchmark, the government can set specific racial targets, hit them, and avoid even an inquiry into discriminatory intent,” so long as it has not explicitly called out race in its process, they wrote in their appeal to the Supreme Court. The case was thrown out in 2022 by US District Judge Paula Xinis. She noted that the percentage of admitted Asian-American students exceeded the percentage of Asian Americans among all applicants to the magnet schools. Xinis also found no evidence that the lottery policy was implemented with discriminatory intent. The school system has consistently argued the new admissions policy, called the “Pandemic Plan” due to the timing of its release, is race-neutral. “The Pandemic Plan is a colorblind lottery,” lawyers wrote in a brief asking the Supreme Court not to take up the case. “Nothing about the Pandemic Plan, its history, or its purpose is offensive to the Constitution.” Supreme Court justices will now consider whether a group claiming to be targeted by a race-neutral policy must show it was disproportionately harmed to prove intentional discrimination.

events.summary: Sea Limited’s financial services arm Monee offers mobile wallets, payments processing, credit and banking services. Sea Limited plans to list its financial services arm Monee, founder Forrest Lee said in an internal memo reviewed by Reuters. Lee said going public would give Monee the “resources and the room to go further and faster than it can today”. It runs mobile wallets, payments, credit and banking in eight markets. SINGAPORE – Singapore-headquartered tech conglomerate Sea Limited is planning a public listing for its financial services arm Monee and will also launch an artificial intelligence enterprise platform business, according to an internal memo sent on Oct 20. Founder Forrest Li, in a memo to employees that was reviewed by Reuters, said he believed going public would give its financial payments and services business the “resources and the room to go further and faster than it can today”. The business operates in Singapore, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam, the Philippines, Taiwan, and Brazil and offers mobile wallets, payments processing, credit and banking services. Sea did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The memo said the tech group would also launch an AI-first enterprise platform named Sea Cloud. In the memo, which was sent on the ninth anniversary of the group’s public listing in New York, Li said the quarterly revenue for the group had grown more than 80 times over that period to US$7.8 billion (S$10 billion). events.title: Indonesia stems market rout ignited by MSCI expulsion threat
events.summary: Jakarta’s benchmark index rose 3% on Oct 20, after hitting a six-year low in the previous session. Indonesia stocks rebounded 4% after a record US$82 billion selloff, as Jakarta moved to curb selling and calm fears after MSCI warned of a possible index downgrade. MSCI said Indonesia may be cut to “standalone” status over weak ownership transparency and concerns about coordinated trading, which could trigger passive fund outflows and hurt confidence. The stock exchange will remove highly concentrated stocks from its benchmark, while officials push reforms and watch Bank Indonesia, as pressure on the rupiah and borrowing costs grows. SINGAPORE/JAKARTA – Indonesian stocks rose on Oct 20 as the authorities in Jakarta introduced measures to restrict selling after a record two-day US$82 billion (S$104.9 billion) rout sparked by index provider MSCI’s warning of possible removal from its global indexes. Jakarta’s benchmark index rose 4% on Oct 20, after hitting a six-year low in the previous session as the world’s worst-performing stock market this year dropped 14.8% over Oct 16 and Oct 19. Still, the index is down about 40% in 2026. MSCI on Oct 16 said it was considering shifting Indonesia to “standalone” instead of “emerging markets” status, a more-severe-than-expected downgrade that shocked investors and officials, and fuelled fears of a selloff by passive funds that track global indexes . The index provider’s latest warning stemmed from concerns that Indonesia had yet to improve ownership transparency or clamp down on coordinated trading and was much worse than the January threat of a downgrade to “frontier” market status. Relegation to “standalone” would be a devastating blow to Indonesia as South-east Asia’s biggest economy grapples with eroding investor confidence over its fiscal health and central bank independence under President Prabowo Subianto. After an online meeting with MSCI on Oct 19, the Indonesia Stock Exchange said it would exclude from its benchmark index any stocks with a high concentration of ownership by any person or entity. “We are doing what is best for our market,” IDX President Director Jeffrey Hendrik said, adding the exclusion would provide a more accurate picture of the index’s movements. He said the affected stocks account for roughly 18% of the total index weight. Gary Tan, portfolio manager at Allspring Global Investments, said excluding tightly held stocks should help address some investability concerns, but implementation would be key, given the potential for domestic pushback. “From here, we think the bigger incremental risk to flows is likely to come from active rather than passive funds,” he said. Jakarta aims to calm nerves with market measures To slow the heavy selling on the market, the stock exchange this week halved the daily down limit on stock prices to 7% from 15%, while setting a 1 rupiah down limit on shares priced at 14 rupiah or less. Also on Oct 19 , Prabowo held talks with finance chiefs, including the head of the Financial Services Authority (OJK), the finance minister and the Bank Indonesia (BI) governor. After the meeting, OJK chief Friderica Widyasari Dewi said the regulator would continue to advance Indonesia’s capital market reforms, particularly regarding transparency, liquidity, and law enforcement against various forms of violations. “A particularly important special message is how we must continuously enforce regulations against those who have committed violations related to coordinated trading and other similar practices,” Friderica said. Market watchers said the stock exchange had taken a constructive step in eliminating stocks with highly concentrated ownership from the benchmark index, but that would not automatically eliminate investors’ exposure to those companies either directly or through products such as mutual funds. “We must ensure that even if a stock is delisted from the Jakarta Composite Index, concentration risk does not continue to accumulate within products purchased by the public,” said Liza Camelia Suryanata, head of research at stockbroker Kiwoom Sekuritas Indonesia. MSCI’s warning has weighed on the rupiah as well, which strengthened slightly to 18,000 per US dollar on Oct 20 but remained close to the record low of 18,190 hit in June ahead of a policy decision from Indonesia’s central bank . BI is expected to hold rates steady on Oct 21, although some economists have raised the prospect of a rate hike to defend the currency, which is down 7% in 2026, making it the worst-performing currency in the region. George Xu, a director in Fitch Ratings’ sovereigns team, said the latest concerns and substantial market selloff reinforced the risks the rating agency identified when it revised the outlook on Indonesia to negative in March.

events.title: CPF maintains A grade in global ranking of pension systems for second year; overall score goes up
events.summary: The CPF was the first pension system in Asia to secure an A grade, with its overall score rising from 80.8 to 82 on the Marsh CFA Institute Global Pension Index. Singapore’s CPF kept its A grade in the Marsh CFA Institute Global Pension Index for a second year, and its overall score rose from 80.8 to 82. The report said ageing populations and longer lives are straining pension systems. Singapore’s CPF is “fully funded” by employer and employee contributions, unlike pay-as-you-go systems. Experts said retirement systems must stay flexible as people work longer. Singapore is moving towards a retirement age of 65 and a re-employment age of 70 by 2030. SINGAPORE – Singapore’s Central Provident Fund (CPF) has retained its A rating for a second consecutive year in an annual global ranking of pension systems. The CPF was the first pension system in Asia to secure an A grade, with its overall score rising from 80.8 to 82 on the Marsh CFA Institute Global Pension Index. It was given the B+ grade in 2024. In 2026, Australia’s social security system also achieved an A rating, meaning the Asia-Pacific region now has two top-tier retirement systems. Other countries that earned the top rating for their pension systems are the Netherlands, which obtained the highest score of 85.8, as well as Denmark, Iceland and Israel. “First-class” retirement income systems that are robust, sustainable, deliver good benefits and have a high level of integrity get an A from Marsh. The professional services firm has collaborated with the CFA Institute, the global association of investment professionals, on the annual index since 2008 . Previously called the Mercer CFA Institute Global Pension Index, it was renamed in 2026 after Mercer adopted the Marsh brand in September as part of a corporate rebrand by its parent company, Marsh McLennan. In 2026, the Index examined the impact of falling birth rates and rising life expectancies on 55 retirement income systems worldwide, up from 52 in the 2025 Index. The study covered pension systems in 66% of the world’s population, including the US, Britain, China, India, South Korea and Japan. Reflecting the focus on the ageing population globally, the report adjusted the Adequacy sub-index to consider the levels of income available at retirement and at age 80. This recognises the fact that more people will live past 80 and into their 90s, needing financial support throughout their long retirement years. The Adequacy sub-index measures whether a pension system provides a sufficient level of income for retirees to maintain a decent standard of living. It is one of three sub-indices that make up a pension system’s overall index score. Singapore’s Adequacy score jumped from 79.4 in 2025 to 82.8 in 2026, but its Sustainability sub-index score dipped from 75.5 to 75.3. The Sustainability sub-index assesses a pension system’s long-term viability and its ability to meet future pension obligations. Meanwhile, the Integrity sub-index rounds out the overall score by measuring the level of public trust and assessing whether the pension system earns the confidence of those who depend on it. On this front, Singapore held its 90.4 score. Rising life expectancies strain government budgets Mirroring the global trend of population ageing, Singapore became a super-aged society in June 2026, when 21.4% of its citizens were 65 or older. The United Nations classifies any nation with 21% of its population aged 65 and above as super-aged. Marsh highlighted in its report that ageing populations are placing increasing strain on government budgets. Public pensions, especially those that operate on a pay-as-you-go basis, will not be sustainable because they rely on taxes from the current working population to fund the retirement payouts of today’s retirees. As the population ages, there will be a smaller workforce to pay for the retirement benefits of a growing pool of retirees. Marsh noted that growing financial strain will prompt many countries to review the funding of their pension systems. Governments will either have to cut retirement benefits or encourage their population to save for their future payouts in advance. Marsh noted that Singapore’s CPF, unlike other pension systems, is “fully funded with contributions from both employers and employees”. These CPF contributions are invested primarily in special Singapore Government Securities, which allow the CPF Board to pay interest of at least 2.5% on Ordinary Account savings and at least 4% on Special Account and Retirement Account (RA) savings. Walter Theseira, associate professor of economics at the Singapore University of Social Sciences, added that because CPF payouts are based solely on one’s own retirement savings, they will not be affected by government tax constraints or public finance challenges. CPF Life, the national longevity insurance annuity scheme, pays out income from each member’s CPF personal retirement savings pot for as long as they live.

events.title: Bank Indonesia faces mounting pressure to hike after MSCI threat fuels market rout
events.summary: Bank Indonesia is under pressure to raise its benchmark rate on Wednesday to stabilize the rupiah. Economists are split on the size of a hike, with Citi expecting a 50-basis-point hike to 6.25% and Capital Economics and others seeing a smaller increase to 6%. Analysts urge credible market governance reforms to address MSCI's fundamental concerns. Bank Indonesia faces mounting pressure to raise interest rates on Wednesday as economists revise their forecasts after global index provider MSCI warned it may downgrade the country's stock market from emerging-market status, setting off a selloff in stocks and the rupiah. Citibank now expects a pre-emptive 50 basis-point increase to 6.25%, abandoning its earlier call for no change. Capital Economics and Permata Bank expect a 25 basis-point hike to 6%. The central bank has held its benchmark seven-day reverse repurchase rate at 5.75% since June. MSCI said Friday it is considering moving Indonesia to "standalone" from the emerging-market status it has held since 1989, causing the Jakarta Composite Index to suffer the worst two-day sell-off recorded, before recovering about 3% Tuesday after authorities announced steps to improve market transparency and price discovery, including expelling tightly held companies from the flagship index. Meanwhile, rupiah weakened to 18,030 per dollar on Tuesday, near its June record low, falling about 8% this year. "Not delivering a rate hike [on Wednesday] would run the risk of disappointing investors and fueling further downward pressure on the currency," said Jason Tuvey, deputy chief emerging markets economist at Capital Economics. "A decision to hold rates on Wednesday could also revive concerns among investors that Bank Indonesia is kowtowing to political pressure." Citi's Helmi Arman said a hike would aim to stop equity outflows spilling into bonds and prompting capital flight by domestic investors. He expects it to be a "one-off" followed by other support such as government foreign-currency borrowing or another round of bilateral currency swaps with foreign central banks. The central bank has already raised rates by a combined 100 basis points since May. Headline inflation quickened to a three-month high of 3.28% in September, within the 1.5%-3.5% target range, while core inflation eased to 2.84%. The governor, Destry Damayanti, has said foreign-exchange reserves of $146.3 billion at the end of September would be adequate to stabilize the rupiah. "Market confidence can deteriorate much faster than economic fundamentals," said Josua Pardede, chief economist at PT Bank Permata, estimating that foreign investors have net sold about $5 billion of Indonesian stocks this year. The risk is that foreign equity withdrawals could further weaken the rupiah and trigger selling in government bonds, he added. An MSCI downgrade could force $3 billion to $5 billion of passive outflows, with another $15 billion of actively managed foreign money exposed to reassessment, he estimates. Pardede expects the market adjustment may come in stages, from precautionary selling through the first half of 2027 and mechanical selling if MSCI confirms the move by June. "BI can provide liquidity and reduce excessive volatility, but only credible market-governance reforms can address MSCI's fundamental concerns," he said, calling for credible free-float data, ownership disclosure and transparent engagement with international institutional investors. "The biggest risk is not simply losing Emerging Market status, but letting doubts about market integrity become a lasting increase in Indonesia's cost of capital."

events.title: ‘Deliberate’ car ramming of Australian MP an isolated incident, police say
events.summary: A 43-year-old man accused of deliberately hitting Helen Haines outside her office remains in police custody. The Australian Federal Police (AFP) have said the alleged targeting of independent lawmaker Helen Haines appeared to be an “isolated incident” and there were no known further threats associated with the attack. Haines was struck by a Toyota Land Cruiser SUV outside her office in Wangaratta, about 200km (124 miles) northwest of the state of Victoria’s capital, Melbourne, on Monday, in what Prime Minister Anthony Albanese called a “deliberate” act. list 1 of 3 Flight from Israel makes emergency landing in Bulgaria after bomb threat list 2 of 3 Police investigating Flydubai co-pilot’s Australia ties list 3 of 3 Melbourne man ‘strongly rejects’ links to flydubai attack suspect The 65-year-old underwent surgery overnight, with Australian media outlets reporting on Tuesday that she has lost a leg and remains in critical condition in a Melbourne hospital. The suspect is in police custody, an AFP statement released on Tuesday said. Local media identified the driver as a 43-year-old man from Tarrawingee, Victoria. Federal and state police were working “to identify potential charges”, including “the offence of causing harm to a Commonwealth public official which carries a maximum penalty of 10 years’ imprisonment”, the statement said. The prime minister said on Tuesday that the vehicle had performed a U-turn before hitting the MP. “It’s clear that there was a deliberate act here. This wasn’t an accident, someone just skidding off the road,” Albanese ⁠told the ABC national broadcaster. The prime minister said the alleged attacker’s motive remained unknown. A former nurse, Haines is an independent federal MP for the Victorian seat of Indi and is known for her socially conscious policy positions on the environment and transparency. Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke told ABC Radio that witnesses said Haines was struck twice by the vehicle before a bystander intervened. Ricky Jefferies ran from his barber shop, restrained the attacker and removed a knife from him after initially believing the incident was a car accident, Australian media reported. “I heard a loud bang with no brakes. It was crazy; I just ran out to the ⁠front to see what’s happening,” Jefferies told reporters outside his shop. “I didn’t realise the seriousness of ⁠the situation initially, and once it became relevant, I just did what I could and what others were already trying to do.” Foreign Minister Penny Wong said she was shocked by the “deeply disturbing attack” and wished Haines a full recovery in a post on X. The attack comes after the federal police documented a steady rise in threats and abuse directed towards the nation’s politicians in recent years. Politicians have historically been highly accessible to the public and usually go about their business without security. Albanese said on Monday that “the temperature has increased in recent times”. Haines entered parliament in 2019 after working as a nurse and midwife, becoming known for stances such as supporting stronger climate action. She has been praised for her efforts to increase transparency in politics and crack down on corruption.

Angel Reese scored 30 points and had 16 rebounds as the Atlanta Dream stymied the Golden State Valkyries in a stunning win in the WNBA Finals to level the series 1-1 in San Francisco. Allisha Gray added 18 points as the Dream took full control at both ends in the second half, winning 79-65 on Monday night to even the best-of-seven series before it heads to Atlanta. Rhyne Howard set a Finals record with six steals, while Jordin Canada contributed 13 points, 10 assists and seven rebounds as the Dream earned the franchise’s first Finals victory after going winless in three previous trips. They now head home, having salvaged a split in front of the boisterous “Ballhalla” crowd at Chase Center. “This environment is tough to play in. Shoutout to the fans. Shoutout to my team, though,” Reese said after the game. “We came and fought. I mean, that Game 1 was tough for us. But we moved on.” Reese became the third player with at least 30 points and 15 rebounds in a Finals game, joining Jonquel Jones of Connecticut in 2019 and Breanna Stewart of Seattle in 2020. “She was definitely way more aggressive; she had a great game,” Valkyries centre Kiah Stokes said. “We let everyone kind of have their way.” Game 3 is Wednesday in Atlanta, where the next two games were moved to the NBA’s Atlanta Hawks’ State Farm Arena so more fans could attend. It holds more than 17,000, as opposed to the Dream’s regular home, Gateway Center Arena, which accommodates only 3,500. Chase Center holds 18,064 and has sold out every game since the Valkyries began playing last year. Gabby Williams finished with 14 points on 3-for-15 shooting after she was the only Golden State player to score in double figures with 26 points in Game 1, going 7 for 24 from the 3-point range. “We shot terribly,” point guard Veronica Burton said. “We missed shots that we make all the time.” Foul trouble almost did in the Dream this time, but Reese simply would not have it. She went scoreless in the second half of the opener, but delivered the big baskets and key defensive stops two days later, finishing 10 for 16 from the floor while dishing out three assists and blocking two shots. “We watched film and saw the things that we messed up on. When I said that they didn’t do anything to mess us up, it was literally just us,” Reese said. “And we can see that tonight. And we’re gonna carry that over in Atlanta. Atlanta, y’all better pull up and pop out; I’m looking forward to it.” Atlanta scored 24 points off Golden State’s 19 turnovers to hand the Valkyries their first loss in regulation since a 73-70 defeat at Chicago on August 21. The Dream had just eight points off turnovers in Game 1, but returned to the defensive formula that advanced Atlanta this far.

events.title: Brisbane council to embrace early morning culture with new dawn plan
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Brisbane City Council to develop economic plan to embrace locals' early-morning habits The Brisbane City Council will conduct a survey about residents' early morning habits. ( ABC News: Brian Hurst ) The Brisbane City Council has launched a survey of residents' early-morning behaviours to inform a new Dawn Economy Plan. The council says the plan will help improve park facilities and public transport options as Brisbane leans into its reputation as a city of early risers. The survey will be open until November 22. The Brisbane City Council hopes to take advantage of residents' tendency to wake up early with the development of a new Dawn Plan, set to highlight early-morning economic opportunities. To inform the plan, the council is encouraging locals to take part in a survey about their experiences in Brisbane between 4am and 7am. Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner said the responses would help improve park facilities, pathways and public transport options in the early hours. Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner says Brisbane has a thriving dawn economy. ( ABC News: Lucas Hill ) "The reality is there's a thriving dawn economy at the moment," Cr Schrinner said. "People are voting with their feet. They want to get up early, they want to get out and about, and they want to get active." Analysis by University of Melbourne research fellow Dr Anna Edwards found Brisbane has one of the most active early-morning trading hours in Australia . About 13 per cent of Brisbane cafes are open between 5am and 6am. ( ABC News: Tim Swanston ) The research showed 13 per cent of Brisbane food and drink businesses are open between 5am and 6am, and by 8am, about half are serving customers. Dr Edwards said it was "wonderful" to see the Brisbane City Council "drawing on this strength and building on it". "We do a lot of planning of places by space, but we don't necessarily always think about timing. "Things have shifted quite considerably over the last five to 10 years, and I think we need to be thinking about this, but mornings generally have been quite overlooked." Blaine Swanborough co-owns a cafe in Mitchelton that opens at 6am. ( ABC News ) Blaine Swanborough co-owns a cafe in Mitchelton which opens at 6am, and said the community is often out and about by then. "We really see a drop off in trade later in the mornings as it heats up, especially in summer," Mr Swanborough said. "We really try and make the most of it in the early morning. "Our balance is with staff as well … but we try and find that line of providing what the community wants." The council says survey responses will help improve park facilities, pathways and public transport options. ( ABC News: Giulio Saggin, file photo ) Committee for Brisbane chief executive Jen Williams said the dawn economy plan was about playing to Brisbane's strengths. "For a long time, Brisbane has shied away from acknowledging that it is an early-rising city," Ms Williams said. "Whereas now, we can see with the global wellness movement and a focus on health, that people really do want to embrace the mornings. "The dawn economy doesn't come at the expense of the night-time economy. It is really about building a 24-hour city." Council opposition leader Jared Cassidy said the dawn survey was unnecessary. "It's shocking that our Lord Mayor, who has served in Council for over 20 years, has just realised Brisbane residents start their day early," Cr Cassidy said. "It's simple — we need investment in the infrastructure and services necessary to improve our uniquely Brisbane way of life. "Early morning public transport services and lighting in parks and bikeways to support active travel in the winter months would be a great start." The dawn economy survey will be open until midnight on November 22.

events.title: UAE tax rules: What businesses can claim for employee expenses
events.summary: Giving employees the tools they need to do their jobs effectively is a timeless business requirement. Whether a company has standard lists of equipment and resources for different grades and functions, which it should to make onboarding easier, most businesses could produce such lists without much difficulty. There are, however, tax considerations, particularly corporation tax and VAT . Thankfully, Federal Tax Authority Decision No 17 of 2026 has helpfully brought together answers to many of the questions businesses might have. There are five main sections, starting with transport provided for staff. It's critical that employees are not charged for the service and that transport is provided only between their homes and workplaces. Could there be a collection point for several employees, provided it is a reasonable distance from their homes? I would imagine so. Cash payments instead of transport cannot be offered, and there should be no identifiable non-business benefit. Could one employee who fails either test affect the entire arrangement? The decision says nothing about separating qualifying and non-qualifying cases. Best not be the person who tests the rules. What about pooling transport between two neighbouring companies? If the company providing the service changes according to a weekly schedule, would that complicate matters? A strict interpretation would require whichever company provides the service to invoice its commercial neighbour. I don't see how this can be avoided. Anything more complicated might best be outsourced for simplicity. Next is the provision of food and beverages. This is permissible where employees live so remotely that returning home is impractical. What constitutes remote is not defined, although I would interpret it as being unable to reach home within a reasonable time, given an individual's circumstances. This raises the possibility that only a small proportion of the workforce might qualify. No guidance has been provided on whether a minimum number of employees must meet the conditions. The provision must be linked to an employee's role and circumstances, including their workplace or residence. Suitable facilities should not be available at their accommodation or workplace, nor should local food outlets be reasonably accessible. Again, cash payments instead of food and beverages should not be an option. Moving on to company-provided accommodation, this must be an operational necessity. Perhaps the work site is in the Empty Quarter, 100 miles (160km) from the nearest town. Difficult access could make it reasonable to accommodate employees on or near the site. Accommodation and communication Accommodation should be suitable but not luxurious. No swimming pools, expansive manicured gardens, extensive household staff or additional reception rooms. The rules for onboarding new employees are a little more relaxed. Accommodation can be provided for up to 30 days, and the expense claimed, provided it is not ostentatious. Notably, the decision does not exclude employees who have already been living in the country, regardless of how long they have been here. I recall benefiting from such an arrangement when starting a role in the late 2000s. I believe there were two reasons for it. First, treating new starters differently would have been inconvenient. Second, with international personnel flying in and out of the region, putting everyone in the same hotel helped employees become familiar with the business and encouraged social interaction. Mobile phones are another area where guidance already existed, and the new decision restates and expands on it. Devices must be required for work and used only for business purposes. Each invoice should be reviewed, with personal calls identified and excluded from VAT or corporation tax claims. A company may decide to absorb the non-deductible cost rather than introduce an internal system for recovering personal expenses. Sometimes the administrative cost can outweigh the value of recovering small amounts spent on company assets. The new requirement is for a formal standard operating policy. This must be communicated to everyone affected, reviewed periodically, updated when necessary and demonstrably enforced. For businesses without standard operating procedures, this would be a good place to start. If I could, as an accountant, give human resources departments one task, it would be to map every business process and identify the roles and individuals responsible for each. This would strengthen both control and continuity. I can think of few projects more valuable when reassessing internal efficiency, particularly in an AI-driven world where automation is the mot du jour . Lastly comes parking, which is subject to the same requirements as mobile phones.

events.summary: Lamine Yamal faces ex-teammate Ferran Torres as in-form Barcelona take on holders PSG in a spicy encounter in Paris. Who : Paris Saint-Germain vs Barcelona What : UEFA Champions League , match day 3 Where : Parc des Princes, Paris, France When : Tuesday, October 20, at 9pm (19:00 GMT) How to follow : Al Jazeera Sport will bring you all the build-up and live updates from 16:00 GMT. One of the most eagerly awaited Champions League matches of the season will be played against the backdrop of turmoil on the streets of the French capital as holders Paris Saint-Germain host Barcelona on Tuesday. list 1 of 4 Will FIFA scrap its peace prize, making Trump its first and only winner? list 2 of 4 Manchester United held at Leeds despite improved performance for Carrick list 3 of 4 Madueke scores only goal as below-par Arsenal beat Nottingham Forest list 4 of 4 Real Madrid demand resignation of La Liga chief after Goebbels comparison The fate of the match has been subject to debate as the French government seeks to control the violent protests gripping the country. However, once the match gets under way at the Parc des Princes, fans can expect a mouthwatering battle between the Champions League’s top two teams as the back-to-back holders welcome five-time winners. Boasting a perfect record across all competitions, Spanish giants Barca are arguably one of Europe’s best teams this season. PSG too have been nothing short of lethal – the Parisians lead the UCL points table and have scored a whopping 10 goals in two games. There will be plenty of star power on display when the match kicks off as the dazzling duo of Ferran Torres and Ousmane Dembele will headline the star-studded home side. Lamine Yamal, who is enjoying one of the best starts to a La Liga season for a forward, will be joined by Raphinha for Barcelona. Here’s everything you need to know ahead of PSG vs Barcelona: After seven matches, PSG are second in Ligue 1 with 14 points, behind Lyon on goal difference. They have won four times, drawn twice and lost once in the French top division. How have Barcelona played this season? Barcelona are five points clear at the top of La Liga table with nine wins from nine. Their blistering attack has scored 39 league goals. What happened in the first and second Champions League rounds? Two-time holders PSG thrashed Slovan Bratislava 6-1 in their UCL opener at home before beating Manchester City 4-2 in a thrilling away fixture. Barcelona thumped Feyenoord 5-1 at home and bounced back from a goal down to smash Galatasaray 4-1 away. Those results keep PSG top of the table and Barcelona second, with both on six points. Will PSG vs Barcelona go ahead amid the protests in France? Despite the violent protests and nationwide arrests, French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said the match will not be postponed or cancelled. Lecornu said on Monday that he had asked regional authorities to impose “partial” and “localised” curfews in some cities to protect businesses after weekend demonstrations spilled over into some of the worst street violence in recent years. “These curfews must be local and partial. It is out of the question to put all of Paris ⁠⁠⁠⁠under curfew.” At the same news conference, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told reporters there were no plans to cancel the ⁠⁠⁠⁠match. Police have arrested at least 2,400 people across France after violent groups clashed with officers and looted shops during nationwide demonstrations that attracted hundreds of thousands of people to denounce rising living costs and poor conditions in schools. Opta’s supercomputer has given PSG a 39.7 per cent probability of winning, while Barcelona have a 37.7 per cent chance. There are 22.6 per cent odds for a draw. (Last five matches across all competitions; latest game first) Ferran Torres and Ousmane Dembele (PSG): Torres, who joined PSG after four seasons at Barcelona, is their leading scorer with seven goals in all competitions, including an opening day Champions League hat-trick. Dembele has had an all-round impact with six assists and four goals. Raphinha and Lamine Yamal (Barcelona): With 14 goals, Raphinha is the most prolific striker in European club football this season. Such is his dominance that even a brief injury absence did not take away his top spot. Yamal, on the other hand, has been unstoppable in his own way – the 18-year-old winger’s nine goals and 10 assists make him a once-in-a-generation talent. PSG suffered a major blow shortly before Tuesday’s trip when left-back Nuno Mendes suffered a thigh injury during their 3-1 Ligue 1 victory at Strasbourg on Saturday. Mendes will be unavailable for the “next few weeks”, according to the team who are also without Senny Mayulu with a similar issue.

( ABC News: Ethan Rix ) The mother of Complainant A in the Alan Jones trial has told a court her son's "mood was different" when he returned home from a trip to the veteran broadcaster's private farm. Complainant A says when he was a 17-year-old schoolboy he was indecently assaulted by Mr Jones at the farm. The 85-year-old has pleaded not guilty to 21 counts of indecent assault and sexual touching related to five male complainants. A mother has told a trial she trusted Alan Jones as a mentor to her son before the broadcaster allegedly indecently assaulted the 17-year-old schoolboy at his private farm. One of Mr Jones's five alleged victims, known as Complainant A, alleges the radio host kissed him, put his tongue in his mouth and touched his buttocks when he visited Mr Jones's property in the Southern Highlands as a 17-year-old schoolboy. The 85-year-old has pleaded not guilty to 21 counts of indecent assault and sexually touching, relating to several alleged incidents against five males between 2003 and 2020. The court previously heard the complainant was 13 years old when he sent a letter to the then-2GB radio host, requesting help for his single mother and their serious financial struggles. Emails read to the court show Mr Jones developed a relationship with the boy over several years, and that the prominent media figure helped wipe $600,000 off the mother's home loan and provided $100,000 to assist with the completion of their home. Mr Jones has pleaded not guilty to 21 counts of indecent assault and sexual touching related to five male complainants. ( ABC News: Ethan Rix ) Giving evidence at the trial on Tuesday, the boy's mother told the court her son met up with Mr Jones on several occasions including for private breakfasts at his Circular Quay apartment and lunch at a pub, but that she was never invited. She recalled when her son was 17 and had been invited by Mr Jones to spend two nights at his Fitzroy Falls farm and that she felt "really comfortable" with him going because she "trusted" the radio host. "[Someone] who saw that my son was intelligent as he is." Mother breaks down reading son's note NSW Sexual Violence Helpline on 1800 424 017 NSW Victims Services on 1800 633 063 Bravehearts (support for child sexual abuse survivors) on 1800 272 831 Child Protection Helpline on 132 111 MARS Australia (for men affected by rape and sexual abuse) on (07) 3857 1222 National Survivors Foundation on 1300 124 433 Full Stop Australia on 1800 385 578. The woman told the court that when her son returned home from the trip, "his mood was different" and she "knew straight away something was up". "He wasn't sleeping, he was just staying up," she said. She said her son wrote her a letter 10 days later, saying "something happened at Fitzroy Falls" and that "someone did something they shouldn't have" but did not go into explicit detail. The mother broke down several times in the witness box, including when her son's letter was placed in front of her during her testimony. The woman said after receiving the note she asked her son if he wanted to report what happened to police. "He [my son] said to me that 'I wasn't raped'," she said. Mother tells court of her 'dire' financial situation The mother told the court that, before the alleged assault that she was in a "dire" situation, with a $1.3 million mortgage hanging over her head and the builder of her unfinished home walking off the job. The trial heard the woman's partner had also left the country and would often miss child support payments. The woman said a family friend suggested she reach out to the broadcaster for help because "he's influential and there might be people he knows who can help you". The mother said she provided information to her son to send to Mr Jones, who replied with an email saying, "you sound a special sort of young man," and asking for additional information. "When he [my son] told me that, I was incredibly grateful that someone of his stature was interested in what we were doing because we got such a prompt reply," the mother said. "I was desperate, people who are being served repossession papers are not cruising along in life." Court told Mr Jones put mother in contact with head of major bank The woman told the court that Mr Jones organised for the head of the Commonwealth Bank at the time to call her to understand more about her circumstances and try to find a "manageable" situation for the family.

events.title: Hong Kong’s rail company MTR bets $6.3 billion on a city that doesn’t exist yet
events.summary: Under the government’s plan, half a million new homes will be constructed, helping increase the area’s population to 2.5 million. MTR is spending at least HK$38.9 billion on the Northern Metropolis rail link, a project built before the city around it exists. The company is borrowing upfront and waiting years for land value returns. The Northern Metropolis plan aims for 500,000 new homes, 2.5 million people, and a tech hub by 2030 and 2034. It marks a shift towards Hong Kong’s border area and away from Victoria Harbour growth. The project brings big risks for MTR, including high interest rates, property market weakness, and past cost overruns. Ratings stay strong, but success depends on on-time delivery and government backing. HONG KONG – Hong Kong’s MTR has built the city’s railways one of two ways: The government handed over land around new stations, or paid directly. Either way, the money arrived with the track. The Northern Metropolis is different. MTR is putting up at least HK$38.9 billion (S$6.3 billion), borrowing to do it, and will wait years to find out whether the land it receives in return – under a funding model that has never been tested at this scale – is worth what the lines cost. “In the past, some projects we developed the area and then we built the railway,” said Dominic Law, the head of project delivery for phase one of MTR’s Northern Link. “But moving into the Northern Metropolis, we focus on the infrastructure first.” At 300 sq km, the Northern Metropolis covers more than a quarter of Hong Kong’s total land area and is two and a half times the size of San Francisco. Under the government’s plan, half a million new homes will be constructed, helping increase the area’s population to 2.5 million from 980,000 over a roughly 20-year period. The economic centrepiece of the project is a tech hub designed to be Hong Kong’s Silicon Valley. To facilitate this, MTR will build 17km of underground rail track and seven new stations for the Northern Link and spur line. Some works have already started. The project is scheduled for completion in 2034 and will be financed upfront by the company. To help pay for the construction, the company has raised more than HK$130 billion in bonds and loans since early 2025, much of it earmarked for capital works including the Northern Metropolis, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. In turn, the government has granted MTR development rights for 10 plots of land along the upcoming lines. The government, which owns virtually all the land in Hong Kong, typically sells plots at a large premium to factor in development potential. In the case of the Northern Link, the government has deducted HK$39.05 billion from the premium MTR owes – roughly equal to the company’s targeted outlay. MTR was established in 1975 with the British colonial government as sole shareholder to build the city’s metro system after the population swelled by almost four million in three decades. In 2000, the government divested a 23% stake to investors when the company was listed on Hong Kong’s stock exchange. For much of MTR’s history, the government has used the “rail-plus-property” model to subsidise construction. That model – selling homes around its stations – has made MTR one of the most profitable railway businesses by net margin. In recent decades, however, three major projects – the West Island line, the high-speed rail link to mainland China and the Shatin to Central line – were directly funded by the government as part of a massive wave of spending on infrastructure. The Northern Metropolis was formally unveiled in 2021 by Hong Kong’s then leader Carrie Lam to help the city better integrate with mainland China, solve a housing shortage, develop advanced tech industries and create jobs. The project signals a notable shift away from the intense development around Victoria Harbour towards the historically underdeveloped, mostly rural land adjacent to the mainland border – as well as reducing Hong Kong’s reliance on the finance and real estate industries for growth. The city’s new five-year plan announced in September sets a binding target of having 900ha of land in the Northern Metropolis ready for construction by 2030, underscoring the strategic importance of the development. All this shows the pressure on MTR to complete the railways on schedule and on budget, at a time when the outlook for the property market is unclear. Existing home prices are down 16% from their 2021 high, and a currency peg with the dollar means the city’s interest rates move in sync with those in US. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority’s base rate is 4.25%, more than double the 1.8% average since 2008. “To fully unleash the potential of this development, we really need the Northern Link to be in operation at the right time,” said MTR’s Law. “It is a very complex project covering a big area and affecting a lot of different stakeholders.” The company’s recent record shows the challenges.

events.title: BlackRock, GIC among investors chasing Indian telecom major Jio's IPO as anchor bids top $26 billion
events.summary: Jio Platforms has garnered bids from top global investors including Capital Group, GIC, and BlackRock for the $854 million anchor book portion of its initial public offering. The company's anchor book received total bids worth $26.3 billion from institutional investors, more than 30 times the anchor book. Meta and Google-backed Jio Platforms plans to raise up to $3.2 billion through an IPO. India's Jio Platforms has seen the anchor investor quota for its initial public offering oversubscribed more than 30 times, according to a source familiar with the matter, drawing bids from top asset managers including BlackRock, Capital Group and GIC. The country's largest telecommunications and digital services company, backed by Meta and Google, plans to raise up to 302 billion rupees ($3.2 billion) through India's largest ever IPO in rupee terms . According to the source, who is not allowed to speak on the matter due to legal restrictions, the company's anchor book received total bids worth 2.5 trillion rupees ($26.3 billion) for the 81.1 billion rupee anchor book portion. Jio Platforms, in a release on Monday, said it had finalized the allocation of 72.47 million equity shares to anchor investors at 1,119 rupees a share, at the upper range of the price band. The anchor book is a portion of the total fundraise set aside for large institutional investors before the IPO opens for public bidding. Some other major institutional investors who have been allocated shares include India's state-owned insurance firm Life Insurance Corporation , Fidelity Investments, JPMorgan Asset Management and Abu Dhabi Investment Authority. The Jio Platforms IPO will be open to the public from Wednesday through Friday. Jio Platforms, owned by Reliance Industries , has been positioning itself as a tech company and not just a traditional utility provider . The IPO price values the company at around $108 billion — lower than the valuations of over $130 billion floated a year ago.

events.title: Witkoff heads to Oslo, plans Russia trip for peace talks
events.summary: White House envoy Steve Witkoff is traveling to Oslo for talks Tuesday with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and European leaders, a U.S. official said. The big picture: The talks will bring together Ukraine, European allies and the U.S. as they seek to develop a peace proposal to present to Russia . The Oslo talks are expected to include Zelensky , Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, representatives of the E4 nations (the U.K., France, Germany and Poland) and officials from the EU and NATO. Driving the news: The U.S. official said that following Oslo, Witkoff is also planning to travel to Russia, where he hopes to meet with President Vladimir Putin and present ideas developed in close consultation with Ukraine and European partners. Trump adviser Jared Kushner has the flu and will not attend the Oslo meeting in person, but will participate virtually, the U.S. official said. The planned meetings in Oslo build on the discussions held at Witkoff's Miami-area Shell Bay club , where Zelensky committed to reviewing and advancing a series of proposals aimed at creating a pathway toward a comprehensive and durable peace agreement, the U.S. official added. Zoom in: The U.S. official said American, Ukrainian and European representatives worked together over the past week to develop the proposals. "Steve and Jared also spoke with President Zelensky on Sunday to review progress and discuss next steps," the U.S. official said. The trip is also expected to include efforts to secure the release of Stephen Hubbard, a retired American teacher whom the U.S. says has been wrongfully detained in Russia. What's next: The U.S. official said the discussions are focused on two parallel tracks: Securing Ukraine's future: Establishing a sovereign, secure, and prosperous future for Ukraine, including credible security guarantees, European integration, and a comprehensive postwar economic framework that addresses Ukraine's financial needs and creates opportunities for long-term growth and investment. Creating the conditions for a durable peace: Developing a comprehensive proposal to Russia that addresses the issues necessary to end the war, establishes a new and enduring security architecture between Russia and Europe, and explores opportunities for postwar economic cooperation. "President Trump has directed an intensive process to develop a comprehensive peace proposal with Ukraine and Europe, and the next step is to test whether that work can form the basis for serious negotiations with Russia," the U.S. official said. "These discussions remain fluid, and substantial work remains. President Trump's objective is clear: to end the killing, bring the war to a close, and establish the conditions for a lasting peace that benefits Ukraine, Russia, Europe, and the United States."

events.title: Shares stumble, oil rises as markets await AI sector results
events.summary: Brent rose to US$109.64 per barrel. Asian shares fell as investors waited for results from Meta, Tesla and chipmakers. AI earnings are seen as a key test of market strength and spending plans. Oil prices rose as Trump’s Russia energy order and French riots lifted safe-haven demand. Brent and WTI both gained, while gold fell. French unrest, weak Asian markets and cautious central bank signals weighed on sentiment. Traders also watched speeches from the ECB and Bank of England, plus crypto losses. TOKYO – Asian stocks retreated broadly on Oct 20 while oil rose as geopolitical risks rattled sentiment ahead of key results from artificial intelligence bellwether companies. The euro recouped some losses from the previous session that were spurred by escalating riots in France. Crude prices resumed their climb as markets weighed an executive order from US President Donald Trump that waived some sanctions and tariffs on Russian energy. The spotlight now turns to corporate earnings, with investors seeking fresh evidence that consumers and the broader economy remain resilient. Quarterly earnings are due from SpaceX and Netflix on Oct 20, with results from AI heavyweights such as Meta and Tesla scheduled for later in the week. “The market is happy to cover shorts and unwind defensive trades, but that’s very different from having the conviction to rebuild aggressive exposure to AI,” Chris Weston, head of research at Pepperstone, said in a note. “French sovereign risk is clearly being priced into European equities, but the euro’s resilience suggests traders aren’t yet treating it as a systemic European problem.” The MSCI Asia ex-Japan index fell 1.14 %, while Japan’s Nikkei 225 dropped 0.98 %. South Korea’s KOSPI tumbled 3.92 %. In early European trade, the pan-region Euro Stoxx 50 futures slipped 0.57%, German DAX futures dipped 0.33% and FTSE futures lost 0.47%. US stock futures, the S&P 500 e-minis, rose 0.12% to 7,743.5. The dollar index, which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies, fell 0.16% to 101.80, with the euro up 0.17% at US$1.1229. The Japanese yen strengthened 0.16% to 158.24 per dollar, and sterling rose 0.21% to US$1.3327. Overnight, the French authorities set curfews in parts of several cities including Paris, Lille and Nice, after a weekend of riots and looting stemming from nationwide anti-government protests. And in the Middle East, dozens were killed and more than 200 were injured after an attack by the Iran-aligned Houthis on a government security forces training camp in Yemen’s Shabwa province. Netflix is expected to report slowing revenue growth in the third quarter, while SpaceX is forecast to report US$12.74 billion (S$16.3 billion) i n quarterly revenue. General Motors, Hasbro, Halliburton, and 3M are among the more established names due to report on Oct 20. Along with quarterly results, markets are increasingly focused on the massive spending plans of the major AI players. Facebook operator Meta is one of five AI hyperscalers expected to increase combined capital expenditure to about US$1.2 trillion (S$1.5 trillion) in 2027, according to Goldman Sachs. “Investors are fine with AI being used more. What they’re questioning is whether every dollar of AI capex earns more than it costs to finance,” said Ninghui Liu, head of investment strategy and research for APAC at State Street Investment Management. “AI has gone from an earnings story to a balance-sheet story, and now a unit-economics story to some extent.” US crude rose 0.18% to US$103.85 a barrel and Brent rose to US$109.64 per barrel, up 0.08% on the day. Spot gold rose 0.13% to US$4,145.25 an ounce. An executive order issued by Trump on the night of Oct 16 waived key Russia-related US sanctions and tariffs, including duties on the country’s goods and penalties for buying its oil and gas. However, Trump said on Oct 17 that he has yet to announce a final decision on the matter. Inflationary pressures from elevated oil prices have put most major central banks on a tightening bias, though with a careful eye on whether economies are resilient enough to absorb higher interest rates. Recent comments from Federal Reserve officials, including Chair Kevin Warsh, suggest policymakers are in no rush to hike rates again. The US Census Bureau is due to release September figures, with housing starts expected to rise to 1.305 million from 1.275 million in August, while building permits are seen at 1.395 million compared with 1.403 million. European Central Bank (ECB) policymaker Martin Kocher is due to speak later on Oct 20, as well as ECB policymaker and Finnish central bank governor Olli Rehn. Bank of England Monetary Policy Committee member Megan Greene will deliver a speech at the London School of Economics. Euro Stoxx 50 futures fell 0.71%, DAX futures slipped 0.40% and FTSE futures dropped 0.44%. S&P e-minis were flat at 7,734.25. In cryptocurrencies, bitcoin gained 0.22% to US$82,117.01, and ether rose 0.63% to US$2,413.64. REUTERS

events.title: Four dead as torrential rain batters eastern Spain
events.summary: Cars swept away, roads submerged, residents isolated in parts of Spain’s Mediterranean coast. Four people have been killed as torrential rainfall sweeping eastern Spain triggered severe flooding, evacuations and shelter-in-place orders for tens of thousands of people, authorities said on Monday. The downpour from Storm Adam, which started on Saturday, dumped as much as 700 litres of rain (185 gallons) per square metre in 24 hours in some areas of the Valencia region. list 1 of 3 Europe swelters in latest wave of extreme heat list 2 of 3 Dangerous summers: How heatwaves and wildfires change life across Europe list 3 of 3 Floods sweep cars through streets after intense rain in Spain Floodwaters have since isolated several towns along the Mediterranean coast, while rivers have burst their banks and streets have turned into torrents, leaving scenes reminiscent of the catastrophic flooding that killed more than 230 people in the Valencia region two years ago. The storm is confirmed to have killed four people: two in the coastal resort of Oliva, a third at a beach in Sagunto, and a fourth who fell into a swollen stream in Catalonia. On Monday morning, 800,000 residents were under shelter-in-place orders, but that was reduced to 87,000 in eight municipalities by late afternoon. Security forces carried out more than 400 rescues in the Valencia region, according to government representative Pilar Bernabe. People stranded on rooftops have been winched to safety amid widespread evacuations. The storm, which also lashed the Balearic Islands and Catalonia, prompted authorities to order about 100 municipalities to remain indoors for several hours on Monday. Most restrictions were lifted by early afternoon as conditions improved, the regional government said. In Els Poblets, northeast of Alicante, cars and vans were piled on top of one another from the force of the water, as residents tried to salvage what they could from their homes. “The village, well, it’s a disaster. Some people have lost everything all over again, just like in 2007, when exactly the same thing happened,” resident Javier Fornez said. More than 2,000 people were evacuated, mainly in Oliva, and authorities carried out nearly 100 rescues in Valencia and Alicante on Monday, the Civil Guard police said. The mayor of Pego, Enrique Moll, told public regional broadcaster A Punt radio on Monday that several people were still waiting to be evacuated by helicopter from their roofs. All access routes to the town were blocked, he added. The deputy mayor of Oliva, Salvador Llopis, told state broadcaster TVE on Monday that emergency services were rescuing trapped residents, particularly elderly people stuck inside their homes with water up to their waists. National weather agency AEMET announced on Friday that last month was mainland Spain’s hottest September on record, after registering its warmest summer between June and August.
