events.title: Is this the beginning of the end of the AI stock market boom?
events.summary: After a wobble on the tech-heavy Nasdaq, some AI market observers think a reassessment of the potential value of various businesses may be under way Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast The world is holding its breath as it waits to find out whether this year’s estimated $US1tn investment in artificial intelligence is resting on a castle made of sand. Last week, the Nasdaq 100 – an index of the 100 biggest non-financial stocks on the American tech-heavy Nasdaq exchange – dropped by 5.5%, triggering the usual angst that the AI boom is about to go bust. The recent rot may have started with the failure of Firmus, an Australian datacentre company, to list on the ASX. The multi-billion dollar initial public offering was, at one stage, on track to make Firmus worth more than Telstra – even before having delivered on its promised earnings. That proved to be a fever dream of its founders and a wake-up call to investors in Australia and around the world to reconsider the potential value of similar businesses. If this is the beginning of the end of the AI boom, it is only the very beginning, and tech stocks bounced back in Wall Street trade on Monday night. Gerard Minack, of Minack Advisors, said his view was that investors were fundamentally overestimating the returns that AI providers will be able to deliver. “While I am becoming more confident that returns on AI investment will disappoint, I have no confidence calling the precise top of the AI market,” Minack said. Despite the recent wobbles, the Nasdaq 100 is still worth nearly three times more than at the start of 2023. On the S&P 500, meanwhile, tech titans Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia and Tesla now account for 35% of the American sharemarket index, up from 12% a decade ago. The total market capitalisation of the so called “magnificent seven” companies has increased by more than 50% in the past two years. Raisah Rasid, a Singapore-based global market strategist at JP Morgan Asset Management, said what she was seeing in the recent sell-off was “a valuation reset, rather than the market questioning the efficacy of AI itself”. “This is still a long-term, structural transformation trend,” Rasid said. “This is very different from the dotcom bubble.” Rasid sees two potentially more meaningful threats. First, that an open source AI model, potentially from China, could undermine the economics of AI and the hundreds of billions of dollars of investment – a concern shared by Minack. The second, said Rasid, is the risk that popular opposition gains a critical mass: for example, anger about datacentre developments or that AI will do more harm to workers and society than good. The imminent quarterly earnings season in the US will deliver the latest verdict on whether the AI companies are worth their extremely high valuations. But Minack said sharemarkets can continue to climb well after warning signs over earnings emerge. Sally Auld, NAB’s chief economist, agreed that last week’s pullback in valuations looked more like investors taking a breath rather than the entire trade running out of puff altogether. Get the most important news as it breaks “When you look back in time, every big new technology, from railroads to the internet, we always overbuild capacity. Why do we think this one will be any different?” “It suggests investors may be taking a more balanced approach. It doesn’t mean the whole thing is a disaster; there’s a reassessment under way.” The recent market action may also be evidence that investors are becoming more mindful of the risks associated with tech companies’ growing reliance on debt. Companies like Amazon, Microsoft, Google and Apple have gone on a borrowing binge to help pay for spending on datacentres and associated AI infrastructure. These American “hyperscalers” spent $US425bn in AI-related capital expenditure in 2025, Minack said, and are on track to invest $US800bn this year and over $US1.1tn in the next. Corporate bonds issued by these companies now account for nearly 10% of the global investment-grade credit market, from 0.5% at the end of 2024, according to the International Monetary Fund. The fast-growing financialisation of the AI story helps explain why the IMF last week put the bursting of the AI investment bubble at the top of a trio of risks that could threaten the global economy, alongside rapidly rising borrowing costs and the threat of a major cyber-attack. Another cause for concern in the AI market is the growing “circularity” of funding arrangements between companies – where, for example, a manufacturer agrees to help pay to build a datacentre in return for the centre owner buying its microchips. These circular financing deals are only as strong as their weakest link. “If the demand for AI is not there, then not only does the datacentre not get built, but also the chips don’t need to be made,” Auld said. “But that’s far more of an issue for the US than in Australia.

events.title: ‘Open your doors for AI’: German chancellor urges businesses to embrace AI as Nvidia announces new investments
events.summary: Nvidia named Agile Robots, Avelios Medical, Mirelo and Reflex Aerospace as investment targets, part of nearly $10 billion commitment for Europe's AI ecosystem. Merz urged German businesses, particularly SMEs, to "open your doors for AI to make use of your data." Nvidia expands collaboration with the German government on industrial AI, while Siemens announced a wider partnership with the chipmaker to advance AI-driven autonomous factories. Nvidia is increasing its investments in Europe's artificial intelligence sector, unveiling plans to back four German startups as the country pushes to strengthen its position in industrial AI. The investments are part of the U.S. chipmaker's nearly $10 billion commitment to invest in companies, universities and research institutions across Europe, as announced at the Invest in Germany Summit in Berlin on Monday. The four startups are Agile Robots, Avelios Medical, Mirelo and Reflex Aerospace. However, Nvidia did not disclose the size of the planned investments. Agile Robots develops AI-powered robots for manufacturing, logistics and healthcare, while Avelios Medical builds AI-powered hospital management software. Mirelo develops AI models that generate audio for videos, while Reflex Aerospace designs and builds satellites. The announcement comes as Germany seeks to accelerate AI adoption across its industrial sector, with Chancellor Friedrich Merz saying the country aims to become a leader in integrating AI into key sectors. Merz, who described the technology as a major opportunity for the country's economy, named manufacturing, machinery and the automotive industry for integrating AI. He also urged Germany's small- and medium-sized businesses to capitalize on the data they already hold. "Please open your doors for AI to make use of your data," Merz said. "This is a real secret and a real advantage for Germany to make use of all the data which is already available in our companies." Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang echoed Merz's remarks while highlighting Germany's expertise in manufacturing, mathematics and science, saying that AI would strengthen rather than replace the country's industrial capabilities. "AI can only augment your capability, it will not replace your capability," Huang said, describing the technology as a new instrument for businesses. Nvidia is also expanding its collaboration with the German federal government and its "Industry 4.0 Platform ," bringing together representatives from government, industry, research and trade associations, to accelerate the adoption of industrial AI. On Monday, the government signed a joint declaration of intent with Nvidia to advance AI models for industrial applications. Earlier in the day, Siemens had also announced new AI solutions developed with Nvidia at its factory in Erlangen, Germany. Siemens said the technologies could reduce engineering work involved in preparing production by up to 85%, while AI-powered production planning could cut costs by as much as 20%. Huang had also visited France last week, where he announced investments in four French startups and met with French President Emmanuel Macron to discuss AI development. The Nvidia boss is scheduled to deliver a keynote address in Berlin on Wednesday.

events.title: Walmart’s Flipkart is quietly building a food delivery challenger in India
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Flipkart, the Walmart-owned Indian e-commerce giant, is preparing to challenge India’s food-delivery duopoly of Zomato and Swiggy. It is entering a fiercely competitive market that has defeated even previous attempts by Amazon and Google to break in. The Bengaluru-based company is testing its food-delivery service internally and has expanded the trial from a few hundred employees to upwards of 8,000, according to two people familiar with the matter. It has also deployed a dedicated fleet of riders through its logistics arm, Ekart, separate from the riders who handle its quick-commerce deliveries, as it prepares for a public launch. The employee-only service appears as a separate tab on Flipkart’s main shopping app, alongside its Minutes quick-commerce offering and travel bookings, TechCrunch has learned. It draws on restaurants listed through ONDC, a government-backed network that connects online buyers and sellers across different platforms , as well as restaurants that Flipkart signed up directly. Riders wearing jerseys bearing the “Eat-in by Minutes” branding have also begun fulfilling orders on the streets of Bengaluru, the southern Indian city where Flipkart is headquartered. As Flipkart expands its food-delivery operations, it is entering a market that the brokerage firm Bernstein estimates is growing 18% to 20% a year. Online delivery, though, still accounts for just over 15% of India’s broader food-services industry. Zomato, owned by Eternal, and Swiggy together serve an estimated 85 million to 95 million paying customers a year, per Bernstein. That figure shows how dominant the two are, and how much room newcomers have to grow online food ordering in the world’s most populous country, which has more than a billion internet subscriptions. Flipkart is not the only company trying to shake up India’s food-delivery market. Ride-hailing company Rapido, which has already given Uber and its Indian rival Ola a tough fight, has been expanding Ownly, its food-delivery service that charges restaurants zero commission. Meanwhile, Swiggy has launched Toing , a separate app aimed at customers looking for cheaper meals. Both moves reflect growing pressure on the industry’s existing pricing model and the commissions that restaurants pay. “Monopoly is bad, but duopoly is more pathetic,” said Sagar Daryani, president of the New Delhi-headquartered National Restaurant Association of India, which represents over 500,000 restaurants nationwide. “What one does, the other follows suit.” Daryani argued that restaurants have long needed alternatives to the two dominant platforms. Flipkart is not the first deep-pocketed company to try breaking into India’s food-delivery market. In 2020, Amazon launched a food-ordering service in Bengaluru , but it shut the service down two years later . Google’s Areo app, which offered food ordering alongside other services, also failed to gain traction. Uber also left the market in 2020, selling its Uber Eats business in India to Zomato. Daryani sees one important difference between Flipkart and the companies that tried food delivery before it. Zomato and Swiggy built their businesses around delivering meals before expanding into quick commerce. Flipkart is doing the reverse, using its established e-commerce business and growing quick-commerce operations as a springboard into food delivery. “Flipkart’s quick commerce benefit will get passed on to food delivery, so it will be leaner, more efficient,” Daryani told TechCrunch. Restaurants are also hoping that new entrants will bring down the cost of selling meals online. Daryani, also co-founder and CEO of the dumpling chain Wow! Momo Foods, said Flipkart has proposed a base commission of about 10%, compared with the 20% to 25% that restaurants typically pay Zomato and Swiggy. Commissions are only part of the expense, though. Once advertising, discounts, and other promotional costs are factored in, restaurants can end up spending 40% to 50% of an order’s value on the established platforms, Daryani told TechCrunch. He expects Flipkart to keep that total cost closer to 15% to 16%, which could mean restaurants keep more money from each order. Nonetheless, getting restaurants on board is one thing and winning over customers is another. Bernstein estimates that new entrants could save customers just ₹20 to ₹30 (around 20–30 cents) per order by operating more efficiently, which may not be enough to draw customers away from Zomato and Swiggy. The two incumbents could also offer deeper discounts to keep them. Flipkart is not planning to stay in Bengaluru for long. The company has told restaurants that it expects to launch its food-delivery service publicly by the end of October and to expand to five or six cities by the end of this year, Daryani told TechCrunch.

events.title: Honeywell Aerospace sees business aviation growth on rising aircraft use
events.summary: Honeywell Aerospace expects global business aviation flight hours to increase about 34% through 2035. Honeywell Aerospace raised its 2026-2035 forecast to 9,950 new business jet deliveries, up 4.4%, as higher aircraft use and fleet growth support demand. It expects about 4,200 turboprop deliveries and a 29% rise in the global business aviation fleet, with flight hours up 34% by 2035. North America stays the biggest market, while Latin America and Asia-Pacific, including India, grow. Middle East conflict has disrupted flights and delayed development. MONTREAL – Honeywell Aerospace said on Oct 19 it expects 9,950 new business jet deliveries worldwide between 2026 and 2035, raising its forecast by 4.4% from 2025 as higher aircraft utilisation and fleet growth support demand. The forecast includes about 4,200 turboprop deliveries through 2035, bringing total aircraft deliveries to roughly 14,000, while the global business aviation fleet is expected to grow about 29% over the next decade. Growing demand for charter and fractional ownership is driving higher aircraft utilisation, helping support business jet demand despite economic uncertainty and geopolitical volatility . Honeywell Aerospace expects global business aviation flight hours to increase about 34% through 2035, outpacing fleet growth as operators make greater use of shared-use models. “Business aircraft owners and operators are consistently flying more, ordering new business jets, expanding fleets and investing in innovations that are driving growth across the sector,” said Linnea Whisler, president of Commercial Original Equipment at Honeywell Aerospace. The company said North America remained the largest business aviation market, while demand was growing in Latin America and parts of Asia-Pacific, including India. However, it noted that conflict in the Middle East has disrupted flight operations and paused development activity in the region. REUTERS

In an Oct 20 press statement, the Singapore Exchange (SGX)-listed company said it welcomed a thorough, evidence-based examination of the ongoing fires and haze situation, and reiterated that it strictly enforces a longstanding zero-burning policy across its operations. It added that it is confident that an objective review of the available evidence would show that it does not clear land using fire, either directly or indirectly. In its statement, First Resources said assessments of where fires originated should be based on verified facts, scientific evidence and a comprehensive understanding of conditions on the ground. The group, which has a market value of $6 billion in Singapore, welcomed documentary and technical reviews, as well as on-the-ground verification where necessary, to provide an accurate picture of the situation. Evidence may include the chronology of hot-spot detections and fire progression based on satellite imagery, documentary evidence of the actions taken to suppress and extinguish fires, and spatial analyses demonstrating the continued protection of conservation areas, it said. First Resources also said it was open to constructive suggestions from regulators, customers, investors, civil society organisations and other industry stakeholders on strengthening fire prevention and management. “Addressing the complex challenge of transboundary haze requires sustained collaboration among governments, companies, local communities and other stakeholders,” it said. First Resources ’ statement comes after the company said on Oct 16 that fires from outside its boundaries had spread into areas under its management, and had not originated from its concessions. It said some fires had become too large and fast-moving to contain despite its firefighting efforts. Other SGX-listed companies, including Golden Agri Resources, Bumitama Agri, Wilmar International, Kencana Agri, Indofood Agri, have also issued similar statements after receiving queries from SGX RegCo over their operations and potential ties to the haze. TSH Resources has yet to respond. Senior Minister K. Shanmugam told reporters on Oct 19 that statements from the companies – no matter how well drafted, are not good enough. Shanmugam, who is also Coordinating Minister for National Security and Minister for Home Affairs, added that the Government will “ask for the full facts, consider all evidence fairly and act based on the facts”. Kang Wan Chern is deputy business editor at The Straits Times.

events.title: Nvidia-backed Nscale, Anthropic in talks for new US$45 billion AI cloud deal, source says
events.summary: The data centre developer is seeking another major deal with Anthropic for a second facility in West Virginia. Nscale is in talks with Anthropic for a new US$45 billion AI cloud deal at its West Virginia Monarch campus, Reuters said. The second building could add 460 megawatts using Nvidia Vera Rubin chips. Anthropic already agreed in August to spend US$45 billion on Nscale cloud power, and may also get first refusal on a third Monarch building. The deal is not final and terms could still change. The talks come as investors question heavy debt used to build AI infrastructure. Nscale also faces setbacks after Microsoft pulled out of a flagship data centre deal over power delays. Nscale is in talks to sell AI computing power to Claude maker Anthropic in a new deal that could be worth about US$45 billion (S$58 billion) , a person familiar with the matter told Reuters on Oct 19 . The data centre developer is seeking another major deal with the AI lab for a second facility at its Monarch data centre campus in West Virginia, the person said. In August, Anthropic struck a deal to spend US$45 billion to ​rent AI cloud computing power from Nscale’s West ‌Virginia data centre campus. A second Monarch building would deliver 460 megawatts of computing power using Nvidia’s advanced Vera Rubin AI chips, according to the source. Anthropic did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment. Anthropic also has the right of first refusal on Monarch’s expected third building, the person said, adding discussions were ongoing and details of the plan could change. Bloomberg, which first reported the news, also said a cohort of investors had urged Anthropic to lower its IPO valuation target after a series of market setbacks for AI companies. Investors have sharpened scrutiny of companies that are increasingly turning to debt-driven AI infrastructure expansion. Last week, Nscale rival CoreWeave’s shares slumped amid concerns over its US$50 billion debt load, fuelling a global selloff in AI stocks. The news of a potential tie-up comes after Microsoft pulled out of a deal to anchor a flagship data centre for Nscale following power ​connection delays that pushed its expected supply date into the 2030s. Nscale has grown rapidly since ⁠launch, increasing ​its total contracted value from US$100 million to more than US$103 ​billion in two-and-a-half years and competing with Nebius, Crusoe and Lambda. events.title: JD Vance refrains from endorsing Israeli leader Netanyahu as Trump offers praise
events.summary: Vance says he is neither “anti-endorsing” nor “pro-endorsing” Netanyahu as he endorses American candidates and is focused on the midterms. Vance refrained from backing Netanyahu even though Trump praised the Israeli leader for the country's war effort. Vance has in the past campaigned for foreign leaders. U.S. Vice President JD Vance declined to endorse Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu , after President Donald Trump offered his backing for the leader's reelection bid next week. "The president has the most effective endorsement in American or international political history," Vance said in an interview on Mark Halperin's 2WAY Tonight published Monday. "I endorse American candidates, and that's where I'm focused on in the midterms," he said. Vance said he was not criticizing Netanyahu: "I'm not anti-endorsing him. I'm not pro-endorsing him," he said, adding that "I'm not getting involved in Israeli elections." Those remarks diverge from the approach by President Donald Trump, who gave the Israeli prime minister his backing in the election next week. Trump on Sunday praised Netanyahu, the country's longest-serving prime minister, on Truth Social as "a Great Warrior Prime Minister , and an even greater Partner for Peace in combating the Islamic Republic of Iran." In a social media post, Netanyahu thanked Trump for his "tremendous support and work together." Vance has weighed in on foreign politics before. He campaigned in Budapest in April to publicly endorse then-Prime Minister Viktor Orban's reelection bid. Orban was later voted out after 16 years in power. Last year in Munich for a security conference, Vance met Alice Weidel, the leader of Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany party, which Elon Musk was also boosting at the time. The Israeli vote next week will be the first national election since Hamas attacked Israel in late 2023. The comments also come as U.S. public support for Israel, historically strong among both Republicans and Democrats, has fallen sharply . There has also been vigorous debate in America about the Netanyahu-led government's response to the Hamas attack. In June, Vance said that Israel has almost no friends left in the world and should think hard before turning on the one it has.

events.title: The human cost of surging US air strikes in Somalia
events.summary: Families recount deaths, injuries and displacement as Trump accelerates US strikes against armed groups in Somalia. Mogadishu, Somalia – Nearly a year after a suspected US strike in southern Somalia left shrapnel embedded in her son’s body, Maryam Haji Abdi Guled still feels compelled to accompany him to school. She fears another child might push him while playing, disturbing a fragment of metal lodged near his hip. Doctors have warned that removing it could leave him paralysed. list 1 of 3 Somalia won’t accept Israeli presence ‘under any circumstances’: President list 2 of 3 Four African leaders issue joint declaration as Ethiopia war escalates list 3 of 3 Labour fends off the Green party in closely watched UK by-election “I hold his hand, take him to school, and I bring him back myself. I watch over him,” she told Al Jazeera. Her son, Abdiqadir Salah, was seven when he was injured during a November 2025 military offensive involving United States air strikes and Somali ground forces around Jamaame, in Somalia’s southern Jubaland state. Maryam is among several survivors interviewed by Al Jazeera in recent months who say family members were killed or seriously injured during the offensive. Their accounts describe deaths, displacement, lost livelihoods and injuries that continue to shape their lives. Their testimonies come as US air operations against armed rebel groups in Somalia have intensified sharply under President Donald Trump. Public records from the US Africa Command (AFRICOM) listed 84 strikes in Somalia through September 2026, while the New America Foundation, which independently tracks the campaign, documented 88 over the same period. The US military has acknowledged conducting air strikes in the area on November 14 and 15, 2025. But it disputes allegations that its aircraft caused civilian casualties. AFRICOM told Al Jazeera it had completed an assessment of reports that US operations killed between 10 and 12 civilians and destroyed homes and businesses in Jamaame. It concluded that the information reviewed did not meet the military’s “more likely than not” threshold for determining that US air strikes had caused the reported harm. That finding does not establish that US strikes caused no harm. Rather, AFRICOM said the evidence did not establish that US operations were more likely than not to have caused the reported casualties and damage. Al Jazeera asked whether investigators had spoken to survivors, relatives of those killed, hospital staff, local authorities or other witnesses. AFRICOM did not say whether they had done so. The command said the assessment could be reopened if new information emerged that might change its findings. The conclusion contrasts with accounts from families who say they witnessed the bombardment and with independent monitoring reports documenting civilian deaths and mass displacement during the offensive. For those who lost loved ones or were left caring for seriously injured relatives, whether they will ever obtain justice remains unresolved. Maryam remembers the morning aircraft appeared over Jamaame. She was preparing breakfast after her children returned from school when they heard a roar overhead. Aircraft had become so common that the family no longer regarded the sound as unusual. “The aircraft never leave us, night or day, and we have become accustomed to them,” she said. Her children ran outside towards the noise. Maryam followed, intending to bring them back inside before the family fled. Then a munition struck nearby, followed by another explosion near the front door. More bombardment followed around the house. Maryam believes the attack on her home was carried out by US drones that had been circling over the town before the bombardment. Ugaas Ahmed Ugaas Said Ali, a Bimaal clan chief who had been in contact with families affected by the attacks, said the suffering extended far beyond those who had managed to leave Jamaame. “Maryam is one of the fortunate people who has been able to obtain medical care. There are many injured people left in the town from that offensive who haven’t been able to make it to Mogadishu,” he said. Maryam recalled one munition hitting the ground without exploding, while other strikes killed people nearby. Amid the explosions, she became separated from her children. Three of her six children were wounded, including Abdiqadir, who suffered the most serious injuries. It took her a day and a night to reach medical care in Mogadishu. During the journey, which lasted more than 24 hours, her son bled and struggled with pain. Her experience was one of several reported during days of fighting in and around Jamaame. According to Jubaland authorities, Somali government and regional forces, including the US-trained Danab commando unit, launched operations against positions held by the armed group al-Shabab in villages surrounding the town. The authorities said at least 56 al-Shabab fighters were killed and 20 captured.

events.title: Top venture capitalist Jenny Lee says Asian startups are speeding toward IPOs
events.summary: The timeline for startups to do initial public offerings has accelerated, according to Granite Asia's Jenny Lee. "At the very early stage ... we do see a lot more funding activity," Lee said. Granite Asia is concentrating on areas including artificial intelligence for creation, AI for science, concepts around Asian subcultures, and robotics, Lee said. Newly formed companies are reaching the initial public offering stage far sooner than they used to, according to venture capitalist Jenny Lee. In the West, companies like to stay private a little longer, but Asian firms are leaning toward a more accelerated timeline, according to Lee, senior managing partner at Granite Asia and the first woman to break into the top 10 of the Forbes Global 100 VC Midas list. "On average the holding period before a company goes public is eight to 10 years," Lee said in an interview on the sidelines of the DBS Asia Future Forward Conference last week in Singapore. "But currently, the later stage companies we are seeing are actually preparing for IPOs when they are four to five years old." Investment platform Granite Asia works with startups from their first round through public listings, and in both equity and credit. Lee said the firm has made more than 40 equity investments in the last two years. "At the very early stage ... we do see a lot more funding activity," Lee said. She added that companies in later stages of investment are seeing productivity gains and getting profitable faster. Granite Asia is concentrating on areas including artificial intelligence for science, and robotics, Lee said. It is also interested in concepts around Asian subcultures such as apps that would appeal in India specifically, or AI tools that help create Japanese content. Also, "we are looking at companies that have energy-related technology, say in storage, to help with the energy issue," she said. "Many of the countries in Asia import a huge percentage of their energy needs, and so as the countries grow onto a path to adopt more renewables, it's then important to have storage technology."

events.title: Beyond money: Why young Tunisians are considering emigration
events.summary: For many young Tunisians, the question is no longer simply how to make a living, but where they can build a future. Tunis, Tunisia – For Maher Qassem, the phrase “beyond money” sums up why he is considering leaving his country. After years of working in the media and trying to secure a stable life for his family, he is now thinking of starting over abroad. Buying a home and planning for a better future have given way to more immediate concerns: covering monthly expenses and meeting mounting financial commitments. Speaking to Al Jazeera, Qassem says almost his entire salary goes towards loan repayments, rent and his son’s education. At times, he adds, he has been unable to help his sick mother pay for medication and treatment. Qassem is among many young Tunisians who see little meaningful change in their daily lives. Seven years into President Kais Saied’s rule, he worries about his son’s prospects and the quality of life the country can offer future generations. Others, however, continue to trust the president. Tunisians remain divided between those who believe the past several years have failed to deliver the change they hoped for and those who still believe reform is possible. These contrasting views unfold against a backdrop of persistent economic difficulties. Ghaith remembers the excitement surrounding the 2019 presidential election and the expectations raised by Saied’s victory. He was 19 at the time, had little interest in politics, and did not vote. But he recalls the hope that accompanied the president’s election. Seven years later, Ghaith says, little has changed in his own life. The cost-of-living pressures that existed then remain, he tells Al Jazeera, while ordinary citizens continue to face recurring difficulties obtaining some essential goods and services. He is also frustrated by the authorities’ communication with the public. Tunisians want clearer answers about government policies and the results they are expected to deliver, he says. They also want accountability and a clear vision for the future. For Qassem, the reasons for leaving extend beyond economic hardship. He believes working as a journalist has become more difficult, too. Not everyone has lost faith in the president. Mohamed Amine, a taxi driver in his 30s, voted for Saied in the most recent presidential election and remains convinced that he can improve the country’s situation. The president is “sincere in his intentions” and wants change, Amine tells Al Jazeera. He believes, however, that various obstacles have hindered Saied’s reform programme. It is too early to judge the outcome, he says. The president should be given more time. Unemployment, particularly among young people and university graduates, remains a major challenge in Tunisia. According to the National Institute of Statistics, the unemployment rate stood at 14.9 percent in the second quarter of 2026, with approximately 622,000 people out of work. The situation is more severe among younger Tunisians. Unemployment among people aged 15 to 24 reached 35.4 percent, while the rate among university graduates stood at 26.6 percent. Among female university graduates, it was 35.6 percent, compared with 14.2 percent among men. The desire to leave is widespread. A study by Afrobarometer, an independent African research network that conducts public-opinion surveys across the continent, found that around two-thirds of young Tunisians had considered emigrating. The proportion who said they thought about leaving “a lot” rose from 38 percent in 2018 to 51 percent in 2024. Among young people considering emigration, 59 percent cited better job opportunities as their main motivation. The findings point to frustration among a section of Tunisia’s youth and growing concerns about the prospects for professional and social stability at home. The desire to leave extends beyond young people seeking their first jobs. Tunisia is also losing qualified professionals trained in the country. Kamel Sahnoun, head of the Tunisian Order of Engineers, said at a press conference organised by the professional body that approximately 6,500 engineers left Tunisia in 2022 alone. The figure compares with an annual average of about 3,000 in 2013 and 2014, highlighting the scale of the departure of skilled workers. The healthcare sector is also losing professionals. Figures from the Tunisian Agency for Technical Cooperation show that 1,839 healthcare and paramedical professionals were recruited to work abroad in 2023. Another 1,022 were recruited during the first nine months of 2024, followed by 1,244 in 2025. The figures, alongside international demand for Tunisian expertise, reflect the search for better working and living conditions abroad. Hamza, a 26-year-old software engineer working for a foreign company, earns what he describes as a good income. Yet he is seriously considering leaving Tunisia. “It’s no longer just about money,” he tells Al Jazeera.

( ABC Eyre Peninsula: Jodie Hamilton ) SA Water says delays on the Eyre Peninsula Desalination Plant will push the delivery of clean water past its original 2026 deadline. Critics argue the setbacks will result in significant budget and time overruns. SA Water says fresh drinking water will now be available to the region by mid-2027. Work on a desalination plant in regional South Australia has been delayed by six months, past when the region was due to run out of clean drinking water. SA Water has announced construction on the Eyre Peninsula Desalination Plant will be pushed back six months, to mid-2027, due to harder-than-usual granite affecting its underground boring Consumer access to water will be "unchanged". Residents of Port Lincoln and its surrounding areas were told they could run out of clean drinking water by 2026. The 35,000 residents of the Eyre Peninsula draw drinking water from the Uley South Basin, which has been depleting at a rate described as "dire" by the state government. The state government funded the then-$330 million Eyre Peninsula Desalination Plant project, which is now expected to cost approximately $470 million, at the Billy Lights Point coastal reserve. Early works began in February 2025 and it was projected to deliver fresh water by the end of this year. "We're a bit behind where we'd like to be," SA Water sustainable infrastructure general manager Peter Seltsikas said. Peter Seltsikas says tunnelling delays have pushed out the plant's completion date. ( ABC News: Brant Cumming ) "The pipelines are done, the desalination plant is substantially complete. "But the tunnelling delay means the first water day is pushing out to the middle of next year." Mr Seltsikas said higher-than-usual rains this year across the Eyre Peninsula had increased the water levels of the Uley South Basin. "We have enough water this year to continue to supply our customers and when the desalination plant comes next year they'll continue to have secure water." Cost blowouts and security concerns Glen Ingham was the spokesperson for community action group Hands Off Boston Bay, which was opposed to the location of the desalination plant. He said the delays were testing the government's claims the site is the "cheapest and quickest" option. Glen Ingham was the spokesperson for Hands Off Boston Bay. ( ABC Eyre Peninsula: Jodie Hamilton ) "Here we are now at the end of 2026 and they're [pushing the end date] to the middle of next year. "I'm certain it will be beyond that and the cost blowout will be huge," he said. In a statement, the state government said the revised budget of the project would be detailed once "contractual processes with delivery partners are complete". Mr Seltsikas said the authority recognised the ongoing need to reduce water being taken from the basin. "So we are very much concerned about water security," he said. The state government said a revised Water Allocation Plan for the Southern Basins meant SA Water could extract water from the Uley South Basin and River Murray to meet consumer demand. SA Water's groundwater allocation will reduce to 3.5 gigalitres per year in 2027-28, as the plant comes online. A spokesperson said "it is not expected that water restrictions will be needed".

events.title: South Korean data centre firm Elice shares plunge in IPO debut
events.summary: Elice shares fell as much as 32% on their Kosdaq debut after South Korea’s biggest IPO of 2026 raised 201 billion won (S$192.92 million) and valued the firm above one trillion won. The weak start tests demand for AI infrastructure stocks, as global peers face lower valuations, cancelled listings and investor doubts about high spending on AI. Elice won strong retail support and reported sharp revenue and profit growth. It plans to use IPO funds to build more AI data centres in South Korea and overseas. Data centre infrastructure company Elice plunged in its trading debut on South Korea’s tech-heavy Kosdaq market after raising 201 billion won ( S$192.92 million) in the stock exchange’s biggest initial public offering in 2026 . The debut is a test of investor appetite for the sector after a series of setbacks around the world. Firmus Grid cancelled its high-profile Sydney listing in October as concerns over borrowing costs, fierce competition and long-term returns from massive AI-related spending weigh on valuations. Coreweave’s shares have more than halved since their May peak, AirTrunk is delaying a planned IPO of a real estate investment trust, people familiar with the matter have said. Meanwhile, Nscale is facing pushback over its target IPO valuation, Bloomberg News reported. “Elice’s debut comes at a time when sentiment toward AI infrastructure companies has weakened, particularly in the US,” said Albert Yong, managing partner and chief investment officer at Petra Capital Management. “Sentiment toward AI infrastructure has been highly volatile and often disconnected from underlying fundamentals.” Elice was able to generate demand among South Korean retail investors, who poured roughly 10.3 trillion won into subscription deposits in hopes of buying shares. The retail offering was oversubscribed more than 400 times. To win over investors, Elice touted a 200% surge in first-half revenue to 34.4 billion won, according to its prospectus. The company swung to an operating profit of 10.3 billion won, while earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation jumped more than 11-fold to 23.2 billion won. The company is expected to record an 83% sales jump in 2026 and an operating margin of about 33%, analyst Douglas Kim wrote in a note on Smartkarma. “While it’s a company that already posts operating profit with the AI cloud business and it plans to respond to private-sector demand with the IPO proceeds, it remains to be seen whether the company can maintain its current profitability,” said Kim Do-joon, chief executive of Zian Investment Management. “Investor sentiment may have weakened due to CoreWeave, but its financial structure is quite different from CoreWeave, so I don’t think investors need to view the company as particularly risky.” Founded in 2015 by three students in the doctorate programme of Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology , one of the country’s top technology universities, Elice began as a coding education platform before pivoting to AI cloud infrastructure, supplying products including servers, liquid-cooled chips, cloud and networking equipment and software. The company has since developed a modular data centre platform with high-density power systems and advanced liquid cooling designed for high-performance AI chip clusters. A successful offering would help break an IPO drought in South Korea, where the primary market has been in the doldrums as fund-raising surged across Asia. First-time listings in Seoul have raised US$1.4 billion ( S$1.79 billion ) in 2026, compared with more than $3 billion in each of the previous three years, according to Bloomberg-compiled data. Meanwhile, SK Hynix completed the biggest-ever US share sale by a foreign company. Backed by venture capital firms including Vertex Ventures and Altos Ventures, Elice plans to use its IPO proceeds to build more AI data centres around South Korea and abroad, according to chief executive Jae-won Kim. Mirae Asset Securities and Samsung Securities served as lead underwriters. “We’re going all-in on becoming a full-stack AI infrastructure leader globally,” Kim said in an interview. “This IPO is about giving ourselves the financial firepower to execute.” BLOOMBERG

events.title: Asia’s wealth transfer to next generation puts family unity to the test: Report
events.summary: Differing valuation expectations is the most frequently cited source of family misalignment that could derail a family’s exit. Asia’s ageing founders are passing wealth to the next generation, but most families are not ready. Only 3.5% of advisers said clients are fully prepared for a sale or transfer. Family conflict is a major risk. The report said valuation gaps, future plans, legacy worries and timing can derail exits, while only 8.4% of Asia respondents said the next generation has an equal say. Most wealthy Asian families prefer a single family office after exit. It helps manage complex wealth, and advisers say early succession talks can protect both wealth and the entrepreneurial spirit. SINGAPORE – As Asia’s first-generation entrepreneurs grow older and prepare to hand over their businesses to the next generation, many are not yet ready for the transition. Key questions around who will lead the business next, how ownership should be distributed, when the founding generation should step back and on whose terms are not addressed openly enough in succession planning, said the latest Julius Baer Family Barometer report. These questions become even more commercially consequential when a business sale is on the table. They can shape valuations, negotiations, and a family’s readiness to act when an opportunity arises, it said. Just 3.5% of wealth professionals advising Asia-based clients said most business-owning families they advise are fully ready for a sale or transfer. Globally, the figure is just as low, at 2.3%. Differing valuation expectations is the most frequently cited source of family misalignment that could derail a family’s exit. This is followed by disagreement over the business’s future, emotional attachment, legacy concerns, and timing, the report said. The Barometer surveyed more than 700 advisers to ultra-wealthy families worldwide, capturing their assessments of their clients rather than the families’ own views. The professionals included relationship managers, tax and legal specialists, family-office professionals, wealth planners, investment advisers and consultants. Asia has the lowest level of active involvement by the next generation in carrying out plans for what happens to a family business or wealth after it is sold. Only 8.4% of respondents report the next generation as having an equal say. In most cases, the next generation is consulted but has no formal vote, is involved in limited discussions or is not consulted at all. More than 75% of advisers to wealthy families in the region said the wealthy prefer to set up a single family office to manage their wealth after an exit. Others may consider creating a family investment vehicle or entity, as well as a new business. A single family office helps families manage increasingly complex finances by overseeing investments, consolidating financial reports and handling administrative matters in one place. Families often retain strategic decision-making while relying on external specialists for investments management and non-investment functions. “Unless you are a large-scale family office with substantial resources, it is difficult to build dedicated teams across every asset class, as well as manage non-investment functions such as legal affairs, operations, and estate planning. Most families will need external expertise in some areas.” said Christos Anagnostopoulos, head of family office solutions and advisory for Asia at Julius Baer. Some Asian founders who are not ready to retire following a sale would separate their wealth into different pools: one professionally managed for long-term preservation and another reserved for new ventures and direct investments. That allows them to remain entrepreneurial while ensuring the majority of the wealth is managed in a disciplined way. “The result is a distinctly Asian model of post-exit wealth management. Families are professionalising the way wealth is owned and managed without losing the entrepreneurial mindset that created it in the first place,” said Anagnostopoulos. The report found that families in Asia and the Middle East place greater emphasis on long-term growth, while capital preservation ranks highest in Europe and Latin America. Succession planning is the leading family priority for the wealthy across Asia as well as the rest of the world. Jimmy Lee, member of the global wealth management committee and region head for Asia at Julius Baer, said the most prepared families are those that make succession a shared strategic priority well before a transaction becomes relevant. “Involving the next generation early and agreeing on the family’s long-term goals can help reserve both the wealth and the entrepreneurial spirit that built it,” Lee said. Early dialogue helps establish whether younger generations want and are prepared to take over. After succession planning, other priorities include building a family legacy, and individual and family growth opportunities.

events.title: Mamdani says feds have abdicated on AI, urges New Yorkers to push back
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Two of New York’s sweethearts, Mayor Zohran Mamdani and activist and “Broad City” star Ilana Glazer, spoke about AI at Webster Hall in Manhattan on Monday night, with Glazer posing questions to the mayor about the future of AI in society. Mamdani encouraged New Yorkers to resist the overwhelming feeling that AI is inevitably coming for their jobs, their kids’ minds, and their dignity, and to take back control instead. His message came at a moment when the federal government is doing little to regulate AI, leaving cities to act on their own. At The People’s AI Assembly, an event hosted by the AI Now Institute , a think tank that explores the social implications of AI, Mamdani argued that the technology’s rapid rollout is not inevitable and that public officials should hold AI companies accountable. Last month, Mamdani ordered a ban on AI use in elementary and middle schools. Glazer, a parent, said the technology’s arrival in classrooms unsettles her. “It just makes me nervous. It feels so non-consensual, as though…this has to be in schools. It wasn’t two years ago. Why does it have to be in schools?” she said. Over the summer, the mayor also introduced a policy that would require landlords, brokers, and real estate platforms to clearly disclose when a property’s listing photos or videos are made with AI. The policy is aimed at protecting New Yorkers from getting “house-phished,” or tricked by misleading listings. Both moves challenge the assumption that schools and the public must simply accept AI as it arrives. “Nothing has to be,” Mamdani said at the event Monday. “There’s a creep that comes with this, and there’s an intent to overwhelm that leaves people feeling as if there is simply no option.” He said there has been a “reckless adoption of technology without any kind of a reckoning with the limitations of that technology,” citing the U.S. military’s February strike on a school in Iran that killed more than 150 people, including at least 123 children . Officials involved in the Pentagon’s internal investigation have told Bloomberg that overreliance on AI in targeting was one factor in the attack. “There is this desire to speak about [AI] as if it is infallible, as if it cannot be questioned, as if the only people who can regulate it are the ones who are currently developing it,” Mamdani said, noting that Facebook made similar arguments back in 2008. “What it really is,’ he continued, “is an attempt to escape any kind of accountability at any level, without also jeopardizing the potential valuation from an IPO.” Anthropic is expected to debut on the public markets this year, and OpenAI has said it will go public in 2027. Mamdani criticized the “complete abdication of federal law” when it comes to AI. “At a national level, when the conversation is about artificial intelligence, it’s so often framed in this language of an arms race with China, and any of the humanistic concern, we just push to the side in a language of national competition,” the mayor said. President Donald Trump’s Superintelligence Task Force , announced earlier this month, largely focuses on allowing powerful AI companies to self-regulate, rather than creating new federal restrictions. That comes despite growing fears about AI’s effect on every facet of human life, including warnings from whistleblowers at Anthropic, Google DeepMind, and OpenAI that AI could lead to human extinction. “As we are looking at what comes after this federal administration, there has to be a very different kind of framework in how we think about AI, talk about AI, the accountability we’re willing to bring forward when it comes to that,” Mamdani said. events.title: El-Sayed pushes back at Republicans who judge him because he ‘might pray differently’
events.summary: The News MARQUETTE, Mich. — Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed on Thursday night accused President Donald Trump and Republican rival Mike Rogers of using his Muslim faith as a political cudgel. “Judge me by my actions and my work, but please do not assume that because I might pray differently than anybody who’s ever held this office, that somehow I am not deeply committed to this Constitution,” El-Sayed said in response to a question from Semafor. Republicans have recently amplified claims that El-Sayed and his family have ties to the Muslim Brotherhood. Trump posted a video Thursday night that directly called El-Sayed a member of the group, which was founded in Egypt; his administration has designated chapters as terrorist organizations. El-Sayed, an American of Egyptian descent who would be the first Muslim senator if elected, has rankled at the GOP accusations, including in a recent TV interview . His comments on Thursday are as close as he has come on the campaign trail to alleging Islamophobia by his opponents. “They don’t want to talk about any of the other issues that people are actually experiencing in their lives. They want to talk about me or point to my mom or my sister,” El-Sayed said. “My mom and my sister are not running for office. I’m running for office.” El-Sayed called it “an insane thing to assume” that members of his family were part of the Muslim Brotherhood, saying he didn’t “know what my mother was doing in Egypt in the 1970s.” Republicans have cited social media posts from his half-sister that appear to refer to his mother’s engagement with the group. “My parents got divorced when I was very young — 3,” El-Sayed said. “I didn’t see my mom for years after I was raised by my dad and my stepmom, and when I was asked, [to] the best of my knowledge, nobody in my family’s been a member of this organization.” Know More El-Sayed said insinuating he might not be loyal to the Constitution because of his faith was “the same thing that was done to JFK when they tried to say that, ‘Oh, well, he’s going to answer to the Pope because he’s Catholic.’ Same thing they tried to do to President Obama.” John F. Kennedy, the first Roman Catholic president, faced some false accusations of “dual loyalties” because of his faith. And the hard right pushed conspiracy theories about the religious practices of Obama, who is a Christian and was the first Black president. El-Sayed was campaigning in Michigan’s Upper Peninsula this week as part of a swing with progressive Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y. El-Sayed and Democrats are hoping they can grow the electorate in what has traditionally been redder territory in the state. events.title: Saudi Arabia cancels 2026 ‘Davos in the Desert’ amid Houthi attacks
events.summary: Riyadh postpones flagship investment conference until 2027, orders government staff to work from home. Saudi Arabia’s Future Investment Initiative (FII) conference has been postponed until next year, according to a statement on the official website, as deadly strikes by the Iran-backed Houthis against the kingdom continue. The annual event was due to start next week on October 26 and run through October 29, with a date next year to be announced “very soon”, the statement released on Tuesday said. list 1 of 3 Saudi-led forces try to break Houthi siege of Taiz with airstrikes list 2 of 3 Fighting intensifies across Yemen as humanitarian crisis deepens list 3 of 3 Iran support for Houthis probed as Yemen war re-erupts and Saudi cities hit FII Institute chief executive officer Dr Maha Bint Mishari Al Saud said the decision “comes from a deep commitment to our partners, members, speakers and delegates”. “Because this is our landmark tenth edition, we want to ensure it delivers the full scale, extraordinary quality, and unforgettable impact that our community has come to expect and truly deserves,” she said. Informally dubbed “Davos in the Desert”, a nod to the World Economic Forum’s annual meeting in Switzerland, the state-backed conference showcases the kingdom’s ambitious investment plans in a bid to attract billions of dollars needed to fund its economic transformation away from hydrocarbons towards tourism, sport and technology. Expected speakers included: Alphabet & Google’s president and chief information officer, Ruth Porat; Goldman Sachs Group chairman and CEO David Solomon; and BlackRock chairman and CEO Laurence Fink, according to the FII website. Fighting between a Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognised government and the Iran-aligned Houthis has escalated in recent weeks. The Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah, have hit military, energy and civilian infrastructure across Saudi Arabia, including Riyadh’s international airport , killing at least 18 people and injuring hundreds more. Government agencies in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, have told employees to work from home, one worker and two consultants told the AFP news agency, as the city comes under repeated attack from the Houthis. The Kingdom Centre, a 99‑storey tower in downtown Riyadh that houses the International Monetary Fund’s regional office, also requested workers stay away until further notice. On Sunday, an employee of a government agency in the capital received a message saying, “It has been decided to implement remote work from Monday to Thursday this week”. The message added: “We ask everyone to continue their activities as normal.” Companies based in the King Abdullah Financial District, which hosts offices of major United States firms, have also asked employees to work from home, according to other sources.

events.title: Keppel Reit to buy 51% stake in Keppel South Central for $610.9 million
events.summary: The total value of the 33-storey Keppel South Central in the central business district stands at about $1.2 billion. Keppel Reit will buy a 51% stake in Keppel South Central for $610.9 million, lifting its Singapore office exposure and raising its presence in the CBD to 82%. The 33-storey Grade A building is valued at about $1.2 billion. The deal needs unit-holder approval and is expected to complete in Q2 2027. Keppel Reit expects a 2.01% distribution per unit uplift and a 4.3% yield. It also has a five-year income guarantee of $2.23 million a month from K-Commercial Investment. SINGAPORE – Keppel Reit is buying a 51% stake in Keppel South Central from its sponsor Keppel for a purchase consideration of $610.9 million, strengthening its footprint in Singapore’s prime office market, it said on Oct 20. The total value of the 33-storey Grade A commercial building in the central business district (CBD) stands at about $1.2 billion. With 522,500 sq ft of net lettable area, this translates to an overall building valuation of about $2,350 per square foot (psf). Based on this total valuation, the agreed property value for Keppel Reit’s 51% interest on a 70-year leasehold basis is $626.2 million. “The proposed acquisition of Keppel South Central increases our presence in Singapore to 82%,” said Chua Hsien Yang, CEO of Keppel Reit Management. It also “reinforces Keppel Reit’s leading position in this supply-constrained CBD office market, which continues to benefit from resilient business demand and limited new supply”, he added. Completion of the deal will be subject to the approval of unit holders at an extraordinary general meeting, expected to be held in the fourth quarter of 2026 . The transaction, which includes repayment of $462.1 million in existing shareholder loans, is expected to be completed in Q2 2027 . Keppel Reit said the acquisition offers a pro forma distribution per unit accretion of 2.01% and an “attractive” initial property yield of 4.3%. Had the proposed acquisition of Keppel South Central and both the divestments of T Tower and KR Ginza II been completed on June 30, Keppel Reit’s portfolio occupancy would be 93.9% with a weighted average lease expiry of 4.5 years, it said. Its portfolio would comprise 13 properties with a total value of about $12.1 billion across Singapore and Australia. An arrangement with Keppel’s wholly owned subsidiary K-Commercial Investment will provide the Reit with a guaranteed monthly income of $2.23 million for up to five years – supported by current rents at the property. Committed leases and leases which are in the process of documentation for Keppel South Central comprised 52.7% of net lettable area at an average rent of about S$11.30 psf per month as at Sept 30. This is above the rent of $11.15 psf per month assumed under the arrangement, said Keppel Reit management. The average rent “largely reflects leasing activity on the lower-to-mid floors, with potential for higher rents from the remaining available space on the mid-to-high floors”, it added. As at Oct 15, committed leases and leases in the process of documentation for Keppel South Central increased to about 60%. Keppel Reit’s manager said it intends to fund the acquisition through a combination of bank loans, perpetual securities, internal cash and/or equity financing, with post-acquisition aggregate leverage expected to be 39.2%. Units of Keppel Reit closed flat at 82.5 cents on Oct 19 . THE BUSINESS TIMES

It will jack up the price of its Kando Jacket, a lightweight, high-performance jacket designed for ease of movement, from 6,990 yen (S$56.4) to 7,990 yen on Nov 10. Moreover, the retailer will end its practice of offering discounted multi-pair deals on socks. In total, prices will rise for 11 products in November. Uniqlo also raised prices on some products in September, along with shipping fees and charges for clothing alterations, including hemming pants and shortening shirt sleeves. events.title: OpenAI seeks to accelerate fund-raising ahead of Anthropic IPO, sources say
events.summary: AI giants OpenAI and Anthropic are increasingly tapping into a similar investor base. OpenAI is rushing a US$30 billion fundraising before Anthropic’s expected IPO, aiming for a valuation above US$1.4 trillion and to secure capital from the same investors. The company says revenue rose after GPT-6 Astra, reaching US$50 billion annualised and targeting US$70 billion by year-end, while also needing funds for infrastructure and a possible 2027 listing. The race reflects wider market jitters, with AI valuations under pressure, IPO plans delayed, and investors comparing OpenAI and Anthropic’s growth, pricing and accounting methods. NEW YORK – OpenAI is racing to secure investor commitments before rival Anthropic’s expected public market debut in mid-November, in an unusually fast fund-raising that could value the ChatGPT maker at more than US$1.4 trillion ( S$1.79 trillion ), according to two sources familiar with the matter. The rapid timetable reflects, in part, a desire to get ahead of Anthropic as the two frontier labs are increasingly tapping a similar investor base, the sources said, adding that OpenAI wants to capitalise on its recent revenue growth after launching new models. SoftBank Group, Abu Dhabi-based MGX and other existing backers of OpenAI are in talks to join the round of about US$30 billion, one of the sources said. The acceleration underscores how closely the two AI developers are competing for capital as both pursue trillion-dollar price tags, amid growing concern about rising interest rates, significant volatility in technology stocks and rising scrutiny of artificial intelligence valuations. OpenAI held meetings with long-only funds and sovereign wealth funds last week while Anthropic was hosting its own investor day. OpenAI’s funding round is expected to move faster than is typical for an offering of its size, the people said. Investors familiar with the company say OpenAI also needs capital to fund its substantial infrastructure commitments and bolster its balance sheet if a deterioration in the initial public offering markets further delays its planned 2027 listing. Though there is high demand for the shares of both companies, investors face the challenge of evaluating and allocating capital to two complex, competing offerings within days or weeks of each other. Some investors view OpenAI’s financing push as an effort to lock in capital from funds that might otherwise devote more of their resources to Anthropic’s IPO, the people said. OpenAI and SoftBank declined to comment. Anthropic and MGX did not immediately respond to requests for comment. OpenAI is pitching investors on growth that accelerated after the launch of its GPT-6 Astra model, saying it had reached US$50 billion in annualised revenue and expecting that figure to rise to US$70 billion by the end of 2026, according to one of the sources. OpenAI has also cut prices on its cheaper models, which it said has boosted usage, and told investors it can further lower the price of AI models, the source added. Anthropic’s annualised revenue reached roughly US$65 billion by July, Reuters previously reported. Its quarterly revenue jumped to US$16.8 billion in the third quarter from US$11.6 billion in the second quarter of 2026 , it told investors, but slowing month-to-month revenue growth has raised concerns among investors about its valuation. OpenAI is seeking to complete the fund-raising before Anthropic’s financial disclosures give investors a fuller picture of its business and invite comparisons between the two companies, one person said. The disclosures could prompt investors to press OpenAI chief financial officer Sarah Friar for more details about the company’s revenue growth and financial outlook, the person added. OpenAI records revenue on a net basis by subtracting partner shares upfront. It has accused Anthropic of inflating its revenue by counting the full, gross value of contracts sold through third-party cloud providers. Anthropic told Reuters earlier that it follows established accounting practices. “OpenAI could want to set its own valuation and not have to worry about a comp (comparison),” said Edward Best, co-chair of capital markets at Willkie Farr & Gallagher, who is not working on the deal and commented on a hypothetical basis. “It’s really a two-horse race in terms of being public.” OpenAI was last valued at US$852 billion in March, after a record-breaking US$122 billion funding round, including a commitment from Amazon.com, which agreed to invest up to US$50 billion in the lab. The Financial Times previously reported some details of OpenAI’s potential fund-raising. events.title: Musk to gift SpaceX shares to American children
events.summary: The News SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said Monday that he would distribute to every American child a share in the AI-and-space-exploration company, a gift that, if realized, would dwarf a similar $6.25 billion gift from Michael Dell. The gift could be worth roughly $10.8 billion, based on SpaceX’s current share price and the U.S. Census’ estimate of under-18s living in the US. It would work out to roughly 1% of Musk’s current SpaceX holdings. Musk and the Trump administration originally discussed the share donations this summer when Trump accounts were first launched, Semafor scooped . Musk made the announcement Monday in response to a social media post from Anthropic , which said it would commit 5% of its listed equities to a “public benefit fund.” President Donald Trump later tweeted a thank you to Musk: “This is exactly what was envisioned when we created Trump Accounts.” Musk and a Treasury spokesperson did not return a request for comment. Rohan’s view The pledge raises some questions about what kind of voting rights the shares would have; SpaceX is a dual-class stock and Musk enjoys supermajority control of the company. Recent regulatory changes allow individual equities to be held in Trump Accounts, the childhood savings program that has been a flagship initiative of this administration. Musk has also not been a big philanthropist, relative to his wealth, and has argued before that the best way he can do good for humanity is by building great companies. Look at this through a strategic, rather than a philanthropic lens, however, and it makes a lot more sense. Musk’s planned donation could generate goodwill from a skeptical public around him, his companies and his goals — space exploration, self-driving cars and AI, among others. If other businesses chose to do something similar, they could also benefit from a public-relations boost, or possibly amass a friendly shareholder block that helps protect against others that might disagree with their strategic direction.

events.title: National Australia Bank to cut 2,500 jobs in cost overhaul as credit growth slows
events.summary: National Australia Bank is Australia’s biggest business lender. National Australia Bank will cut up to 2,500 jobs, about 6% of staff, by 2027 to simplify operations as credit growth slows. Most cuts will hit corporate roles, and NAB will reduce consultants and contractors. Chief executive Andrew Irvine said the strategy stays the same. The overhaul will cost about A$300 million before tax in 2027. The move comes as weaker housing, higher costs and tax changes pressure bank earnings. National Australia Bank (NAB) said on Oct 20 that it will cut up to 2,500 jobs, or about 6% of its workforce, in 2027, in a bid to simplify its operations while grappling with a more challenging outlook for credit growth. The bank, which is Australia’s biggest business lender and third-largest home lender , said up to 1,500 roles would go by the end of 2026. The biggest cuts will target corporate roles rather than customer-facing bankers, it said. It also plans to materially reduce its use of consultants and contractors. “Our ambition and strategy remain unchanged. We will improve productivity, risk outcomes and execution to be a simpler and more efficient bank,” chief executive Andrew Irvine said in a statement. NAB stock was down nearly 2.5% on Oct 20, and recorded the largest share price decline of Australia’s “Big Four” retail banks in the session. The S&P/ASX 200 was down 0.9%. NAB said it would begin consultation with the Finance Sector Union, whose national assistant secretary Nicole McPherson said the job cuts would not help simplify the organisation. “To take a wrecking ball to 6% of one of Australia’s largest workforces this close to Christmas is disgraceful and shows that NAB’s leadership is completely detached from the lived experience of their workers,” she said. The overhaul will result in a restructuring charge of about A$300 million (S$268 million) before tax in 2027, related to redundancy, redeployment and organisational redesign costs. The charge compares with about A$80 million before tax incurred in each of 2025 and 2026, NAB said. The job cuts follow a period of mounting pressure on Australia’s banks as weaker housing activity, rising competition and higher operating costs weigh on earnings. In August, NAB warned that housing credit growth would slow sharply in 2027 following the federal government’s property tax reforms, which the bank said had dampened demand from homebuyers and investors. At that time, Irvine said the combined effects of geopolitical uncertainty, higher domestic interest rates and tax changes were creating challenges for customers. NAB employed 41,880 people globally as of Sept 30, 2025, according to its latest annual report. The move follows a similar restructuring drive at rival ANZ, which in 2025 announced plans to cut about 3,500 jobs by September 2026 as part of a simplification programme under EO Nuno Matos to reduce duplication and lower costs. events.title: The affordability question Republicans can't escape
events.summary: One issue is breaking through even among the most loyal Republican supporters: gas prices . Why it matters: Republicans promised to slash gas prices. But the Iran war sent them soaring, up 37% since President Trump took office . Republicans call it temporary. But there are limits to what voters will accept. On recent campaign trips with House Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) and Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.), gas prices were the most frequent concern raised at events attended by Axios. These weren't rooms full of undecided voters. They were GOP donors, activists and supporters who had turned out to help Republicans win in November. Zoom in: The first question Scalise fielded at a campaign event for Republican Marty O'Donnell in Nevada was about high gas prices. "Everyone's always worried about gas prices," the attendee said, asking whether Republicans could do more to promote Trump's efforts to expand domestic energy production. Another attendee pointed to the gas-price difference between California and Oregon on a recent trip, and asked whether Congress could intervene to ease state restrictions. Scalise acknowledged the impact of the Iran war on gas prices — and said they'd fall once it's resolved — but blamed Democratic energy policies for making the U.S. more vulnerable to rising costs. Zoom out: Emmer faced similar concerns during a recent campaign trip through North Carolina and Virginia. "Four-dollar gas, five-dollar diesel, six-dollar diesel, totally unacceptable," Emmer told supporters at a North Carolina fundraiser. "But it ain't enough to make me vote for communists." "[Democrats] are talking about affordability. That's the problem. We need to be sensitive to the fact that gas and diesel are way up. Just sensitive to it because people are struggling," he told Axios in an interview. The big picture: Republican candidates are feeling the pressure too. Texas Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton privately blamed the Iran war and gas prices for his campaign struggles, according to audio obtained by Axios. "It's the war, it's gas prices, it's diesel," Paxton told donors at a closed-door fundraiser last month, calling affordability "by far our biggest problem." The bottom line: "I don't think gaslighting works," House GOP conference Chairwoman Lisa McClain (R-Mich.) told Axios in an interview last month. "I think if you meet voters where they're at and you have an honest conversation with them ... that's pretty refreshing to them."

events.title: Inside the GOP's fight to avoid a House wipeout
events.summary: House Majority Leader Steve Scalise won't talk about defeat, even as his outside GOP allies are pulling money anyway. Why it matters: Republicans face brutal political headwinds, but Scalise (R-La.) stands out from his fellow leaders for refusing to even contemplate losing the House. Zoom in: At an event for Republican Marty O'Donnell, who's challenging Rep. Susie Lee (D-Nev.), Scalise argued that his presence in the district was evidence Republicans are still on offense. "If it's some horrible cycle for Republicans, then why am I here?" Scalise told supporters at a Las Vegas country club Thursday. "This is a winnable race," he said. But MAGA Inc., a super PAC allied with President Trump, pulled nearly $1 million in advertising from the race last week. The big picture: House Democrats lead the generic ballot by eight points in new Washington Post-ABC polling . Trump's approval is at a record low of 31% ( Reuters/Ipsos ) and 72% say the country is on the wrong track (Post/ABC). He's making 56 campaign stops between August and Election Day as part of what he's dubbed the "Save America Tour," complete with T-shirts featuring a map of his travels. "This is like better than a rock band," Scalise told Axios during an in-flight interview while campaigning in Arizona and Nevada last week. Scalise identified 35 competitive districts , including 15 Democratic-held seats Republicans believe they have a chance to flip. He pointed to Reps. Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.), Juan Ciscomani (R-Ariz.), Rob Bresnahan (R-Pa.) and Ryan Mackenzie (R-Pa.) as races he'll watch closely as bellwethers for how the night could unfold. The pro-Scalise super PAC Save American Freedom is also launching a $3.5 million get-out-the-vote and digital advertising blitz to help 52 House Republicans, Axios' Alex Isenstadt reports. Among the Republicans benefiting are Reps. Brad Finstad (R-Minn.), Mike Carey (R-Ohio) and Rob Wittman (R-Va.), along with GOP candidates Ralph Alvarado (KY-6), Alex Mealer (TX-9) and Jenny Costa Honeycutt (S.C.-1). The intrigue: The GOP's pullback in some districts has fueled speculation that Republicans are giving up on the House to save the Senate. But Scalise argued it will still benefit his members. He pointed to Iowa, where the Congressional Leadership Fund, a super PAC allied with House Republicans, pulled financial support from Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks' district. Senate Republicans subsequently bought the airtime for Ashley Hinson. "You actually get a three for one, " Scalise said, arguing that shifting the ad time to Hinson will benefit Miller-Meeks, Rep. Zach Nunn and the Republican running to succeed Hinson in her House district. "You're going to probably see that in some other areas too," Scalise said. He pointed to Senate races in North Carolina and Texas, where he acknowledged "challenges" at the top of the ticket. The bottom line: Scalise isn't ready to look beyond Election Day, even as Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) publicly weighed in on that very scenario last week. Johnson said he intends to remain the top House Republican even if Democrats win the majority. The race for the top job could become a three-way fight among Johnson, Scalise and Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio). Scalise repeatedly declined to say whether he would endorse Johnson for minority leader or consider running himself. "Anybody who's thinking about planning for us losing is in the wrong business," Scalise told Axios.
