events.title: 'I'm fed up of swiping': Why singles now want to meet IRL
events.summary: Olivia says she chose to attend this dating event because she has "app fatigue" Checking in at a dating event in a bar in Guildford, Olivia Miller-Davis is understandably apprehensive. Even bringing a friend with her doesn't remove the awkwardness at the start of the night. "It's always nerve-wracking when you're meeting new people," the 28-year-old admits before downloading an app that will match her to other daters based on their star signs. This is speed dating 2026-style and Olivia, like many people we speak to, is here because she's fed up of "endlessly swiping" or as some describe it "app fatigue". She says she hates judging people with "really limited information and just a couple of pictures" because she doesn't feel she can "really fully commit" with so little to go on. According to a recent study from online regulator Ofcom 11% of adults use dating sites but it suggests the time we spend on them is dropping, from a peak of almost four hours a month in 2023, down to three hours last year. Edward believes apps are designed so you don't actually find "the one" Olivia's first match on the night is Edward and he agrees that recent dating trends leave him feeling cold. "I mean, they're designed so that you don't find 'the one', because they want you to come back and use the app forever. They don't want you to get married from the app." The event is organised by Love at First Sign, a dating company that uses an app to match people based on astrological connection, but most people are just using it as an icebreaker. Director of events Lissy Cleminson says the way people date is changing and a big factor is more home working since Covid, which means people do not meet in offices or on the commute. "The little meet-cutes don't happen so much when you're at home with your shirt up top and your pyjamas down bottom," she jokes. As you may expect at a dating event many of the singles told us they were keen for that in-real-life or IRL experience. There are a lot of #SingleTok and #Singlelife accounts on TikTok and Instagram reviewing dating events. Candice Gallagher runs an account called @Candilicious and recently went to 10 different dating events in 10 weeks. She describes herself as an entrepreneur and thinks in business terms dating events deliver "much greater return on investment". The 40-year-old says all too often dating online can lead to "chat graveyards" with very limited conversation. "At a dating event, everyone is single, everyone's ready to mingle, and your chances of having a good conversation are much greater." Dating events provide a better "return on investment" than apps, says Candice Gallagher Many people at the event in Guildford agreed dating events were better value for money because "you get to meet a range of people" in person for a similar cost to one date from an app. These events typically cost around £15 to £30 and often include a drink and activity or icebreaking gimmick, in this case an app that is used throughout the night. Olivia believes money plays a big factor in dating. "I wasn't working for a bit because I changed careers and because of that I put dating on hold." Olivia remembers thinking it "couldn't be a priority" and feeling she needed to wait until she was "earning enough" before dating again. She is not alone in finding dating expensive. More than a quarter of daters surveyed by Barclays suggested rising costs had changed how they date. And a couple of recent studies suggest the monthly cost of dating - from apps to entertainment and clothes - can add up to around £130. Many people at the event in Guildford agreed dating events were better value for money Those running apps are quick to point out online is still a big part in the way people meet. New research from Match Group, which owns Tinder and Hinge, suggests that out of those who had ever had a romantic relationship, about 21% of baby boomers surveyed met their most recent partner at a pub, bar or club. The survey of 3,007 single people also suggests that of those who had ever had a relationship, 20% met their most recent partner on a dating app and 20% met through friends. Chine Mmegwa, head of strategy, corporate development and operations at Match Group, said Tinder has made tweaks to its service in the past year to win back younger daters. As well as helping users find out more about each other in advance of dates, through interactive music and astrology features, it has introduced "double date mode" for friends who want to date together. And she said Tinder is doing more to encourage people to connect IRL. "They want to be in person. You've seen us launch events across the US and now the UK. We are bringing IRL experiences into the app. "What we're doing is putting IRL into our experience. And so we are bringing that gap to what they're looking for in person, using the apps." In Guildford, Olivia says her night was a success because she met some men she might want to go on a first date with.

events.title: CNBC's The China Connection newsletter: Navigating a tech-heavy world
events.summary: China's seen growing "misallocation" of resources, Krishna Srinivasan, the International Monetary Fund's Asia and Pacific Department Director. Local businesses have tried to fill the gaps where they can. International investment is always an option. Hi, this is Evelyn, writing to you from Shanghai. Welcome to the latest edition of The China Connection — a snapshot of what I'm seeing and hearing from local businesses. While economists and former central bankers discuss tech and monetary policy at the Bund Summit , companies are moving faster to capture new revenue. What risks bear watching? China's seen growing "misallocation" of resources, Krishna Srinivasan, the International Monetary Fund's Asia and Pacific Department Director, told me on the sidelines of the Bund Summit on Monday. That "needs to be corrected," he said, urging policymakers not to "pick and choose sectors" to support, but to allow capital to work according to market forces. It's a tough ask as China has doubled down on technological development, while struggling to transition away from real estate, which once accounted for more than one-fifth of the economy. In Shenzhen, a local partner for Kickstarter, called INNO100, is making about 5 million yuan ($750,000) a month at its retail store, said Baron Wang, founder of the parent entity Longham Group. That's thanks to a combination of retail sales, 3D printing service fees and events, he said. The store showcases new tech products, similar to its Beverly Hills-based cousin. Wang plans to open about 10 more stores in China, and five overseas, saying he sees the chance to get customers especially from the U.S. "It's really hard for us to control the relationship between China and the U.S.," he said. "But I think the technology should not be too politic[al]," he said, especially in consumer electronics. Yuan Minglun, co-founder and CTO of Kunwei Technology, said the company already supplies major Chinese humanoid robot companies with sensors, and is planning to set up a factory in the U.S. in coming months so that it can more easily sell to American humanoid startups. It reflects a persistent gap between U.S. and Chinese supply chains. Cyril Nader, founder and CEO of outer space-focused startup Phenix, has aimed to use a non-China supply chain. But he pointed out that the lead time for non-China-made parts such as gear boxes can be 56 weeks. "56 weeks from now, I don't know what I will be doing," he said. "We'll be way ahead. We'll be on [the] third phase." Visa gets Beijing's green light for bank card business after 40 years of working with China The news comes as the U.S. and Chinese presidents plan for their third meeting this year. " For more than 40 years , Visa has been an active contributor to China's dynamic payments landscape," Visa CEO Ryan McInerney said. He became chair of the U.S.-China Business Council in June. U.S. presses China on Mastercard, Citigroup market access in bilateral Bangkok talks, official says U.S. officials raised market access issues for Mastercard and Citigroup in China during bilateral meetings in Bangkok last week, according to a U.S. Treasury official. China's GDP picks up speed, up by 4.5% in Q3 Surging exports helped lift overall economic growth in the third quarter, while retail sales grew by a faster-than-expected 1.1% in September from a year ago. Producer prices last month rose by their fastest since June 2022. events.title: Embedded AI evaluators won’t be an easy solution, Hugging Face’s policy chief says
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. AI labs have staked their reputations on model benchmarking — the supposedly neutral and accurate system of evaluations that are designed to measure whether one AI product is better than another. However, the methods behind these evaluations are complicated and still maturing, said Irene Solaiman, Hugging Face’s chief policy officer, during a discussion at TechCrunch Disrupt last week. Testing needs to come together into a more consistent science if the industry is to rely on them in the future. With that in mind, can we trust the current tests that are being released? “Trust is such a weighted term,” said Solaiman. “In terms of whether we can trust results, one big part [of that] is can you reproduce the results of an evaluation? Do you have the level of access that you need to the model itself — this is where open weights come in in a big way,” she added. Reproducibility in model evaluations has long remained one of the stickier aspects of benchmarking — and remains a topic of significant debate in the industry. Outside of an individual test’s validity, there’s also the added question of how that test compares to other evaluations. “They are an evolving science — where we don’t know how to meaningfully compare them to each other,” Solaiman said. “They start to get ineffective relatively quickly, and we don’t have as much of a thriving ecosystem as we need,” she added. “There’s this hunger for an embedded evaluator ecosystem now, but the qualifications that determine who is an effective evaluator across what tasks need a lot more standardization.” The idea of embedded evaluators — in which supposedly “neutral” third-party observers are placed inside AI organizations — has been popularized over the last several months, as AI labs grapple with a rash of safety incidents that have spurred concerns over the potential harms of their technology. Hugging Face was famously the target of one of those incidents. Instead of active government regulation to identify and mitigate model safety concerns, labs have pushed for the third-party solution. However, doubts remain over how neutral or effective those evaluators will actually be. Anthropic’s decision to hire Accenture as its first evaluator spurred a good amount of backlash, with some critics mocking the idea that the consulting firm was qualified to do the task at hand. Evaluations are now moving from merely a test of the model itself to a test of the entire system around the model — including the harness and agent. The harness — or the tool the user is using to access the model — specifically, has a lot to do with a model’s performance, and a weaker model with a better harness could easily outperform a frontier model, Solaiman shared. “Agentic evals are really hard and really expensive,” said Solaiman. “We have just more evaluations for models. … We don’t have as many evaluations for harnesses, and we are developing better evaluations for the holistic agent — because that’s what a lot of folks are getting value out of,” she added. In other words, the evaluation space is a bit of a free-for-all at the moment, and if benchmarking is going to continue to be seen as a useful tool for industry leaders, a more uniform, industry-wide approach — where everyone is on the same page — may be necessary. events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts NAB to slash up to 2,500 jobs in massive restructure National Australia Bank plans to make about 6 per cent of its staff redundant by the end of this financial year. ( ABC News: Stephen Cavenagh ) National Australia Bank has announced plans to cut up to 2,500 jobs, or about 6 per cent of its workforce, this financial year. NAB chief executive Andrew Irvine said there would be no material impact to customer-facing banking roles. Up to 1,500 roles will be cut by the end of the year, NAB said. It will book $300 million in restructuring costs. National Australia Bank says it will cut up to 2,500 jobs, or about 6 per cent of its workforce, by mid-2027. That would include up to 1,500 roles before the end of this year, NAB said in a statement to the stock exchange. The union representing bank employees said it was "appalled" by the announcement. "To take a wrecking ball to 6 per cent of one of Australia's largest workforces this close to Christmas is disgraceful and shows that NAB's leadership is completely detached from the lived experience of their workers," Finance Sector Union (FSU) national assistant secretary Nicole McPherson said. In addition to the internal cuts, NAB also plans to "materially reduce its use of consultants and external contractors". The announcement, lodged with the ASX this morning, said it was part of "actions to simplify its operating model and better align its workforce to prioritise growth and technology initiatives for customers". The bank has flagged a restructuring charge of about $300 million, pre-tax, with more details to come in its full-year results announcement on November 5. Australian banks, large and small, have been cutting their workforces, with a major restructure at ANZ leading to thousands of job losses in the past year . Last month, Bendigo and Adelaide Bank proposed cutting 137 jobs as part of an ongoing restructure. 'Rapid technological change' contributes to cuts While there was no direct reference to artificial intelligence in the NAB release, it did refer to "rapid technological change". "NAB is implementing these changes as part of a broader review to identify the nature of the workforce required to support NAB's strategic ambition in an evolving operating environment," the bank said. "These actions will help make NAB a stronger bank, better placed to navigate risks and opportunities arising from more challenging economic conditions, increasing customer expectations, competitive intensity and rapid technological change." NAB cited economic conditions as one factor behind the major overhaul. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) NAB chief executive Andrew Irvine said there would be no material effect on customer-facing banking roles. "We are particularly focused on reducing the size of corporate functions … we have also deliberately made deeper changes to senior management positions, which will broaden leadership responsibilities across the bank." Mr Irvine acknowledged it would be a difficult period for the employees affected and pledged to treat everyone "with dignity and respect". events.title: Microsoft says AI agents are like insider threats as ‘frontier models can’t be trusted’
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Microsoft on Monday introduced new security features designed to protect enterprises from the growing threat of AI agents. The launch comes as Microsoft continues to warn enterprises about the dangers of AI and agents. Perhaps the most notable addition is Guardian Agents , a new feature intended to monitor the AI agents a company uses. Guardian Agents is part of Project Perception, a product introduced in June. Project Perception was Microsoft’s answer to powerful hacking models like Anthropic’s Mythos and Fable and OpenAI’s security vulnerability scanning system Daybreak. Project Perception originally launched three classes of agents: a “red team” that acted like hackers and attacked, a “blue team” that detected the red team and assessed the vulnerabilities they found, and a “green team” tasked with fixing them. The product was designed around the assumption that AI hackers would come from outside the company. But lately, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has been warning that the AI enemy may be the very agents enterprises have deployed and are paying for, much like a rogue human employee, otherwise known as an “insider threat.” Earlier this month, in his private blog , Nadella warned that it’s time to stop trusting AI model providers, even if they offer assurances of safety and security with their agentic products. He wants enterprises to implement separate systems, not controlled by the AI labs, to watch and control the agents that those AI labs’ products launch. “We are deploying these complex agentic systems and models, with access to our most sensitive data and giving them the ability to take mission-critical actions on our behalf!” he wrote. “We simply can’t outsource responsibility for what intelligence does on our behalf. A model provider’s assurances do not relieve us of that responsibility. … In other words, we need to separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it.” When announcing Guardian Agents, Microsoft’s security business chief Hayete Gallot was even more straightforward. “Unfortunately, frontier models, regardless of their origin, cannot be trusted,” she wrote , adding that this isn’t because they are malicious or easily hacked, but because they are unpredictable. They have been trained to achieve tasks, not follow “organizational norms or judgment.” On top of that, they are often given the keys to the kingdom, with access to data and tools that could do serious harm. Microsoft’s solution is both surprising and self-serving. The surprising side is that Microsoft is famously close to OpenAI and Anthropic, having invested in both. OpenAI is also one of its biggest cloud customers, and Microsoft has its own AI lab developing models. So, Microsoft is sowing distrust against some of its own business interests. The self-serving side is that Microsoft wants enterprises to buy agent security products from it, the cloud provider, rather than from Anthropic and OpenAI. But conflicting interests aside, its logic is sound. The software that monitors agent behavior should be separate from the suppliers of agents, just as auditors should be independent of the organizations they audit. Or as Nadella puts it: “We need to separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it.” Microsoft is now seizing that business opportunity in a variety of ways. In addition to Guardian Agents, it has added an agent detection feature to its Microsoft Defender product that can find up to 60 types of agents that employees bring into the workplace, including Claude Code, Codex, and OpenClaw. It has also added features that limit agents’ access to data and systems, and dynamically adjust their agent permissions based on the task. That includes requiring human approval if an agent appears to be making risky decisions. This idea of agents as untrustworthy insiders is taking hold across the broader industry, too. Microsoft was an inaugural member of Nvidia’s new Open Agent Safety Platform, which garnered the support of more than 100 other tech companies . The platform isolates agents in secure environments and can monitor and stop behavior through hardware, functioning something like a kill switch. This follows Microsoft’s announcement of the new Surface Laptop Ultra PCs built for agents , which run on Nvidia chips and have agent security and controls baked in. events.title: Ex–OpenAI engineer accused of bugging office stays in jail as prosecutors allege Saudi ties: ‘Once he leaves, there’s no getting him back’
events.summary: A federal judge on Monday ordered a former OpenAI engineer accused of bugging an executive conference room to stay in jail , after questioning whether a $1 million bond the Saudi government offered to guarantee would bring him back if he fled. Abdulrahman Alfozan, the 35-year-old former OpenAI engineer, appeared in court today wearing an orange jumpsuit and white face mask while escorted by two U.S. marshals. He will remain in federal custody until his next court date, a preliminary hearing on Nov. 6. He has been in jail since the FBI arrested him on Oct. 9, alleging he planted the device in a conference room where executives, and sometimes government officials, discussed sensitive information, on Sept. 28. Magistrate Judge Alex G. Tse said a $1 million bond had to be weighed against the possibility that Alfozan “potentially has access to much greater wealth.” “Once he leaves, there’s no getting him back, and that’s why this is a bigger case,” Tse said in the courtroom Monday morning. OpenAI terminated Alfozan’s employment on Oct. 9, although Alfozan’s lawyer said Monday in court the company never formally told him that. However, per his defense motion, he was told before his arrest that he had been placed on administrative leave. Tse noted that OpenAI would not have fired him if it had no concern about what it found. Fortune was in the San Francisco courtroom for the hearing, as were about 60 others, including a group of high school students who had come to witness a case involving one of the most prominent companies in the world. Ahead of the court hearing Monday, both prosecutors for the federal government and the defense, Alfozan’s attorney William Pernik, filed court documents revealing new details about the case. Alfozan sought release from federal custody, with supervision, such as an ankle monitor, while the U.S. argued there was reason to believe he would leave the country and that he posed a danger to the community and to U.S. national security. Alfozan faces one count of using or attempting to use a device to intercept oral communications, which carries a maximum of five years in prison. He was charged by criminal complaint and has not been indicted or entered a plea. The complaint does not charge him with espionage, theft of trade secrets, or acting as an agent of a foreign government, a point his defense stressed in its motion. OpenAI has said it has “no indications” that he inappropriately accessed or took model weights, source code, or customer data. The filings reveal far more than has been known to date about Alfozan and some of the most controversial details of the case, including why Alfozan had a one-way flight booked to Saudi Arabia three days after his arrest. Alfozan’s lawyer said he is a citizen of Saudi Arabia, although he has been in the U.S. for 15 years; got his green card in 2020; and joined OpenAI in 2025. A one-way ticket to Saudi Arabia and potential plans to move back Alfozan booked the flight to Saudi Arabia on Sept. 13, according to the defense motion, along with his wife, also a Saudi national, and 3-month-old baby. The economy fare for all three cost $1,897.59 and could be changed for a $180 fee, the defense said, adding this wasn’t unusual for its client: Alfozan often books one-way tickets to allow for scheduling flexibility around his work schedule, the defense motion says. In fact, 70% (96 of 138) of the airline bookings “in his email since January 2021 were one-way tickets.” His naturalization application lists 25 trips abroad between 2020 and 2025, 20 of which included Saudi Arabia, and he returned from every one, according to the defense. As for the date of Oct. 12, Alfozan booked it for then because that’s the day his wife’s 60-day grace period ended after her work permit in the U.S. expired on Aug. 13. Since giving birth, she has “struggled with postpartum depression and anxiety,” the defense motion says. Alfozan filed for paternity leave from OpenAI, set for Oct. 19 to Dec. 20, after which he planned to return to the Bay Area and his role at OpenAI. After Alfozan’s arrest, his wife allegedly told authorities that she and their baby intended to permanently move to Saudi Arabia, according to the court filing. She told them her husband intended to move there at some point to be with them, but for now, was spending two months of his paternity leave in the country before returning to the U.S. In court Monday, however, the defense said she now plans to return to the U.S. on a temporary, short-term B-1 visa. The defense also said she left the U.S. rather than overstay her visa. That is consistent with a letter one of Alfozan’s friends submitted for the defense motion, in which the friend says he spoke to Alfozan about his plan to continue working in the U.S. and supporting his wife and baby when they returned to Saudi Arabia. As further evidence of Alfozan’s intent to return to the U.S., his lawyer notes that on Sept. 26, two days before he allegedly planted the device, Alfozan registered to attend the Consumer Electronics Show (CES), a convention in Las Vegas scheduled for early January 2027. In court, Pernik argued that Alfozan stayed in the country for about eight to 10 days after OpenAI confronted him. “If he really were an agent of a foreign government … why wouldn’t he just leave right away?” Pernik said in court. Evidence found on his iPhone The U.S. filing also reveals the results of a federal search of Alfozan’s home and cell phone. They found “several electronic components similar” to the recording device Alfozan allegedly installed behind a TV in the conference room, and a second one OpenAI security staff found in his bag. On Alfozan’s iPhone were several photographs, dated from Sept. 22 to Sept. 28, 2026, of another recording device. Other photos showed what appeared to be the input and output panels on televisions and other devices in “various locations in OpenAI buildings” including another conference room where “sensitive meetings” frequently occurred, according to the filing. This suggested Alfozan “had done reconnaissance at OpenAI to determine where he might install additional devices,” the U.S. filing says. Also on Alfozan’s iPhone was a note he had deleted from September 2026, which had links to different recording devices, including ones made by Seeed Studio, the type of device Alfozan allegedly put in the conference room and which had been found at his residence. Two other notes stood out. One titled “Riyadh tasks,” last modified Sept. 13—the day he booked the flight—listed finding an apartment and a job for his wife and getting a Saudi passport for his son. Another, titled “OpenAI leave” and last modified Oct. 7, suggested he planned an “early … pick up” of the devices and extending his leave “to full,” according to the U.S. filing. events.title: Andy Burnham outlines new rules to outlaw ‘rip-off’ private parking fines
events.summary: Drivers to get five minutes to decide whether to park and 10 minutes to leave after their session ends Drivers will get a guaranteed five minutes to decide whether to park and 10 minutes to leave after their parking session ends before they face a fine under new rules for private car parks that Andy Burnham said were designed to outlaw “rip-off” charges. In the latest in a series of “everyday fixes” to ease the cost of living and give consumers a “fairer” deal, the prime minister said a new official code of practice for the industry meant motorists in England, Scotland and Wales would enjoy a range of new rights. The consumer body Which? said the “long overdue” rules appeared to fall well short of what was needed to help drivers fight back against private parking “cowboys”, however. Each year in the UK, private firms dish out millions of parking tickets, and the number has been climbing. In August, the RAC said the number issued rose 17% in a year to reach a record 16.9m in 2025-26. Complaints about poor behaviour by some operators are rife, and campaigners say reform is years overdue. Legislation was passed in early 2019 , and an official code of practice was unveiled by the then government in early 2022 – but lasted less than six months after legal challenges by several parking firms forced it to be withdrawn. In a fresh push, a new private parking code of practice is due to be laid in parliament on Tuesday, though it is unclear when this will take effect. Ministers said they would look to bring the code into force “as soon as possible”. New rights for drivers include “a guaranteed five minutes to decide whether to park, and 10 minutes to leave once their session ends”. The government is sticking with the existing industry maximum parking charge of £100 despite calls to halve it. Which? said: “It is particularly concerning that the government has shied away from a £50 price cap.” The consumer body had called for a maximum £50 fine, and this was also the amount at which some charges were capped under the withdrawn code. Meanwhile, fines will be scrapped on appeal for “honest mistakes”, such as stopping briefly to check directions, and for situations such as a medical emergency, vehicle breakdown or broken ticket machine. For “smaller slip-ups”, such as forgetting to display a parking permit or entering the wrong vehicle’s registration, the government said drivers would face a maximum charge of £20 on appeal. This appears to be a less generous system than under the original rules: the code that was withdrawn required the cancellation of a parking charge “in all mitigating circumstances”. Which? said the government had also shied away from an independent appeals body “that could rein in the industry’s worst practices” and had failed to take action on private parking debt recovery fees, which it said were regularly added without motorists’ knowledge and pushed unfair charges even higher. On the latter point, the government has promised to consult on these fees – which are added when a fine becomes overdue – “as soon as possible next year”. These fees are currently capped at £70, and the consultation will look at whether they should be cut or scrapped altogether. Burnham said: “Being a few minutes late back to your car or typing one digit of your number plate wrong shouldn’t end with a hefty fine landing on your doormat. “These charges leave people feeling ripped off and out of pocket, so I’m putting a stop to them. We are introducing clearer rules, longer grace periods and lower charges for genuine mistakes.”

events.title: Zelensky lobbies senators to press White House on alleged intel and weapons curbs
events.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Monday lobbied a bipartisan group of senators to press the Trump administration to remove what he claimed are restrictions on intelligence sharing and weapons supplies. Why it matters: Ukrainian officials say the Trump administration has quietly imposed these limits without admitting it publicly in an attempt to press Zelensky to accept a deal to end the war that includes more concessions to Russia. Trump and White House officials have denied for days that they've imposed any restrictions on Ukraine. Driving the news: The crisis began 10 days ago when Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia during a round of negotiations between his envoys and Ukrainian officials in Miami. The Ukrainians claimed that Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner threatened that Trump could cut off Ukraine from U.S. intelligence and stop selling weapons if it continued to ignore requests not to target Russian oil refineries . U.S. officials denied such a threat. They said Witkoff and Kushner told the Ukrainians that the U.S. was a strong partner, providing munitions and intelligence. Ukraine therefore shouldn't take actions that hurt American consumers, Witkoff and Kushner said.​ Behind the scenes: During a virtual meeting with a bipartisan group of senators led by Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) and Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), Zelensky laid out the various problems Ukraine has been experiencing since the Miami meeting. Axios obtained a transcript from Ukrainian officials. Elon Musk's Starlink and the U.S. military's Starshield satellite systems remain partially restricted — despite claims by the White House to the contrary. "We still have no explanation for this. Just different strange stories we're hearing, unfortunately," Zelensky told the senators. It's hampering Ukraine's ability to shoot down Russian attack drones, he added. On three occasions the past week, including on Sunday, Ukraine didn't receive early warnings from the U.S. about Russian ballistic missile attacks, Zelensky said, suggesting it was a sign that intelligence sharing has been curbed. "We have received no clear explanation from Washington – why this is happening," he added. Zelensky said Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is not signing off on the delivery of Patriot interceptors and AIM-9x missiles for the NASAMS air-defense system, even though NATO countries have already paid for them. "We have almost no Patriot interceptors left from the U.S. partners," he said. "All of this suggests that some political decision has been made to slow down support for us," Zelensky said. ​"We want to understand what is happening, why it's happening, and where all of this is heading." What they're saying : Tillis said after the meeting that Congress "remains committed to standing with Ukraine and our European allies to end Russia's brutal aggression and secure lasting peace." Blumenthal said afterwards that "bipartisan support for Ukraine was clear and unequivocal, which we'll be expressing in upcoming action." "Appeasement won't work with Putin, a thug who understands only strength and force," he added. The other side: President Trump told reporters on Monday that the U.S. is still sharing intelligence with Ukraine and said he didn't know who ordered the throttling of the Starlink satellite system. "But I am gonna find out," he said. "Frankly Zelensky is not helping matters much. He doesn't want to stop the war. Zelensky doesn't know what he is talking about," the president said. "Maybe it's time for Zelensky to let somebody else negotiate on behalf of Ukraine. … We have given a lot to Ukraine. They have given nothing to us." State of play: Zelensky spoke with Witkoff and Kushner on Sunday. They asked Ukraine again to stop attacking Russian oil refineries, Ukrainian officials said. Zelensky told the senators that he proposed to the U.S. envoys that Ukraine halt strikes on refineries for 30 days. In return, the U.S. would supply Ukraine with Patriot interceptors so it could defend itself from Russian ballistic missiles during that 30-day period. Zelensky told the senators that Witkoff and Kushner haven't shown any openness to the idea. What to watch: Zelensky told the senators that he'll be in Oslo, Norway next week and could meet with Witkoff and Kushner on Tuesday or Wednesday. Kushner and Witkoff could then continue on from Oslo to Moscow to meet with Putin, a source familiar with the matter said.

events.title: Ex-OpenAI worker accused of planting device had Saudi support, says court filing
events.summary: A Saudi national charged with secretly planting a recording device in one of OpenAI's meeting rooms has been accused of having "considerable support" from the Saudi government, according to a court filing , external in California. US prosecutors claimed Abdulrahman Alfozan, who worked for the AI firm, was in "frequent communication... with a member of the Saudi royal family", and say a member of the country's military paid for a one-way flight to Saudi Arabia for his wife and son after his arrest. The 35-year-old engineer was on Monday deemed a flight risk and denied bail, pending trial. The Saudi government did not immediately respond to BBC requests for comment. Alfozan had worked at OpenAI for around a year before he allegedly made his attempt to plant an audio recorder. The AI company discovered the device, which was plugged into the back of a TV in a conference meeting room and covered up with toilet paper, on 30 September. A camera was placed in the room and on 5 October, Alfozan was filmed entering and appearing to look behind the television where the audio recorder had been inserted. He was arrested by the FBI on 9 October and his contract with OpenAI was terminated. The court filing claimed the suspect's alleged conduct could pose "a danger to the national security of the United States", because executives from the tech firm met with government officials in the room during the days the device was believed to have been installed. It said Alfozan's arrest came three days before he was scheduled to fly from San Francisco to Riyadh on a one-way itinerary with his wife and son. Following the arrest, the document claims the defendant's wife told FBI agents who interviewed her that "her US visa was expiring" and so she and her son were "permanently moving back to Saudi Arabia", and her husband intended to do the same. On 10 October, the day after Alfozan was arrested, his wife and son flew from San Francisco to Doha, Qatar. They travelled on a one-way business class ticket booked and paid for by a Saudi military official. "Ultimately, the defendant has little incentive to remain in the United States to see this case through," the prosecutors argued. US district judge Alex Tse on Monday denied Alfozan's attorneys request for his release on bail, saying "there is a risk of non-appearance that is significant". Alfozan was scheduled to ‌appear ⁠in federal court in San Francisco later on Monday. If convicted, he faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 (£188,000) fine. events.title: Trump says he'd meet with Putin and Xi, criticizes Zelenskyy
events.summary: President Donald Trump said he would meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping. Trump again lashed out at Volodymyr Zelenskyy after the Ukrainian leader criticized Trump's recent decision to waive new sanctions against Russia. Zelenskyy has claimed that the Starlink and Starshield services from Elon Musk's SpaceX have recently been degraded, and that U.S. intelligence sharing has also been disrupted. President Donald Trump said Monday that he would meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping to discuss how to end the Ukraine war, while ramping up his criticism of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy . Trump suggested that a meeting between the world leaders, which Putin reportedly proposed, could take place without Zelenskyy present. "Anything I can do to end the war, whether somebody's there or not," Trump told reporters when asked about the potential meeting as he departed the White House for a campaign rally in Kansas. The comments came as tensions between Trump and Zelenskyy have steadily risen in recent weeks, while Russia — which invaded Ukraine in 2022 — has received multiple breaks from the U.S. Trump had initially suggested that he would be more interested in discussing "denuclearization" with Putin and Xi, saying, "Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine. They haven't been doing much." The Wall Street Journal had reported that Putin in an Oct. 9 phone call with Trump floated the idea of a trilateral summit with Xi next month. That meeting could take place at the upcoming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, which is set for Nov. 18 and Nov. 19, the Journal reported. "If President Xi wants to have it, I'd have it. I'm sure we'd talk about other things like trade too. But yeah, I would do that," Trump said in Monday's remarks. He also said that Russia and China, which have both been accused of supporting Iran in its ongoing military efforts against the U.S., have done "very little" for Tehran. And when asked about Zelenskyy's criticism of Trump's recent decision to waive new sanctions against Russia — and his recent claim that Trump is on the wrong side of history — the U.S. president once again lashed out at the Ukrainian leader. "Zelenskyy doesn't know what he's talking about," Trump said. "Zelenskyy is a man that should have had this war settled a long time ago." "I think it's time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine," Trump added, echoing his prior call for Kyiv to "get a new president." Zelenskyy says that Starlink and Starshield, the critical satellite services offered by Elon Musk 's SpaceX , have recently been degraded, and that U.S. intelligence sharing has also been disrupted, leaving Ukraine without advance warning of Russian strikes. "No explanation for either of these issues has been provided to Ukraine by the American side," Zelenskyy said earlier Monday after a call with bipartisan U.S. lawmakers from the House and Senate. Trump said outside the White House that he does not know who ordered the interruption to the Starlink service, "But I'd like to find out." Musk said last week that the U.S. government and Trump are "ultimately" responsible for any slowdowns. But Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied that the U.S. caused the interruption, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned Zelenskyy to be "very careful about making statements like this that aren't true." Zelenskyy also once again criticized Trump's decision to waive key provisions of a new Russian sanctions bill, which was signed last month after passing Congress with broad bipartisan support. He said he showed the lawmakers photos from the scene of a Russian attack in the Kharkiv region that killed six people, including a mother and her 1-year-old child. "This is how Russia responds to the lifting of sanctions and the easing of pressure," Zelenskyy said. Sens. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., and Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said in a joint statement after the meeting, "Funding Russia's war machine, disabling Ukraine's satellite communications, and crippling its air defense are all impediments to peace." "Trying to appease a murderous thug like Vladimir Putin will only prolong this war and bring greater casualties," the senators said. Trump had already been criticized by members of both parties after announcing a deal allowing Russia to supply diesel fuel on the global market, despite existing sanctions. But in Monday's remarks, Trump pushed back, saying he is "not looking to break up negotiations" with Putin on deals pertaining to Ukraine, Iran, diesel and the release of hostages.

events.title: Tech stocks had a nice oversold bounce on Monday. Earnings this week will determine if it's for real
events.summary: This week's major earnings hold the key to whether this technology comeback has legs, investors said. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite rallied Monday, largely due to a rebound in artificial intelligence companies. Chip stocks surged, with the iShares Semiconductor ETF ( SOXX ) on pace to snap a nine-day slump. The Magnificent Seven outperformed, as did memory chip makers. The iShares MSCI South Korea ETF ( EWY ), dominated by SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, surged 4% after also suffering steep declines over the past week. That comes after the S&P 500 fell nearly 2% last week, its worst weekly decline since late June. The Nasdaq Composite dropped 4.5% over the same five-day span. Monday looked like a bounce from oversold conditions, but a bigger move will depend on this week's big tech earnings — which include results from major names such as Meta Platforms and Tesla — to clear some of the recent worries about the sustainability of the AI trade. SpaceX reports after the bell Tuesday. "Tech earnings are key this week. Fundamentals are unchanged, but given fragile price action, we turn neutral [on] risk assets and stay neutral duration," wrote Ajay Rajadhyaksha, global chairman of research at Barclays. This week will be especially crucial for the S&P 500 and Nasdaq, which need to hold support so as not to confirm a further breakdown, Katie Stockton, founder of Fairlead Strategies, said in a Monday note. For the time being, however, widespread, short-term oversold conditions suggest support can hold, she said. Of the 47 S&P 500 companies that have reported their third quarter thus far, 85% have beaten expectations, and the broad market index is on track to post a blended earnings growth rate of 29%. But the bulk of tech results are still to come, and they have a high bar to clear. "Investors are going to need proof statements from any company that is considered part of the AI trade that they can deliver on the earnings growth expectations being built into their pricing," said Ron Albahary, chief investment officer at LNW. "We don't have a valuation-potential bubble here like we had in the internet bubble. We have an earnings-expectation-potential bubble in this cycle." As a result, the market will take a "more discriminating" approach to tech, which Albahary views as a healthy move that will lead to "more of a dispersion of winners and losers within the AI trade universe." In that environment, some AI beneficiaries may continue to rise, while others like the neocloud platforms may sell off due to the amount of debt they're taking on to finance the build-out, he said. "Previously, the AI headlines would drive the bulk of the AI universe stocks up or down," the CIO said. "I don't think we're going to see that kind of uniformity going forward." As it stands now, action in the AI trade appears to be more of a "reality check" than a "full-blown unraveling," according to Wells Fargo Investment Institute's Sameer Samana. But he still believes there may be more pressure in the days and maybe even weeks ahead. "We recently downgrade[d] tech because we thought expectations had gotten too optimistic, and while the recent selling has taken some of that optimism out of the equation, we don't think it's fully done and may last through the midterms given the politicization of AI/data centers," the Wells Fargo head of global equities and real assets told CNBC.

events.title: OpenAI bugging suspect Alfozan held without bail after Saudi government offers to pay
events.summary: The Saudi national charged with planting a recording device in a sensitive OpenAI executive conference room was "in frequent communications via WhatsApp with a member of the Saudi Royal Family" throughout 2025 and 2026, federal prosecutors said in a court filing. Federal prosecutors warned that the alleged actions of Abdulrahman Alfozan "could pose a danger to the national security of the United States," and want him detained without bail. The Saudi Consulate in Los Angeles has offered to pay Alfozan's full bail if he is released. The Saudi national accused of planting a recording device in an executive conference room at OpenAI 's headquarters was ordered detained without bail pending trial Monday by a San Francisco federal judge who said that there is a "significant" risk he would flee. The order came at a court hearing where Judge Alex Tse sharply questioned the value of an offer by the Saudi Consulate in Los Angeles to pay the full bail for Abdulrahman Alfozan , 35, who was working for OpenAI as an engineer when he allegedly planted the device in a television on Sept. 28. Tse said he found the Saudi offer "problematic." "It seems like a blank check: 'We're gonna pay whatever the court wants to make sure he gets out," Tse said in the courtroom, as Alfozan and several dozen of his supporters looked on. "The Saudi government is saying, 'We'll take care of everything, we'll have supervision, we will pay the bond, we're not going to approve any travel documents.'" Tse noted. "But what confidence do I have that they're going to protect the interests of the [U.S.] government?" "That he's not going to flee? He doesn't have to go all the way to Saudi Arabia," the judge said. "He just has to go to Canada or Mexico ... I don't see how that is in his favor." Saudi Arabia has no extradition treaty with the United States, which the judge referred to at the hearing. Tse also noted that OpenAI has terminated Alfozan. Alfozan has been in jail since his arrest on a charge of using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. He faces a maximum possible sentence of five years in prison if convicted. Tse ordered Alfozan to return to court on Nov. 6. Prosecutors from the San Francisco U.S. Attorney's Office during Monday's hearing, and in a detention memo, detailed Alfozan's ties to Saudi Arabia as they argued he was a flight risk. Those ties include his wife and their 3-month-old son, who left the United States shortly after his arrest. Prosecutors in that court filing Sunday said that Alfozan's alleged bugging of the artificial intelligence giant "could pose a danger to the national security of the United States." The filing says, "OpenAI executives met with government officials" in the company's San Francisco headquarters in the same conference room on days close to when it is alleged Alfozan planted the device. "This is an ongoing investigation that may yet result in more serious charges," the filing says. Prosecutors said in the filing that Alfozan has access to "ample resources ... and what appears to be considerable support from a foreign government that has (i) no extradition treaty with the United States; (ii) limitless resources; and (iii) the ability to provide extraordinary travel assistance, including based on similar circumstances in this District," the filing said. "He has the connections needed not only to flee, but to build a new life in Saudi Arabia. The Court should order the defendant detained pending trial," prosecutors wrote. Prosecutors in their filing said Alfozan had been "in frequent communications via WhatsApp with a member of the Saudi Royal Family" throughout 2025 and 2026. Alfozan communicated with the Saudi royal as recently as Oct. 5 — four days before he was arrested, prosecutors said. Prosecutors did not identify the Saudi royal or say how Alfozan knew that person. "Among other things, the individual [the royal family member] told the defendant [Alfozan] that an artificial intelligence initiative was being launched in Saudi Arabia and wanted the defendant to join it," the filing says. "In May 2026, the individual told the defendant, 'Saudi needs you more then [sic] the US!' to which the defendant responded '100,' indicating he agreed," prosecutors wrote. "The individual repeatedly tried to recruit the defendant and asked when he planned to leave OpenAI," prosecutors wrote. "At the time, the defendant said he wouldn't leave until his stock vested." The filing does not say the Saudi royal directed Alfozan to install a recording device at OpenAI or steal information from the AI giant. Alfozan, who lives near the San Francisco airport, is a venture partner at Raed Ventures , a Saudi venture capital firm. Prince Khalid bin Bader Al Saud, a member of the Saudi royal family, joined Raed as a venture partner in 2025.

events.title: 3 years after releasing "Flowers," Miley Cyrus sang new lyrics at the Hollywood Bowl. Here are the song's rumored Liam Hemsworth references.
events.summary: Miley Cyrus ad-libbed lyrics for her hit single "Flowers" after selling out the Hollywood Bowl. Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for Live Nation, Presley Ann/WireImage via Getty Images Miley Cyrus changed the lyrics to her hit song "Flowers" after selling out the Hollywood Bowl. She held a two-night run at the venue in October, her first full solo concert in four years. Some fans say "Flowers," released in early 2023, is a diss track to her ex-husband, Liam Hemsworth. After selling out a two-night residency at the Hollywood Bowl in October, Miley Cyrus changed the lyrics of an integral part of her hit song, "Flowers." She ad-libbed about selling out the iconic venue before the chorus: "Started to cry, but then remembered I sold out the Hollywood Bowl!" She added similar lyrics to "Flowers" in 2024 when she performed it after winning her first Grammy. The ad-lib now seems to be a way for Cyrus to celebrate her wins, and fans have suggested since its release in 2023 that the song was written as a diss track against her ex-husband, Liam Hemsworth. The two married in 2018 and divorced a year later. Representatives for Hemsworth did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Here are the Easter eggs you may have missed in "Flowers." Miley Cyrus released her single "Flowers" in 2023 — and many fans think the song takes aim at her ex-husband Liam Hemsworth. Fans think "Flowers" is a dig at Hemsworth. Miley Cyrus/YouTube As Business Insider previously reported , Cyrus and Hemsworth met on the set of "The Last Song," which was released in 2010, and dated on and off for several years. The couple married in 2018 and divorced a year later. The split was finalized in January 2020. While Cyrus hasn't confirmed that "Flowers" is about her relationship with Hemsworth, the single's release date, lyrics, and other hidden details offer a few clues to the song's meaning. The song was released on Liam Hemsworth's birthday. Liam Hemsworth and Miley Cyrus attended the "Avengers: Endgame" premiere. VALERIE MACON / Getty Images The buzz around "Flowers" began when fans noticed its release date. The single dropped on January 13 — Hemsworth's 33rd birthday — a detail that was not lost on Cyrus' fans.    Miley’s telling the world she can love herself better ON LIAM’S BIRTHDAY?! she definitely didn’t lie when she said she’s got nerve https://t.co/Pp7fi5yuqa — 𝒉𝒂𝒍𝒆𝒔 (@mileywrld) January 1, 2023 "She definitely didn't lie when she said she's got nerve," one user tweeted.  Many fans think "Flowers" resembles Bruno Mars' song, "When I Was Your Man." Theo Wargo/Getty Images In "When I Was Your Man," Mars sings that he wishes he " bought you flowers, and held your hand." Although Mars isn't credited as a songwriter on "Flowers," Cyrus sings "I can buy myself flowers," and "I can hold my own hand" in a similar tune to Mars' hit.  According to Billboard, some fans have speculated that Hemsworth dedicated Mars' song to Cyrus during their first engagement — though those theories are unconfirmed. The song's opening verse could refer to the 2018 Woolsey Fire. Chris Pizzello/Invision/AP "We were good, we were gold/ Kind of dream that can't be sold/ We were right till we weren't/ Built a home and watched it burn," Cyrus sings in the opening verse.  According to Us Weekly , the fire metaphor could be referring to the home Cyrus shared with Hemsworth, which burned down during the 2018 Woolsey Fire. It’s been a heartbreaking few days. This is what’s left of my house. Love. Many people in Malibu and surrounding areas in California have lost their homes also and my heart goes out to everyone who was affected by these fires. To help: https://t.co/YQCE1cLaej &amp; @happyhippiefdn https://t.co/vtLFytFmNw — Liam Hemsworth (@LiamHemsworth) November 13, 2018 Cyrus has said that the loss of the couple's Malibu home is partially what led her and Hemsworth to get married.  Some fans have drawn comparisons between a clip from the song's music video and a past red-carpet moment. Evan Agostini/Invision/AP In 2019, while attending the Vanity Fair Oscars party, an Access Hollywood reporter asked Cyrus and Hemsworth what a dance number would look like between the couple. WAIT A MINUTE https://t.co/YA76DVsz7T — out of context hannah montana (@OCHannahMontana) January 4, 2023 When Cyrus began dancing on Hemsworth, her then-husband, he shut it down, saying, "We're not doing this. Not on the carpet." One Twitter user put that video side by side with a promotional clip Cyrus posted on the platform, in which she appears to do a similar dance move — while the lyrics "I can love me better" play in the background. In October 2026, Cyrus changed the lyrics to "Flowers" and performed it at the Hollywood Bowl. LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 16: (EXCLUSIVE COVERAGE) Miley Cyrus performs onstage at Bass Persuades Live at Hollywood Bowl on October 16, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for Live Nation) Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for Live Nation After selling out shows at the Hollywood Bowl in October 2026, Cyrus changed the pre-chorus lyrics to "Flowers." In the original version, Cyrus sings: "I didn't wanna leave you/I didn't wanna fight/Started to cry, but then remembered I," before belting out the chorus. This past weekend, however, Cyrus changed that to: "I didn't wanna leave you (but I had to)/I didn't wanna fight (but we did)/Started to cry, but then remembered I sold out the Hollywood Bowl." Cyrus has ad-libbed her hit single before: At the 2024 Grammys, she sang, "Started to cry, but then remembered I just won my first Grammy!" Fans took to social media to applaud Cyrus' lyric change, with one YouTube commenter saying they "love how she's filling it in with different achievements." Cyrus also paid tribute to Dolly Parton, her late godmother, during the concert, breaking down in tears as she recalled memories of Parton. Cyrus then performed Parton's hit song "Jolene." Editor's Note: This story was originally published in January 2023 and was most recently updated in October 2026. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: ASX closes down, NAB shares drop on 2,500 planned job cuts — as it happened
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts NAB shares drop as it plans to cut 2,500 job by mid-2027, NextDC in trading halt — as it happened National Australia Bank says it will cut up to 2,500 jobs, or about 6 per cent of its workforce, by mid-2027. Local data centre giant NextDC has been suspended from trading ahead of an announcement that appears linked to a dispute about power poles in a suburban Melbourne street. Look back on the day's financial news and insights from our specialist business reporters on our live blog. Disclaimer: This blog is not intended as investment advice. Australian dollar: flat to 69.81 US cents Brent crude: +0.3% to $US119.91/barrel Live updates on the major ASX indices: Choose what information you see below by using filters We'll end our markets live coverage here and thank you for staying with us. If you miss anything during the trading day, you can catch The Business on ABC News at 8:44pm, after the late news on ABC TV, and any time on ABC iview . Our team will be back on deck tomorrow morning with the latest. NAB job cuts raise 'serious questions': Senator Tony Sheldon NSW Senator Tony Sheldon has urged NAB to "come clean" about how much of a role AI and technology have played in its decision to axe 2,500 jobs announced today. "We already know banks like NAB are using AI to automate tasks, analyse customer data and monitor risks. "For NAB to use buzzwords like 'future fit' to justify cutting 2,500 people is deeply disappointing and raises serious questions about whether its vision for the future is one powered by Australians or by AI and an offshore workforce. "Banks need to give their staff a genuine voice in this technological transformation instead of subjecting them to an AI dictatorship." Citi's Dirk Willer seems to take as a given that shares are in a bubble, the question is only when it ends. "Whenever the equity bubble bursts, we will go back to this correlation that rates will fall," he says. And that's it for the Citi Investment Conference today. I'll be back here tomorrow morning at 8:45am AEDT sharp for RBA deputy governor Andrew Hauser. Mining stocks lead local decline: analyst Betashares investment strategist Hugh Lam says mining stocks led the local decline today, with BHP under pressure after its September-quarter copper production missed estimates. Mr Lam said gains in health care and consumer staples had helped cushion the index, with Cochlear rising around 5%. "Our local market may also be reflecting the caution seen across Asia, where South Korea's KOSPI index and Japan's Nikkei 225 index failed to participate in Wall Street's tech-led relief rally," he noted. "The US rebound followed last week's sharp sell-off over the cost of financing AI infrastructure, but one strong session has not settled questions about the returns on that spending. "Higher US bond yields and Brent crude above US$100 a barrel are keeping inflation and borrowing costs in focus with Australia's relatively limited direct exposure to AI infrastructure offering some insulation to other major markets, although weakness in miners and banks are weighing on the index today." Mr Lam added that third-quarter US earnings season would be an important test for markets over the next few weeks. "Investors will look for evidence that AI demand remains durable and that revenue growth can justify the scale of investment in chips and data centres. "Until then, rallies in US tech may struggle to translate into broader gains across Asian and Australian equities." 'No-one wants to jump off the train too early' An interesting insight into investment psychology and strategy from Citi's global head of macro strategy and asset allocation Dirk Willer . He does believe there is a bubble in the AI boom. "We always over-capitalise the opportunity and the bigger the opportunity the more we over-capitalise it," he explains at the bank's annual Investment Conference in Sydney. However, that doesn't mean Citi is bailing out of equity investments in the tech sector ... yet. Willer points out that the Nasdaq rose 50% in a quarter just before the tech wreck of the early 2000s, meaning investors who exited too far before the bust missed out on a lot of potential returns. "No-one wants to jump off the train too early," he says. Dirk Willer is doing a one-on-one interview with Alicia Barry tomorrow , which you can watch on The Business at 8:44pm AEDT on Wednesday. The ASX has finished the day lower, down 0.3% at 8,816 points. When looking at the sectors, Consumer Staples led the gains, up 1.2%, followed by Healthcare and Consumer Discretionary , both up 0.9%.

events.title: The reporter who exposed Elizabeth Holmes' fraud responds to people who say he's 'missing the point of the film'
events.summary: John Carreyrou says the doc deserves its early Oscar buzz. Michael Loccisano/Getty Images John Carreyrou told Business Insider that he loves the new Elizabeth Holmes doc as "a great piece of art." But audiences who want an accurate retelling of Theranos' downfall should read his book, he said. It comes as people allege that he's "missing the point of the film." John Carreyrou has seen " You Can See Everything " twice. The reporter, whose award-winning investigation for The Wall Street Journal helped bring down blood-testing startup Theranos, told Business Insider that he liked the documentary. It follows Elizabeth Holmes, the startup's CEO, in the 34 days before she reported to federal prison in 2023. The film — co-directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim — has inspired a mix of reactions from viewers , ranging from shock to boredom to sympathy for Holmes. Carreyrou doesn't see that ambiguity. "The film is a great piece of art, but let's not confuse that art with the underlying facts," he told Business Insider. It mirrors what he's been writing on X. Carreyrou has been pushing back on people who, he said, had accused him of "missing the point" of the film — namely, that Holmes is unknowable. "She went after Tyler Shultz and Erika Cheung with everything she had," he wrote, referring to the two company whistleblowers at the center of his 2015 story. "I was threatened with litigation on a daily basis for months on end. It was a ruthless cover-up of a breathtaking fraud, and she was at the controls." A few readers have taken me to task for “missing the point of the film,” which is apparently that Elizabeth Holmes is unknowable and everything is ambiguous. Here’s my response: She went after Tyler Shultz and Erika Cheung with everything she had. I was threatened with litigation on a daily basis for months on end. It was a ruthless cover-up of a breathtaking fraud, and she was at the controls. Just a little context for those who have forgotten or didn’t follow the original story. By the way, I loved the film. #BestPicture, IMO. — John Carreyrou (@JohnCarreyrou) October 18, 2026 He has also reposted a Monday morning interview with Schultz, who said that Holmes "knows that she did something wrong," and alleged that, during the film, she brought out a different device when she was asked to show Theranos' hardware. The documentary does not retrace every detail of the Theranos scandal or the reporting that exposed it. Instead, it puts viewers inside Holmes' home as she insists that she was wrongly convicted. For audiences, it's raised bigger questions about performance, self-deception, and whether the film's subject can ever be fully believed. Carreyrou has told Business Insider that if audiences "have questions afterward or want more context about the Theranos saga, I would encourage them to read my book." He ended his X post by saying he "loved the film." He also gave a nod to its early Oscar buzz. "#BestPicture , IMO," he wrote. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Fired OpenAI engineer accused of bugging office won't be released from jail
events.summary: San Francisco's federal courthouse held the detention hearing for Abdulrahman Alfozan, the arrested and fired OpenAI engineer, on Monday. Brennan Smart/Bloomberg via Getty Images Abdulrahman Alfozan will stay jailed pre-trial, a San Francisco judge decided Monday. The engineer is accused of bugging a conference room at OpenAI, and he has been fired. Alfozan posed a risk of non-appearance, the judge said, after discussing his ties to Saudi Arabia. A former OpenAI engineer accused of bugging the AI startup's office was denied release by a San Francisco judge on Monday, meaning he'll have to mount his defense from jail. The Justice Department arrested Abdulrahman Alfozan on October 9 and charged him with using or attempting to use a device to intercept oral communications. He's accused of placing a recording device behind a television in an OpenAI conference room — an FBI affidavit includes photos of the device wrapped in toilet paper, and a man they say is Alfozan peering behind the TV. On Monday, the engineer wore a yellow surgical mask and a jail-issued orange sweatshirt to the San Francisco courthouse. Magistrate Judge Alex G. Tse prodded Alfozan's legal team about the risk that he might not appear for a future court hearing. Tse said that Alfozan's wife and son had traveled to Saudi Arabia with no plans to return, and went back and forth with Yasin about a one-way ticket that Alfozan had previously booked to the country. Tse said that Saudi Arabia and the US do not have an extradition agreement, and expressed skepticism that he had sufficient ties to the Bay Area to prevent his departure. William Pernik, Alfozan's attorney, argued that, rather than being detained, Alfozan should be fitted with an ankle monitor, ordered to stay home, and have limits placed on his use of technology. The lawyer also said Alfozan is willing to put up "essentially all the money his family has" as bond, including a roughly $1 million investment account. "Everything this man has, he's willing to surrender, and say, 'I'm not going anywhere,'" Pernik said. Pernik and Nas Yasin, another of Alfozan's attorneys, cited his coming naturalization interview as evidence of his local ties. "He was weeks away from achieving every immigrant's dream in this country," Pernik said. Yasin told Tse that she learned Alfozan's wife had obtained a short-term visitor visa to return to the US, to help improve her husband's case for ties to the Bay Area. Tse also asked Alfozan's legal team a slew of questions about his relationship with Saudi Arabia, including a commitment by the Saudi consulate to pay his bond and support his legal effort. Nick Parker, an assistant US attorney, appeared for the prosecution. He argued that the threat of forfeiting a $1 million bond wouldn't be enough to convince Alfozan to return if he made it out of the US, because he might be able to earn more money in Saudi Arabia. "There is a real threat here that once he leaves, the case is over," Tse responded. The judge scheduled the case's next hearing for early November. OpenAI called the recording device "sophisticated" when the arrest went public, though it said it hadn't found signs that he'd taken AI model weights, source code, or customer information. OpenAI fired Alfozan. Alfozan's charge carries a maximum penalty of 5 years. Pernik said in a statement last week that the allegations "appear wholly out of character for him." Alfozan, 35, has a green card that makes him a lawful permanent resident of the United States. He attended MIT, then worked at Facebook (now Meta) from 2017 to 2023. After a stint at the engineering startup Nash Technologies, Alfozan joined OpenAI in 2025. FBI agents have already taken Alfozan's Saudi passport. Have a tip? events.title: Citing ProPublica, Lawmakers Introduce Bill to Help U.S. Citizens Sue ICE for Wrongful Detentions
events.summary: Photo illustration by ProPublica. Source images: Congress and videos obtained by ProPublica. What Happened: A New Mexico Democrat in the House introduced a bill last week that would make it easier for U.S. citizens to sue immigration agents and the federal government over wrongful detentions and arrests. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández credited ProPublica’s reporting as the catalyst for the bill, the Justice for Citizens Wrongfully Detained by ICE Act. Earlier this month, we revealed that more than 500 U.S. citizens have been detained in warrantless arrests during the second Trump administration. Leger Fernández said the legislation would roll back the protections from lawsuits that agents and the federal government currently have. It would also establish a minimum level of compensation for people who win their suits, and extend the statute of limitations for such cases. The legislation would also take back any unspent Immigration and Customs Enforcement funding from President Donald Trump’s so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Leger Fernández’s bill was introduced with co-sponsor Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman, a New Jersey Democrat. Why It Matters: It can be difficult to sue federal officers for wrongful arrests or excessive force, or for local prosecutors to bring charges . Federal agents can claim immunity in response to civil lawsuits or to state charges and can move their cases to federal court. People who accuse immigration agents of wrongdoing can currently only sue in a narrow set of circumstances, and p revious Democratic bills aiming to change that have not passed. Some local prosecutors have announced investigations into the wrongful arrests of U.S. citizens or prosecuted federal agents accused of wrongdoing during immigration enforcement actions. What They Said: In an interview with ProPublica, Leger Fernández emphasized that accountability could not only address past wrongs, it may also help head them off in the future. “We know that when there are consequences, bad actors start behaving better because they don’t want to face those consequences,” she said. Without legislation, Leger Fernández said, agents “will continue to violate the law, to violate their own policy, and to violate the Constitution without any consequences.” Asked about the legislation, the Department of Homeland Security, ICE’s parent agency, repeated claims that it is not arresting U.S. citizens and defended its immigration operations as “highly targeted.” Background: The federal government denies that there is any pattern of immigration agents detaining U.S. citizens, but according to ProPublica’s count, more than 100 citizens were held after agents questioned their citizenship. At least 70 children and teens were also detained. Last year, congressional Democrats announced a wide-ranging investigation into immigration agents’ detention of U.S. citizens after our earlier investigation found that more than 170 citizens were detained by immigration agents . Read the Investigation More Than 500 U.S. Citizens Have Been Detained, Including Handcuffed or Held at Gunpoint, in Trump’s Immigration Crackdown The post Citing ProPublica, Lawmakers Introduce Bill to Help U.S. Citizens Sue ICE for Wrongful Detentions appeared first on ProPublica .

events.title: Prosecutors say ex-OpenAI employee accused of planting recording device received 'what appears to be considerable support' from the Saudi government
events.summary: A man described as Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi national employed as an OpenAI engineer, looks behind a television where a recording device has been placed in a conference room at OpenAI. DOJ/Reuters Prosecutors say an ex-OpenAI employee accused of planting a recording device appears to have received support from the Saudi government. A federal magistrate judge ruled on Monday that Abdulrahman Alfozan should remain in custody. Prosecutors said that Alfozan frequently communicated with a member of the Saudi Royal Family. Federal prosecutors say that a former OpenAI employee accused of planting a recording device received "what appears to be considerable support from" the Saudi government. Prosecutors made the disclosure in a motion to keep Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi national and former OpenAI employee, in custody pending trial. US Magistrate Judge Alex G. Tse ruled on Monday that Alfozan should remain in custody . Alfozan had been in contact as recently as October 5 with an unnamed member of the Saudi Royal Family, whom he frequently communicated with on WhatsApp over the last two years, prosecutors said. "In May 2026, the individual told the defendant, 'Saudi needs you more then [ sic ] the US!' to which the defendant responded '100,"' indicating he agreed," prosecutors wrote. The FBI arrested Alfozan on October 9. According to a criminal complaint, Alfozan planted a recording device in the back of a TV in an OpenAI conference room where sensitive discussions take place. OpenAI's security cameras caught Alfozan near the conference room on multiple occasions, despite his lack of authorization to the high-level meetings held there, prosecutors said. "In the days surrounding the time period that the device was installed, OpenAI executives met with government officials in that very room," prosecutors wrote in a filing on Sunday. "Defendant's conduct could pose a danger to the national security of the United States." The complaint included a photo of what prosecutors said was Alfozan peering behind the TV where the recording device was found. In addition to his WhatsApp messaging, prosecutors wrote that an unnamed member of the Saudi military booked a flight for Alfozan's wife and son on October 11, despite an existing reservation for an October 12 flight, which prosecutors said was "paid for by the Saudi government." Prosecutors also disclosed more information about Alfozan's alleged efforts to plant the device. According to the filing, Alfozan's iPhone had photos of "what appear to be the input/output panels on televisions and other electronic devices in various locations in OpenAI buildings." Those locations, prosecutors wrote, included "another conference room where sensitive meetings frequently occurred." Other files on the phone, including a note modified as recently as September 13, listed "Riyadh tasks" like "finding an apartment and a job for the defendant's wife, as well as obtaining an ID and a Saudi passport for his son," the filing said. Another note titled "OpenAI leave" suggested that Alfozan "was planning an '[e]arly … pick up' of the devices he had installed or intended to install and then extending his planned parental 'leave to full.,'" prosecutors wrote. As part of their reasons for requesting that the former OpenAI engineer remain in custody, prosecutors wrote that Alfozan's wife and son left the US without him and are now in Saudi Arabia. The filing also said "both of his parents and all (or all but one) of his siblings" are in Saudi Arabia. In a separate filing, William Pernik, Alfozan's attorney, said that the former OpenAI engineer did not pose a flight risk. "Mr. Alfozan was made aware of OpenAI finding the device per its own filings and OpenAI's public statements, approximately eight to ten days before he was arrested," Pernik wrote. "If his intention was to flee, he would have done so at that time." Pernik said that prosecutors' previous disclosure that Alfozan had purchased a one-way ticket to Saudi Arabia lacked context. "Seventy percent of the airline bookings in his email since January 2021 (96 of 138) were one-way tickets," Pernik wrote. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: US sanction waivers are Russian economic boon
events.summary: The Trump administration is delivering a string of victories — for the Russian economy. Within weeks of waiving sanctions on Russian diesel, President Donald Trump waived sanctions on Russia’s trading partners , prompting a fresh wave of GOP pushback that is building by the hour. “I want to see those used,” Sen. Katie Britt, R-Ala., said earlier Monday . Neither waiver is projected to have much long-term effect on US prices. But one expert estimated the diesel waiver alone could help Russian exporters net $30 to $40 more per ton, in turn padding Moscow’s tax revenue. The UK last year estimated that global sanctions had previously deprived Russia of $450 billion in war funds , including $154 billion in lost oil revenue and $285 billion in frozen central bank reserves. White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers told Semafor both waivers were necessary to “see this brutal war [in Ukraine] come to an end,” echoing an argument Trump made on Truth Social . “Enforcing the sanctions provisions now would impede ongoing US efforts to negotiate a durable and comprehensive peace agreement between Ukraine and Russia,” Rogers said. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, meanwhile, has argued that the latest waiver did not provide Russia with sanctions relief because “no sanctions were lifted.” “There is a 60-day period so we can examine what’s going on,” he told NBC News . — Eleanor Mueller
