events.title: Amazon is taking its biggest shot at Nvidia yet with new TorchNeuron dev tool
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. On Monday, Amazon Web Services released a tool called TorchNeuron that lets AI startups easily move their AI apps onto Amazon’s AI chip, Trainium. In doing so, Amazon is also taking a direct stab at the software advantage that has helped Nvidia become the default hardware choice for AI apps and spurred its rise as AI hardware provider of choice. TorchNeuron works with PyTorch, a free, open source toolkit that developers use to build, train, and run AI models. It lets AI apps written with PyTorch run on Trainium by changing just one line of configuration, according to Amazon — no code rewrite required. Amazon says about 85% of AI apps are written with PyTorch. Facebook originally developed it, but since 2022, it has been part of the Linux Foundation, which maintains open source projects. Nvidia has spent years ensuring its CUDA software — the software infrastructure that allows apps to run on Nvidia GPUs and its other hardware — seamlessly supports AI apps written with PyTorch. As a result, Nvidia’s hardware is now deeply embedded in the toolkit, essentially by default. TorchNeuron is adapted from PyTorch, so developers who know PyTorch already know how to use it. Amazon isn’t the first company to attempt to easily bring their chips to the platform. PyTorch users can also port their apps to AMD GPUs or even Apple’s chips with a simple configuration change. However, Amazon argues that porting to Trainium is not only easy, but it also gives AI startups access to Amazon’s entire cloud. Unsurprisingly, AWS claims that this is a better choice for startups than using neoclouds, many of which are tied to Nvidia and its hardware, like CoreWeave, Nebius, and Firmus. “You’re building on AWS. You’re not betting on a single-purpose compute provider and scrambling to build everything else around it,” Colin Brace, VP of Technology Software at AWS Annapurna Labs (the unit that makes Amazon’s custom chips), told TechCrunch via email. “On AWS,” he continued, “the infrastructure to go from prototype to production is already there, allowing a founder to move fast and scale when they need to.” AWS says that because the same chip both handles training (teaching the AI model) and inference (putting the finished model to work, as when it answers a user’s question), and is tightly integrated with the cloud infrastructure that startups need, its cloud will save them money, even if AWS doesn’t offer the cheapest per-token price. “Trainium’s value is price-performance plus the fact that it’s one platform for both training and inference, which improves the economics across a full workload,” Brace said. “Look at Deepgram — they moved to Trainium using native PyTorch support and they’re processing 70% more audio per dollar at production-grade accuracy.” Deepgram is an AI voice app provider, a competitor to ElevenLabs. But Amazon isn’t content to just give PyTorch app developers an easy option to move to its cloud. Amazon also says it is pushing PyTorch to be less automatically centered on Nvidia, and it will contribute the code to do that to the main PyTorch project. In the blog post announcing the new tool, the company wrote : Amazon’s approach extends beyond its own hardware. The company is contributing changes upstream to PyTorch itself, working with the PyTorch community to remove code that ties the framework to specific chips. The goal is to make PyTorch more hardware-agnostic for the entire developer community, not just Trainium users. While such a tactic is undoubtedly good for those who are selling hardware and cloud services that compete with Nvidia, one of the points of PyTorch is to hide all the pesky difficulties of getting AI code to run on hardware. We’ll have to wait and see if pushing Nvidia out that far gives developers more choice and more affordable options, as Amazon promises, or just more configuration headaches. Either way, if Amazon succeeds in deeply uncoupling PyTorch from Nvidia, this could have much bigger ramifications for the GPU giant than simply dealing with chip competitors. As Brace said: “The real story is removing the lock-in that kept developers from having a real choice at all.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . This doesn’t affect our editorial independence.

events.title: Trump open to summit with Xi and Putin — to discuss denuclearization
events.summary: President Trump wants to hold a trilateral summit with Chinese President Xi and Russian President Putin in China next month to discuss "denuclearization" — but not necessarily Ukraine. Why it matters: Such a summit between the leaders of the U.S., China and Russia would be unprecedented. Trump has been talking for two years about his aspiration to reach a deal with Russia and China to reduce the number of nuclear weapons. But so far Putin and Xi haven't shown much openness to the idea. Driving the news: Trump is expected to travel to China in mid-November to participate in the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders' meeting in the city of Shenzhen. The Kremlin has been floating the idea of holding such a meeting since July. Putin raised the issue in two phone calls with Trump, including one last week. The Chinese government hasn't expressed willingness to hold such a summit. What he's saying: When asked on Monday whether such a summit could discuss ending the war in Ukraine, Trump said he wants to hold such a trilateral meeting, but in order to discuss other issues. "I would do it, not so much for Ukraine, we would have it to talk about denuclearization," he said.

events.title: Nvidia CEO urges German manufacturers to adopt AI, saying digital tech won't replace heavy industry
events.summary: Nvidia's Jensen Huang is urging German manufacturing companies to combine their expertise in physical machines with artificial intelligence to, as he put it, “re-engineer” the economy FRANKFURT, Germany -- Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang urged Germany's makers of cars and industrial machines to quickly adopt artificial intelligence to “re-engineer” the country's struggling business model by tapping its wealth of manufacturing data and expertise. Huang, whose company designs the powerful computer chips and software used by companies like Anthropic and OpenAI to develop AI applications, said that digital technology would never replace manufacturing and the engineering world of cars and robots where Germany has vast experience. Or, as he put it, “electrons will never replace atoms.” But he said industry would benefit by leaning into technology. “The next wave of AI is physical. This is where AI interacts with the physical world: robotics, manufacturing, cars, heavy industry,” Huang said Monday during a discussion with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz at an investment conference in Berlin. "And so AI can only augment your capability. It will not replace your capability. So take advantage of the technology." Huang said Germany's data and expertise on manufacturing “is your natural resource, it belongs to the nation" but it needs to take better advantage of AI. "This industrial revolution is so mighty, so powerful. You don't have another chance,” he said. European leaders like Merz are looking to AI as a potential source of growth but are also concerned about the extent of European dependence on U.S. tech companies in the field. Europe's wealth of high quality public-sector and machine-readable manufacturing data could serve as grist for AI, an opportunity cited by former European Central Bank head Mario Draghi as an area where Europe could compete with the U.S. and China in the AI field. DOJ official clashes with judge in DC golf course case after Trump attacks her Man who took bird from Las Vegas' Flamingo casino could face prison if convicted Massive meat recall includes bacon, hot dogs, sausages Huang and Merz said AI was an opportunity for Germany's so-called “mittelstand,” the hundreds of small- and medium-sized companies in highly specialized industrial sectors. Merz is struggling to revive growth in Germany after years of near-stagnation after the pandemic. Among the economy's headwinds are high energy prices after losing cheap Russian natural gas due to the invasion of Ukraine , competition from China in sectors like autos where Germany once dominated, and excessive red tape and permissions that hold up projects for years. All that has put a damper on an economy heavily oriented toward building complicated machines for export, including cars, trains, aircraft and factory equipment. Europe lags the U.S. in building out the data centers that offer the massive computing capacity to train artificial intelligence applications, and faces concerns over the security of European companies' sensitive data against subpoenas and criminal warrants on servers owned by U.S. companies and thus exposed to the U.S. legal system even if they're in Europe. Huang appeared to address such concerns by urging Germany to import AI technology but adding that “you should not export your culture, export your values, export your knowledge." Huang said Germany should “take advantage of artificial intelligence. events.title: OpenAI Engineer Accused of Spying on Executives Ordered to Remain in Custody
events.summary: The former OpenAI engineer accused of bugging a company conference room must stay in custody while he awaits trial, a federal judge ruled on Monday after expressing concerns about his ties to Saudi Arabia. US prosecutors alleged Abdulrahman Alfozan is a flight risk because the Saudi Arabian government has offered to support him with no strings attached. They cited, for example, the Saudi consulate’s offer to work with a bail bonds firm to help fund Alfozan’s release. Federal magistrate judge Alex Tse questioned whether Alfozan is an “asset” for the kingdom and how a bond backed by the government could keep him in the country. “I find that problematic,” Tse said. “It seems like a blank check. ‘We’re going to pay whatever the court wants to get him out.’ I’m more interested in people from his family wanting to put up assets.” William Pernik, an attorney for Alfozan, dismissed the flight risk worries as baseless. But he failed to convince the judge that Alfozan was committed to his life in the US. “There is a real threat here that once he leaves the case is over,” Tse said. Aflozan appeared in an orange prison uniform and a medical face mask pulled down over his neck on Monday in Tse’s San Francisco courtroom, which was filled to capacity with journalists, students on a field trip, and about 20 people supporting Alfozan. Employee attempts to steal confidential company information are common in Silicon Valley. But Alfozan’s case has drawn international attention for the alleged amateur spycraft and geopolitical tensions at the center of it. Authorities haven’t offered a potential motive but have noted Alfozan has worked for a Saudi venture capital firm, offered consulting services to Saudi companies, and is supposedly friendly with people high up in the Saudi government. Pernik said there is no evidence of Alfozan spying for Saudi Arabia or engaging in something covert. “It’s not as if he sneaked in under the covers of darkness,” he said of the OpenAI conference room. “This was an open room where anybody could work in.” After the hour-long hearing, Pernik told reporters he was disappointed with the custody ruling and would continue to try to fight it. While Alfozan is a US permanent resident who had been on the path to obtaining citizenship, his ties to his native Saudi Arabia have come under scrutiny. Prosecutors allege that Alfozan was “in frequent communications via WhatsApp” with a member of the Saudi royal family throughout 2025 and 2026. The Saudi royal, who is not identified, was allegedly recruiting Alfozan to return to the country for a job working on a forthcoming AI initiative, according to a court filing. “Saudi needs you more then [sic] the US!” the individual wrote to Alfozan this past May, per the filing. Alfozan allegedly “responded ‘100,’ indicating he agreed.” US authorities also allege that the Saudi government bought Alfozan's wife and infant son a ticket to return to the country a few days after his arrest. She ended up leaving sooner on another flight booked by her sister’s husband, who works for the Saudi navy, according to attorneys for both sides. Alfozan's wife has not been accused of wrongdoing, and the FBI last week declined to comment on whether she would face any charges. Alfozan was at OpenAI for just over a year when the AI lab discovered a covert audio recording device hidden in a wad of toilet paper behind a TV in an executive conference room used for confidential business meetings. OpenAI found the device in late September, connected it to Alfozan, and then fired him earlier this month just before the FBI arrested him. Alfozan faces five years in prison on a single count of using a device to intercept communications, but prosecutors say additional charges are possible. Included among the government’s evidence are alleged conversations between Alfozan and an AI chatbot in which he asked for help setting up listening devices. Prosecutors also produced a photo taken of Alfozan looking behind the TV after OpenAI had removed the recorder. It’s unclear what, if anything, was recorded, because the device’s data was encrypted, according to authorities. Authorities say they also found components for recording devices at Alfozan’s home and photos of other OpenAI monitors and another OpenAI conference room on his phone. OpenAI previously said it recovered a second listening device in a bag Alfozan brought to the office and left unattended. Pernik claimed the electronics at Alfozan’s home were for home monitoring projects, including trying to improve a smart litter box for their cat. “This is a gentleman who spent 15 years of life immersed at this intersection of technology and personal life,” Pernik told the judge. Authorities said ahead of the hearing that they believed Alfozan had the means to flee.

events.title: PSA: Patch your Plex media server before someone hacks it
events.summary: Recently fixed vulnerabilities in the Plex Media Server are under active exploitation in attacks that, when successful, install malware, including cryptominers and residential proxy apps, a researcher said. Plex fixed four vulnerabilities at the start of last month. Three weeks later, published CVE designations revealed five vulnerabilities, with one of them carrying a severity rating of 8.6 out of 10. A researcher last week revealed an exploit that chained four of them together to achieve remote code execution of the device running a vulnerable Plex version. The researcher named the chain "Plex2Shell." Complex exploit chain The new details allowed a separate researcher to create a honeypot that could track attempts in the wild to exploit the vulnerability chain. Within a day, the researcher began seeing active scanning of the simulated Plex server and eventually successful attempts to infect devices. So far, successful attacks are installing two payloads. One is a cryptominer, which uses the device to mine cryptocurrency and deposit it into a wallet controlled by the attacker. The other payload is residential proxy software, which allows people to anonymize their Internet activity (much of it illegal) by connecting to the infected box and then using it to send the user’s traffic to a final destination. events.title: Saudi Arabia postpones big investor conference to 2027 as Iran-backed Houthis escalate attacks on kingdom
events.summary: The Future Investment Initiative, originally scheduled to take place in Riyadh from Oct. 26 to Oct. 29, has been postponed until 2027. The decision to postpone comes after Houthi militants attacked the international airport in Riyadh, leaving at least 12 people dead and hundreds injured. Some of the biggest names in finance were listed as speakers for the conference, including JPMorgan's Jamie Dimon and Goldman Sachs' David Solomon. Saudi Arabia on Monday postponed its big annual investor conference until 2027 as Iran-backed Houthi militants have escalated missile and drone attacks on the kingdom in recent weeks. The Future Investment Initiative was originally scheduled to take place in the Saudi capital Riyadh from Oct. 26 to Oct. 29. "We will announce the new 2027 dates very soon," the conference organizers said in a statement . The decision to postpone the conference comes after the Houthis attacked King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Oct. 10, leaving at least 12 people dead and more than 300 injured. Some of the biggest names in business and finance were listed as speakers for the conference. They included JPMorgan Chase's Jamie Dimon, Goldman Sachs' David Solomon, Blackstone's Stephen Schwarzman, BlackRock's Larry Fink and Citigroup's Jane Fraser. CNBC was told some participants and speakers had planned to travel to Saudi Arabia by flying first to Bahrain and then driving five hours to Riyadh. Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund launched the Future Investment Initiative in 2017. The conference has played a key part in Riyadh's plans to diversify its oil-dependent economy. Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman unveiled the ambitious megaproject NEOM at the first conference in 2017. The decision to postpone the conference underscores the deteriorating security situation in the Middle East as the U.S-Iran war spreads across the region. Houthi militants have launched repeated waves of missile and drone strikes at Saudi Arabia since the deadly airport attack earlier this month. The Houthis claimed on Monday to have attacked King Khalid International Airport again; Abha International Airport in southwestern Saudi Arabia, close to Yemen; Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu on the Red Sea Coast; the Shaybah oilfield and Saudi naval forces. The Saudi military destroyed several drones launched at the Riyadh region on Friday and Saturday, a spokesperson for the kingdom's armed forces said. Missiles launched over the Red Sea were also intercepted Friday including one heading toward the port city and oil terminal Yanbu, the spokesperson said.

The diamond-encrusted bra was always extravagant and worn by a top model at the VS Fashion Show. Kylie Jenner brought it back in 2026, modeling the most expensive Fantasy Bra ever created. Victoria's Secret brought some extra sparkle to its runway on Sunday night. The brand's annual fashion show, which returned in 2024 after being canceled five years earlier , was held in Los Angeles, with models including Adriana Lima and Barbara Palvin donning their wings for the occasion. Since making its comeback, the fashion show has been more than a spectacle for Victoria's Secret. It's also been a way to attract a new generation of shoppers by leaning into nostalgia . Elizabeth Preis, Victoria's Secret's chief marketing officer, previously told Fast Company that the show was about "brand consideration for the audience that doesn't currently shop with us." This year, the brand ramped up its social media promotion and made 17 times as many runway items available to purchase, Barron's reported. The 2026 show also brought back a symbol of Victoria's Secret's heyday: the Fantasy Bra , an elaborate piece of lingerie often worth millions that hadn't appeared on the runway since 2018. Kylie Jenner modeled the bra for its comeback. Designed by Jacob & Co., it's the most expensive Fantasy Bra ever created at $50 million. Take a look back at other Fantasy Bras Victoria's Secret has designed over the years. The Fantasy Bra was first introduced by Victoria's Secret in 1996 via a massive New York City billboard. Evan Agostini/Getty Images Worn by Claudia Schiffer, the diamond-encrusted lingerie was dubbed the "Million Dollar Miracle Bra." It was modeled for the Victoria's Secret catalog and advertisements, such as the massive one displayed in New York City. Tyra Banks wore the next one in 1997. Tyra Banks models the Victoria's Secret Fantasy Bra in 1997. Ron Galella/Getty Images The " Diamond Dream Bra " was much more understated than the original. It was crafted from white satin, lined with diamonds, and had one 42-carat teardrop gem hanging from its center. Gisele Bündchen modeled the "Red Hot Fantasy Bra" in 2000. Gisele Bündchen models the Victoria's Secret Fantasy Bra in 2000. DMIPhoto/Stringer/Getty Images The ruby-covered bra and matching panties modeled by Bündchen for a catalog were the most expensive lingerie set created by Victoria's Secret at the time, costing $15 million when they were designed. It also featured the Mouawad Excelsior Diamond —a 69-carat piece cut from the second-largest diamond in the world — hanging from its center. Valued at $6.5 million, the silver bra was covered in tiny diamonds from its straps to its cups. It also had two thin straps in the middle, with a 10-carat flower-shaped pendant hanging from them. Victoria's Secret put a holiday twist on the famous lingerie in 2007. Selita Ebanks models the Victoria's Secret Fantasy Bra in 2007. Gabriel Bouys/Getty Images The diamond-covered, $4.5 million "Very Sexy Holiday" bra — modeled by Selita Ebanks — stood out thanks to the rubies, emeralds, and yellow sapphires arranged in the shape of holly across its cups. Its Mouawad gems totaled 1,662.51 carats. Victoria's Secret fans saw the dark side of the Fantasy Bra in 2008. It was covered in black diamonds and had strings of rubies and white diamonds across it, for a total of 3,900 gems. Victoria's Secret kept the edgy aesthetic going in 2009. Marisa Miller models the Victoria's Secret Fantasy Bra in 2009. events.title: I Am Australian co-writer 'not happy' song used at conservative conference
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts I Am Australian co-writer says song used at conservative conference without permission Dobe Newton says associating his song I am Australian with a call to end migration is ironic. ( Supplied: Tamworth Country Music Festival Youtube ) Musician Dobe Newton says his co-written song I Am Australian was used without permission at the Conservative Political Action Conference this month. Mr Newton says it is inappropriate to use the song at an event that included talks about migration from Pauline Hanson and Angus Taylor. The ABC has contacted Conservative Political Action Conference Australia for comment. One of the writers of a classic Australian song has called out a conservative political conference for using his work without permission. I Am Australian was co-written by Dobe Newton from the folk and country group The Bushwackers in 1987, along with Bruce Woodley of The Seekers. Mr Newton said he never gave permission for the song to be played at the Australian Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC), which took place in Brisbane on October 10 and 11. "I was surprised and I'm not happy, Jan," he said. According to a CPAC program, the song was sung by opera singers in an opening ceremony, along with Advance Australia Fair and Waltzing Matilda. Mr Newton said he was not approached by anyone from CPAC and was only informed of its use after being approached by media. Bruce Woodley recently told other media outlets permission had not been sought or granted from him either. The ABC has contacted CPAC for comment. I Am Australian is often considered an unofficial Australian anthem , played at major sporting events and covered for significant national occasions. In 2023, a cover of the song by Judith Durham, Russell Hitchcock and Mandawuy Yunupingu was added to the National Film and Sound Archives' Sounds of Australia. Mr Newton said it was not appropriate for the song to be played at an event that included speeches mentioning proposed migration cuts from One Nation leader Pauline Hanson and Opposition Leader Angus Taylor. Angus Taylor spoke at the 2026 Australian Conservative Political Action Conference. ( ABC News: Luke Bowden ) "People will interpret it how they want but its specific use to promote a certain political point of view, as far as we're concerned, isn't appropriate," he said. "The whole point of writing it was to celebrate our multicultural nation. Mr Newton said other attempts to use the song by political groups had been denied. "When we had The Voice Referendum, both sides of the argument got in touch with Bruce and myself to ask for permission to use it as part of their campaigning," he said. "We politely declined to give either of them permission." Mr Newton said artists had moral rights to their work that theoretically protected against derogatory uses. "If your song is used in a situation where you think it's derogatory to the song itself or your reputation, then you have the ability to say, 'No, you don't have permission,'" he said. Louise Buckingham says copyright law is complex. ( Supplied: Louise Buckingham ) But CEO and principal lawyer at Arts Law Australia, Louise Buckingham, said the complexity of copyright law made it challenging for artists to push the rights. "We all benefit from [I Am Australian] and it's been used to such good effect in so many meaningful contexts that's enriched so many people's lives. Louise Buckingham says copyright laws need to be respected. ( 774 ABC Melbourne: Simon Leo Brown ) "It's such a kick in the teeth for artist when it's misused and when it's used without their consent and permission." Mr Newton said more needed to be done to protect artists. "The kindest interpretation would be that people aren't familiar with the fact that if you're going to use somebody's song in a political context, you need to seek permission," he said.

events.title: Hackers hit AI coding tool OpenCode, running up charges on users’ AI accounts
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. OpenCode , an open source AI coding agent that has been gaining ground among developers as an alternative to Claude Code and Cursor, said Saturday that attackers broke into an older system overnight, affecting 1.4% of users of its online platform, OpenCode Console, where some users store the API keys, or digital passwords, they use to access AI services. As the OpenCode team struggled to keep pace with the attack, the scramble to respond highlighted a growing problem: Companies without vetted access to AI models with fewer safety restrictions have a hard time defending against large-scale, AI-driven cyberattacks. “We had a security breach last night related to a large-scale distillation attack that impacted 1.4% of OpenCode Console users,” the company wrote on X. “We have notified them all this morning via email.” Users who did not receive an email were not impacted, the company said. While the company didn’t specify how the distillation attack occurred, leaked API keys can help users in countries with restricted access to American models generate the high volume of outputs needed for that process. Some skeptics called the framing an overstretch, arguing that the incident was a straightforward breach whose use for distillation remains unproven. Overnight, developers began posting spending alerts and unauthorized charges on Reddit and X: “I saw my Open AI, Anthropic, and Google AI spend alerts all fire off before going to bed wondering what was going on,” a developer wrote . Other users reported charges in the hundreds of dollars on individual accounts; a few described totals above $1,000. Anthropic and Google both blocked the API keys they believed were exposed, while OpenAI said it worked with OpenCode to restore access and refund its API customers for credits used in the attack. OpenCode said refunds for unauthorized charges are underway. The exposed keys were confined to Console, where some users had them in workspaces. The open source app and command-line tool were not affected, according to co-founder Dax Raad. “Note this is the OpenCode Console, not OpenCode itself, those keys never come to us,” he wrote on X. Even as users and AI companies moved to disable the exposed keys, the OpenCode team was still under pressure. Raad said attackers had been trying to break into its systems nonstop for 48 hours, requiring the team to keep AI defensive agents running around the clock. AI models that the OpenCode team turned to for analysis helped for a while, but started refusing to work when the malicious code they were asked to examine activated safety filters. “[T]hat was a bit frustrating,” he wrote on X. OpenCode later received access to OpenAI’s Daybreak Blue program, which gives vetted users AI models that are less likely to refuse requests for defensive security work. Raad said the access improved the team’s ability to investigate the attack. OpenCode isn’t the first company to hit this wall. In July, AI platform Hugging Face said commercial AI models blocked its attempts to analyze activity logs from an intrusion by autonomous AI agents, which OpenAI later revealed were its own models running with safeguards lowered during a test. In a section of its blog post titled “The asymmetry problem,” Hugging Face wrote that guardrails “cannot distinguish an incident responder from an attacker.” Security researchers have raised similar complaints , saying the restrictions are inconsistent and have pushed some toward foreign open-weight models, which anyone can download and run. The weekend episode drew a response from David Sacks, co-chair of the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology. “OpenCode (and earlier Hugging Face) hit the same wall mid-attack: frontier models refused to analyze the very exploits needed for defense because the payloads tripped safety filters. The guardrails backfired,” he wrote on X . The breach occurred the same night OpenCode made GLM-5.3-Flash free for users. The broader GLM-5.3 family has drawn attention from researchers who study open-weight models and note that its cybersecurity capabilities approached levels previously associated with restricted-access models like Anthropic’s Claude Mythos Preview. OpenCode has not detailed how attackers gained access to the older system, how keys were stored, or the full extent of any misuse. It has told affected users to revoke and replace their keys directly with each provider. The company said the incident remains ongoing . The breach lands amid a run of AI-enabled cyber incidents. Earlier this month, cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike said a China-based hacker likely used an AI penetration-testing agent, which probes computer systems for weaknesses, and Claude in attacks on South Korean banks .

events.title: Germany Wants to Lead the World in Industrial AI: How NVIDIA Will Help
events.summary: In the cavernous hall of Kraftwerk, a former power station in Berlin, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang sat down to discuss Germany’s AI roadmap, and in particular, the industrial applications of AI. Huang opened by tracing NVIDIA’s longstanding relationship with German industry, beginning with gaming systems, workstations and automotive design in the early 2000s and leading to today’s partnerships in autonomous vehicle development and digital twins for manufacturing. The conversation focused on how Germany can make the most of the AI revolution by playing to its strengths in manufacturing and automotive — and by encouraging AI adoption across the country’s ecosystem of small and medium-sized companies. Earlier in the day, as part of the Invest in Germany Summit, Chancellor Merz, the Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy and the Federal Ministry for Research, Technology and Space signed a Joint Declaration of Intent with NVIDIA. The German federal government’s aim is to merge traditional German engineering and manufacturing expertise with cutting-edge research and AI technology. The declaration sets out an agreement to work on a joint initiative with NVIDIA to advance cutting edge AI models for physical AI. Formalizing and expanding NVIDIA’s collaboration with Germany’s federal government and its “Industry 4.0 Platform,” which is comprised of representatives from politics, industry, research and trade associations, helps achieve the government’s stated goal to “systematically bring industrial AI into widespread use and to establish a state-of-the-art industrial AI ecosystem in Europe.” Germany’s Ambition to Integrate AI With Industry Merz and Huang dug into industrial AI and how NVIDIA can help Germany lead the way. The German Chancellor first laid out his government’s ambition. “We are fully committed to be one of the most advanced places in the world, not just in the European Union, but in the world to work with AI, to integrate AI into our industry,” Merz said. “I’m really optimistic that we will be one of the leading, if not the leading, country in the world in terms of the spread of AI for all the companies — our manufacturers, machinery, automotive industry and suppliers of the automotive industry. I think this is a great opportunity.” Merz called out the leaders of the small and medium businesses — the Mittelstand — in the audience. “The biggest advantage we have in Germany is our so-called Mittelstand,” Merz said. “Please open your doors for AI to make use of your data. This is a real secret and a real advantage for Germany to make use of all the data which is already available in our companies.” Huang agreed, and praised Germany’s world-class expertise in manufacturing companies both large and small, as well as its math and science excellence. That national expertise and knowledge is what sets the German economy apart, he said, and AI will only amplify it. “That knowledge belongs to you,” Huang said. “It cannot be replaced. AI can only augment your capability, it will not replace your capability. Take advantage of the technology. It’s a new instrument.” Germany’s expertise with physical technologies is a differentiator, Huang and Merz agreed, and a powerful accelerator for the German economy when AI is included. “If we are successful in bringing these two aspects and parts of the business of the future together,” Merz said. “I’m really very optimistic that Germany can be one of the most successful economies in the world.” Huang described AI’s impact across virtually every industry as a new industrial revolution. “This industrial revolution is so mighty, so powerful,” Huang said. “In the Chancellor’s words, you are re-engineering Germany. This is your chance to do it well.” Merz envisioned a regular reunion with Huang to assess the progress Germany is making with AI. “I would like to see him regularly, let’s say at least once a year, and discuss the progress we made,” Merz said, “And see a guy sitting in my office being extremely happy about Germany as a place to invest.” Huang also announced new investments in four German startups, part of a nearly $10 billion commitment by NVIDIA to support companies, universities, research institutions and more across Europe. NVIDIA has been investing across Germany’s startup ecosystem, supporting leading technology companies including n8n, Neura Robotics and Black Forest Labs . Today, Huang announced new planned investments in Agile Robots, Avelios Medical, Mirelo and Reflex Aerospace. Agile Robots, a Munich-based robotics company, builds AI-powered robots, from robotic arms to its Agile ONE humanoid, for manufacturing, logistics and healthcare. Avelios Medical, a Munich-based healthcare technology startup, develops an AI-native hospital information system that serves as the core system of record for clinical and administrative workflows, integrating AI directly into hospital operations to free up doctors and nurses to deliver better patient care. Mirelo , a German startup, develops AI models that generate sound effects, speech and music for video, helping creators and production teams produce high-quality audio that perfectly matches their visuals on screen. Reflex Aerospace, a Berlin-based space scaleup, designs and builds high-performance satellites ready for launch in about 12 months instead of years. Siemens and NVIDIA Advance Autonomous Manufacturing; Record-Breaking Quantum Simulation Earlier in the day, Siemens announced it’s partnering with NVIDIA to advance AI-driven, autonomous factories. Siemens showcased new AI solutions at its Erlangen factory , advancing its role as a global blueprint for autonomous manufacturing. Fully virtual production ramp-up reduces engineering effort by up to 85%, while agent-based production planning enables more adaptive manufacturing and cost savings of up to 20%. NVIDIA researchers used JUPITER, Europe’s largest supercomputer at the Jülich Supercomputing Centre, to run a record-breaking simulation of a fault-tolerant quantum computer. The 104-qubit simulation is the largest and most detailed of its kind to date. events.title: KI ferries close temporarily as ramps upgraded for new vessels
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts The Spirit of Kangaroo Island ferry, also known as SPOKI, is being retired as SeaLink prepares for a new vessel to take on the route. ( ABC News: Daniel Taylor ) Ferry services to Kangaroo Island will close temporarily as SeaLink prepares to introduce the first of two new vessels. Locals are hoping the larger vessels will help to grow the island's economy after a long wait. Services are scheduled to resume on a limited timetable, weather permitting. Kangaroo Island's ferry service has shut down for three days as part of preparations for the first of two new vessels to begin operating, with locals describing the wait as "frustrating". The SeaLink service will be closed until Friday, as crews work around the clock to install new vehicle ramp infrastructure at Cape Jervis, south of Adelaide, and at Penneshaw, on Kangaroo Island, to accommodate the larger ferries. The first new ferry, Wanggami, is expected to be brought into service later this month, while SeaLink has launched legal action in the Federal Court to have the second ferry, Ruwi, delivered to Australia from a shipyard in Indonesia . Kangaroo Island Regional Tourism manager Megan Harvie said the delays that plagued the arrival of the new vessels were "frustrating". "We need the ferries here to help us to grow the economy for both tourism and agriculture alike," she said. Megan Harvie says the new ferries were needed to help grow the island's tourism and agriculture. ( ABC News: Daniel Taylor ) But, she said locals were "excited" by the arrival of Wanggami, which was expected to be carrying passengers before the end of next week. She said the retirement of the Spirit of Kangaroo Island, which was affectionately known as SPOKI, was "bittersweet" after it had served the island for 22 years. The two new ferries were initially expected to begin service early last year , but last October the company adjusted the start date to June 1 this year. Kangaroo Island electrician Frank Colman, said it had been two or three years "without any real clear idea of what's going on". "We’ve been getting little updates here and there as far as how the boats are tracking and what’s happening with the ramps either side," he said. "But I feel like a lot of us have been a bit left in the lurch as far as not being able to honour timelines and not a lot of certainty around what's gonna actually happen here on in." Frank Colman says there had been uncertainty about the arrival of the new ferries. ( ABC News: Daniel Taylor ) He said the three-day shutdown may impact some services, but said locals were "generally pretty considerate when it comes to timelines on things, so I think we’ll be fine". Peter Wallis from Island Earth Works, a company working on the ramp changeover on Kangaroo Island, also said three days without a ferry could be frustrating for some people, but he said most locals were used to coping with periodic stops. “All in all, I think the sentiment's quite positive that we've just gotta get through this little bit now and get ahead and get with the new ferries and I think all the problems, they'll all go away once it gets going." The SeaLink ferry service will be closed until Friday. ( ABC News: Daniel Taylor ) James Meredith who owns Millie Mae's Pantry on the island said the existing ferries were full of "quirks and personalities" and welcomed the new vessels. Kangaroo Island Mayor Michael Pengilly said it was "imperative to the island that we have the ferries operating, operating well". He said the next three days would be inconvenient for some, particularly because it was "the busiest time of year" for livestock movement, but expected the ferries would quickly return to "business as usual". "When livestock are ready to go they have to go, you can't keep them. And they've got to be booked into the abattoirs," he said. Kangaroo Island Mayor Michael Pengilly says the ferries were "imperative" for the island. ( ABC News: Daniel Taylor ) He said the delays in delivering the new ferries had been "a mess", but it was time to "put that behind us". According to a statement on the SeaLink website, the planned closure was subject to weather conditions, with limited services expected to resume on Friday, October 23, with SeaLion 2000 the only ferry operating for "an anticipated three to four days". The website states that Wanggami would then begin operating alongside SeaLion 2000 once training, testing and familiarisation has been completed. SeaLink has also been contacted for comment.

events.title: Former coalmine site at centre of $12 billion plan to build trains
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Former Teralba coalmine preferred site for state-owned train manufacturing factory The NSW government says the Teralba site could accommodate train manufacturing, assembly, commissioning and testing. ( Supplied: NSW government ) The New South Wales government has chosen a former coalmine site in Lake Macquarie to be its state-owned train factory. The facility will build the next generation of NSW passenger trains, starting with the Tangara replacement fleet. The government says it is progressing with detailed site investigations and due diligence with the site's owners. A former coalmine site in Lake Macquarie is set to become a train factory where the next generation of NSW passenger trains will be built. NSW Premier Chris Minns pledged $12 billion to revive local train manufacturing capability in July , earmarking two sites near Newcastle for the state-owned facility. On Tuesday, the government announced a former mine site at Teralba, owned by Macquarie Coal, as the preferred location, chosen over the Broadmeadow locomotive depot in Newcastle. In a statement, the government said the location was selected after a preliminary assessment of both sites found Teralba was "a larger and more flexible site that could accommodate train manufacturing, assembly, commissioning and on-site dynamic testing" with capacity for future expansion. It said the location also provided an opportunity to transform former mining land into a major "manufacturing and employment hub". The facility is part of the government's $12 billion Future Fleet Program to rebuild train manufacturing capability in the Hunter. ( Supplied: NSW government ) The development, funded under the Future Fleet Program, is expected to support up to 780 jobs during construction and about 550 ongoing jobs across the facility and supply chains. Business Hunter chief executive Bob Hawes said the announcement was "fantastic" news for the region. "This is the sort of industry development that we want to see in this region," he said. "It digs into a deep vein of experience and opportunity that the region knows it can deliver on, with our skills and workforce here as well as the developed industries that already exist that can service and operate in this environment." The Hunter has a long history of rail manufacturing, with Newcastle firm Goninan, founded in 1899, building the Tangara trains at Broadmeadow in the late 1980s and 1990s, and the Millennium fleet later built at Cardiff. The facility will manufacture the Tangara replacement fleet. ( ABC News: Declan Bowring ) Mr Minns said the project would build on the state's manufacturing capacity. "For more than a century, workers in the Hunter proudly built the trains that carried millions of people around Sydney," Mr Minns said in a statement. "Then those jobs were sent overseas. We're bringing them back, because we believe NSW should build more of the things we need right here at home." The Lake Macquarie facility will host the next 30 years of train manufacturing in NSW, starting with the new Tangara replacement fleet before future replacement programs for the Millennium and OSCAR fleets in the 2040s and the Waratah fleet in the 2050s. The government said it would progress detailed site investigations and due diligence with Glencore, which part-owns Macquarie Coal, to enable further site planning, design and procurement work to start. The timeline for the facility's completion has not been finalised. It said Broadmeadow remained an alternative option at this stage, while detailed investigations, due diligence and acquisition activities continued at Teralba.

events.title: Fashion brands fail to show ethical commitments being met, new report shows
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Australian fashion ethical practices stalling, Baptist World Aid report finds Baptist World Aid has released its 11th Ethical Fashion Report. ( Supplied: World Baptist Aid ) The biennial Baptist World Aid Ethical Fashion Report, which scores brands on sustainable and ethical practices, found brands have improved just 0.2 per cent in the past two years. It found many companies had made commitments to supply chain improvements but failed to show any follow-through. Industry experts are calling for the Modern Slavery Act to be strengthened. Sustainable and ethical practice within the Australian fashion industry has stalled and is at risk of falling behind, a report has found. Baptist World Aid's Ethical Fashion Report analyses 500 brands across 48 different measures including governance, supply-chain tracing, supplier relationships, worker empowerment and environmental sustainability. The 11th edition of the report, released today, found on average that brands scored 31.5 points out of a possible 100, representing an 0.2 per cent improvement from 2024. Baptist World Aid ethical fashion lead Katherine Halliday said brands were failing to follow through on supply chain improvements. Katherine Halliday says this year's results are disappointing. ( Supplied: World Baptist Aid ) "Over the lifetime of the report, we've seen that fashion companies are getting better at setting policies and outlining their commitments for ethical practice, but they're falling short of really implementing those to make change for the workers," she said. The report found 93 per cent of companies had policies for workers' rights and sustainability but many lacked visibility beyond direct suppliers. Ms Halliday said brand transparency was improving thanks to growing consumer awareness and modern slavery legislation, but it was not reaching the areas that were the most impactful for workers, such as living wages or the ability to advocate for workers' rights. "We know that almost no garment worker in the supply chain is being paid a living wage. And that's not a luxury. It's just enough to make ends meet," she said. The report found while some companies offered grievance mechanisms, these were only accessible to 20 per cent of workers at less than a quarter of the brands. Luxury and fast fashion rank similarly Outdoor and technical brands were among the highest ranked by the report, including Patagonia, which scored 70 points. Ms Halliday said the sector had performed well for some time. "I'm really heartened when those brands that look environmental and ethical can actually back it up with strong certified material use and strong supply chain practices," she said. Ms Halliday encouraged shoppers to check the ethical fashion guide rather than rely on a brand's image. Despite vast price differences, the report found luxury and premium brands (38.63), on average, only scored marginally better than fast fashion brands (37.91). Thirty-eight per cent of brands used sustainable fibres, which was an improvement from 30 per cent in 2024. But the report found the overall rise in fibre production, particularly petroleum-based synthetics, outpaced any environmental benefits of the materials used. Harriette Richards, from RMIT University's School of Fashion and Textiles, said it was difficult for fast fashion brands to be considered truly sustainable, based on the volume of production alone. She said use of natural or recycled fibres did not mean a garment was built to last and could also leave questions about how the fibres were made. "I think it can sometimes be used, dare I say it, as a greenwashing tactic, or as simply a distraction from some of the other more complicated issues that are at play when it comes to mass production," Dr Richards said. Seven per cent of brands received a perfect score for responsible purchasing practices, a criteria assessed on whether brands conducted business in a way that enabled their suppliers to act ethically. Ms Halliday said a brand might have a code of conduct that asked suppliers not to make workers do overtime, but then undermine that by setting short timelines or having "a lot of pressure in turnaround and the pricing negotiations". Dr Richards said deadlines set by Australian brands could put expectations on offshore producers that they could fulfil, so they had to pass the work on to subcontractors operating under unethical conditions. "There's this real, like, trickle-on effect, just by someone saying, 'I need this order by this date,'" she said. What needs to be done to improve fashion ethics?

events.title: Alleged investment scam leaves Australians missing millions
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts From Sydney to the Caribbean via Dubai: How a CEO with possible terror links allegedly took millions A licensed investment company allegedly scammed its customers out of their life savings — and now its CEO may have links to terrorism. It has sparked concerns about deep flaws in Australia's financial regulatory regime. Shirtless, adorned in reflective sunglasses and holding a pineapple, Karim Farag looks like an ordinary holiday-goer. But the 32-year-old Egyptian has landed in a web of lies involving a suspected sham investment, ghost addresses leading to the Caribbean, a famous Australian cricketer and alleged links to terrorism. Karim Farag is the former chief executive of Main Group FX, a licensed investment firm in Australia that disappeared three years ago, leaving at least 13 investors collectively $2 million in the red. Now the ABC can reveal Mr Farag has alleged connections to an organisation accused of funding terrorism. Mr Farag maintains he has nothing to hide and is willing to cooperate with authorities. The 'euphoric' Sydney event that lured investors It all began at a four-star hotel in the heart of Sydney in 2023. As they enjoyed free food and cocktails, Main Group investors could never imagine that, by the end of the year, the company hosting the event would vanish, and their life savings along with it. Investor Jean Giles, a former public servant from Western Australia, thought she bonded with her account manager over a glass of red wine as he confided that his daughter had died in a hit-and-run in New York. "The Sydney event was the clincher for me. I came away from there feeling quite euphoric," she said. Do you know more about this or have a similar story? Email turner-cohen.alex@abc.net.au Main Group claimed to trade in futures and commodities, including oil and gold. Its headquarters were in Sydney, and it spruiked algorithmic trading software that allowed investors to "set and forget" their money. With monthly dividends and the ability to cash out at any time, users could start with as little as $US250 ($350). Ms Giles invested a small amount and, over several months, with moderate returns, was coaxed into giving away more, to the tune of $176,000. Also at the Sydney event was Melbourne truck driver Dean Butterworth, who eventually invested $217,000 from a workers' compensation payout he received after injuring his back. He was among an estimated 40 guests who met several Main Group FX staff flown in from the Cyprus head office to "put a face to the voice", as the event was advertised. It was to be the first and only time meeting Robin Mahfouz, the Australian director of Main Group FX, and account managers Oscar Allison and Alex Morrison. Mr Allison and Mr Morrison did not respond to requests for comment. The ABC is not suggesting they were aware of any wrongdoing. "Going to this event sort of made me feel comfortable knowing that we're meeting real people, it's not over the phone, it's not emails or anything like that," Mr Butterworth said. Adding to the appeal, cricket legend Shane Watson was spruiked as a potential special guest as Main Group's "Australian ambassador" but ended up being a no-show. The firm's enigmatic chief executive Mr Farag was quoted in a paid advertorial saying: "We are thrilled to partner with a world-class talent like Shane Watson!" Mr Watson had previously posed for the company in a photo shoot that included a Main Group FX-branded cricket bat and clothing. "Being able to partner with Main Group FX, that's one of their incredible strengths, is educating people, educating traders and people who don't really know a lot about trading to be able to give them the best chance of success," Mr Watson said in the video. He told the ABC he cut ties with the group in November 2023, had no involvement in its management, and had tried to get the photos removed. A few months after the lavish conference, investors said monthly dividends stopped, they could not withdraw their money, and all trace of Main Group FX disappeared. Main Group FX never entered administration or bankruptcy and the company is now deregistered, with customers no longer receiving returns and unable to recover their initial investment. It has essentially vanished, and there is no established way for investors to salvage their missing money. They now have to take matters into their own hands, with some pursuing action from police and regulators. "At the moment, financially, I'm barely holding it together. Bankruptcy is on the books," Mr Butterworth said. He was forced to return to work despite his back injury, while Ms Giles sold her home.

events.title: The ultramarathon legend who ran 350 miles nonstop says the key to doing hard things is simpler than most people think
events.summary: Courtesy of Dean Karnazes Dean Karnazes holds the world record for the longest distance a human has ever run nonstop. His advice for going farther than you think you can: redefine success before the race begins. When the pain hits, Karnazes says there’s one rule: keep moving — even if you have to walk. For decades, scientists have tried to understand what separates people capable of extraordinary endurance from everyone else. Is it genetics? VO₂ max? Pain tolerance? Mental toughness? Dean Karnazes has spent more than 30 years giving them a remarkable case study. He's run 50 marathons in 50 states in 50 consecutive days, crossed Death Valley in the middle of summer , and in 2005 set the record for the longest nonstop run — covering 350 miles in 80 hours and 44 minutes. Even that wasn't enough. "I actually made it 350 miles, which was somewhat of a letdown because I thought maybe I could run 500 miles," Karnazes told me. "That was kind of the ultimate goal." His world record still stands today, 21 years later. After decades of ultrarunning , Karnazes says he's learned that doing hard things comes down to a handful of simple habits that anyone can practice. Don't make winning the goal Dean Karnazes has traveled the world, running ultramarathons for more than 30 years. Courtesy of Dean Karnazes Karnazes has finished on the podium plenty of times, but he says that's never been what pulled him to the starting line. "I do it for the adventure," he said. "Both the inner and the outer adventure. I've never really said I want to win a race. I just thought, be the best Dean that Dean can be on race day." He says approaching races that way has changed how he defines success . The podium, if it comes, is just the cherry on top. That mindset, he says, has kept him motivated through hundreds of marathons and ultramarathons, long after chasing trophies stopped being interesting. Redefine what success looks like Karnazes ran 350 miles nonstop, setting the world record for the longest continuous run by any human. Courtesy of Dean Karnazes When Karnazes gives advice to new ultrarunners, he doesn't start with mileage or pace. "Just set your goal on finishing," he said. "Don't say I want to do it in sub five hours or sub six hours. Just say, 'For me, success is reaching the finish line before the cutoff.'" Karnazes says that approach has a way of changing how you see your own limits. "You'll prove to yourself that you're better than you think you are. And you can go further than you think you could." Keep moving, even if you have to slow down Karnazes has placed in many races, but he says that's not what drives him. Courtesy of Dean Karnazes The advice sounds simple, but following it is another story. At some point during his 350-mile run, Karnazes stopped trusting what he was seeing. After nearly three days without sleep, he said he started hallucinating . He felt as though he had left his own body and was watching himself from above. "When you're in these altered states, it's as though you don't have conscious control of your mind," he said. "You're fighting your mind to stay present, but your mind gets away from you." Despite that, he kept running . I asked Karnazes for his advice to aspiring ultrarunners who worry they'll hit a point where the pain becomes too much. "You walk if you have to," he said. "You slow down, you push through the pain, and you come out the other side, and you're rejuvenated." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Tolan snags $30M for its AI companion that helps users navigate life
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Tolan , the AI companion designed to help people manage their daily lives, navigate relationships and emotions, and accomplish their goals, has just expanded its runway with another $30 million in capital. The startup’s investors in the latest round include Union Square Ventures, Khosla Ventures, and Homebrew, doubling the total amount it has raised to date and pushing its valuation beyond the previous $120 million, according to a new report by Upstarts Media . (The startup didn’t disclose its new valuation, but PitchBook estimates it at more than $268 million, with “medium confidence.”) Users engage with Tolan’s app through a cartoonish character that’s meant to offer support and help them get through their to-dos. Tolan generates revenue from its tiered memberships, which are required for full access to all features. The company told Upstarts Media its annual recurring revenue is now in the “double-digit millions.” The startup is one of the few AI companions that have found some traction, as it claims to have more than 250,000 active users who have had more than 70 million conversations over the past year. Around 70% of its users are women, and 40% are parents, Tolan’s team told the news outlet. (Anecdotally, the app is said to appeal in particular to neurodivergent people , who may benefit from additional support, whether that’s emotional support or help with organizing tasks.) Compared with other companions, Tolan seems to have found a balance between being helpful without being perceived as too weird. Compare that with the public shaming that Friend’s pendant-based AI companion faced; users dubbed Friend “ very cringe ,” The New York Times called it “hated,” and Wired said it “has no soul.” Meanwhile, another former top contender in the space, Character.AI, recently filed for bankruptcy after its founder’s return to Google . (Its remaining staff is transitioning to Disney, which bought some of its assets.) However, Tolan could end up facing increased competition from the more recent crop of AI agents, which help users plan, organize, and accomplish their tasks and goals, not just talk their way through them. For instance, Meta gave its AI agent Muse a cute avatar for its users to talk to, which it also plans to release as a hardware product in the future. The startup also has to navigate the risks of offering AI-powered emotional support, given that multiple lawsuits have been filed against general-purpose AI app makers alleging that chatbot interactions contributed to users’ suicides. Nicole Stuart/US Marine Corps The Marines are fielding new medical gear to treat casualties when evacuation is delayed. New portable blood coolers and warmers will help corpsmen treat wounded troops closer to combat. AI-assisted ultrasounds could help front-line medics identify internal injuries and prioritize evacuation. The US Marine Corps has begun fielding new medical equipment meant to help troops survive when wounded service members can't be quickly evacuated from the battlefield. The new technology is designed to store blood, identify internal injuries, and treat wounded service members closer to the battlefield as the military prepares for future wars in which casualties may be unable to reach a hospital for hours or even days. The equipment includes improved, lighter-weight mobile blood coolers, better blood warmers, and small AI-assisted ultrasound devices and is designed to help Navy corpsmen and other providers treat casualties with less bulky equipment and less reliance on extensive medical infrastructure . During the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, US air supremacy frequently allowed helicopters to quickly evacuate wounded troops to well-equipped and defended medical facilities near the battlefield. The proliferation of drone warfare and other technological advancements seen in Ukraine has, however, raised doubts about whether rapid casualty evacuations will be possible in future conflicts. Now, military planners assume that a sophisticated foe is likely to possess tools that could severely disrupt military tasks such as casualty evacuation , resupply, and communications. Throughout the post 9/11 wars in the Middle East, the military planned on getting wounded troops to advanced medical facilities within an hour, said Navy Capt. Shari Gentry, the Marine Corps' deputy medical officer, speaking to reporters at a media event near Quantico, Virginia. "And we do not foresee that being the case." The Corps has already begun distributing the systems to medical units, with some equipment reaching troops deployed to the Middle East. Among the new devices is a portable refrigerator capable of storing approximately 30 units of blood, potentially enough for four seriously wounded Marines, according to military medical guidance. Each battalion aid station is set to receive one, giving medical personnel a supply of blood closer to the battlefield. Weighing about 60 pounds, it replaces a system that weighs over twice as much and uses rechargeable batteries already common throughout the Marine Corps. The smaller refrigerator allows medical teams to maintain blood supplies without relying continuously on generators or fuel deliveries, said Navy Cmdr. Kyleigh Hupfl, the Corps' clinical lead for Expeditionary Medical Systems. The capability has already proved useful in the Middle East, Hupfl said. The Corps accelerated delivery after units raised concerns about the reliability of existing refrigeration equipment. One unit told her that the new device allowed it to maintain a ready supply of blood throughout its deployment. Small deviations in temperature can render blood and other pharmaceuticals unusable. "We need to be able to bring cold chain distribution forward without relying on heavy generators, and we need to be able to do that in a sustainable way," she said. The service is also fielding new portable blood warmers that can deliver warmed fluids faster than the previous equipment. The warmer works by passing blood through a tube, warming it before it flows into a patient's veins. Such warmth is crucial to prevent hypothermia, a serious complication in injured patients. Another major change involves portable ultrasound machines equipped with AI-assisted imaging. Previously held only at higher levels of battlefield medical care , the new machines are now being pushed toward the lowest level of tactical care, known as Role 1 facilities, where Navy corpsmen and physicians provide immediate life-saving care for wounded Marines. The AI software helps users identify anatomical structures on ultrasound images, allowing providers with less ultrasound experience to spot signs of internal bleeding or other injuries that might otherwise be difficult to detect. That information can also help medical teams determine which casualties need evacuation or surgery most urgently, said Navy Chief Petty Officer Matthew Brown, the chief biomedical equipment technician for the Corps' Expeditionary Medical Systems. "I have 10 people that are hurt. Who should I get out?" Brown said of the dilemma and the new ultrasounds being fielded to front-line medics to address it. "And at the end of the day, that's what's going to save their life." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Federal spending on climate change before 2024 election boosted incumbents of both parties
events.summary: The U.S. House of Representatives votes on the Inflation Reduction Act in August 2022. AP Photo/Patrick Semansky A massive federal spending effort to combat climate change passed in 2022 without a single Republican vote in the U.S. House or the Senate . But the billions of dollars it authorized benefited Republican and Democratic politicians alike – so long as they were already in the House of Representatives – according to an analysis I conducted with several fellow researchers. The results suggest that incumbents can still reap electoral rewards when federal money reaches their districts, even if they opposed the bill that provided it. Enacted in 2022, the Inflation Reduction Act squeaked through the Senate only through a tiebreaking vote cast by Vice President Kamala Harris . It authorized spending US$370 billion to combat climate change and lower greenhouse gas emissions , primarily through subsidies such as a tax credit of up to $7,500 for buying an electric vehicle and incentives for making commercial buildings more energy efficient , rather than by imposing new fees or taxes. Before the 2024 election, over $204 billion had been spent on clean energy projects around the country, through a combination of private investment and federal incentives. While Republicans opposed the legislation, 79% of the law’s investment went to Republican congressional districts. Even when Republicans vote against climate legislation at the national level, at least some favor investing in clean energy technology at the state and local level, because those investments bring local economic benefits. Many Republican districts, which are often large and more rural, are well suited to these kinds of projects. Benefits of federal investment Elected officials are sometimes accused of “ pork barrel politics ,” seeking to direct federal taxpayer spending to their own congressional districts. In part that’s because voters see federal investment as creating local jobs and stimulating economic growth. Although no Republican voted for the Inflation Reduction Act in 2022, some Republican lawmakers began defending parts of the law as investments reached their districts. In August 2024, heading into the election, 18 Republican House members urged House Speaker Mike Johnson to preserve the law’s clean energy tax credits, which they said “created good jobs in many parts of the country – including many districts represented by members of our conference.” That support continued after the election. In March 2025, after Republicans retained control of the House and party leaders began considering cuts to the law’s programs, even more Republican House members called for preserving the clean energy tax credits, which could be used, for example, to finance a large wind energy project or construction of a battery factory. The lawmakers argued that repealing the credits while major projects were still under construction would jeopardize investments already underway and the jobs tied to them. A Toyota battery-manufacturing plant in Liberty, N.C., received billions in support through the Inflation Reduction Act. Logan Cyrus/AFP via Getty Images The bill’s funding affected the 2024 election Our analysis finds that Inflation Reduction Act funding helped incumbent House members of both parties in the 2024 election. During the campaign, both Democrats and Republicans highlighted benefits of the investments funded by the act. Republicans usually used language like “ economic development opportunities ,” while Democrats directly mentioned the act itself. Some districts got nothing, and one got nearly $8 billion. Some of the largest investments were in Republican-held districts in North Carolina and Georgia to expand capacity at electric vehicle plants already under construction. These companies were eligible for corporate tax breaks from the law and hoped to benefit from increased consumer demand because of the law’s tax credit for people purchasing electric vehicles. In Mississippi’s 2nd Congressional District, which got $588 million in funding from the Inflation Reduction Act, Rep. Bennie Thompson, a Democrat, received 61.8% of the vote in 2024, up from 60% in 2022. In Michigan’s 5th District, which got almost $2 billion under the law, Rep. Tim Walberg, a Republican, received 65.7% of the vote in 2024, up from 62% in 2022. We found that the more money a representative’s district got from the Inflation Reduction Act, the more the candidate improved their electoral performance in 2024 over how they had done in 2022. When we conducted our statistical analysis, we accounted for multiple factors that could influence election results, including the district’s support for Trump, the incumbent’s previous vote share, campaign spending and district demographics. Using statistical methods to isolate the effects of Inflation Reduction Act funding, we found that doubling the amount of federal investment in a congressional district led to about a 0.9 percentage-point increase in the incumbent’s 2024 vote share relative to their 2022 result. Our analysis showed that both Democratic and Republican incumbents saw electoral benefits from Inflation Reduction Act investment, even though Republicans in Congress had universally opposed the legislation. While some incumbents still lost votes or their seats, the data showed that greater Inflation Reduction Act investment helped them perform better than they otherwise would have. These results indicate that voters may respond more to the money coming into their districts than to the underlying purpose of that funding. While previous federal spending projects helped incumbent House members in elections , we found no direct evidence that district economies improved between 2022 and 2024. Instead, it’s more likely that incumbents claiming credit for the investments on the campaign trail explained why election results improved with Inflation Reduction Act funding. The lesson is that voters pay attention to actual or promised investments that might come into their areas. President Donald Trump signs a major tax cut and spending cut bill on July 4, 2025. Samuel Corum/Getty Images Dismantling the subsidies and tax breaks Upon taking office in 2025, the Trump administration and the Republican majority in the House rolled back many of the law’s climate provisions . A massive package of tax breaks and spending cuts sometimes referred to as the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” removed tax credits for energy efficiency improvements and electric vehicle purchases. The Trump administration has also moved to expand fossil fuel production on federal lands. This evidence indicates that presidential priorities can outweigh even direct benefits to House members on highly polarized issues. The fact that some climate-related tax credits remained even after passage of the big budget bill does indicate that economic development policies may remain appealing to Republican leadership.
