events.title: How far can we push computing?
events.summary: MIT Technology Review Explains: Let our writers untangle the complex, messy world of science and technology to help you understand what’s coming next. You can read more from the series here . On the evening of December 29, 1959, at an American Physical Society meeting at Caltech, the physicist Richard Feynman gave a lecture called “There’s Plenty of Room at the Bottom,” on how we might manipulate and control things on an extremely small scale. There is no physical law stopping us from writing the entire Encyclopædia Britannica on the head of a pin, he argued, or from storing every book ever written in something the size of a dust speck—or, ultimately, from arranging matter atom by atom. Biology already did versions of this (a living cell keeps its instructions in a wisp of DNA), so all of this was plainly permitted by the laws of physics. We simply had not built the tools yet. In other words, there was plenty of room at the bottom. He was right, and for decades we descended into that space almost for free. The transistor—the switch at the heart of computer chips—repeatedly halved in size so that chips doubled in density; a computer that once filled a room now fits inside a watch. But that easy descent has now stalled, and the clearest sign is the buildout of data centers. Six of the biggest hyperscalers, the companies that run the world’s largest such facilities, are on track to spend more than $700 billion this year on computing infrastructure, about twice the record they set in 2025, pouring concrete and copper and silicon into new sites faster than the electrical grid can feed them. That buildout buys performance by brute force, adding more of what we already know how to make. The other kind of progress, the kind that made computer chips better, is the one that is quietly running out. The trend lines that tracked the dramatic improvements of the 20th-century information age are now bending—or breaking—with the dawn of the 21st century’s intelligence age. Moore’s Law, which plots how densely transistors can be constructed on silicon, has slowed down; Dennard’s Law, which states that power consumption in a given patch of computer chip stays the same even as it gets more and more packed with smaller and smaller transistors, has ended; Koomey’s Law, which traces how much computation we can wring from each joule of energy, has begun to flag; Kryder’s Law, which describes how tightly bits can be packed to build magnetic storage, has slowed to a crawl; and Keck’s Law, which charts the exponential rise in the amount of information a single conventional optical fiber can carry, is flattening.  But these scaling laws are merely observations about systems that we have engineered; they are not fundamental physical laws. The physical limits of computing and communications—dictated by quantum mechanics, general relativity, and information theory—lie far below anything in a data center today. The scaling laws chart the descent behind us. The fundamental physical limits chart the room that remains. Some of these limits may be far out of reach in practice. But they are still worth exploring, because the work pays twice: once in technology development and once in fundamental science. A proof-of-­concept system that approaches a limit is at once a technology that forces stalled paradigms to give way and an experiment that deepens our understanding of the physical laws themselves.  The descent During his 1959 lecture, Feynman offered two prizes of $1,000 each out of his own pocket. One would go to the first person to build a working electric motor smaller than a 0.4-millimeter cube. He expected the challenge to force someone to invent a genuinely new microtechnology. Instead, about a year later, a Caltech-trained engineer named William McLellan turned up with the motor built and running. The ­quarter-­milligram machine, roughly the size of a grain of sand, had been assembled by hand with a toothpick and a watch­maker’s lathe, under a microscope. Feynman, by his own account, was only slightly disappointed. The prize had proved his point in the least interesting way imaginable. The room really was down there, but reaching this first milestone had taken no new technology at all—just an unusually patient man with steady hands. The second prize aged differently, and more instructively. It was offered to whoever could shrink a page of text by a factor of 25,000 in each direction, small enough for the whole Britannica to fit on a pinhead. That one stood unclaimed for a quarter of a century. It was finally won in 1985 by Tom Newman, a Stanford graduate student who used an electron-beam lithography machine—an ancestor of pattern-making tools used in chipmaking today—to transcribe the opening page of A Tale of Two Cities at the required scale. The descent was already well underway, however. The year before Feynman’s talk, Jack Kilby, newly hired at Texas Instruments and with no vacation yet to take, spent that July nearly alone in the lab while his colleagues enjoyed time off, and by that September he had wired together a transistor, a capacitor, and three resistors, all made from a single sliver of germanium. This proved that an entire circuit could be carved from one block of semiconductor.  The machine, roughly the size of a grain of sand, had been assembled by hand with a toothpick and a watch­maker’s lathe, under a microscope. The idea took off, and the number of components on a chip kept doubling on a schedule so regular that Gordon Moore, in a 1965 trade-magazine article, simply drew a line through the trend and extended it into the future. That line became Moore’s Law. Moore, though, never claimed transistors could shrink forever. He observed that at any given moment there is a certain number of components that makes each one of them as cheap as possible to manufacture. In 1965, that number was 50. Put in too few transistors and you waste the chip; cram in too many and manufacturing errors multiply and yields collapse. It was this cost-minimizing number that was doubling at a steady pace.  For four decades the descent came with another gift: Dennard scaling, so named for the IBM engineer Robert Dennard, who spelled it out in 1974. Each time transistors shrank, they also switched faster and drew proportionally less power, so every generation was an automatic win. Around 2004, though, the gift ran out. Chips could no longer shed the heat of running every transistor flat out; clock speeds, which had raced past three gigahertz, stopped climbing, and Intel canceled the four-gigahertz processor it had promised. The industry pivoted to packing multiple processing cores onto a chip rather than making one core faster, and the texture of progress changed.  Progress is now bought mostly by scaling up the system—more chips wired together, more memory feeding them, more power and cooling around them—rather than by shrinking the transistor. events.title: Trump Appointees Asked a Federal Cybersecurity Agency to Secretly Acquire a Voting Machine — and Hack It
events.summary: Photo illustration by Shoshana Gordon/ProPublica. Source images: Christopher Mark Juhn/Anadolu via Getty Images, Erlon Silva - TRI Digital via Getty Images, Mironov Konstantin via Getty Images. A few months into President Donald Trump’s second term, political appointees at the Department of Homeland Security made an unusual request of its agency focused on cybersecurity: Secretly acquire a voting machine and hack it. The appointees wanted the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency to procure the machine, examine it and report back the findings so they could be given to the White House, according to two former administration officials with knowledge of the request.  The proposition was shocking to CISA’s career staffers, according to one of the former officials. CISA typically worked to thwart hackers. Moreover, the agency had been directed not to alert the voting machine company if it uncovered flaws, contrary to its standard practices. The request made the CISA employees fear they were being asked to take part in political interference. “My thought was they could keep it in their back pocket to invalidate any [election] results they don’t like,” one of the former officials said. “This goes against everything CISA represents.” The CISA employees repeatedly told the political appointees that their request was impossible, in part because the agents capable of pulling off such an operation had just been laid off by Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency initiative. The appointees eventually stopped pressing CISA. Though not acted on, the request shows how the Trump administration has tried to use the agency for its own ends while draining it of resources for one of its critical missions: protecting the nation’s voting systems.  In Trump’s second term, his administration has laid off or pushed out more than 1,000 CISA employees, shrinking the agency by about one-third. The president’s 2027 budget proposal would reduce funding for the agency by another $700 million, which could necessitate 900 additional layoffs.  In response, Democratic lawmakers have called for an investigation into CISA’s ability to do its job and demanded answers as to why federal funds are not being used to support election security as directed by Congress. Since Trump signed the CISA Act in 2018, the agency has worked with state authorities and voting machine vendors to help protect election infrastructure from cyberattacks. During Trump’s second term, though, CISA has abandoned much of this work. Several state election authorities said the agency provided them no assistance — and no explanation for its absence — during the most critical planning stages for the upcoming midterms. “There is a difference between deprioritizing and being nonexistent,” said Ryan Macias, an election technology and cybersecurity expert who has worked as a consultant for CISA. In 2025 and through mid-September 2026 — when the bulk of preparations for the election typically would have been completed — “they were nonexistent. Literally nonexistent.” While Trump has repeatedly warned that America’s elections are vulnerable to hacking, in some cases repeating disproven claims, experts said his administration is undermining the federal government’s role in helping secure them. Though CISA re-emerged in September with a last-minute security plan for the election, some state officials told ProPublica they fear that what is left of the agency has been compromised by a conspiracy-obsessed presidential administration. In recent months, in reviving debunked theories about the 2020 election, the Trump administration has declassified troves of records, including sensitive material that state officials provided to CISA. Some state authorities said they no longer trusted the administration enough to share information with CISA, a key to the agency’s success in past elections. “They’ve violated the entire premise of that information-sharing relationship,” said one former high-ranking federal cybersecurity official who now advises state governments on national security. “There’s no fucking way they’re ever going to give any information to CISA. And it’s unclear if they ever will in the future.”  A spokesperson for the White House declined an interview request but defended Trump’s handling of election security in an emailed statement. “President Trump has done more than any other President to ensure we have free and fair elections,” said Lauren Bis.  Bis referred specific questions about CISA’s handling of elections to DHS. DHS and CISA did not respond to interview requests or to a detailed list of questions. “There’s no fucking way [state governments are] ever going to give any information to CISA. And it’s unclear if they ever will in the future.” A former federal cybersecurity official who advises state governments Current and former CISA employees and state election officials describe an agency that has become significantly less equipped to help states fight legitimate cyber threats. State leaders say they have used their own resources to shore up gaps left by CISA, such as paying for sensor technology that can detect unusual activity in election networks. But some services, like intel on foreign actors, can’t be replicated. Some people interviewed said they were worried that Trump and his allies continue to ratchet up rhetoric about voting security, particularly about threats to voting machines. Officials in one large voting jurisdiction said they have met privately with machine vendors to come up with a contingency plan if the federal government seizes their machines or declares them unusable. “I don’t pay attention to what the president says. I pay attention to what his administration does,” Arizona Secretary of State Adrian Fontes said. “And what they’ve done is basically cut us off and left us on our own.” Defending elections from hackers wasn’t always part of DHS’s remit. Throughout the mid-1990s and 2000s, a series of cyberattacks rocked the federal government, demonstrating the emerging threat. In 2007, hackers broke into the Pentagon and stole terabytes of sensitive data. The digital heist, by an unknown foreign adversary, was so damaging that one intelligence leader later described it as an “espionage Pearl Harbor.” Under George W. Bush, DHS underwent a reorganization to more effectively combat terrorism and respond to disasters like Hurricane Katrina. The department dedicated resources under an office called the National Protection and Programs Directorate to help fortify advanced cyber defense systems and important infrastructure. The office’s work ranged from helping secure events like the Super Bowl to protecting chemical plants to issuing cybersecurity warnings to the private sector and the public. events.title: Democrats face Gaza litmus test
events.summary: The News FREDERICKSBURG, Va. — In a matter of weeks, when the midterm results are tallied and the next campaign begins, Democrats with presidential dreams know the question will be coming. Do Israel’s actions in Gaza constitute genocide? The question flew at Democrats all year. Progressives generally said “yes.” Pro-Israel Democrats said “no.” Many rejected the idea that they had to use that word or were otherwise endorsing every action taken by the Jewish state. As potential Democratic 2028 contenders fan out across the country this month, campaigning with battleground Democrats and building their win/loss scorecards, just two have said “yes” to the question: Reps. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y. Khanna has been particularly direct , using interviews and public appearances not only to insist that Israel committed genocide, but also that Democrats who won’t say so are too weak to lead the party. “Israel has committed a genocide in Gaza, and we should have the courage to say so,” Khanna said at the Democratic National Committee’s summer meeting in Texas — a historically red state where this year’s top statewide Democratic nominees, Senate candidate James Talarico and gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa, have not gone as far. The question hasn’t dominated the last few weeks of campaigning, with primaries long over and stark differences on Israel between most Democrats and Republicans. Last week, when Ocasio-Cortez made three campaign stops for Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, neither Democrat — and no audience members — brought up the topic of Gaza. But the question still looms over the party’s first wide-open primaries in eight years. They’ll be the first since small armies of activists pressed Democrats to take more progressive positions on immigration , the environment , and criminal justice reform . In retrospect, many Democrats now think that the candidates in 2020 were too willing to bow to pressure with cameras rolling. There is no sign that anyone but Khanna or Ocasio-Cortez is moving towards a new Gaza answer that activists might prefer. “I think we have to acknowledge the seriousness of the issue, the seriousness of what’s happening in Gaza, the seriousness of what’s happening in the West Bank,” Maryland Gov. Wes Moore told Semafor earlier this month at a campaign stop, when asked why he thought the word “genocide” was so important to many Democrats. Moore has accused Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of committing war crimes, but hasn’t called the violence in Gaza a genocide. “I think it’ll be up to the voters to decide whether or not they feel that people are meeting the moment,” Moore continued. Know More When the Gaza questions do pick up again, most Democrats are likely to punt to the International Criminal Court — already a popular way to dodge them. The ICC has issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu for war crimes and crimes against humanity, but hasn’t accused Israel of committing genocide. “The question of genocide is a question of whether a government has the specific intent to destroy a national or ethnic group,” Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., said in his first debate against challenger Mike Collins this month. “And that is a question for the International Criminal Court.” That answer is unlikely to satisfy many Democratic primary voters, according to a poll of six early primary states conducted by YouGov on behalf of the Institute for Middle East Understanding Policy Project. In South Carolina, where Democrats opted to hold their first primary, 57% of likely primary voters said that Israel was “committing genocide against Palestinians.” In the other five early-voting states, the number was much higher: 78% in New Hampshire and Nevada, 76% in New Mexico, and 72% in Virginia. And in Michigan, where El-Sayed has said he will play an active role in the primaries if he wins his Senate race, eight in 10 likely primary voters agreed with the “genocide” term. These are more lopsided numbers than other pollsters have found, but according to an Associated Press survey this summer, half of all Democrats now agree that “genocide” was the appropriate word to describe what they saw happen in Gaza. “It’s certainly been a question that keeps coming up in debates,” said the IMEU Policy Project’s spokesman, Hamid Bendaas. “And I’d expect there will be a key 2028 moment where the candidates are asked to raise their hands with a yes or no.” Some Democrats have tried to cancel the test before they can take it. In March, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear told Politico that “genocide” was “becoming one of those new litmus tests that we said we would never do as a party again.” He wouldn’t answer the question, but assumed he’d be asked again. Democrats uncomfortable with the term have watched how even using it does not stop questions about their commitment to cutting off arms to Israel — the policy fight they expect, with a little less dread, next year. In August, two months after he defeated Rep. Dan Goldman in New York’s Democratic primary, Brad Lander joined a protest of a Hindu nationalist politician in Manhattan and was filmed being heckled as a “zionist” — even though he said that the war “meets the definition of genocide.” Last month, after Drop Site and New York magazine reported that consultants were urging Maine Democratic Senate candidate Troy Jackson not to say “genocide” so much, supporters began asking him about the war again, worried that he’d gone wobbly. David’s view If Israel elects another government led by Netanyahu, just days before the US midterms, the nuanced answers that many Democrats give to the “genocide” question will grow even trickier to land. The party has already shifted leftward. Rahm Emanuel’s endorsement of conditions on aid was an early signal that the field engaged in the “invisible primary” would be less pro-Israel than Joe Biden. But most of the likely Democratic candidates simply don’t agree that a genocide happened in Gaza, and reject the question’s premise. “Having one conversation about one country means you are politicizing a term that has huge, historic, moral complications,” Emanuel told Meet the Press this month. Still, it’s possible public pressure — including demonastrations organized by interest groups — changes their stances. Eight years ago, protesters frequently drove coverage in their preferred direction by disrupting candidates (Movimiento Cosecha pushed Biden to endorse a deportation moratorium, for instance) and showing up to press them at Q&As. Kamala Harris’ defeat convinced some Democratic strategists, like the big-tenters at Third Way and the Searchlight Institute, that Democratic candidates were too easily moved by activists, and that voters held this against them. It in turn fostered a reluctance to let activists shape their next primary. This is the topic that will stir those emotions next. events.title: The national intelligence chief steering AI
events.summary: Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton has received mostly positive marks so far in Washington as chair of the Trump administration’s AI task force , which is focusing on using current law to get AI companies to behave responsibly. A number of people familiar with Clayton’s work tell Semafor his experience at the Securities and Exchange Commission and Office of the Director of National Intelligence aligns well with the two areas threatened the most by advanced AI: finance and national security. “He is hyper-competent and a problem-solver with good instincts, and that’s why he’s so valued,” one former White House official told Semafor. “He’s just a guy who doesn’t f*ck up and delivers results that they need and want, and so they just keep promoting him, because there aren’t a lot of those.” Paul Lekas, executive vice president for policy at the Software & Information Industry Association, said Clayton’s role atop the task force “signals that the White House is focused on the national security dimension of super intelligence.” Three industry sources told Semafor that the task force is now focused on staffing up to carry out its work. As far as Clayton’s future goes, one tech lobbyist told Semafor to watch what happens on day 121 (the task force’s work is supposed to be completed in 120 days). “If [Clayton] can get agencies approaching AI from very different directions to keep sharing information, coordinating decisions and agreeing on responsibilities … his influence will last well beyond any one appointment,” the lobbyist said. Others are skeptical the task force can accomplish much in such a short time period, arguing that eventually sweeping new legislation will be needed to regulate AI.

events.title: White House allies play midterms blame game
events.summary: Trump administration officials and allies are starting to debate who will shoulder the blame if Republicans perform poorly in November. The White House has witnessed an uptick in drama driven by the midterms, from maneuvering to replace chief of staff Susie Wiles to finger-pointing at James Blair, President Donald Trump’s outside adviser whose recent work trip to Republika Srpska frustrated the president because of its proximity to the November elections. Wiles seems safe; Trump has issued multiple emphatic endorsements of his chief of staff. Some suggest Blair will get blamed, though his tension with Trump has subsided for now. Others predict Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth could draw ire due to the unpopular Iran war. It all depends on how Republicans measure up to the dire predictions — sources close to the White House say Republicans holding onto the Senate is likely to satisfy Trump at this point. The White House dismissed the talk as “armchair” speculation. “These armchair experts peddling their baseless speculation to Semafor have no idea what they’re talking about and are focused on themselves, not helping the President,” White House spokesman Davis Ingle said. “President Trump is laser-focused on maintaining Republican majorities in Congress this November, which is why he is traveling across the country highlighting the historic victories his Administration has delivered for the American people.” — Shelby Talcott

events.title: Tropics attract city dwellers in regional migration trend
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Tropics welcome city dwellers in regional migration trend Small rural towns like Atherton on the Tablelands near Cairns are seeing an influx of residents from capital cities. ( ABC News: Nathan Morris ) The Regional Australia Institute says new data shows city-to-regional migration is on par with pandemic levels. The Sunshine Coast was the most popular destination for people moving to regional Australia, while other areas of Queensland recorded significant annual growth. Sydney and Melbourne recorded the largest losses of residents to regional Australia. City dwellers are moving to regional Australia at rates not seen since the COVID pandemic, according to new data. The movement of people out of Sydney and Melbourne is captured in data from Commonwealth Bank, which the Regional Australia Institute (RAI) has analysed to track migration trends. Sydney accounted for 52 per cent of the net population outflow to Australian regions in the June 2026 quarter. ( ABC News: Liam Patrick ) The not-for-profit organisation said migration from capital cities to regional Australia during the June 2026 quarter matched the record set in June 2021. Those moving to the regions outnumbered those moving to the cities by 30 per cent, and Sydney and Melbourne recorded the largest losses of residents. Sunshine Coast is the region that city movers are favouring most. ( Supplied ) The Sunshine Coast remained the most favoured region for those leaving capital cities, followed by Greater Geelong in Victoria. In the 12 months to the June 2026 quarter, the Sunshine Coast received 8.7 per cent of total net migration share. Victoria's Central Goldfields and the New South Wales Snowy Mountains were the most popular for movers already living in regional Australia. Beyond the stand-out markets, the RAI highlighted significant growth in north Queensland in the 12 months to the June 2026 quarter. Geelong trailed the Sunshine Coast with the second-largest share of total net internal migration. ( ABC News: Harrison Tippet ) The sugarcane and horticultural mecca of the Burdekin, south of Townsville, saw a 238 per cent annual increase in the number of city movers choosing the region. Retail operator Candace Young moved from Dalby to the Burdekin in 2023. She said since the move, she had noticed a stream of southerners moving to the shire of 17,000 people. "We are getting a lot of city people coming up here, customers coming to the shop who have moved from Victoria or Tasmania," she said. "Here, you can drive five minutes in any direction and take the kids fishing or camping, and those things are free activities. The Atherton Tablelands region, south of Cairns, received a 131 per cent annual increase in residents from capital cities. RAI chief executive Liz Ritchie said the latest quarterly data showed people still wanted to move to regional Australia in droves, years after the pandemic-inspired tree and sea changes. "It is those southern states that are really feeling the pinch in terms of how people are measuring their lifestyle and what they're hoping for," she said. "It is a good-news story for Queensland." Liz Ritchie says one in three city dwellers were planning a regional move within five years. ( ABC News: Luke Stephenson ) Ms Ritchie said the RAI was lobbying to establish a national population plan to assist regional planning. "We continue to under-project population in regional Australia, and our regional communities suffer because of that," she said. "People on the ground know when their town is growing, and they know when they're feeling the pinch.

events.title: Six-year plastics factory fight takes toll on Moss Vale residents
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Moss Vale residents tell court of personal toll after six-year plastics factory fight Hundreds of residents gathered at the proposed Moss Vale plastics recycling factory site as the Land and Environment Court began hearing an appeal against the project's rejection. ( ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale ) Hundreds of Moss Vale residents have gathered as a developer appeals the rejection of a proposed plastics recycling factory. The court heard emotional accounts of how six years of uncertainty has affected local families. The hearing will continue for another nine days, with council offering live stream access at the Moss Vale Civic Centre from Tuesday. A mother described fearing for her children's health, a doctor recounted the psychological toll on families, and a retiree told of plans for a quieter life put on hold. They were among the eight residents who addressed the NSW Land and Environment Court at Moss Vale on Monday, as hundreds gathered for the opening of an appeal hearing into a proposed plastics recycling factory. Developer Repoly is appealing the Independent Planning Commission's decision to reject the project last year. The proposed factory would process up to 120,000 tonnes of mixed plastic waste a year at a site on Beaconsfield Road. For Jean McKern, who lives immediately beside the proposed site, the dispute has overshadowed what she hoped would be peaceful retirement years. Jean McKern (sitting) surrounded by people who also spoke at the appeal hearing. ( ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale ) Now in her late 80s, she told the court she was a healthy, active 83-year-old when the proposal first emerged in 2020. She described disrupted sleep, mounting stress and health problems she believes have been exacerbated by the uncertainty. Ms McKern became emotional as she described fears about noise, lighting, pollution and fire risks, saying she could be forced to leave the home where she has lived for 30 years. Another neighbouring resident, Graham Horden , said he and his wife had downsized in retirement, hoping to restore native vegetation on their property and spend time with their grandchildren. "From a feeling of justified satisfaction in our retirement years, we have regressed to a situation of prolonged stress and anxiety," he told the court. He said the uncertainty had also raised concerns about their financial position as self-funded retirees. Families living in 'suspended animation' Moss Vale mother Natalie Swainston described watching her two young sons play cricket at nearby Lackey Park on Saturday and worrying about potential pollution if the factory were operating less than a kilometre away. Natalie Swainston told the court she feared the potential impacts of the factory on children attending a nearby childcare centre. ( ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale ) Her children had previously attended a childcare centre about 300 metres from the proposed development, where they spent much of their days playing outdoors. "It's quite hard to explain what it's like to live in suspended animation for this long," she told the court. "You put your life on hold and wait for the next amendment, the next deadline, the next hearing. You think you can finally rest and then there's an appeal." Palliative care doctor Jacqueline Duc, speaking on behalf of local health professionals and Doctors for the Environment Australia, raised concerns about potential health risks and the psychological toll of the prolonged dispute. She urged the court to adopt a precautionary approach. Dr Duc also shared a deeply personal account of how the dispute had affected another member of the community. Jacqueline Duc told the court years of uncertainty over the proposed factory had affected the wellbeing of local families. ( ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale ) She told the court the family's daughter's eighth birthday wish was for the factory proposal to go away. She said their daughter is now 11, and the dispute continues. The Independent Planning Commission refused approval in January 2025, citing concerns including fire risks and the suitability of the location. Repoly has since amended its plans, including moving one building further from neighbouring homes and proposing to transport process wastewater offsite for disposal. Wingecarribee Shire Council maintains the location remains unsuitable. More than 500 people attended the appeal hearing at the site of Repoly's proposed facility in Moss Vale.

events.title: UAE amends e-invoicing regulations as implementation deadline draws closer
events.summary: The UAE's Ministry of Finance has made amendments to its e-invoicing system that will apply to value-added tax filing in the country from next year. Authorities are introducing a temporary exclusion for business transactions between entities that are members of the same tax group for two years, starting from January 1, 2027, the Ministry of Finance said on Monday. Such transactions will be treated as "excluded transactions" throughout the 24-month period, "giving businesses greater flexibility and more time to adapt to the system", the ministry said. David Daly, a partner at Gulf Tax Accounting Group, said the move was "welcome", but more clarity would be needed to understand specific details. For instance, in a scenario where each entity also issues invoices to non-tax group members, it still needs to be known whether these must be managed through the e-invoicing system, he said. The ministry's latest decision also amends article 11 on the storage of electronic invoice and electronic credit note data. Under the amended provision, entities must retain all electronic invoices, electronic credit notes and any associated data for the period prescribed under the Tax Procedures Law, and ensure that such records can be provided to the Federal Tax Authority on request, the ministry said. The decision "removes the previous requirement that such data be stored within the UAE, thereby shifting the focus from the location of storage to the retention and accessibility of records for tax compliance purposes", it added. The amendments also remove the requirement for companies to notify the FTA of a system failure within two business days of it happening. The ministry said the amendments are aimed at improving the ease of doing business in the UAE "by reducing operational burdens on businesses, providing greater flexibility during the implementation of the electronic invoicing system, and ensuring that regulatory requirements support an efficient and business-friendly environment". The latest decision comes as the first major compliance requirement in the phased transition to e-invoicing approaches on October 30. The ministry extended the deadline for appointing an accredited service provider (ASP) for businesses in the UAE with annual revenue of Dh50 million ($13.6 million) or more to October 30, from July 1, under the first phase of the programme. Under the UAE's unified e-invoicing model, all qualifying transactions must be validated and sent through an ASP.

events.title: Khosla Ventures doubles down on Even Healthcare to challenge India’s hospital economics
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Even Healthcare has raised $50 million in a funding round led by Khosla Ventures, as the Indian startup seeks to change how hospitals in the world’s most populous country make money and how doctors are rewarded. The all-equity Series B round also saw participation from Alpha Wave and valued it at $300 million, triple its valuation 18 months ago, according to Even. The latest funding brings Even’s total capital raised to more than $120 million. Hospitals in India typically earn more when patients undergo additional tests, procedures, or longer stays, even when they may not need them. Even wants to change that by focusing on patient care rather than pushing unnecessary treatments that drive up medical bills. That approach has continued to appeal to Khosla Ventures, which has invested in Even since its seed round in 2021. The Silicon Valley venture firm is doubling down as Even moves to build and operate hospitals of its own, giving it greater control over patient care and costs. Vinod Khosla, founder of Khosla Ventures, said Even’s approach goes beyond fixing individual parts of a fragmented healthcare system by bringing financing, technology, and care delivery together. The goal, he said in a prepared statement, is to reward better health outcomes rather than greater use of healthcare services. “The clinical and economic results so far give us conviction that this can become an important new model for healthcare in India and beyond,” Khosla said. Initially, Even relied on partner hospitals to treat its members, but Mayank Banerjee, who founded the startup in 2021 with Matilde Giglio and Alessandro Ialongo, said in an interview that the startup began questioning that model after finding that patients had undergone tests or been recommended surgeries it considered unnecessary. “We think patients are getting not only a bad experience, but insurers are getting a bad economic deal. And as a result, we decided to fix it by building our own hospitals,” Banerjee told TechCrunch. Even has since opened two hospitals in Bengaluru, both of which reached operational profitability, excluding depreciation, within a year of opening, Banerjee stated. The startup plans to open five more hospitals in the southern Indian city over the next six months, funded by its latest round. Banerjee told TechCrunch that Even leases hospital buildings on 20-year agreements and spends on fitting them out and buying medical equipment. Unlike hospitals where doctors may have financial incentives to recommend more procedures, Even pays its doctors fixed salaries — not tying their compensation to the number of tests or surgeries they perform, though Banerjee said doctors can earn bonuses based on patient-reported clinical outcomes. The same principle extends to hospital management, whose compensation is not linked to the number of procedures performed, Banerjee told TechCrunch. Managers, he said, receive salaries and company-wide incentives, while marketing teams focus on bringing in patients instead of the revenue those patients generate. Moreover, every employee, including doctors and other hospital staff, receives equity in Even. The idea is to give employees a stake in the startup’s long-term performance, not to reward them for generating more medical bills. Most of Even’s revenue comes from patients paying for treatment, Banerjee said. The startup also generates revenue through its relationships with insurers. It is also working with insurer partners on a model that could compensate it for hospitalizations it helps prevent, not simply for providing more treatment. Banerjee told TechCrunch that Even tracks how patients recover after treatment using established medical scoring systems. In the case of knee replacements, for instance, it uses the Oxford Knee Score to measure pain and mobility. The startup publishes results on its website , alongside figures from other healthcare systems for comparison. Even says its hospitals have an unplanned readmission rate of less than 1%, compared with an industry benchmark of 8% to 15%. Furthermore, it claims patients spend 40% less time in the hospital and that its approach has saved insurers more than ₹500 million (about $5.27 million). Jai Sajnani, a partner at Khosla Ventures, told TechCrunch that the early performance of Even’s hospitals was a key reason the firm led the round. “We look forward to helping the Even team put quality care within reach of every family in Bengaluru and across India,” he said. Even is still losing money, though. The startup posted a net loss of ₹902 million (about $9.50 million) in fiscal 2025, nearly 25% more than the previous year, on revenue of ₹272 million (about $2.86 million), regulatory filings show. In August, Even also laid off about 350 employees , according to Indian startup news website Entrackr.

events.title: Australia could be without structural and rail steelmaking for up to five years
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Whyalla blast furnace closure could leave Australia without major steel production for years The coal-fired blast furnace at Whyalla's steelworks closed last month after being offline since April. ( ABC News ) Unions predict Australia could be without domestic structural and rail steelmaking for up to five years, as about 500 employees are made redundant at the Whyalla Steelworks. About 250 employees are expected to take voluntary packages, but there will be forced redundancies . About 100 contractors will also go, after attempts to repair the plant's 60-year-old blast furnace failed. "Steel production is not possible without a blast furnace," Australian Workers Union branch organiser Shane Karger told 7.30. Shane Karger from the Australian Workers Union says the future of the Whyalla steel plant is uncertain. ( ABC News: Carl Saville ) Seventy-five per cent of the nation's structural steel comes from the Whyalla plant, and has been used in construction of the Western Sydney Airport and Optus Stadium in Perth. The steelworks is also the sole domestic manufacturer of rail steel. The plant will keep operating using stockpiled as well as locally and internationally sourced semi-finished steel product. "The iron ore mines will obviously still operate and export any product that they produce but for this period of time, Australia is reliant on the rest of the world for its structural and rail steel," Mr Karger said. Australian Industry Group CEO Innes Willox said it would become increasingly difficult to bring back structural and rail steelmaking capacity in Whyalla as time went on. "A clear, transparent path back to production is essential to give both the people of Whyalla, South Australia and industry more generally, confidence that there is a path forward. Right now, it's not so clear that there is one." Innes Willox says it will be harder for steelmaking to resume at Whyalla the longer production is paused. ( ABC News: Dan Fermer ) The South Australian and federal governments have publicly pledged almost $2 billion to help a new owner invest in a less emissions intensive electric arc furnace. Federal Industry Minister Tim Ayres didn't rule out putting more money on the table and told 7.30 his government was committed to the "fastest possible resumption" of steelmaking capacity. "The commitment from the two governments here ... is to deliver a pit to port mining facility, iron and steel making and of course, finished steel products," Mr Ayres said. "We're working closely with the final two bidders in the process to deliver the best outcome." Tim Ayres says the federal government is working to resume production at Whyalla as soon as possible. ( ABC News: Shaun Kingma ) The shortlisted bidders are Indian industrial company Jindal and Australian business M Resources, while Australia's largest steelmaker Bluescope holds a right of last offer. It had been hoped the coal-fired blast furnace would last a few more years, which would smooth the transition to that proposed electric arc furnace but Mr Karger believes cost cutting under previous owner Sanjeev Gupta's GFG Alliance shortened its life span. "A decision was made … to throttle back the furnace," Mr Karger said. "A typical blast furnace of that type likes to run at near capacity, keep the temperature up and the iron flowing. Whyalla Steelworks is the only producer of structural and rail steel in Australia. ( ABC News: Lincoln Rothall ) A spokesman for GFG told 7.30 in a statement that Whyalla's problems did not begin with GFG and they have not ended since the company's removal. "Despite significant losses, over six years GFG preserved jobs and Australia's sovereign steelmaking capability while battling an aging plant and grossly inadequate protection against unprecedented levels of steel dumping," it said. "The blast furnace did not fail under GFG's watch … those now seeking to place all responsibility on GFG should also acknowledge Whyalla's long decline across successive owners, governments and policy regimes." GFG Alliance has been struggling to stay afloat globally since the collapse of key financier Greensill Capital in 2021. When the steelworks was placed into administration by the South Australian government in February last year, it was losing $1.5 million a day. The town of Whyalla depends on the local steel industry. ( ABC News/Carl Saville ) Administrators said they took control of a plant that had sustained a "long period of underinvestment, inadequate or no maintenance" and "poor health and safety practices".

events.title: Why Physical AI Is So Hard To Engineer
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Physical AI is the deployment of machines with autonomy, acting within the real world. It is not a single product, but a philosophy built on modular architectures. These systems can only be developed with a full systems approach, integrating sensors, actuators, and distributed compute systems, in a multi-physics methodology. Real-time constraints become much more important than in the past, and at the same time much more complex. Physical AI is changing how chips are designed and used, integrating sensing, AI inference, and real-time control into machines that can safely and predictably interact with the physical world. The challenges extend well beyond just performance. Engineers need to account for corner cases stemming from unpredictable environments, ensure these systems are safe and reliable, and they need to future-proof these systems by ensuring they are serviceable and upgradable. This will require new tools and methodologies, as well as some new design approaches. “AI is leaving the screen,” says Anthony Matarazzo, head of physical AI, digital twins, simulation-driven AI, and accelerated computing at Synopsys . “It is no longer about generating text or code. It is entering the physical world. It needs to understand, interact, sense, make decisions in a physical environment. We are moving from generative AI to agentic workflow orchestration to physical AI (see figure 1.) That is literally making intelligence actionable. But the consequences of being wrong fundamentally change. Life or death, plus or minus 1%.” Fig. 1: Three Eras of AI. Source: Synopsys Physical AI must see and interact with the real world. “It is challenging to make artificial intelligence see the world correctly,” says Chun-Ting “Tim” Wang-Lee, signal integrity application scientist at Keysight EDA . “Real-world information comes from the sensors, and the data has to be moved somewhere and processed so that the AI can decide and then act. There are decisions that need to be made.” This changes the design priorities. “Physical AI usually gets framed as a compute story,” says Justin Endo, director for marketing and sales at Mixel , A Silvaco Company. “But from our perspective it has really been an imaging story. Every robot, drone, and autonomous system comes down to cameras feeding an inference engine.” Physical AI builds on some of the connectivity and sensing technologies developed for the Internet of Things. “IoT was largely about connecting and monitoring things,” says Brad Rex, head of physical AI, UX at Renesas Electronics. “Physical AI is about giving machines the ability to perceive and act autonomously in unstructured environments. This is a completely orthogonal engineering problem, and it requires a step-change in system-level content — more sensing, more real-time compute, more sophisticated power management, and more safety considerations per device.” Within physical AI, there are two distinct classes of devices: “Those that can rely on a cloud connection and those that must operate fully locally without relying on connectivity,” says Ashley Stevens, director of product management and marketing at Arteris . “For example, vehicles cannot rely on continuous connectivity, as there are many locations where cellular coverage is inadequate. In contrast, an industrial robotic arm moves but is constrained to a particular location within a factory setting, and therefore can be connected to the cloud.” Others agree. “Unlike traditional AI applications that primarily generate information, physical AI systems influence real-world outcomes through continuous interaction with their environment,” says William Chen, product marketing group director for design IP at Cadence . “Traditional IoT often focused on collecting and transmitting data. Physical AI adds real-time interpretation and action. The result is a shift from connected devices to intelligent systems operating within sensing and control loops.” This requires new architectures and new methodologies. “The entire architecture is very different,” says Satish Radhakrishnan, head of semiconductor and electronics at Vinci . “Time-to-market is going to be much slower because people are still learning. Physical AI is the next step that they want, but the switch to it is not going to be easy. The easiest entry point will be a repetitive action, but people are not willing to pay much for that. They want it to do a lot more. That’s why it is going to take a more complex architecture to build, make reliable, and make it work for at least a day on a single charge.” It also requires significant processing power. “Robotics and drones require powerful, efficient compute capable of multimodal processing and accurate, real-time responsiveness in dynamic settings,” says Sameer Sharma, associate vice president for MediaTek’s IoT business. “Because of latency and bandwidth constraints, these devices require silicon capable of handling AI workloads at the edge, including AI acceleration for machine vision and object classification.” As systems get larger or more capable, additional challenges emerge. “You need longer reach through moving joints, aggregation of many cameras into few ports, and the functional safety expectations coming over from automotive,” says Mixel’s Endo. “But the standard is already moving in that direction. At a high level, PwC estimates the global physical AI market will reach ~€430 billion by 2030, with “significant upside potential as systems scale and mature.” Deloitte, meanwhile, found that 58% of companies report at least limited use of physical AI today, with that number projected to rise to 80% within two years. events.title: Consumer apprehension grows as US retailers adopt AI-assisted pricing tools
events.summary: U.S. consumers are uneasy about the increasingly high-tech ways that restaurant chains and major retailers are setting prices U.S. consumers aren't just frustrated with high prices . They're angry and confused about the increasingly high-tech ways that restaurant chains and major retailers are setting those prices. Digital price tags are rapidly replacing paper ones in grocery aisles. Artificial intelligence tools help businesses decide what to charge by predicting how customers might respond. Terms like “dynamic pricing” and “surveillance pricing” are stirring anxiety on social media, where users wonder if different people are getting different prices for the same product. Americans have grown accustomed to changing prices when booking flights, hotel rooms and rides, but the prospect of everyday spending shaped by algorithms they don’t understand and personal data they may not realize they’re sharing has touched a nerve. “There are major tensions happening right now between who’s really going to have the power with some of these algorithms and usage of bots and AI: the companies or the shopper,” said Katie Thomas, who leads an internal consumer behavior think tank at the management consulting firm Kearney. Companies using the technology say some concerns stem from misconceptions about how their pricing tools work. Walmart CEO John Furner said in a blog post last month that digital price tags save workers’ time and keep prices up to date. He said the labels aren’t used to raise prices based on the weather, time of day or individual shopper. “We price the product, not the person,” Furner wrote. But companies aren't always transparent about the customer data they collect and how it's used, which has made consumers suspicious and led to speculation. For example, social media posts falsely imply that electronic shelf labels Walmart plans to put in all its U.S. stores scan shoppers’ faces or cellphones to set individualized prices, Thomas said. Lawmakers and regulators are taking action. Legislators in at least 30 states have considered pricing bills this year, including measures addressing algorithmic and personalized pricing, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. The Federal Trade Commission has proposed an enforcement policy warning businesses that failing to disclose their use of personal data to set individualized prices could violate consumer protection law. Here are some of the pricing practices and technologies drawing scrutiny. What it is: Dynamic pricing means adjusting prices in response to changing market conditions, including supply and demand . An airline that adjusts ticket prices as departures approach is using dynamic pricing. Uber's practice of lifting fares when demand outstrips the supply of available drivers, such as during rush hour, is a type of dynamic pricing known as surge pricing. Why it matters: Frequent price changes extend well beyond food. Decodo, a web data company, tracked price changes in 2025 across products ranging from electronics to clothing and home improvement supplies. About half the U.S. changes it recorded were decreases, contrary to consumers’ assumptions that dynamic pricing only raises prices, said Gabriele Vitke, a senior product marketing manager. What they are: Digital displays that let stores update shelf prices electronically instead of replacing paper tags. Why it matters: Digital price labels, long used in Europe and Asia, are drawing more attention as they spread to major U.S. retailers like Walmart and Whole Foods. Consumer advocates have argued that digital labels could eventually be used for surge pricing or personalized pricing. Labor unions also have opposed the technology. The electronic shelf labels make frequent changes easier but don’t necessarily lead to higher prices during periods of strong demand. Retailers typically update electronic shelf prices on a regular schedule, often weekly, because shoppers value consistency, said Asa Farquhar of Relex Solutions, a retail technology company. Researchers who tracked prices at an unnamed grocery chain found “virtually no surge pricing” after the labels were introduced. “Changing prices throughout the day, the way airlines or rideshare apps do, is exceedingly rare in grocery and general merchandise today,” Farquhar said. 2 dead, 11 injured after Kansas mother drives onto soccer field during game: Police Iran updates: Trump admin prepares options, including 'mother of all bombs' Bend, Oregon, shooting: Suspect ID'd, had attended elementary school, police say What it is: Personalized pricing means offering customers different prices and discounts based on their locations, incomes, web-browsing habits and other information about individuals or groups of shoppers. Some advocacy groups and regulators use the term “surveillance pricing" for the same practice. Why it matters: It’s unclear how widely businesses use personal information to customize prices.

events.title: NSW government drafts law to allow Upper Hunter mine to increase output
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Mount Pleasant mine legislation to allow increased output weeks away The NSW government will table legislation it says will protect 400 jobs at MACH Energy's Mount Pleasant mine. ( Supplied: Climate Media Centre ) The NSW Labor government will introduce legislation to the state's parliament aiming to shore up 400 jobs at an Upper Hunter coal mine. The legislation, if passed, will allow MACH Energy to operate its Mount Pleasant mine with its current workforce and output until 2032. The High Court earlier this month ruled planning authorities must consider global fossil fuel impacts in mine extension decisions, effectively halting a proposed extension by MACH. The NSW government will introduce a law to allow a Hunter Valley coal mine to keep operating at a higher output, despite a High Court ruling that invalidated the mine's expansion approval. NSW Premier Chris Minns argued the legislation, to be introduced in the coming weeks, would authorise MACH Energy to increase annual coal production at its Mount Pleasant mine from 12.5 million to 16.5 million tonnes until 2032. Mr Minns said the proposed allowance was "consistent with the current workforce profile and current coal extraction on the site". "It's become apparent that there are 400 jobs on the line that will go before Christmas without this intervention," he said. If the plan passes, the deal will see MACH Energy enter a "jobs guarantee" to shore up the 400 direct jobs until 2032. Chris Minns says the proposed legislation will be introduced in the coming weeks. ( ABC News ) It comes after the High Court found the NSW Independent Planning Commission (IPC) failed to consider the project's downstream emissions, invalidating approvals for a 22-year extension slated by MACH. The Denman Aberdeen Muswellbrook Scone Healthy Environment Group (DAMSHEG) successfully appealed the IPC's 2022 approval of an extension, arguing the commission failed to consider Scope 3 emissions. Subsequent appeals from MACH Energy, including in the High Court earlier this month, were dismissed, effectively thwarting the company's hope to extract a total of 444 million tonnes of coal from the site by 2048. High Court ruling on coal and climate An expert says a High Court ruling on coal said "the quiet part out loud". Scope 3 emissions are indirect emissions stemming from outside the initial production or extraction phase, and are largely not produced by the company itself. It includes coal that is sold overseas, and then burned, creating emissions elsewhere. The group has called for the premier to release more details on the proposed bill announced today. "We have never wanted anyone in the Hunter to lose their livelihood," DAMSHEG president Wendy Wales said in a statement. "A law written for one company, days after the High Court ruled against that company, is an inappropriate use of the NSW legislative process. "The laws should reflect a balance where the overall welfare of citizens and environment is paramount and industry serves the needs of all citizens." Mr Minns said the legislation included a requirement that MACH Energy would need to adhere to Scope 3 limiting rules, and only sell to countries that were signatories to the Paris Agreement. Mr Minns stressed the proposed legislation was not a "full approval for the mine". "They'll continue their applications through the Land and Environment Court for the full scope of their original application, which was granted by the Independent Planning and Assessment Commission in 2022," he said. "This is, in effect, a partial approval to keep pace with the current workforce that's on the ground in that community." Greens spokesperson for climate change, Sue Higginson, said in a statement the premier had taken the coal company's side. "Minns's new law is explicitly to allow more coal to be mined and exported, contrary to the High Court's decision," she said. "This is significant overreach by Premier Minns and NSW Labor, writing special laws to protect specific projects sets a dangerous precedent. The Mount Pleasant mine, near Muswellbrook, extracts thermal coal largely for export. ( ABC Upper Hunter: Amelia Bernasconi ) "Nobody and no coal company should be above the law of the land and receive such special treatment." When asked by a journalist if the proposed legislation set a precedent for government interventions in controversial mine approval cases, Mr Minns rejected that, and said Mount Pleasant was in a "unique" position.

events.title: China's growth accelerates as AI boom helps boost exports
events.summary: China's economic growth picked up in the three months to the end of September, rebounding from a three-year low as the artificial intelligence (AI) boom helped boost exports. The world's second largest economy grew by 4.5% in the third quarter, up from the previous period but below the 5% expansion recorded from January to March, according to official Chinese data. The latest figure is at the bottom end of Beijing's annual growth target of 4.5%-5%, which analysts have said gives policymakers room to address the country's economic challenges. While exports have helped offset weak spending at home, global trade tensions and uncertainty over AI investments are clouding its outlook. China's National Bureau of Statistics said on Monday that the economy "sustained steady development against pressure" and showed "momentum with new growth drivers and improving structure". With exports climbing, China's trade surplus - the amount of goods and services it sells abroad compared to what it buys from other countries - is on track to overtake the record $1.2tn (£900bn) seen last year. Sales of high-tech goods rose by 14.3% while the production of both batteries and industrial robots grew by more than 29%, official figures showed. Oxford Economics researcher Sheana Yue said manufacturing and high-tech exports have boosted China's growth, despite weak investment and domestic spending. But property investment fell by more than 20% in the first nine months from the same period last year, official data also showed. China's economy has been struggling to shake off a long-running property slump, after years of overbuilding and excessive borrowing by private developers. There are still no signs that this trend will end soon, Yue said. Trade uncertainties and geopolitical issues have also made Chinese consumers more "pessimistic" and unwilling to spend, she added. 'Investing in people': Can China's new push to boost spending revive the economy? Published 10 March Faisal Islam: Why China and AI are worrying global finance bosses Published 3 days ago The effects of Beijing's targeted support measures for businesses have yet to be seen, said Dave Chia, an economist at Moody's Analytics. Several risks stand out from the data, including China's reliance on a "single external engine" in exports, he added. The technology industry has been a key driver of China's growth in recent quarters. Global demand for computer chips and other components used to build AI data centres has helped to ease pressure on Beijing and cushion the impact of sluggish domestic consumption. Chinese businesses have leaned heavily on exports as a prolonged property slump, weak wage growth and high youth unemployment have weighed on consumer spending at home. In September, Beijing unveiled a raft of support measures, including lower interest rates for some businesses and subsidies for property buyers, in an effort to boost the economy. But Beijing is facing a backlash from Western economies - including the US and European Union - as manufacturers struggle to compete with large amounts of cheap Chinese goods. There are also concerns over the billions of dollars being spent on AI infrastructure and whether the companies making those investments can deliver on their promises of generating huge profits. Why is China spending billions to get people to open their wallets? events.title: Dubai Investments to list DIP Holding shares in first DFM IPO this year
events.summary: Dubai Investments , a Dubai-listed conglomerate, is selling a 20 per cent stake in its subsidiary DIP Holding in the first initial public offering in the UAE this year. The deal will comprise the sale of 1.74 billion shares by existing shareholders in DIP Holding, which owns the mixed-use development Dubai Investments Park, the company said on Monday. Parent Dubai Investments will continue to control the remaining 80 per cent shareholding in DIP Holding, contingent on the offering size remaining unchanged and all shares on sale being allocated to investors, it said. Subscriptions for the sale are set to open on October 27 and will run until November 3. Final pricing for the deal will be announced on November 4. DIP Holding shares are expected to start trading on the Dubai Financial Market on November 11, according to the offer document. "Our IPO marks an important milestone in DIP Holding’s journey and reflects the strength and resilience of our differentiated, infrastructure-like business model, said Omar Al Mesmar, chief executive of DIP Holding. "Looking ahead, we see clear opportunities to build on this foundation." The deal breaks the lull in the IPO market in the UAE. The Arab world’s second-largest economy was a hotbed for public floats, with the DFM and the Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange both attracting a steady stream of IPOs over the past few years. The Middle East IPO market last year slowed after it was hit by lower oil prices , geopolitical unrest and weaker post-listing performances. Companies in the region raised $7.1 billion from 61 listings, down from $13 billion a year earlier. UAE companies raised a total of $1.1 billion through three IPOs in 2025, Dealogic data shows. The US-Iran war, now in its eighth month, has further disrupted the already slowing momentum as companies put their plans of tapping equities markets to raise capital on hold. Dubai Investments , in which the sovereign investment fund Investment Corporation of Dubai holds a stake, was among the UAE companies that expressed intentions to list shares in its units before war-driven volatility sapped deal volumes. The company in September last year said that it was in talks with banks and planned to list up to 25 per cent of Dubai Investments Park. Dividend policy Situated near Al Maktoum International Airport and Jebel Ali Port, Dubai Investments Park is home to 1,000 tenants, 5,700 subtenants and more than 150,000 residents. The district was established in 1997 and hosts warehouses, hotels, retail outlets, schools and medical centres, making it one of the largest mixed-use developments in the emirate. DIP Holding intends to adopt a semi-annual cash dividend distribution policy. The company expects to pay annualised dividends of Dh700 million, Dh725 million and Dh750 million for 2026, 2027 and 2028 financial years, respectively. In 2029, the company expects to pay dividends in line with, or above the 2028 payout, it said in the offer document. "Our intention to list DIP Holding on the Dubai Financial Market represents a natural next step in a journey that began more than 25 years ago," said DIP Holding chairman Khalid bin Kalban. "What began as an ambitious vision for an integrated mixed-use destination has developed into a fully established and highly sought-after platform supporting businesses and communities across the logistics, industrial, commercial and residential sectors."

events.title: Charities 'busier than ever' with furniture poverty
events.summary: BBC South visited charity Scratch's warehouse ahead of deliveries being made Charities say they are "busier than ever" helping people living in furniture poverty. BBC South spoke to people and organisations affected in Hampshire after national charity End Furniture Poverty said about six million in the UK were living without essentials such as beds, cookers and fridges. And a group of MPs is calling on the government to develop a national strategy to address the problem. They said they believed that a safe, secure and sustainable home should include access to the basic furniture necessary for everyday living. The government said it was already taking action to support households. Among those who have needed help is Yana Osibchuk, who moved to the UK from Ukraine after the war began with her son, her dog and two suitcases - and was placed into social housing. "It was absolutely empty - no furniture, no cooker, no fridge, nothing and no flooring," she said. Yana Osibchuk spoke to the BBC about her experience of furniture poverty Yana was referred to charity Southampton City and Region Action to Combat Hardship (Scratch). "It's really changed my life," she said. But Yana's situation is not unusual. The overwhelming majority of social housing is let unfurnished. Scratch has been running for 27 years and its managing director Mike Taylor said the charity was "busier now than it's ever been". "We are always chock-a-block, our diaries are full every week," he said. "We have two vans going out every day." Mike Taylor, from charity Scratch, said demand for furniture was increasing He said household budget pressure were a factor but that there were lots of reasons people found themselves needing help. "It could be that they've had a crisis in their life, they've had to flee a relationship or flee domestic violence and they've ended up somehow in a property with no furniture," he said. "They may have children with them. They haven't got disposable income. They just don't have the facilities or the money to get going again." Scratch relies on donations and grants from the council. It then makes up packs and sells them on to people at minimal prices. The charity does not deal directly with the public but takes referrals from the council, housing association or other professionals like social workers. National charity End Furniture Poverty defines furniture poverty as the inability to access or afford to buy or maintain any household furniture or appliance item that is essential to achieve a socially acceptable standard of living. Claire Donovan, from End Furniture Poverty, said not having access to household essentials had a significant impact on people's lives Charity director Claire Donovan said: "There are harmful physical, emotional, social, and financial consequences to furniture poverty, and it's not just about material needs as furniture poverty is a consequence of the broader issue of poverty. "Over a quarter of social housing tenants live in furniture poverty and yet only around 3% of those are let as furnished." End Furniture Poverty questioned people living in furniture poverty and 30% said their physical and mental health had been impacted. Claire added: "Not being able to get a good night's sleep because you haven't got a bed. Not being able to store or prepare fresh food because you haven't got a cooker or a fridge - and just the grinding stress of that day in day out - it really affects every area of your life." It is not a problem confined to one area. The Moving on Project Portsmouth charity helps people in the city struggling with furniture poverty. Every day it sees people in desperate need. Sarah Knight, from Moving On Project Portsmouth, said the problem had become "huge" Sarah Knight, from the charity, said: "It's huge. People are digging deep - the only other alternative is to enter loans which have a high interest rate and can lead to problems along the line. "It used to be people on benefits - now it's not, it's people from all walks of life. Reduced hours, higher bills - it affects everybody. "The foodbanks and pantries are on the increase and it's the same with furniture - there are so many families struggling. "Some may not have a bed, they may have a couple of kids sharing a bed. It's horrendous to think that we are in 2026 and to think this amount of poverty is still going on." End Furniture Poverty is calling on the government to ensure 10% of social housing is let as furnished. A government spokesperson said in a statement: "No one should have to live without essential furniture in the place they call home. "We're taking action to support renters by launching a £1bn fund that can be used to help households get furniture.

events.title: Oman could become a cornerstone of Gulf energy security, but risks remain
events.summary: In its heyday, Oman’s maritime empire stretched from Mozambique and Zanzibar to Gwadar in Pakistan. The modern sultanate does not extend so far, but it still holds an important position overlooking the Strait of Hormuz. Oman has gained economically from the conflict, while seeking to mediate peace. Now it could make itself a foundation stone of Gulf security. The war has forced the IMF to downgrade economic growth forecasts across the region. But Oman is expected to expand by 4.1 per cent. It has managed to bring down its debt burden from a worrying 68 per cent of GDP in 2020 to a much more comfortable 35 to 36 per cent of GDP. The sultanate benefits from record oil and gas exports at a time of high prices, as well as from the rest of its heavy industrial base in refined petroleum, fertilisers and aluminium. The endless queues of lorries to and from the UAE border tell eloquently of Oman’s essential role as a transit route for goods . In May 2024, in a fortunate piece of advance planning, construction began on Hafeet Rail, which will link the industrial city of Sohar with Al Ain and Abu Dhabi . This is intended to be finished by the final quarter of 2027 and will be an invaluable route for industrial inputs to the UAE and for the export of finished products such as steel and aluminium. By late next year, Oman should also finish a direct connection to the GCC electricity grid, allowing it to exchange more power. This will benefit its fast-growing renewable sector. Oman has not stayed entirely out of the front line during the war. The oil terminals of Mina Al Fahal, Duqm and Salalah, and Sohar were attacked by drones, and several ships have been struck in its mainland waters, not to mention all those hit while crossing the Omani lane of the Strait of Hormuz. But the sultanate has suffered much less physical damage and disruption than its Gulf neighbours. New energy routes In 2016, the oil minister at the time, Mohammed Al Rumhi announced plans for an enormous 200-million barrel petroleum storage terminal at Duqm on its south-east coast. By comparison, Fujairah, which has also emerged as a strategic node during the war and is a central global refuelling point, has about 120 million barrels of capacity. Muscat’s intention was to reorient its crude oil exports from the crowded northern coast to a new terminal, which would also have the happy effect of shifting them further from Iran. It also had in mind that other GCC nations might connect to Duqm, to give themselves an option in case of a blockade of the Strait of Hormuz. Kuwait, which has no alternative outlet, was said to be interested. Kuwait Petroleum Corporation eventually invested in the major new refinery there. But it seemed far-fetched that a new pipeline route would be needed. Eventually only 5.2 million barrels of crude storage were built, mostly to serve the refinery. Drones, missiles, and Washington’s decision to confront Tehran on the battlefield changed that. Now Saudi Aramco is studying a pipeline to Duqm, estimated to span 1,000 to 1,200 kilometres through the dunes of the Empty Quarter, and expected to cost $7 billion. This new node has the advantage of bypassing not just Hormuz, but also the Bab Al Mandeb strait. Saudi exports through the kingdom's East-West pipeline to the Red Sea port of Yanbu have been hampered by attacks from the Houthis in Yemen and Iranian allies in Iraq. A Kuwait Oil Company representative told the World Energy Congress in Riyadh last week that his country was evaluating a possible route to Duqm, as well as through the UAE or Saudi Arabia. This would most probably involve delivering oil by tanker to a Saudi or UAE port for onward transport, rather than transporting it all the way overland. State energy investor OQ has announced plans to expand Duqm’s storage to 10 million barrels within three years, and eventually 40 million barrels. It is also considering buying two tankers to hold 4 million barrels in floating storage. In September, it signed an agreement with a German company to design a new marine bunkering site at the port of Shinas, just south of the UAE border. This would be about a third the size of Fujairah, which ranks as the world’s second or third-largest ship refuelling hub. Strategic risks Nevertheless, Oman’s centrality to the Gulf’s new infrastructure carries three risks. First, its sites are not much further from Iran than the rest of the Gulf is, and can still be attacked if hostilities escalate. Indeed, Muscat might even put itself in the line of fire if Tehran decides it cannot tolerate too much by-passing of the totemic Strait of Hormuz. The second is almost the opposite: if peace breaks out, much of this infrastructure might seem unnecessary. New pipelines will take from three to five years to build. By then, regional politics and security may look very different. Projects may be terminated halfway through, or left little-used. Oman does not have the deep pockets of its neighbours, who are able to invest heavily in strategic security. Third is that many of these projects are clearly competing with existing Gulf terminals. There is already some disquiet over Muscat’s apparent closeness to Tehran at times during its mediation. Most notably, this surfaced in the debate over tolls for use of the Strait, or essentially Iranian extortion. The other Gulf nations have suffered and spent heavily in the conflict. Of course, they want to leverage Oman’s strategic depth. But they do not want to make obsolete their own decades of massive investment in centres such as Fujairah, Jebel Ali and Yanbu, and new projects at sites such as Khor Fakkan, Al Rugaylat and Dibba. Past such ventures across Iraq, Syria, Turkey and Saudi Arabia have suffered from sabotage, nationalisation, or commercial breakdowns. Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman wisely pointed out that successful multinational pipelines require stakeholders from all sides. Tying Gulf security to Oman needs not only sinews of steel, but political harmony.
